title: ஆசாரக்கோவை 1-20
theme: The book opens by rooting ஆசாரம் in eight ethical virtues and promising its rewards, then sets out the rules of the period for the day: rising and worship, the kinds of எச்சில் and what they bar, the occasions and manner of bathing, reverence owed to elders and sacred things, and the purifying acts and posture of the meal.
structure_note: Verses 1-3 frame conduct ethically; 4 and 9 give the morning; 5-8 define எச்சில் and its bars; 10-14 bathing, dress and oil; 15-17 reverence and calendar rules; 18-20 the meal.
source_issues: Verse 2 line 4 reads ஒழக்கம், most likely ஒழுக்கம் miswritten.

Verses 4 and 11 close with the same line (என்பதே முந்தையோர் கண்ட முறை), and verse 19 line 3 recurs at verse 42: a formulaic close of the work, flagged by the tool as a repeated line, not a corruption.
Verse 10 says ten (ஈரைந்தும்) but the tenth occasion is only reached by splitting ஊண்பொழுது from வைகு துயில்; ஏனை மயலுறல் is obscure.
Verse 13 lines 3-4 on oil and water are hard to order; the sense of நீர்தொடார் after oiling is unclear.

reading: The verse names eight things as the seed from which the conduct called ஆசாரம் grows: gratitude, forbearance, sweet speech, doing nothing painful to any living being, learning, knowing how to do oppuravu fully, wisdom, and friendship with good company.
nuance: The book that goes on to list rules of bathing and eating opens by rooting them in inner virtues; வித்து makes the ritual rules the plant and the ethics the seed, so the order of the work is itself a claim.

reading: The verse says that those who never fail in conduct gain eight things by right: good birth, long life, wealth, beauty, ownership of land, high renown, learning and freedom from disease.
nuance: Birth heads the list of rewards, so good birth is treated as something conduct earns, presumably in a later life, rather than as the ground of conduct; the verse does not say which life the eight arrive in. ஒழக்கம் on line 4 is read as ஒழுக்கம்.

reading: The verse says that gifts to priests, sacrifice, penance and learning are to be kept and carried through by the threefold discipline, and that if they are not, they come to nothing on any side and perish.
nuance: முப்பால் ஒழுக்கு is not explained in the verse; it can be the discipline of mind, speech and body, or conduct in the three aims of aram, porul and inbam. On either reading the claim is that rite and penance are void without conduct to hold them.
domain_note: the man who gives fees and performs sacrifice

norm.note: a rule of the period on the Vedic acts of fee-giving and sacrifice and how they are kept fruitful

reading: The verse reports the order the ancients saw: to wake in the last watch before dawn, think over the good deeds and the honest wealth one will pursue that day, and rise worshipping father and mother.
nuance: Aram and porul are planned before rising, and the first act of worship is to the parents, not to a god. வாய்வதில் on line 2 is not clear to me; it may mean 'in what is fitting' or 'as far as it comes to hand'.

norm.note: an order-of-the-day rule of the period: the hour of waking and the first act of the day

reading: The verse lists five things that, it says, no one in a state of எச்சில் touches: the cow, brahmins, fire, the gods and the crown of one's own head.
nuance: பார்ப்பார் is a birth-group term; the verse sets brahmins beside the cow, fire and the gods as things an impure hand must not reach, so the rule ranks people by birth as well as regulating purity. The crown of the head is the one item on one's own body.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: what the unclean hand is barred from touching, with brahmins ranked among sacred things

reading: The verse lists five things those in a state of எச்சில் do not look at: புலை, the moon, the sun, a dog and a falling star, and says those who know this well keep it daily and promptly.
nuance: புலை is a caste term here most likely naming the outcaste person, set in a list with a dog and the heavenly bodies as sights barred to the unclean; it could also be read as an impure thing such as flesh, which is why the verse is marked uncertain. தக்கவீழ் மீன் is read as a falling star.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: what is barred from sight while the mouth is unclean, with a birth-group among the barred sights

reading: The verse says there are many kinds of எச்சில் and singles out four: the two excretions, sexual union and the mouth's desire, eating.
nuance: The count of four is reached by taking இயக்கம் இரண்டும் as two (urine and faeces), so three items are listed here; வாயின் விழைச்சு is read as eating. Eating, the body's most ordinary act, is put in the same class as excretion and intercourse.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: the classes of bodily act that make a person unclean

reading: The verse says those who would become learned observe the four kinds of எச்சில் carefully and never recite, speak or lie down to sleep while in them.
nuance: The reward named is மேதை, learning or brilliance, not merit: keeping the purity rules is tied to the power of recitation. வளரார் is read as 'do not lie down to sleep'.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: recitation and speech barred while unclean

reading: The verse sets the morning rite: at dawn twilight one chews the tooth-stick, washes the eyes and rises after worshipping the deity in the way one knows, and it calls worship standing at evening twilight a fault.
nuance: தானறியும் ஆற்றால் leaves the form of worship and the deity to the worshipper; only the hour and the posture are fixed.

norm.note: an order-of-the-day rule of the period: cleansing and worship at the two twilights

reading: The verse lists ten occasions on which, it says, one bathes without hesitation: worship of the gods, a bad dream, uncleanness, vomiting what one has eaten, cutting the hair, mealtime, rising from sleep, sexual union, bodily contact with low people, and the other, falling into confusion.
nuance: Ten is reached by taking ஊண்பொழுது and வைகு துயில் as two occasions; ஏனை மயலுறல் is obscure and may mean any other bewilderment. கீழ்மக்கள் can be a moral term (the base), as often in the Kural, but a contact that calls for a bath points to a birth-group, so it is read as a caste term here. வாலாமை, uncleanness, may include menstrual or death pollution; the verse does not say whose.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: the occasions that require bathing, one of them contact with a ranked group

reading: The verse reports the ancients' rule that the worthy do not bathe unclothed, do not eat wearing a single cloth, do not wring the cloth they wear inside the water, and never enter an assembly in a single cloth.
nuance: உடுத்தலால் is read as உடுத்து அலால், 'except clothed'. The single-cloth rule joins the meal and the assembly, so dress is a matter of both purity and public standing.

norm.note: a rule of the period on dress at bathing, eating and in the assembly

reading: The verse says the worthy do not touch any limb with the oil rubbed on the head, do not touch the soiled cloth another has worn, and do not beg for sandals even when they lack them.
nuance: The last item moves from pollution to self-respect: a want as small as sandals does not license begging, so the verse joins bodily purity and the refusal to ask.

norm.note: a rule of the period on oil and others' worn cloth as sources of uncleanness

reading: The verse lists things the worthy avoid: gazing at their reflection in water, scratching the ground at night, going near trees at night, rubbing on oil without first touching water even in distress, and, once oiled, touching water or looking at புலை.
nuance: The order of oil and water on lines 3-4 is hard to fix: one reading is that water is touched before oiling and not again after, until the bath. புலை is again a caste term most likely naming the outcaste person, though it could be an impure thing; the bar on seeing it here attaches to the oiled state, not to எச்சில்.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period on night, oil and water, with a birth-group among the barred sights

reading: The verse says that those who keep the path never, while bathing, swim, spit, splash about or play, and do not bathe leaving out the head even when it is dry.
nuance: The ritual bath is set against the bath as pleasure: every banned act is play in water. காய்ந்தது எனினும் is read as 'even if the head is dry'; it could also mean 'even if the water is cold'.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the manner of the purifying bath

reading: The verse says that one who scorns the five elements, brahmins, the cow, the moon and the sun, not reckoning them as his own elements, has the five elements of his own body perish at once.
nuance: தம்பூதம் makes the outer things kin to the elements of the body, so contempt for them is self-destruction. பார்ப்பார் is a birth-group term, and the verse places brahmins among cosmic and sacred things owed reverence by birth.

norm.note: a rule of the period that ranks brahmins by birth among things owed reverence

reading: The verse names the king, the teacher, the mother, the father and the elder brother as the peerless elders, and reports as the way all have seen that they are to be worshipped as gods.
nuance: The king heads a list otherwise made of household and teacher, so political and family authority are given one kind of reverence; the wife's duty to the husband, which the Kural treats this way, is not among them.

reading: The verse gives the settled view of the wise: they do not act against their elders' word, do not forget to complete vows left unfinished, do not chew the tooth-stick on the full-moon day, and do not cut trees.
nuance: நிறையுவா மேல் may mean the full-moon day and the days after it, or the full and new moon; and the tree-cutting bar may belong to the same day or stand alone. The list joins obedience, vows and calendar rules as one kind of thing.

norm.note: a calendar and vow rule of the period

reading: The verse says that only those who eat after bathing, washing the feet, rinsing the mouth and drawing the circle on the ground are said to have eaten; the others, rinsing their mouths as if they had eaten, go off, and the rakshasas, resenting this, take their meal as their own.
nuance: The sanction is not illness or sin but theft: an unritualed meal is not eaten by the eater at all, because demons claim it. மண்டலஞ்செய்து is read as marking the circle for the leaf.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the purifying acts before a meal

reading: The verse reports the settled view of the very wise that one eats before the water on the feet has dried, and does not climb into bed before the wetness has dried.
nuance: The same wet feet are required for the meal and forbidden for the bed; the rule turns on timing, not on water as such.

norm.note: a rule of the period on wet feet at meal and bed

reading: The verse sets the posture of the meal: one faces east, sits well, does not doze or sway, looks at nothing else and does not speak, and eats after worship, carefully, without spilling.
nuance: Every item governs the eater's body and attention; none governs the food, its amount or its kind.

norm.note: a rule of the period on direction, posture and silence at the meal

title: ஆசாரக்கோவை 21-40
theme: The chapter reports the period's rules for the meal (whom to feed first, direction, posture, order of tastes, rinsing the mouth), for the evening and for sleep, and for spitting and excretion, and it sets among them two ethics verses that bar even the sight and the thought of the gravest wrongs.
structure_note: Verses 21-26 the meal; 27-28 rinsing and the hands; 29-31 twilight, sleep and deference; 32-36 spitting, excretion, rinsing water and clothes; 37-38 ethical bars on sight and thought; 39-40 the hearth and kin at table.
source_issues: Verse 38 line 1 had ௌ written as ெ + ள (repaired to வௌவல்), and the comparison site's text lacks line 1.
Verse 22 is obscure throughout; the sense of முகட்டு வழி decides the reading.
Verse 36 line 2 (மாசுணி கீழ்) is obscure.
Verse 32 counts ten (ஈரைந்தின்); the ten are reached by taking புற் and பைங்கூழ் as two and தேவ குலம் and நிழல் as two; வெண்பலி is doubtful.

reading: The verse says that those who never stray from conduct never eat without first serving food to five: guests, elders, the cow, caged creatures and children.
nuance: The list joins people and animals in one order of precedence at the meal: the guest stands first, and the cow and the caged creature (சிறை, read as birds or beasts kept in confinement; it could also mean captives) rank with elders and children as dependants of the house. The verse has no count word, so no items are given.

reading: The verse appears to say that the other directions too are good in their proper order for eating, and that those who approved eating along the line of the roof-ridge disapproved of laying the bed along it.
nuance: The verse follows 20, which fixes east for the meal, and allows the remaining directions in sequence. முகட்டு வழி is read as the line of the roof-ridge; it might instead name an upward or northern direction, and the contrast between food and bed turns on that word.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the directions for eating and for the bed

reading: The verse reports that the worthy do not eat lying down, standing, or in the open, do not eat to excess even when the food is choice, and do not eat on the bed, and it adds that one should not, breaking the rule, eat anything standing.
nuance: Excess (மிகவுண்ணார்) is set among rules of posture and place, so moderation is presented as part of a code of bodily decorum rather than as a matter of health. வெள்ளிடை is read as open ground; இறந்து on line 3 is read as transgressing the rule.

norm.note: a rule of the period on posture, place and amount at the meal

reading: The verse says that when people sit at a meal with those greater than themselves, they do not eat first, do not rise first, do not press close, and whatever they receive do not sit far to the right.
nuance: The greater ones (பெரியார்) are greater than oneself, by age or standing; the verse does not say by birth. மிக்குறார் is read as not crowding them and ஆற்றவலம் இரார் as not taking the right-hand seat, both doubtful.

norm.note: a rule of precedence of the period at a shared meal

reading: The verse sets the order of the meal: the sweet things first, the bitter things last, and the rest in between in the approved way.
nuance: The rule governs the food itself, its sequence by taste, where most of the meal rules govern the eater's body; the verse gives no reason, medical or ritual.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the order of tastes in a meal

reading: The verse seems to say that one does not seat the aged beside oneself at the meal, by rule takes a little of each thing eaten, and, without failing in affection or leaving ஆசாரம், puts away the vessel courteously.
nuance: Line 1 is doubtful: பக்கத்து வையார் may bar seating elders at one's side as equals, or may bar leaving them aside. Affection (அன்பு) and ஆசாரம் stand side by side as the two things not to lose, so the rule of the meal is tied to feeling as well as form.

norm.note: a rule of the period on seating, portions and clearing the vessel

reading: The verse describes the mouth-rinsing that the great have seen as the way: spitting out well so no எச்சில் is left and nothing drips, wiping well to the root, sipping three times and wiping, and touching the organs of the face with the fingers in the fitting manner.
nuance: This is a step-by-step procedure rather than a list of bars; வாய்பூசல் names the rite and the steps exist to clear எச்சில். அடியோடு is read as the root of the teeth or gums.

norm.note: a purification rule of the period: the manner of rinsing the mouth

reading: The verse reports that the worthy do not drink water with both hands, do not take from or give to their elders with one hand, and do not scratch their body with both hands.
nuance: The hands are counted in each rule: two hands are wrong for drinking and scratching, one hand is wrong for exchange with elders, so the same count is courtesy in one place and indecorum in another.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the use of the hands in drinking, giving and touching the body

reading: The verse says that at evening twilight people do not lie down, walk about, eat, grow angry or scorn the lamp, and that the way is to take the night meal and settle to rest.
nuance: Anger sits in a list of acts barred by the hour, so a moral fault is treated as untimely rather than wrong in itself. முன்னந்தி on line 2 is unclear: it may mean before the twilight, which would put the meal before dusk, or the twilight itself.

norm.note: an order-of-the-day rule of the period for the evening twilight

reading: The verse says that on lying down one joins the hands and worships the deity, does not lay the head to the north or to a corner, and sleeps with the body covered by an upper cloth.
nuance: கோணம் is read as the intermediate directions; with வடக்கு it leaves only east, south and west for the head.

norm.note: a rule of the period on worship before sleep and the direction of the head

reading: The verse says that one does not pass between two gods or two பார்ப்பார், that when one sneezes and one's superiors bless one, one rises worshipping them, and that one goes along gladly with one's equals.
nuance: பார்ப்பார் is a caste term for brahmins, used here to mark persons who may not be walked between, alongside the gods. இருதேவர் பார்ப்பார் may be two gods and brahmins, or two brahmin 'gods'; either way brahmins are given the deference of sacred things. The verse ranks people three ways in three lines: brahmins, superiors (மிக்கார்) and equals (ஒப்பார்).

norm.note: a rule of the period giving brahmins, by birth-name, the deference due to gods

reading: The verse lists ten places where those with understanding neither spit nor void the two excretions: grass, green crops, cow-dung, the cremation ground, a path, sacred water, a temple, shade, a cow-pen and the place of the white offering.
nuance: The ten mix the sacred (temple, sacred water, the white offering), the useful (crops, shade, path) and the cow's things (dung, pen), so the bar protects both holiness and common use. வெண்பலி is read as the place of a white offering or of ash; it is doubtful.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: places barred for spitting and excretion

reading: The verse says that by day one does not face south and by night does not face north, and that by day one does not pour water into fire.
nuance: The verse does not name the act for which the directions are fixed; set between 32 and 34, both on spitting and excretion, it most likely concerns those acts. The water-and-fire rule is a separate bar tied to the same hour.

norm.note: a rule of the period on directions by day and night and on quenching fire

reading: The verse says that those who claim to live by the rule-book, having veiled the ten directions in their mind, spit and void only in a secluded place, and would not slight this even to gain the throne of Indra.
nuance: மனத்தான் மறைத்தபின் makes the screening an act of mind as well as of place. அந்தரத்து is read as a secluded spot; it could mean the open air. தந்திரத்து வாழ்துமென் பார் may carry irony toward those who only say they live by the text.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period on where spitting and excretion are allowed

reading: The verse says that when rinsing from a vessel is not possible, people do not rinse the mouth standing in running water or in water lying on the path, nor without first marking off the place in their mind.
nuance: The conditional on line 4 makes the vessel the norm and natural water the fallback. நடைவரவு நீர் is read as flowing water and வழிநிலை நீர் as standing water on a road; both readings are tentative.

norm.note: a purification rule of the period on the water fit for rinsing the mouth

reading: The verse says that those who know their duty never pass between lamps, never spit on a wall, never take on themselves a soiled cloth worn below even in trouble, never go with their cloth blowing in the wind even if an army comes, and never shake out their cloth among many people.
nuance: The conditions rise in pressure (இடரெனினும், படைவரினும்): the rule holds in distress and even under attack. Line 2 is obscure: மாசுணி கீழ் is read as a soiled lower garment.

norm.note: a rule of the period on fire, spitting and the handling of clothes

reading: The verse says that those who know aram do not even look at five things: another's wife, toddy, theft, gambling and killing, because besides being scorned as worthless they are driven down the road to hell.
nuance: The bar is on looking (நோக்கார்), not only on doing. The verse gives two sanctions, one in this world (scorn) and one after it (hell). An ethics verse inside the ritual book, it needs no norm.

reading: The verse says that those of clear insight do not even think of four things: lying, slander, seizing what is another's and envy, because thinking of them brings suspicion, drives one into hard hell, and makes even the deity destroy one.
nuance: The bar moves inward from the eye in 37 to the mind (சிந்தியார்). ஐயம் புகுவித்து is read as bringing one under suspicion; it might instead mean bringing doubt into one's own mind.

reading: The verse says that the worthy do not set a pot on the fire for themselves alone, do not take food for their own sake, do not let the kitchen be touched by எச்சில், and eat only after seeing the house offering fed.
nuance: Sharing and purity are joined in one rule of the hearth: cooking for oneself and defiling the kitchen are barred together, and the offering (மனைப்பலி) must be fed before the household eats.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the kitchen and the household offering before the meal

reading: The verse says that where elders and young kin are eating, one does not sit above them and does not wound them inwardly, even if they have done one great harm.
nuance: Forbearance is placed at the table and limited to kin: the meal is a time when even a grave wrong is not to be answered. உள்ளழிவு is read as hurt to the feelings.

norm.note: a rule of precedence of the period when kin are eating

title: ஆசாரக்கோவை 41-60
theme: The third twenty move from the body to the household and the road: rules of touch and of marital union timed by the wife's cycle and the calendar, the cleansing and auspicious ordering of the house, days without Vedic recitation, festival days and the welcome of guests, the measure of dress and speech, sights and places to avoid, omens at departure, and deference to elders on the road.
source_issues: Verse 41 line 2 (தலையோடு றுப்புறுத்த) is damaged; the word division and the sense of the rule are uncertain.
Verse 42 line 3 (பேரறி வாளர் துணிவு) repeats the close of verse 19, a formulaic line.
Verse 44 has doubtful forms (இரியார், பாடஅர்) on lines 1 and 3.
Verse 47 is flagged by the tool as missing from the site edition (site_diff).
Verse 48 names only four occasions plainly against its count of five (ஐவகை).
Verse 55 line 3 and verse 59 line 3 are obscure.

reading: The verse reports that those with subtle knowledge of the texts do not put the eye's discharge into the eye, do not rub one foot against the other, and do not let other limbs touch the head, which it calls holy.
nuance: Line 2 is damaged: தலையோடு றுப்புறுத்த is read as the head with the other limbs pressed to it, a rule that the head, called புண்ணியம், is not touched by lower parts; the first rule, கண்ணெச்சில் கண்ணூட்டார், may instead bar touching the eye with a hand soiled by spittle.

norm.note: a purity rule of the period on how the body's parts may touch, with the head treated as holy

reading: The verse gives as the settled view of the greatly wise that a man does not look at his wife on the three days she may not be touched, and that after she has bathed he does not leave her for the twelve days that follow.
nuance: தீண்டாநாள் names the menstrual days by the bar on touch; the verse does not say why the twelve days after the bath matter, but setting them right after the bath ties the rule of pollution to the timing of marital union. The closing phrase பேரறி வாளர் துணிவு recurs from verse 19.

norm.note: a menstrual pollution rule of the period: the wife is not touched or looked at for three days, and the husband stays with her for twelve days after her bath

reading: The verse lists the times on which, it reports, husband and wife do not come together: noon, midnight, the two twilights, the days of the two great gods, the uvā tithi days, the eighth day of the moon, and one's birthday.
nuance: இருதேவர் நாள் is not explained; it names the festival days of two gods without saying which. டுவாத்திதிநாள் is read as உவா joined to திதிநாள், the new- and full-moon days, and taken as one item; ஏனைப் பிறந்தநாள் is read as the birth-star day.

norm.note: a rule of the period setting the hours and calendar days on which marital union is barred

reading: The verse reports household rules: one does not set the measuring vessel down on the seat-plank or turn the plank over, does not unfold new cloth in the doorway, does not lie on a cot at the threshold without thought, and does not let strangers stand at one's head.
nuance: இரியார் and பாடஅர் are doubtful forms; பாடஅர் is read as படார், 'do not lie down', and the last rule, அறியாதார் தந்தலைக்கண் நில்லா விடல், can also mean keeping unknown people from standing at the head of the house. These look like rules of omen rather than of pollution.

norm.note: household omen rules of the period about the seat, new cloth, the threshold and strangers

reading: The verse names five things that are not to be spread inside the pandal: a broom, sweepings, dried grass and leaves, a black pot, and a torn cot.
nuance: துகள்காடு is taken as one thing, a heap of dust and sweepings, to reach the verse's five; split into dust and refuse the list would run to six. The pandal is presumably the booth raised for a wedding or festival, though the verse does not say so.

norm.note: a rule of the period keeping unclean and inauspicious things out of the festive booth

reading: The verse says that those who want good to come to them clear away the refuse, wash the vessels, sprinkle cow-dung water all through the house, fill the water-pot and the karakam early in the morning, adorn them with flowers, and light fire in the hearth so that the house shines.
nuance: The reason given is the household's fortune, நல்லது உறல், not purity as such: cleaning and lighting the hearth are read as making the house auspicious.

norm.note: a rule of the period for the morning cleansing of the house with cow-dung water and the first lighting of the hearth

reading: The verse lists the days on which brahmins do not recite the shining texts: the eighth day, the new and full moon, the fourteenth, a time of affliction to the one who guards the land, a great earthquake, thunder in the sky, and a state of impurity.
nuance: பார்ப்பார் names a birth-group whose duty is set here; the verse does not rank them against others but makes Vedic recitation theirs. The king's distress stands in the same list as earthquake and thunder, as a disturbance of the world that halts recitation.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the days a birth-group, the பார்ப்பார், suspend Vedic recitation, impurity among them

reading: The verse says that on five kinds of day, a wedding, the festivals of the gods and of the ancestors, other festivals and a sacrifice, one does aram without slighting it, and serves food to guests as well.
nuance: Line 1 names four occasions; the five of ஐவகை are reached by taking தேவர் and பிதிர் each with விழா and விழா again as festivals in general. விருந்திற்கும் 'for guests too' makes feeding guests the added duty of the day, after aram.

norm.note: a rule of the period for the festival and rite days of the household calendar

reading: The verse says that dress, gait, slackness of speech and rebuke, these four, are to be done as befits one's standing, learning, manliness and family.
nuance: Even the faults, slackness of speech and abuse, are to be kept in measure with one's place; the rule is not to avoid them but to fit them. Family (குடிமை) closes the four measures, so outward conduct is graded by lineage as well as by learning.

norm.note: a rule of the period that grades outward conduct by one's family rank among other measures

reading: The verse says that those of rare learning by listening do not blame others, do not lower themselves, do not sleep among many, do not promise and then hold back, and do not, even by a slip, mock and deride the poor without cause.
nuance: இசையாத நேர்ந்து கரவார் is doubtful: it may mean they do not agree to what is unfitting and then hide it, or do not conceal after consenting; தள்ளியும் is read as 'even by a slip'.

reading: The verse says that those who want their own radiance do not look at lightning, a falling star, the finery of harlots, or the sun at its rising and setting.
nuance: The reason given is the viewer's own lustre (நம்மொளி), not pollution; the harlots' finery sits among dangerous lights in the sky. The sun's முன்னொளி and பின்னொளி are read as its light at dawn and dusk.

norm.note: a rule of the period on sights to be avoided, with harlots' adornment among them

reading: The verse says that those of unshaken mind never speak deceit, useless words, loose talk, abuse or backbiting.
nuance: The five kinds of speech are tied to one cause, a mind that does not waver (அசையாத உள்ளம்); the verse treats bad speech as the sign of an unsteady mind.

reading: The verse lists acts that those who keep the path do not practise: flicking with the fingers, throwing stones, whistling, calling out, grimacing, anger, concealment, clapping, and harming a limb so that it shows.
nuance: Bodily habits and two moral faults, anger and concealment, stand in one list of things not to be made a habit (பயிற்றார்). விகிர்தம் is read as grimacing, and தோன்ற உறுப்புச் செகுத்தல் is uncertain: maltreating a limb in view, or a gesture of the limbs.

reading: The verse says that a smile, a sweet word, water for the feet, a mat and a bed, these five, are the honours paid together with food to one who has come.
nuance: Food is assumed, and the five are what goes with it: the welcome begins with the face and ends with a place to sleep.

reading: The verse says that people of peerless understanding do not wish to stay long at a hostile battlefront, at a drinking bout, in the street of those without a steady mind, where one taken on for his qualities has lost his hold, or at a water's edge where many crowd.
nuance: குணநோக்கிக் கொண்டவர் கோள்விட் டுழியும் is unclear; it may be a place where a man chosen for his virtue has been dropped, or where those who chose by virtue have given up their resolve. The rule is about lingering (நீடு நிலை), not entering.

reading: The verse says that people do not go into dry grass or forest or kindle fire there, do not run with legs spread when rain falls, do not travel alone through a pathless forest, and, even if the rain fails and poverty swells greatly, do not take up work that departs from their ancestral line.
nuance: The verse moves from bodily prudence to a rule of hereditary occupation: தொல்வரவின் தீர்ந்த தொழில், work cut off from the old descent, is barred even in famine. That last line is a birth rule of the period, set beside rules of safety as if of one kind.

norm.note: a rule of the period binding a person to the occupation of his descent even in poverty

reading: The verse says that those who wish to be free of disease do not enter alone a ruined house, a temple, the burning ground or the lone old tree that rises by a village road, and do not sleep by day.
nuance: The reason given is health, not pollution: the four places are lonely and feared, and தமியர் 'alone' is the condition of the bar.

reading: The verse reports that when someone sets out, people do not call after him from behind, do not sneeze, do not even by a slip ask 'where are you going?', do not step in front and speak face to face, and keep their elders on their right on both sides.
nuance: The first four rules protect a departure from ill omen; the last, கொள்வர் குரவர் வலம், moves to reverence, keeping the elders on the right. இருசார்வும் may mean going and coming.

norm.note: omen rules of the period for a departure, and the rite of keeping elders on the right

reading: The verse reports that people do not say 'my body is well', do not blow out a lamp, do not take fire from a hearth so that it goes out, and do not warm themselves at it with the fire turned toward themselves.
nuance: Saying the body is well seems to court misfortune; the last clause, படக்காயார் தம்மேற் குறித்து, is obscure and may bar warming oneself directly at the hearth fire.

norm.note: rules of the period about the household fire and about words that invite ill

reading: The verse says that when travelling a road together with the full, self-controlled, elder and eminent, one mounts nothing, wears no sandals and does not shade oneself from the sun.
nuance: Deference takes the form of matching the elder's hardship on the road: one gives up mount, sandals and shade beside him.

title: ஆசாரக்கோவை 61-80
theme: Verses 61-80 set out reverence to Veda-knowers, elders and the vulnerable, and then a long code of conduct in the presence of the great: in the great house, before the lord and in his counsel, the attendant governs gaze, gesture, speech and the body itself.
structure_note: 61-64 reverence to Veda-knowers, elders and those owed the road; 65 the senses and kinswomen; 66-79 conduct in attendance on the great and the lord; 80 forms of address.
source_issues: Verse 64 is lacking on the source site the corpus was checked against (tool flag site_diff); it is marked from the core text.
Verse 66 line 4 (கடைபோக வாழ்துமென் பார்) recurs as verse 83 line 4: a formulaic close, flagged as a repeated line.
Verse 75 line 1 செவிசொறுண்டார் is not a clear word, perhaps a scribal form of ear-scratching.
Verse 76 line 3 காலந்தால் is unclear, perhaps காலத்தால்.
Verse 72 line 3 அணங்கொடு நேர்பெரியார் செல்லுமிடத்து is hard to construe.

reading: The verse reports it as the settled view of those versed in the treatises that the knowers of the four Vedas, who came by the order of heaven, are to be treated in the higher way, as one's own elders are.
nuance: The verse does not name the brahmin by a birth word; it names him by the four Vedas and by a coming வான்முறையான், 'by the order of heaven', so the rank is grounded in a sacred origin rather than in conduct. குரவர் here takes the sense verse 16 gives it, the five elders worshipped as gods.

norm.note: a rule of the period that ranks the Veda-knowers with one's own elders by a heaven-given order

reading: The verse reports that the elders call three acts the ஆசாரம் owed to elders, stated in essence: bowing at the feet, attendance at the proper time, and rising when they come.
nuance: சமயம் is the doubtful item: it can be waiting on the elder at the fit time, or keeping the elder's own creed; the first fits the bodily acts beside it. The verse says the three were told சாரத்தால், as the gist, so it offers them as a summary of reverence, not a full code.

reading: The verse names three things as the path seen by those who saw the right manner: caring for those who have renounced, modesty, and not speaking before elders, even by lapse, of what one has learned.
nuance: The third item is a restraint on learning itself: the learned man keeps his learning silent in the presence of elders, so learning is ranked below reverence.

reading: The verse names eight to whom one gives way on the road (brahmins, ascetics, those carrying loads, the sick, the old, the young, cows and women) and says those who step fully aside for them are called praiseworthy among births.
nuance: பார்ப்பார் is a birth term and heads the list, followed by the ascetic; the rest are the burdened and the weak, so a rank by birth and a care for the vulnerable are given one gesture. பிறப்பிடைப் போற்றி may mean praised among men, or praised in their births to come; the verse does not settle it.

norm.note: a road rule of the period that puts brahmins first among those one gives way to

reading: The verse reports that the worthy should not stay alone even with their own mother, daughter or sister, because the five senses are hard to hold back.
nuance: The reason given is not the woman's conduct but the man's senses: even சான்றார் are not trusted to restrain the five, so the rule removes the occasion rather than relying on restraint.

norm.note: a rule of the period separating men from their nearest kinswomen when alone

reading: The verse says that those who mean to live on to the end (in a great one's service) are not angered when stopped at the gate, do not take excessive liberties of intimacy, are not careless at the giving of gifts, do not dress as their lord does, and do not cut in between to go and join another.
nuance: கடை is the gate of the great house, which sets the verse in attendance on a lord. கோலநேர் செய்யார் is read as not matching the lord's dress; இடையறுத்துப் போகிப் பிறனொருவன் சேரார் can be not breaking off to attach oneself to another patron, or not passing between two people to reach a third. கடைபோக வாழ்தும் is survival as much as virtue.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse says one should not speak a pronouncement about oneself, a retort answering what one's betters have said, or a pronouncement about others, and that speaking them turns into a fault that scars.
nuance: The three speeches cover self, superior and third party, so the verse closes off every subject on which one might pronounce; வடுக்குற்றம் makes the fault a lasting mark, not a passing lapse.

reading: The verse says they do not take pleasure in what the great take pleasure in, do not enter a house bringing lowly men, and do not speak slightingly even of an undiscerning child in a place where they are not on familiar terms.
nuance: The child that may not be slighted is most naturally the great house's own child; தம்மோடு அளவளாவில்லா இடத்து limits the rules to a house where one is not intimate, so the verse is about the stranger's caution in another's household.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse says they do not show anger or sulk, do not stand facing the great one, do not speak of their own affairs to him in private, and do not say 'we know what is pleasant', even if he says without kindness that the crow is white.
nuance: The closing clause gives the measure of the whole rule: the attendant does not contradict the great one even on a plain falsehood. The verse does not call this truth; it calls it conduct.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse names five things they do not do in the house of the great: spitting, climbing to a high seat, chewing areca, speaking out of order, and lying down.
nuance: வளர்ச்சி is read as lying down (வளர், to sleep); a reading 'growing familiar' is possible. The list mixes bodily acts and speech as one class of liberties.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse says that those of good family do not speak before their lord of their own wealth, learning, lustre and virtue, spreading them out again and again as an enemy would.
nuance: பகைவர்போல் gives the reason: display of one's own excellences before the lord reads as a rival's challenge, so the restraint is prudence. குலமுடையார் makes it a mark of good birth.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse says that in the house of the great and in a temple they do not bow even to their own elders when they see them, nor when the great go with the deity.
nuance: Reverence is ruled by place: where a greater object of worship is present, bowing to another, even to the elders verse 16 says to worship as gods, is withheld. The third line, அணங்கொடு நேர்பெரியார் செல்லுமிடத்து, is hard; it may mean when the great go in procession with the deity.

norm.note: a rule of the period on where obeisance to elders is withheld

reading: The verse names laughter, yawning, hawking and sneezing as things they do not do before the great, and says that if done, blame stays fixed.
nuance: Involuntary acts of the body are treated as conduct: the verse holds a man to blame for a sneeze as for a laugh.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse says that when the great one stands one stands in restraint, when he sits one does not leave unless sent, one listens with attention when he speaks, and one does not ask again once his word is over.
nuance: The rule on questions is the sharpest: the hearer may not reopen what the great one has closed, so listening is complete when he stops.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse says that in the house of the great they do not let their garment slip, do not speak with the hand raised, do not look at the women, and do not take in whispered words.
nuance: செவிசொறுண்டார் on line 1 is not a clear word; it may be a scribal form of 'scratching the ear'. The bar on looking at the women of the house sets them inside the lord's domain.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

norm.note: a rule of the period barring the attendant's gaze on the women of a great house

reading: The verse says that one does not speak hastily, on and on, in false and sprawling ways, or at length, but speaks knowing the right moment, with few syllables that hold the whole sense together.
nuance: செவ்வி is the hearer's fit moment, so brevity and timing are one rule. காலந்தால் on line 3 is unclear, perhaps காலத்தால்.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse says they do not look at their own body, do not tousle their hair, do not snap their fingers, and look at no body but that of the chief.
nuance: The gaze itself is disciplined: the attendant's eyes belong to the chief, as in verse 75 they may not fall on his women.
domain_note: one who attends on the chief (தலைமகன்)

reading: The verse says they do not take counsel with others in the lord's presence, do not go near the lord or listen in, and if near, stand turned away as if attending to something else.
nuance: Line 3 gives a posture, not only an abstention: one acts out inattention so as to be seen not to be listening.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse names three things found in the capable: sharing the sorrow when there is sorrow, conducting oneself in joyful ways when there is joy, and, out of loyalty, not entering the house of those who have fallen under wrath.
nuance: The sorrow and joy are most likely the lord's, whose moods the attendant mirrors; செறப்பட்டார் are those who have incurred anger, presumably the lord's, so avoiding their house is loyalty, not unkindness.
domain_note: one who attends on the great one, the lord or king

reading: The verse says that even when provoked they do not utter their elders' names, do not stay long in a house clearing the throat, do not address the great by terms of kinship, and that those who know well do not address even the புலையர் by terms of kinship.
nuance: புலையர் is a caste term for a birth-group held outcaste; here it plainly names persons. The final rule withholds kin-address from them as from the great, at the opposite end of rank; முறை may also mean addressing them with honour. நன்கறிவார் repeats the close of verse 6.

norm.note: a rule of the period withholding kinship address from those ranked outcaste

title: ஆசாரக்கோவை 81-100
theme: The book's last twenty verses turn to conduct before the king, elders and other households, with a few rules of the funeral rite, of leavings and of the day of a rite, and close by naming the persons freed from ஆசாரம்.
structure_note: Verses 81-85 conduct at and toward the court; 86-89 and 91, 93-94, 97 courtesy and self-restraint; 87, 90, 92 ritual, purity and caste rules; 95 the four things to guard; 96 animals as models of keeping to one's work; 98-99 places not entered; 100 the nine exempt.
source_issues: Verse 82 line 1 reads மகளிரி, most likely மகளிர் miswritten.
Verse 81 line 3 reads தொழிற்குரிவர், most likely தொழிற்குரியவர்.
Verse 91 line 2 பழித்தாரமாம் is unclear; read as 'are blamed'.
Verse 96 line 1 நந்தெறும்பு may be one word or two (the snail and the ant), so the creature count is three or four.
Verse 97 is missing from one of the source texts (the tool flags site_diff); its last line is hard to construe.
Verse 100 counts nine (ஒன்பதின்மர்); உயிரிழந்தான் is obscure.

reading: The verse says that the upright who do not hold the office concerned do not enter by the back gate and do not look into the king's assembly or the women's quarters of the palace.
nuance: The bar is tied to office: அவ்வத் தொழிற்குரிவர் அல்லா தவர் (read as தொழிற்குரியவர்) leaves the same doors open to those whose work lies there, so the rule is about trespass, not about the places being forbidden as such. செவ்வியார் may name the upright or those who watch for an opening; the reading takes the first.
domain_note: those who move about the king's palace

reading: The verse says that those who count themselves wise do not take a seat near the place of the women, even when they have a very close claim of intimacy, because what pleases women turns out to be other than one supposes.
nuance: The reason given is a claim about women's liking, not about the men's desire, so the rule rests on a generalisation about women. Line 1 is hard: மகளிரி is likely மகளிர் miswritten, and whether வண்ண மகளிர் are the king's women (as the neighbouring verses would suggest) or any women of a house is not said.

norm.note: a rule of the period keeping men from sitting near women, justified by a claim about women's changeable liking

reading: The verse lists what those who mean to live long and to the end do not do: walk along in a row, stand treading on a shadow, speak by picking at another's talk in its midst, do what the town resents, or tell even the size of the king's army.
nuance: Whose shadow and whose row the verse means is unstated; the last item, the king's army, sets the list at court. The close, கடைபோக வாழ்தும், makes the rules a means of survival rather than a virtue.
domain_note: those who live near the king and would keep their place

reading: The verse names four things that bring harm if one slights them, thinking them young, weak or familiar: the snake that lives in a hole, the king, fire, and the lion that lives in a cave.
nuance: The three reasons for contempt (இளைய, எளிய, பயின்றன) map loosely onto the four things: a young king, a small fire, a snake or lion one has grown used to. The king sits second, among beasts and fire, so his claim to respect is his power to harm.

reading: The verse says that capable men, even when their charity, weddings, enterprise and houses grow very great, do nothing that outdoes the king, and that if they do, their lasting wealth is ruined.
nuance: Even அறம் is under the limit: a subject's giving must not outshine the king's. The rule is prudential, with ruin of wealth as its sanction.
domain_note: a wealthy subject of the king

reading: The verse says that one does not ask elders and superiors what they have eaten, does not change countenance on meeting them wherever they are met, and does not ask even mean people what they have eaten.
nuance: The question 'what did you eat' is barred upward and downward alike: புல்லரையும் extends the courtesy to the lowly. The syntax of lines 1-2 is loose; the reading takes குரவரை மிக்காரை as the object of both clauses.

reading: The verse says that people do not wash the feet of one lying down, do not put flowers on him, never smear him with sandal paste even by oversight, and do not stand on the cot where someone lies.
nuance: Washing the feet, laying flowers and anointing with sandal are acts done to a body laid out in death, so the rule most likely keeps the living sleeper from being treated as a corpse; the verse does not say so. கட்டின் மிசை is read as the cot.

norm.note: a rule of the period barring toward the sleeping the acts of the funeral rite

reading: The verse says that those who mean to live in the right way do not speak of the return on help they gave, do not find fault with food, and do not marvel at their own charity and the vows they kept.
nuance: All three are faults of the tongue about one's own goods: help given, food set before one, merit earned. Faulting food sits between the two boasts, so ingratitude to the host is grouped with self-praise.

reading: The verse says that those of true vision do not want what cannot be had, do not grieve over what has passed, and are not troubled at heart by a hardship that has come beyond their power to prevent.
nuance: Each item is scoped: only the unattainable, only the past, only the trouble கைவாரா, beyond one's hand. The verse does not counsel calm before everything, only before what cannot be changed, and calls that calm a matter of vision (மெய்யாய காட்சி) rather than of will.

reading: The verse says that people do not take up flowers already worn on the head or wear flowers already smelled, do not accept a cow from a brahmin's hand when one is given, and never hold out leavings to the புலை.
nuance: புலை is a caste term for the outcaste, set here as one to whom even leavings are not held out, so the rule bars a contact through food; it could also be read as an impure thing, hence the doubt. The cow rule is unclear: it may bar taking back a cow from a brahmin, as brahmins receive and do not give.

norm.note: rules of the period on used flowers and leavings, with a birth-group barred even from receiving leavings and brahmins set apart as receivers

reading: The verse says that a thick wrap worn over the body, a stiffly raised neck and the noise of the feet are blamed even in the forest, since there are always those older than oneself.
nuance: The reason, தம்மின் மூத்த உள, makes the rule hold where no one is watching: even in the forest there are elders, perhaps the old trees and beings of the forest themselves. தாளிசைப்பு is read as the sound of the feet; it may be crossing the legs.

reading: The verse says that when one performs an important auspicious rite one never fixes the day by asking the புலையர், and that one acts on the word of the unfailing அந்தணர், whose word never errs.
nuance: புலையர் and அந்தணர் are set as two birth-groups whose word on the day is untrusted and trusted; புலையர் is a caste term for the outcaste and here names persons, not a thing. That the புலையர் could be asked at all implies they were reckoners of days in the period.

norm.note: a rule of the period on who may fix the day of a rite, by birth-group

reading: The verse says that people do not stand and bustle in the public square, do not go about smeared with dirt, never speak harsh words, and do not go to a place where two stand together.
nuance: The last item guards a private talk from intrusion; the first keeps one from making a show in the common square. உஞற்றார் is read as 'do not exert or bustle'.

reading: The verse says that those of clear vision do not point with the hand while speaking, do not write with the foot, do not compare the poor with the rich by pointing at them, and do not sit while receiving what elders hand them.
nuance: The third item makes a comparison of rich and poor a discourtesy to the poor, not only to the rich. கால்மேல் எழுத்திடார் is obscure: writing with the toe, or writing on the leg.

reading: The verse names four things to be guarded like gold and used with care, one's own body, one's wife, a deposit placed in one's keeping, and wealth set aside for one's own life, and says that failing to do so brings lasting harm.
nuance: The wife stands between the body and a deposit held in trust, so she is listed among goods in the man's keeping; the deposit, another's property, is guarded as closely as one's own body.

norm.note: a rule of the period that lists the wife among the goods a man guards

reading: The verse says that ஆசாரம் comes in any case to those who, like the ant, the weaver bird and the crow, hold fast to their own good work and strive to keep it in that manner.
nuance: The creatures are named without their qualities, so the model is their steady keeping to their own work. நந்தெறும்பு may be one word, 'the good ant', or two, the snail and the ant; it is taken as one item.

reading: The verse says that before the great one says nothing except with folded hands or a covered mouth, and that speaking while looking into their eyes is a fault.
nuance: The last line can also be read as an instruction to speak looking at them; the reading takes பழி as naming the direct gaze a fault. The verse is missing from one of the source texts.

reading: The verse says that those who are not fools do not enter the gamblers' hall or the ground where the din never stops, and that one who enters them meets many harms.
nuance: The danger is in the place, not only the play: entering is the fault, and the noisy ground is ranked with the gaming hall.

reading: The verse says that those of steady vision do not look at the pounding place, the kitchen or the women there, do not raise their voices, and do not enter the house.
nuance: The pounding place and the kitchen are where the women of a house work, so the bar on looking is a bar on looking at women at their work; the verse ends by keeping the visitor out of the house altogether.

norm.note: a rule of the period keeping a man's eyes off women and their working spaces in another's house

reading: The verse names nine who, rightly spoken of, are freed from ஆசாரம்: one from an unknown land, the destitute, the old, the young, one who has lost a life, the frightened, one who has eaten, one who has put the king's work first, and the bridegroom.
nuance: The code closes by bounding itself: the stranger who cannot know the local rule, those too weak or too young, those in fear or grief, and those taken up by the king's work or by their own wedding. உயிரிழந்தான் most likely means one bereaved by a death, though it can read as one near death.

norm.note: a rule of the period naming who is exempt from the rules of conduct

title: ஏலாதி 0-20
theme: After a payiram that says the book joins the householder's and the renouncer's codes and an invocation to the twenty-four, twenty verses count five to eight things under one predicate, moving between the household's giving and hospitality, the king's and minister's duties, and a Jain code of non-killing, truth and restraint; three verses close by setting the books of learning aside for conduct.
source_issues: Verse 17: show flags that the site's text lacks line 1.
Verse 16 line 1: துறவார்(கு) is likely துறவார்க்கு with the க் lost.
Verse 3 line 1: அரிதுக் கார்க்கேல் is obscure and may be corrupt; the middle easy/hard pairs are uncertain.
Verse 10 lines 3-4: the predicate (அறியலம்ஒன்(று) ஆற்ற எனைத்தும் அறியாமை யான்) is hard to construe.
Verse 13 line 2: the division of உட்குடைத்தா வென்று is doubtful.

reading: The payiram says that Kanimethai, an ornament of good learning, gathered and told without lapse the books of virtue, joining the renouncer's code to the householder's, and mixed into the work the good way to release as well.
nuance: It names the book's plan rather than its title: two codes, the household and the renunciant, made one, with release added. கணிமேதை is the author's name, and அணிமேதை puns on it.

reading: The invocation says that one who tends and gives to the four, holding to the red feet praised by the twenty-four and following the four scriptures, will by nature leave the earth and live as lord over the gods.
nuance: அறுநால்வர் (six times four) is most likely the twenty-four Tirthankaras, which fits a Jain author, but the verse names no one. Who the four that are tended and given to are, and which four scriptures (நால் மறை) are meant, the verse does not say; our reading of a Jain fourfold canon and fourfold gift is a guess.

reading: The verse names six things (fame that has spread, wealth, eminence, valour in service, steadfast learning and liberality) and says, to a woman with flowered hair, that they are beauty only in those who walk the way of the scripture.
nuance: The goods named are worldly ones, but the closing line makes them beautiful only on the virtuous, so the verse ranks conduct over the goods it lists. நின்ற நிலை is taken with கல்வி as one item (steadfast learning); read apart, the list has seven.

reading: The verse says that one who, though entitled to kill, does not kill, is not deluded by flesh, does no sharp torment, does not deceive and never swerves from his state rises above not only those on earth but those in the sky.
nuance: கொலையுரியான் கொல்லான் is taken as one item, one who has the right to kill (a king or a judge) and does not; read as two negatives (does not abet killing, does not kill) the verse has six items, the table's count. உரியான் is a positive form, which is why we read five.

reading: The verse sets easy things against hard ones: penance is easy and giving hard; [avoiding] waste is hard and falling into it easy; when blameless joy slips, joining with [grief] is easy, but wiping away that grief is hard.
nuance: Only the first pair is clear: the verse ranks giving as harder than penance. Line 1 ends in the obscure அரிதுக் கார்க்கேல், and the middle pairs are our construal of a damaged line; the six items follow the verse's easy/hard predicates.

reading: The verse names six practices (relieving distress, not scorning, not joining the base, relieving grief, giving up conduct blamed by all, and speech that those who see it desire) and says that where these are seen, the books of those who expound learning can be let go as unneeded.
nuance: The closing line sets conduct above book-learning: the list does what the books are for. கண்டவர் காமுறுஞ் சொல் is read as the sixth item and காணின் as 'if [these] are seen'.

reading: The verse says that one who is always his own companion, does not lie and makes his word true, claims nothing as 'mine', does not trust the words of women adorned like konrai blossoms and is not intoxicated, has what the support of other books would give.
nuance: Like verses 4 and 14, the verse ends by setting the books aside, but சாலும் பிறநூலின் சார்பு can mean either that he needs no other book or that he is enough to be one; தனக்கென்றும் ஓர்பாங்கன் may instead mean one who keeps a single friend. The distrust of women's words is a gender rule of the period.

norm.note: a rule of the period that a man of virtue does not trust women's words

reading: The verse says, to a woman with bamboo-like shoulders, that one who has self-restraint, a gentle nature, giving, patience, and a door shut to falsehood and to flesh is fit to be called a mother to all living beings.
nuance: மறையுடைமை governs both பொய்ம்மை and புலால், so the last two items share one predicate of keeping them out; the six are counted that way. The reward is not heaven but a title: mother to every life.

reading: The verse says that if a man, putting away harsh words, gives to everyone sweet speech, warm mingling, a place to sit and good food, the gods in the sky will hasten to receive him as their guest every day.
nuance: The four gifts are graded from words to food, and the fifth item is a removal (harsh words) that frames them all.

reading: The verse says that one who does not consent to killing, does not kill, relieves the sickness of the afflicted, does not fall into folly, and enters the excellent books of the excellent, studying them widely, will be raised by those who raise men, who come close to him.
nuance: ஆக்குமவர் ஆக்கும் அணைந்து is obscure: 'those who make [men great]' may be the gods or the virtuous. Consenting to a killing is counted as an act separate from killing.

reading: The verse says that those who, not rating the learned only by their learning nor their kin only by kinship, give food, shelter and clothing to the destitute will live as learned men, practised in it.
nuance: The reward is a paradox: giving, not study, makes one a பண்டிதர். Lines 1-2 are hard to construe; we read them as giving without regard to the receiver's learning or kinship.

reading: The verse sets the wealth of subjects under a just sceptre against the ruin of subjects under a cruel and worthless one and the work of a cruel sceptre's ministers, and says that 'we' cannot know these fully for not knowing anything at all.
nuance: Lines 3-4 (அறியலம்ஒன்(று) ஆற்ற எனைத்தும் அறியாமை யான்) are obscure; the speaker's disclaimer may be ironic, or the sense may be that a ruler who cannot do even one thing fully cannot know these. The three items are clear, the predicate is not.

reading: The verse says that one who has set out to cut desire does not slacken, that cutting the desire for those five fully is enough, and that one who does not cut it is tossed about by the five elephants and goes sullen into the hole.
nuance: The verse does not list its five; ஐங்களிறு (five elephants) makes them the senses. புழை, the narrow hole, is most likely rebirth. The three items are the verse's three states of desire, not a counted list.

reading: The verse names five places (the killing ground, the ground where men gamble with strips, the place of torment, the ground where war elephants are trained, and the place where the three circlings are made) and says it is good neither to desire them nor to look at them.
nuance: Even looking is barred: the rule reaches past doing violence to watching it. வார்குத்து and முச்சாரிகை are rare words; the latter is perhaps the wheeling of horses or elephants in drill.

reading: The verse says that not sowing, not eating, not bathing, not fretting greatly, conquering so as to inspire awe, and not plucking out are, on inspection, the six marks kept by those who hold to the books and stand in their portion.
nuance: Our division of line 2 (உட்குடைத்தா வென்று, களையாமை) is doubtful. Read as a Jain ascetic's code, not sowing and not weeding would avoid harm to life in the soil, and not bathing is a known renunciant rule, the reverse of the householder's bathing rules elsewhere in this group.

reading: The verse says, to a woman with fish-like eyes, that for one who does not lie, has put away flesh and toddy, does no evil, does not join the base and does not revile, the books are, on reflection, always beside the point.
nuance: Flesh and toddy are joined by ஒடு but counted as two, giving six. The predicate (அயல அயலவாம் நூல்) puts the books outside such a man, the third time in the chapter conduct replaces the book.

reading: The verse calls good five things: not being angry with those dear as one's eyes, joining the company of the learned, not clinging to those whose speech is like music, not letting a precious secret slip to those whose words are melodious, and relieving the distress of the poor even a little.
nuance: Items 3 and 4 both guard against sweet speakers: one forbids attachment, the other forbids trusting them with a secret. பண்போல் கிளவியார் may be women, but the word does not say so.

reading: The verse says that if a man draws near to renunciants, gives to those who have not renounced, speaks well of the dead, and honours and tends the kin the dead leave behind, his life is sweet and without ruin.
nuance: Four items, not six: the verse pairs those who renounced with those who did not, then the dead with their kin. இறந்தார்க்கு இனிய இசைத்தல் may also mean rites for the dead.

reading: The verse names what makes a trusted minister: guarding the people, resolve, strength in learning, secret counsel, the power to keep off sloth, and, guarding the crown and discerning in smell, taste and hearing, keeping the company of the good.
nuance: Six nominal items are counted; முடியோம்பி நாற்றம் சுவைகேள்வி is read as a phrase qualifying the last, which is doubtful. கூடம் may be secret counsel or stratagem. The last line (தேற்றானேல் தேறும்) may mean that even untested, such a man is to be trusted.

reading: The verse says that if a king guards against sensual indulgence, waste of wealth, deer-hunting, evil toddy, gambling that brings grief, harsh force of words, cruel and wrathful punishment, and lack of restraint, other kings will have no wrath that can destroy him.
nuance: The first seven items match the old list of a king's seven vices (women, hunting, drink, dice, harsh words, harsh punishment, waste); அடங்காமை closes them as their sum. Eight items against the table's six.

reading: The verse names as belonging to one greater than a king: not killing, not causing killing, not lying, not going after another's wife, not joining the base, being deaf to secrets told, and dumb to evil speech.
nuance: Seven items against the table's six. இறையில் பெரியான் can be 'one greater than a king' or 'the great one without fault'; either way the list is a measure of greatness.

reading: The verse says that one who does not trust the words of women with lightning-slim waists, does not heed desire, does not rage in vain, does not kill, delights in giving even when it is like cutting off a limb, and has cut hatred out of himself has no equal even in heaven.
nuance: The giving that cuts like a limb is the hardest gift, which recalls verse 3's ranking of giving above penance. The distrust of women's words repeats verse 5's gender rule.

norm.note: a rule of the period that the virtuous man does not trust women's words

title: ஏலாதி 21-40
theme: Verses 21 to 40 move from Death and impermanence as the reason to seek release (21 to 24, 37), through faults sorted by mind, speech and body (27 to 29) and an envoy's excellences (26), to the twelve kinds of legal son (30, 31) and rewards in heaven or kingship for restrained speech and for feeding the needy (32 to 36, 40), closing with what is easy and what is hard (39).
source_issues: 24 line 1: புறப்பு is most likely a misprint for பிறப்பு (birth).
30 line 3: ஓளரதனே looks like a misspelling of ஔரசன் (aurasa); line 4: கிரிதன்பென கற்பவன் appears corrupt, probably கிரிதன் and a garbled பௌனர்ப்பவன்.
31 line 3: புத்ரனப வித்தனோடு runs புத்ரன் and அபவித்தன் together with a broken word division.
34 lines 1-2: உரைய and உரையாள் look like misprints for உரையான், matching the other clauses.
39 line 2: (எளிது) is an editorial restoration in parentheses, not in the verse as transmitted.
29 line 3: மையெனநீள் கண்ணாய் is spelled as one run; the address is clear but the division is editorial.

reading: Youth passes, disease and old age arrive, and wealth and strength wither, so the verse, addressing a woman of milk-sweet speech, says that while one's days remain the rule is to seek release rather than worldly toil.
nuance: The verse counts five things, not six: two that leave (youth, and with wealth, strength) and two that come (disease, old age), with wealth and strength sharing one verb; பாடு is read as worldly toil, set against வீடு. வீதி in line 4 is taken as விதி, 'the rule'.

reading: Death, who does not let one's days run their full count, fears neither sword nor fierce courage, neither beauty nor men nor wealth, and seeing that he comes, the verse says one should take up the book of verse of the one who reached release.
nuance: The five things are what a person might use against Death, and each is named only to be refused; the remedy is not a deed but a book, பாவின்நூல், apparently the scripture of the Jina who attained வீடு. ஆம்பொருள் தானஞ்சான் could also be split to include தானம், 'gifts', as a sixth thing Death does not fear; the reading here takes தான் as emphatic.

reading: Death regards neither a person's virtue nor his wealth nor his looks, neither a wedding nor an auspicious rite nor the moment, and accepts no guard set at his feet, so the verse calls it beautiful to take the great ones' book as a guard against his mouth.
nuance: Six நோக்கான் clauses make the count; கால்காப்பு வேண்டான் is a seventh refusal that turns toward the remedy, a guard (காப்பு) of a different kind, the scripture, closing the mouth that eats. கணம் may be the moment (no right time to die) or a crowd; the reading takes the moment.

reading: Disease, birth, old age, death, sorrow and unabating want do not hold back, so the verse says the way of release is good if one fulfils it rather than becoming like dancers who play on a decorated stage.
nuance: Birth is counted among the evils, not as a beginning: the list is the round of births itself, closed by want. The dancers on the stage are those who play out a life's roles and leave; the image makes worldly life a performance rather than a sin. The count word இவை is fused into நிரப்பிவை, so count_word is left null; the six are counted as written.

reading: The verse names not frequenting the anklet-wearers and not frequenting the shows that the shareless desire, for once one takes to such shows, enmity, blame, evil talk and death come and do not leave, though they seem to.
nuance: The six things are two abstentions and four consequences: the verse sets the cause beside its fruits. பாடகம், the anklet, stands for those who wear it, most likely dancing women; பாத்திலார், 'those without a share', is obscure and may mean men of no settled portion or the women themselves. தீர்ந்தால்போல் தீரா: the harms seem to end and return.

reading: For envoys the verse names six excellences: a beauty of mind matured and tested, courage, learning well mastered, power of speech, knowing the time, and fame the world knows.
Coveting, anger and wrong view, which a person goes on doing even after learning and weighing the warning that they diminish him, are named three faults that belong to the mind.
nuance: This verse opens a sequence (27 to 29) that sorts faults by the faculty that commits them: three of the mind here, four of speech in 28, three of the body in 29, ten in all. தீக்காட்சி, 'evil seeing', is wrong view, a doctrinal fault, counted with two passions. கள்ளத்த அல்ல is hard: it may say these are not hidden faults or not deeds of the hand; the reading takes the contrast as mind against outward act.

reading: Addressing a woman of kohl-dark wide eyes and a peacock's grace, the verse says those who know the truth hold that lying, slander, harsh words and useless words are four faults that come by the mouth.
nuance: The four are the faults of speech in the three-faculty scheme begun in 27. மறலையின் is obscure; it may be 'of the wicked' or a form of மறலி, Death, which would make the mouth Death's own; the reading keeps only that the four belong to the mouth.

reading: Killing, theft and a life of burning lust, which the great who stand firm in their vows do not consent to, are named three opposed acts whose rule is that they belong to the body.
nuance: It completes the ten faults of 27 to 29 with the three of the body. நிலையளவின் நின்ற, 'who stood in the measure of their station', points to those keeping vows, but the counsel itself is general.

reading: The verse names the first six of the kinds of son that the wise recognise when they take up and protect children: the son of one's own wife, the son of the field, the son of an unmarried girl, the hidden son, the bought son and a sixth whose name is garbled.
nuance: These are Sanskrit law-book names of legal sonship (ஔரச, க்ஷேத்ரஜ, கானீந, கூட, க்ரீத, and probably பௌநர்ப்பவ, the son of a remarried woman) in Tamil spelling; with 31 they make the twelve. The verse makes a son a status the household can acquire, not only beget. The identifications are from the Sanskrit names, not from the verse.

norm.note: a classification of legal sonship of the period by the circumstances of birth: from the wife, from the wife by another man, from an unmarried girl, born in secret, bought

reading: Addressing a woman with the grace of a maddened peacock, the verse names the remaining six kinds of son: the given son, the son taken with the bride, the made son, the son of an appointed daughter, the cast-off son and a son of a sixth kind.
nuance: It completes the list of 30 (தத்தன் dattaka, சகோடன் sahodha, கருத்திரமன் kritrima, புத்திரி புத்ரன் putrika-putra, அபவித்தன் apaviddha, and உருகிருதன், perhaps svayamdatta, the self-given). Line 3 runs புத்ரன் and அபவித்தன் together; பொய்யில் may praise the last or the list.

norm.note: the rest of the period's twelve kinds of legal son, sorted by how the boy came to the house: given, brought by the bride, adopted, through a daughter, found abandoned

reading: One who does not speak of his own lineage and family standing, does not speak of others' defects, does not speak of his wealth, his way of life or his span of years, and who gives before he eats, is to be known, the verse says to a woman of bee-sought tresses, as god of gods.
nuance: Five of the six restraints are silences about oneself (birth, standing, wealth, life, age); the one about others is not to name their defects. The reward is given to the giver, ஈத்துண்பான், so the silences frame the giving.

reading: One who does not lie, does not revile, does not backbite, speaks truth to everyone, speaks openly of what he has and does not speak to wound will, the verse says to a peacock-like woman, leave this world and become king of the assembled gods.
nuance: All six are about speech; உள்ளனவும் விட்டுரையான் is read as one who does not hide what he has from those who ask, which joins speech to giving. எய்யுரையான் is uncertain: 'not speaking words that pierce' or 'not mocking'.

reading: One who does not speak destructive words or speak in hatred, has no anger, does not proclaim his own nature, does not speak of baseness, and gives what fits to those who want it is, the verse says to a woman with lips red as the kovvai fruit, sought with love by the gods.
nuance: Verses 32 to 34 form a run: restraint of speech joined to giving, rewarded each time in heaven, rising from god of gods to king of the gods to sought by the gods. The fruit is put in the gods' wish, not in his merit.

reading: One who gives blameless food as their share to renouncers and to those not renounced, to the powerless, the unseen, the bereaved, the destitute and the young, and to the excellent as well, will, the verse says to a woman of musical speech, rule the earth as king.
nuance: The recipients run to eight, not six: the verse adds சிறந்தவர்க்கும், 'to the excellent too', after the needy, so the list closes by widening, not narrowing. தோன்றார் may be those who keep out of sight (the shamed poor), and இறந்தார் those whose support has died; துறவாதார் may be householders in need. பாற்படுத்தான், 'set as a share', makes the gift a portion due, not a favour.

reading: Those who prepare a deeply satisfying meal for the lame, the blind, the mute, those with no kin at all and those with no learning to hold to will swiftly, the verse says, be desired by the gods.
nuance: The count is five: three bodily lacks, then a social lack (no kin) and a lack of learning, so the unlearned are set among the disabled as people owed food. சாலவும் ஆழப் படும் is taken with the meal ('filling deeply'); read as 'those deeply sunk in need' it would make a sixth.

reading: Death does not go away when people weep, does not fear, does not listen when they cry out, does not leave for the helpless, does not go away when they worship, and regards no worth, so the verse calls it a failing to sit idle without striving at penance.
nuance: Each item is a plea that fails (tears, threats, cries, helplessness, worship), so worship itself is counted among the useless defences; only தவம், practised beforehand, is set against Death. The six are actions Death refuses, not things.

reading: The great penance of those who fully understand that one does not reach it except by noble conduct is something not removed by letters, not ended by numbers, not altered by praise and hymns, and failing to go that way is utter baseness.
nuance: The verse sets penance against three learned or ritual substitutes, script, number (counting or astrology) and praise, and makes conduct the only road. புலை here is baseness, not a caste term. The syntax is compressed and the subject of the three negatives may instead be the bond of deeds that penance alone removes.

reading: Dying is easy and fullness of character hard; to reach for the good is easy and to guard truth hard; to go toward what will be is easy and to stand firm hard; to win by being clever is easy and the right word hard.
nuance: Four easy-and-hard pairs make eight things; each hard thing is the lasting form of its easy partner. Putting death among the easy things reverses the death verses earlier in the chapter. The last pair ranks speech above victory; (எளிது) in line 2 is an editorial restoration.

reading: Not wavering, hastening to what has befallen others, not tormenting living beings, not doubting, choosing the way that ends impermanence, and removing hunger where it is found make one whose gaze is on the heights of heaven.
nuance: The list joins inner steadiness (not wavering, not doubting), care (running to help, removing hunger), non-harm and the choice of release, so feeding the hungry stands beside the way out of impermanence. The division of line 1 is uncertain: உற்றதற்கு ஓடி may go with உலையாமை ('not shaken by what befalls').

title: ஏலாதி 41-60
theme: Nineteen of the twenty verses name about six marks of a giver (refusals of killing, flesh, toddy, lies and theft, and gifts of food, goods, water works and cures to the ruined, the sick, mothers and ascetics) and pay each with a reward, mostly kingship in a later life; the run closes with a learner's six habits and the six evils of bad company.
source_issues: 41: the site lacks this verse; line 2 had ௌ written as ெ + ள (repaired).
45: the site's text lacks lines 1 and 2; line 2 had ௌ written as ெ + ள (repaired).
54: lines 2-3 (தூப்பால / நிண்டாரால்) look corrupt; a recipient may be lost there.
56: line 2 has an unassigned Tamil code point (உயை஡ளர், U+0BA1); ஊண்ஈய்ந்தபர் and மாக்கடால் on line 3 look miscopied.
58: ஆயந்தார் on line 2 looks like a miscopy of ஆய்ந்தார்.

reading: The verse names six marks of a man (he does not draw near the mean, does not take flesh, does not stray into falsehood, does not seize others' goods, is not close-fisted, and gives to those who have no means) and says that, if he is such, the books of the path will recite his worth beyond measure.
nuance: The reward is not a rebirth but praise in the texts themselves (நெறிநூல்கள் ... பன்னும்): the giver becomes a subject the books recite. The last two items turn from refusals to giving: not being tight (இறுகான்) and giving to the resourceless.

norm.note: the Jain abstention from flesh of the period, counted among a giver's marks

reading: The verse says that one who does not kill, does not consent to killing, does not join the company of killers, does not cling to what is others', does not stray into the delusion of flesh, and has fed people, settling them in households, will rule the earth as a king, mounted on a killing elephant, bringing foes under his feet.
nuance: The non-killer's reward is a killing elephant (கொல்யானை) and enemies trodden under: the verse sees no strain in paying non-violence with conquest. புல்லான் பிறர்பால் may mean not embracing another's wife or not attaching himself to others; குடிப்படுத்து may be 'settling families' or 'establishing his own house'.

norm.note: the Jain rule against killing and flesh of the period, extended to consenting and to company
