reading: Addressing a woman with long makara earrings, the verse says that one who does not delight in gambling, does not swerve, does not speak deceit, does not relish disputes with anyone, does not trust women's words, and has given food to great ascetics will dwell in a mansion with makara-mouthed ornament.
nuance: The makara of the woman's earring returns as the makara mouths of the reward mansion, a verbal rhyme of the frame. பேரான் (does not move away) and கலா(வு) (theft, or a form of கலாம், strife) are unsure. The distrust of women's words recurs in verses 5 and 20.

norm.note: a rule of the period that a man of virtue does not trust women's words

reading: The verse says that one who does not lie, does not take to falsehood, does not eat flesh, does not revile anyone, clears the road, and gives fine white rice without grudging before he eats will become a king of the sea-girt earth whose lot is to share his food and be praised.
nuance: The reward repeats the act: one who gave before eating (ஈத்துண்பான்) becomes a king who shares before eating (பாத்துண்பான்), so kingship is the same virtue on a larger table. Clearing the road (வழிசீத்து) is a public work set among private restraints.

norm.note: the Jain abstention from flesh of the period, set among a giver's marks

reading: The verse says that one who does not slip from the proper way, does not covet harmful things, does not err, does not seize the house and goods of others, walks by right conduct and gives faultless food will rule, conquer, and quickly let go.
nuance: விடுப்பான் விரைந்து closes the reward: on one reading the king soon lets the kingdom go, a Jain turn in which rule is a stage before renunciation; on another he quickly releases those he has conquered. மனைபொருள் may be another's house and goods or another's wife and goods.

reading: The verse says that if one does not revel, does not drink toddy, does not look upon drinkers, neither hides from nor flinches at guests, does not scorn the poor, and eats only after giving, he will rule a land without harm and his family will thrive abundantly.
nuance: Three items circle toddy (revelry, drinking, the sight of drinkers) and three circle the table (guests, the poor, eating after giving), so abstention and hospitality are one portrait. ஒளியான் விருந்துக்(கு) உலையான் is taken as one item; split, it gives seven.

norm.note: the period's rule against toddy, extended to the sight of drinkers

reading: The verse says that one who keeps the words of the great and stands without swerving, does not despoil servants who do not desert him, does not trust the words of the black-hearted, does not join them, gives food with a clear mind before he eats, and does not change, will rule the earth.
nuance: பரியா அடியார் is unsure: servants who do not run off, or the unpitied poor at one's feet. கரியார் may be the black-hearted or, since கரி is a witness, false witnesses.

reading: The verse says that if a man does not join in strangers' clamour, does not turn away guests, calls out the sound of the meal in his house before he eats, does not listen to hostile talk, and cherishes his kin, he will come as an unfailing king ruling the earth by the sword.
nuance: Three அரவம் words (sound) carry the verse: strangers' noise he avoids, the rice-call he makes, hostile noise he will not hear. Calling out before eating makes the meal public. Five things, not six; கிளைஓம்பின் is counted as the fifth.

reading: The verse names elephants, horses, gold, a maiden, herds of cattle and all other gifts besides, and says that one who, with these in mind, gave food with cow's ghee to great ascetics will live as Vaisravana, the lord of wealth.
nuance: The relation of the list to the food gift turns on எண்ணனாய்: either the food with ghee is reckoned as worth all these great gifts, or the giver gave all these and food as well. On the first reading the verse ranks a meal for ascetics above the royal gift catalogue. The maiden (கன்னி) stands in a list of goods given.

norm.note: a period gift-list that counts a maiden given in marriage among goods given away

reading: The verse says that one who gave sesame, cotton, oil, cloth to wear, a vessel and cloth, and with them food given with love, saying 'take it', will live happily joined with his companion.
nuance: The goods are household stuffs, and the reward is household joy: a life with one's partner. வள் is unsure (a vessel or a measure), and உடுத்தாடை and துணி may both be cloth, one worn and one uncut.

reading: The verse says that one who made over to common use a tank rich in drinking water, a well, a wayside shelter, a water-booth and a public hall will live abundantly amid tuneful song and dance, in love's union and its quarrels.
nuance: The reward is pleasure, not heaven or kingship: music, dance, and the akam pair of union and sulking (கூடல், ஊடல்). Five works are counted; உண்ணீர் வளம் could be read as a sixth (a source of drinking water) rather than as the tank's quality.

reading: The verse says that those who toil by day to cook and feed people who have lost their house, their eyes, their gathered wealth, their paddy or their herds will become kings with many elephants and eat with considered plenty.
nuance: Every recipient is defined by a loss (இழந்தார் five times), so the list is a census of ruin: blindness sits among the losses of house, grain and cattle. Five things.

reading: The verse says that those who, consenting and having the means, feed in their own houses the indebted, the unprotected, those with nothing in hand, the lame, the old and the young will live on earth as masters of armies.
nuance: The feeding is in the house (இல்லுள்), not at a public charity. தங்கான் is read as தம் கால் (their own legs) before முடம்பட்டார்; மூப்பில்லார் may be the young or those with no elders to keep them.

reading: The verse says that those who, without calculating, gave food to brahmins, the hungry, ascetics, children and those who have no one at all to protect them will rule the earth with a full treasury.
nuance: பார்ப்பார் is a caste term, here naming brahmins by birth as a class of fit recipients, set first beside the hungry and the unprotected. The end of line 2 and start of line 3 (தூப்பால நிண்டாரால்) are corrupt; a sixth recipient may be hidden there.

norm.note: a period list of fit recipients that names brahmins by birth (பார்ப்பார்) first

reading: The verse says that those who, treating them as their own, fed and relieved the grave ills of women who have given birth, those weakened at delivery, the pregnant, infants, the distraught and those stricken by wind-disease will live joined with great wealth.
nuance: Four of the six recipients belong to the birth-room (mothers, those weak in labour, the pregnant, infants), so the verse makes childbirth a field of charity. The giver both feeds and cures (ஊண்ஈய்த்து உறுநோய் களைந்தார்).

reading: Addressing a woman with a deer's glance, the verse says that those who, as kin, gave food to those who were heads of houses, the distressed, the fallen, women, the toiling poor and those with no food at all will rule the island of Jambu girt by the great sea.
nuance: Line 2's உயை஡ளர் is corrupt (an unassigned code point) and several words (தாப்பாளர், ஊண்ஈய்ந்தபர், மாக்கடால்) look miscopied, so the recipients after the first are guesses. The reward, rule of நாவலம்தீவு, is the widest in the chapter.

reading: The verse says that those who took hard pains to feed and cure sufferers of black scab, white leprosy, stone, wind-disease, burning great sores and the fire of a swollen belly will become kings who protect and eat in honour.
nuance: Divided into six by reading கல்வளி as stone and wind-disease and காயும் as qualifying the great sores; read கல்வளி as one ailment and the count is five. The giver here is a healer as well as a feeder (அவை தீர்த்தார்).

reading: The verse says that those who do not sport in lust, do not desire, do not join the unlearned, do not say yes lightly, stand in the way of those who have inquired, and, without boasting, gave to those who asked so that they rejoiced, will in this very life overcome their enemies.
nuance: The reward is in this life (இம்மையான்), where most verses of the run look to a later birth. காமாடார் and ஆமாடார் are obscure; the second may be 'do not dance to every yes'. ஆயந்தார் is read as ஆய்ந்தார்.

reading: The verse says that one who bows, follows the right way, takes the words of the excellent, studies the subtle books and penetrates them, and lives attending to what is fitting will live as a blameless king, examining the books closely.
nuance: The only verse of the run without a gift of food: the six things are a learner's acts, and the reward, a blameless king who still reads (நூல்நோக்கி), returns to the study of line 2. நுழையா is read as the old participle 'having entered'.

reading: The verse says that if one draws near those without worth, who neglect greatness, fame and virtue, are given to anger and lack the rare books, then sin, blame, enmity, death, ruin and fear will cling to him in both worlds like a curse.
nuance: Line 1 may describe the unworthy (neglecting greatness, fame and virtue) or list what is lost by the company. கேடச்சம் joins ruin and fear in one word, so the five items counted here are six evils; 'both worlds' (இருமைக்கும்) makes the cost run past this life.

title: ஏலாதி 61-80
theme: Twenty verses mix the renouncer's code (the defects of the soul, the path and timetable of release, the high state and the seven hells, the teacher's fitness) with the householder's giving, naming in sixes those to be fed, the gifts to students and ascetics, and the marks of love.
source_issues: elathi 61 line 2: ஒர்வமே is not a common form; perhaps for ஓர்வம்.
elathi 62 line 2: முனையுள்ளம் is probably for முனையுள்ளும்.
elathi 67 line 2: இரு ளோ(டு) is split by a space inside இருள்.
elathi 68 line 1: புணர்வுலத்தல் may be for புணர்வு உவத்தல்.
elathi 77 line 4: வல்லைளீ(டு) is corrupt; the sense requires வல்லை வீடு.

reading: The verse names desire, hatred, anger, partiality, avarice and pride without worth, and says that those rid of defect declare, by the scripture, that these are defects of the soul.
nuance: The six are called ஊனம், a flaw of the உயிர், not wrongs against others; the list holds the passions that Jain teaching treats as stains of the soul (anger, pride, greed) beside desire and hatred. ஒர்வமே is a rare form, read here as ஓர்வம் 'leaning to one side', and மானம் is pride, not the honour the word often means in the Kural.

reading: The verse says that those who keep both scripture and conduct do not go to dances, festivals, weddings, killing grounds, the roaring battlefront or other such places, and that if they go it brings them lapse and loss.
nuance: Pleasures and violence are barred together: a wedding sits beside the killing ground. முனையுள்ளம் is probably for முனையுள்ளும் 'within the battlefront', and வேறிடத்தும் 'other places too' leaves the sixth item open.
domain_note: those bound to a rule of conduct; barring weddings and festivals points to the renouncer

reading: The verse says that those who gave food, clothing, a stylus, a book and, with care, the leaf for figures and letters to those who live by hearing, writing and reciting will in this very life live amply, writing as they wish.
nuance: The gift is the material of study, and the reward named seems to be learning itself within this life (இம்மையான்), not a later heaven. பேணொடும் is read as 'with care', not as a sixth thing, so five things are counted; வேட்டெழுத is doubtful.

reading: The verse reports that those who did great penance said release comes if one regards the Exalted one as the lord, recites the Exalted one's book, holds oneself in, and fully performs the Exalted one's hard penance.
nuance: உயர்ந்தான் is repeated three times, tying regard, study and penance to one figure. The order (taking him as lord, his scripture, then penance) is close to the Jain sequence of right faith, knowledge and conduct; that is our reading, not the verse's word. ஒப்புடைத்தான் is obscure. The verse does not count; the four items are the steps it names.

reading: The verse asks whether one who wishes to see Death's strength cut down and who, delighting in the scripture of the all-knowing one and looking at nothing else, performs a pure high penance that harms nothing will not, having understood, rise to the upper world.
nuance: The penance must be ஊறுபாடு இல்லா, causing no injury, so non-harm is a condition of the austerity, not a separate virtue. பாலனார் and பாராது are uncertain; the question form (ஏறுமோ) expects 'yes'. The verse does not count; the three items are the conditions it sets.

reading: The verse says that when the faultless learned who have searched its meaning describe the greatness of the stainless high state, there is no light, no speech, no opposition, no weariness, no trouble and no sweet sleep there.
nuance: The highest state is described only by what it lacks, and the list denies the goods of life (light, speech, sleep) as well as its ills; even rest is not offered as its pleasure. மாறு can be change or opposition.

reading: The verse names sharp arrows, hot sand, hanging gems, the wet, smoke, darkness and the darkness beyond it, and says the great, having examined the scripture, declared these in order to be the seven low states of ruin.
nuance: We read the seven as the Jain sevenfold hell, whose names run from gem and gravel through sand, mud and smoke to darkness and great darkness; the verse's words fit that scheme only roughly, and கூரம்பு and ஈர்மணி தூங்கல் are hard to place. The sixth item is copied with its sandhi (புகையிரு ளோ(டு), 'with darkness' after smoke). The verse counts seven (ஏழு), not six, and we follow it.

reading: The verse says that the gentle set out six qualities in those who love: dying for the beloved, giving wealth, sweet speech, delight in being together, pain at their pain, and grief at separation.
nuance: Love is defined by six acts and feelings, ranging from the gift of life to the grief of parting. புணர்வுலத்தல் is read as புணர்வு உவத்தல் 'rejoicing in union'; as written it could mean wasting away in union.

reading: The verse reports that the exalted set out lifting, bending, straightening, standing, lying down and moving as the six distinct actions that attend a living being.
nuance: The verse makes no moral claim; it classifies the body's movements. Why an ethics work keeps this list is not said; it may serve the Jain care over every act that could harm a creature, but that is a guess.

reading: The verse says that one who, knowing and without doubt, gave alms, begged food, food and clothing to those of hard penance will rule earth and sky in due order, every day, sweetly and without lack.
nuance: ஐயம் is used twice in two senses, alms in line 1 and doubt in line 2, so the gift must be given without hesitation. The reward is rule over both worlds, set out in order (வரிசையால்). The verse names four gifts, taking ஐயம் and பிச்சை as two kinds of alms.

reading: The verse says that one who arranged food for wayfarers, for those who bore heavy loads, for those lying sick, for kin, for those of the sky and for those of the other side lives fittingly in his own house.
nuance: The householder's table is set for six, most of them with no claim of kinship. வானகத்தார் with கேடின்று உடல்சார்ந்த is unclear (the dead, or gods); மறுதலையார் may be enemies or those of another creed, and பொறைதாங்கினார் may be porters or the forbearing.

reading: The verse says that from not understanding comes fault, from fault comes karma, the one without understanding makes the karma that brings birth, and through birth the great suffering follows on, so that it becomes a circle.
nuance: The chain closes on itself (மண்டிலம்): suffering in birth feeds the same ignorance. ஒத்தான் and தொண்டு are obscure, and the exact links of the chain are our reading; the six items are the links of the chain as the verse names them.

reading: The verse says that household life and great penance are both desired as noble ways of acting, and, as far as the words allow, that household life is letting go without clinging while penance is a clinging that is undivided.
nuance: Both ways are called வினைவாழ்க்கை and neither is ranked above the other; each is defined by its relation to பற்று. The second half is obscure: பாத்தில் may be 'without share' or 'without division', and the reading of it is tentative. The verse counts two (இரண்டும்).

reading: The verse says that the beauty of the waist, of the shoulders, beauty beyond compare, the beauty of gait, of modesty and of the neck are not beauty, and that the beauty of numbers and letters alone is beauty.
nuance: The six rejected beauties are the conventional marks of a woman's body, and the list includes modesty, a virtue, among them. Learning is named as எண் and எழுத்து, numbers and letters.

reading: The verse says that the fitness of a teacher lies in knowing the books of the six schools, holding to understanding, removing what runs against the doctrine, and refuting the contrary words of a false teacher.
nuance: The teacher is defined as a debater: he must know the rival systems in order to answer them. மறுவரவு and மாசாரியன் are hard: the second is read as மாசு ஆரியன், a stained teacher, set against ஆசாரியன். The verse does not count; the four items are the parts of fitness it names.

reading: The verse tells a woman with spear-like eyes that, examining what one can do of the good things possible, giving brings enjoyment, penance brings heaven, and the penance that does not cling brings release.
nuance: The three are a ladder of means and fruits, and the top rung is a further kind of penance, not knowledge. அடையாத் தவம் is read as penance that holds to nothing; it could be penance that does not stop. The verse names three means and fruits, not six things.

tamil: எல்லை உயர்த்தார் தவமுயலின் மூன்(று) ஐந்(து) ஏழ்
reading: The verse says that one who wishes to end the suffering and harm of the four states of birth and, examining the scripture's path, strives in penance to reach the pure state will gain release quickly, in three, five or seven births.
nuance: Release is given a term in births, not promised at once. நாற்கதி is the four states of birth of Jain teaching; வல்லைளீ(டு) is read as வல்லை வீடு 'release quickly', which the sense requires. The items are the three spans of births the verse names, not a list of things.

reading: The verse says that those who keep and give to the motherless child, the widow, those whose living has lost its means, those ruined in trade, those who lost the wealth that fed them and the blind will live well.
nuance: Each recipient is named by what was lost (mother, husband, livelihood, trade, wealth, sight), so the list is of the newly helpless. வைத்து வழங்கி asks that one keep in order to give. வாயிழந்த may also mean the mute.

reading: The verse says that death, ruin, enmity, sorrow, joy and banishment from the land all come by the tongue, and, as far as the obscure close allows, that one's character is what passes the lips when speech suits friends.
nuance: Joy stands among the outcomes, so the tongue is the source of good as well as ill. நாக்காடு and the last two lines are obscure; நாட்டறை போக்கு is read as exile from one's country.

reading: The verse says that those who gave food to and were a spring of help for outcastes, the wounded, the blind, those unable to move, those who have lost their former state and the eminent will live as kings, giving audience among their people.
nuance: புலையாளர் is a caste term for those of outcaste birth; here it heads a list of people to be fed, marking a low station rather than barring contact. போக்கில் நிலையாளர் is read as those who cannot move, and தலையாளர் as the eminent fallen on need; both are doubtful.

norm.note: a birth-rank term of the period names outcastes as a class among the needy; the verse sets no bar on them

title: இனியவை நாற்பது 0-20
theme: The invocation and first twenty verses set the book's form, three or four things each named sweet, often ranked 'foremost' (முன்) or capped with 'nothing nobler', and spread it across the king's pleasures of horse and elephant, the householder's joys of children, kin and harvest, and restraints such as not killing, not eating flesh and not looking at another's wife, which the list counts as sweetnesses rather than duties.
source_issues: Verse 1 line 2: நற்சலையில் is not a known word; read as நற்சவையில் 'in a good assembly'.
Verse 16 line 1: சுற்றார்முன் is likely a misprint for கற்றார்முன், which the sense and Kural 722 support.
Verse 17 line 1: நாட்டார்க்கு where Kural 679, which lines 1-2 nearly quote, has நட்டார்க்கு; possibly a misprint.
Verse 19 line 1: வாழ்தால் is a misprint for வாழ்தல்.
Verse 5 line 3: the line was repaired (யார்மட்டும் to யார்மாட்டும், as tamilvu); எய்துங் திறத்தால் also has an odd sandhi (expected எய்துந் திறத்தால்).
Verse 8 has five lines; the second item runs over lines 2-3.

reading: The invocation names three acts of worship as sweet: reaching quickly the feet of the three-eyed god, bowing to the one who wears the ancient, glorious tulasi garland, and going with first care to praise the four-faced one.
nuance: The three gods are not named but are marked by their emblems: the third eye, the tulasi garland and the four faces, so the opening honours Siva, Vishnu and Brahma in turn without ranking one sect over another. The first is 'quickly' sweet (கடிதினிதே), which gives the opening its only note of urgency.

reading: Learning even if one must go begging for it is named very sweet, offering a hand in a good assembly sweet, the speech of women whose smile is like pearls sweet, and joining those clearly superior sweet as well.
nuance: The first item sets learning above the shame of begging, the one thing the book elsewhere treats as a loss of dignity. நற்சலையில் in line 2 is not a known word; it reads best as நற்சவையில் 'in a good assembly', and the item is held on that reading.

reading: The just dealing of a man of means is named sweet; household life is foremost sweet when it is carried through in harmony; and if it does not prosper, renouncing without delay in view of impermanence is sweet above all.
nuance: The verse ranks the two lives by a condition: the household comes first (முன்) while it goes well, and renunciation becomes the highest sweetness (தலையாக) only when it fails, so renouncing is the remedy for a household that has not prospered, not a higher calling in itself. உடையான் வழக்கு is compressed; it may be the fair conduct of the householder (the 'one who has') or a lawsuit settled fairly, so the first item is uncertain.

reading: Young kin who never refuse what they are bidden are named foremost sweet, learning every day without straying into fault very sweet, the farming of a man who owns his plough sweet, and, on reflection, friendship made for a far region sweet too.
nuance: The four together are the supports of a house: obedient young kin, daily learning, a plough of one's own and friends abroad. The last line is compressed; தேரின் 'if one considers' and திசைக்கு 'for a region' allow the friendship to be one formed in, or for the sake of, distant parts, so the fourth item is held loosely.

reading: Seeing an army that has elephants is named foremost sweet, not swelling one's flesh by eating flesh foremost sweet, a village on the shore of a forest river sweet, and the regard of men who have honour sweet as well.
nuance: The list sets abstinence from flesh between a royal spectacle and a pleasant village, as one more sweetness, and gives it the same 'foremost' (முன்) as the elephant army. It mirrors Innaa Narpathu 22 almost item for item.

reading: For a ruler the verse names as foremost sweet not killing and not granting honours by bending the sceptre, names being a just-sceptred king sweet by the means that achieve it, and calls not speaking ill of anyone good.
nuance: மாராயம் is the honour a king confers; the second item is about favour bestowed unjustly, not about punishment. The last item, not speaking ill of anyone, is closed with நன்கு 'good' rather than இனிது, and applies beyond the king.

reading: Doing dharma to the extent of one's strength is named foremost sweet, the fruitful words spoken by those on the right path sweet, and taking as one's guard men who are capable and not shameless sweet.
nuance: வலவை usually names a shameless or wanton person; the third item asks that protectors be chosen both able (வாய்ப்புடையர்) and not of that kind, which fits a householder's or a chief's guard alike.

reading: The verse names brahmins' keeping of the Veda very sweet, the leading of an army by a man with bonds of loyalty foremost sweet, and not attaching oneself even to a father if he will not restrain himself sweet.
nuance: The first item ties Vedic recitation to a birth-group as its proper excellence. The third is the hardest claim in the chapter: it puts self-restraint above filial bond, so an unrestrained father is to be kept at a distance. பந்தம் may be the bond of loyalty to the king or the tie of kin among the troops.

norm.note: a norm of the period assigning Vedic recitation to the brahmin as his proper excellence

reading: The strength of the spirited horse one rides is named foremost sweet, seeing the fury of dark mountain-like elephants in the fierce battle of garlanded kings foremost sweet, and the eager hearing very good things without confusion sweet.
nuance: This is a five-line verse; the second item takes two lines. The first two items are a warrior's pleasures and the third turns to listening, so the list moves from the field of battle to the hall of learning.

reading: The well-being of those who love us is named foremost sweet, seeing the wide moonlight in the beautiful sky sweet, and being of faultless deeds and, with tenderness, loving toward everyone sweet.
nuance: The list widens love outward: first the circle that loves us, then a sight open to all, then love given to everyone (யார்க்கும்), so the moonlight sits as the image between the private and the universal.

reading: The verse names sweet seeing that one lives without taking on debt, putting away women who lack the excellence of self-restraint, and fearing and keeping away from those of mean mind, which is sweet in every way.
nuance: கடம் is debt; the first item is living without borrowing. The second is a gender rule of the period: it treats a woman's நிறை as the condition of keeping her, and says nothing of the man's.

norm.note: a rule of the period that women lacking chastity or restraint are to be sent away

reading: Not living by going on the road is named very sweet, a keenness that does not go crooked to take sweet, and nothing is as noble as the greatness that will not eat from the hand of the unworthy even if life should go.
nuance: The last item is ranked by negation ('there is nothing nobler'), not called sweet, so it caps the list. அதர்சென்று வாழாமை may mean not living as a wayfaring beggar or not living by highway robbery, and உண்ணார் may be those who do not share their food or simply the base; both turn the verse on dignity, but the exact sense is uncertain.

reading: A child's living without illness is named sweet, the learning of one who does not fear the clamorous assembly sweet, and the wealth that comes to excellent men who are not fools sweet if it does not run out.
nuance: Each item carries a condition: the child without illness, learning without fear of the assembly, wealth without exhaustion. Sweetness is in each case the thing kept safe from its typical failure.

reading: Not living on after honour is destroyed is named foremost sweet, living restrained so that one's gifts do not fail sweet, and possessing high wealth without a single flaw sweet for all people.
nuance: Verse 27 repeats the first claim in nearly the same words (மானம் படவரின் வாழாமை). தானம் may be gifts or one's standing; either way restraint is what keeps it.

reading: Seeing a child's tottering walk is named sweet, hearing its babble sweeter than amrita, and having a mind that does not fear when the fruit of one's deeds arrives and burns sweet.
nuance: The third item turns from the nursery to adversity. வினையுடையான் is most likely the bearer of past deeds whose fruit now comes upon him; it could also be an enemy with a task in hand, so the item is held loosely.

reading: The nobility of not looking back after another man's wife is named very sweet, rain falling on green crops suffering drought sweet, and hearing the rut-roar of mountain-like elephants at the gates of valiant kings sweet.
nuance: பின்னோக்கா is 'not looking after', not even turning the eye to follow her; the restraint is in the glance. Innaa Narpathu 38 names the same act from the other side.

reading: Speaking one's learning before the learned is named very sweet, joining one's betters foremost sweet, and giving of oneself without begging even a sesame's worth sweet in every measure.
nuance: The text reads சுற்றார்முன், which as written would be 'before those around one'; கற்றார்முன் 'before the learned' fits the sense and the Kural's phrase, and the reading here follows that, uncertainly. The third item sets giving against asking: one gives without ever asking even a little.

reading: Doing good to the people of the land is named sweet in every measure, winning over those who are not one's allies sweeter still, and having many kinds of grain and joining true companions drawn from many sweet.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 nearly quote Kural 679, but read நாட்டார்க்கு 'to the people of the land' where the Kural has நட்டார்க்கு 'to friends'; this may be a misprint, and on the Kural's wording the verse's audience would be anyone, not a ruler.
domain_note: a ruler or chief: the people of his land, foes won over, granaries and allies

reading: A town where the elders of the assembly live is named sweet, the excellence of ascetics who live by their discipline sweet, and rising in the morning to see one's two aged parents of unfailing worth sweet.
nuance: Three kinds of elder are honoured in turn: the town's elders, the ascetics, and one's own parents (இருமுது மக்கள்), and the last is placed at the start of the day.

reading: Living without speaking ill of friends behind their backs is named very sweet, keeping to the truth and conducting oneself humbly foremost sweet, and, once one has made great wealth without lack, giving it where it is fit sweet.
nuance: வாழ்தால் in line 1 is a misprint for வாழ்தல். The gift is to go தக்குழி, 'where it is fitting', which makes the recipient's worth, not his need, the test.

reading: Letting go of the fickle without approaching them is named sweet, cherishing the true words of the learned sweet, and living fittingly toward all the lives of the wide world sweet.
nuance: The chapter closes on the widest scope in the book so far: right conduct toward every living being of the world (மன்னுயிர்க் கெல்லாம்).

title: இனியவை நாற்பது 21-40
theme: The book's second twenty verses keep its form of three sweet things, often ranked from 'foremost sweet' to 'nothing sweeter', and spread it over giver and asker, king and servant, householder and renouncer, so that restraint of speech and desire, honour, and faithfulness to what others entrust are presented as pleasures rather than duties.
source_issues: 22 line 2: பங்கு where tamilvu reads பாங்கு; the sense changes little.
28 line 2: வாழ்வனிதே looks like a misprint for வாழ்வினிதே.
34 line 4: கொள்ளர் is most likely கொள்ளார்.
35 line 3: பற்றினலாய் and பாத்தூற்று are obscure, possibly corrupt; line 4 வெற்வேறில் is corrupt (Project Madurai prints the variant வெற்றல் வேல்).
38 line 4: சுற்றா is an irregular form, read as சுற்றம்.
40 line 2: வித்துற்குற் றுண்ணா is irregularly written; read as வித்து குற்று உண்ணா, not pounding and eating the seed-grain.

reading: The verse names three things sweet: living without seizing wealth held in another's hand, doing dharma and putting away what is not dharma, and living with the discernment never to join unworthy, deluded men, even by forgetting.
nuance: The third item asks for more than avoidance: மறந்தேயும் ('even by forgetting') makes keeping out of bad company a matter of trained discernment (திறம்), not of a single decision.

reading: The verse names three things sweet: giving with knowledge of one's income, a zeal that does not make one another's dependant, and living without swerving as one who does not do what he craves even when it would delight him greatly.
nuance: Line 2 reads பங்கு ('share') where tamilvu reads பாங்கு ('side'); on either reading the zeal is one that does not hang on someone else. All three items keep a person inside his own measure: of income, of independence, of desire.

reading: The verse names as very sweet digging a charity tank together with a grove, as foremost sweet giving gold together with cows to brahmins, and as sweet leaving the சூதர் who, not fearing even sin, speak the language of a grasping trade.
nuance: சூதர் may be gamblers (சூது) or men who deceive with speech; பற்றுந் தொழில்மொழி ('speech of a grasping trade') fits either, and the line does not settle which. The verse grades its items (மிக, முன்), and the gift to brahmins is the one called foremost.

norm.note: a gift norm of the period that names brahmins as the foremost recipients of cows and gold

reading: The verse names three things sweet: the austerity of one who wants to win and yet does not rage, the forbearance of one who carries a thing through as far as his strength allows, and doing what is to be done without craving what one lacks and grieving in distress.
nuance: Calling the first item நோன்பு, a word for austerity, makes holding back anger in a contest a kind of penance. ஒன்று உய்ப்பான் in line 2 is compressed; 'one who sees a single thing through' is a reading, not a certainty.

reading: The verse names as foremost sweet curbing the craving of the five senses, as sweet keeping away from the unlearned even when wealth would come to hand, and as sweet leaving without embracing men of unsteady views and no self-containment.
nuance: The first item turns inward and the other two outward: the senses are a gate to be guarded and so is one's company, and the second item sets a price on the guarding, wealth given up.

reading: The verse names as sweet the worth of not killing the hope of those who come to one in desire, as very sweet the spirit that will not live where it is held in no regard, and as sweetest of all a bond that in no way hides what it can give.
nuance: The first and last items are about the giver and frame the middle one about honour, so the giver's open hand and the self-respect that will not cringe are made one temper. கரவாத names the Kural's fault of concealment (கரவு) by its absence.

reading: The verse names as foremost sweet the noble bearing of one who gives gifts and not living on when dishonour comes, and as sweet taking what has lasting worth by the proper manner of receiving, as those do who do not make much of what is lacking.
nuance: ஊனங் கொண்டாடார் is hard: 'those who do not celebrate a defect' is the plainest sense, but the line could also mean those who do not dwell on their losses. கோள்முறையாற் கோடல் uses the grammarians' word for a pupil's receiving of instruction (கோடல்), so the third item may be about receiving teaching; this is a reading, not a certainty.

reading: The verse names as foremost sweet not going about crying to others to relieve one's distress, as sweet living mindful that Death's coming is real, and as sweetest of all the judgment of one who speaks no wrong even when his fortune is falling.
nuance: All three items face loss: distress one could beg relief from, death, and ruin of fortune. The closing item makes integrity of speech under ruin the sweetest.

reading: The verse names three things sweet: living with the base put out of one's hands, zeal born of thinking of rising high, and living in brightness without speaking in scorn of people as lowly.
nuance: The aspiration in the middle is fenced on both sides: one leaves the base but does not scorn the lowly. Line 1 is nearly the opening line of Thirikadugam 77.

reading: The verse names as very sweet living with the worth of a kindness weighed, as sweet the excellence of saying nothing crooked in the assembly, and as finest of all the goodness that does not seize a thing given in trust on the thought 'who knew of it then?'
nuance: நன்றிப் பயன்தூக்கி most likely means weighing a kindness received, as gratitude does; it could be read as weighing the return before doing good, but the verse's other items, both about honesty owed to others, favour gratitude. The third item names the temptation precisely: the deposit has no witness left.

reading: The verse names three things sweet: the strength that does not let the sorrow of those who came for refuge grow, doing what one must do even by borrowing, and, however excellent one's learning by listening, speaking only after examining and knowing.
nuance: செய்வன ('what is to be done') is not specified; with the first item about refugees it most naturally covers duties of help, so the second item would accept debt as the price of duty. The third denies that learning excuses one from examining.

reading: The verse names as sweet the counsel on a task given by those who know all its surroundings, as foremost sweet not living under a king who has no care, and as finest of all the loyalty that does not plot harm against those who trusted one.
nuance: பற்றமையா வேந்தன் may be a king who has no regard for his people or for his servants; either way the servant is free, even advised, to leave. Line 3 (தெற்றென இன்றித் தெளிந்தாரை) is compressed: 'those who trusted without asking for certainty' is a reading.

reading: The verse names as very sweet the zeal of conducting oneself in ways the town does not resent, as foremost sweet the effort that never sits idle by itself, and as sweet checking the army of great kings who do not give way in the crowded battle.
nuance: The list moves from the town to the self to the battlefield, so the same exertion is praised as civic conduct, as industry and as a warrior's stand.

reading: The verse names as foremost sweet not going about at night, as sweet speaking without a slip whenever one speaks, and as sweet leaving, not taking up, the friendship of worthless people even when they embrace one.
nuance: வழங்காமை could also mean not giving at night, but with எல்லிப் பொழுது 'not moving about after dark' is the likelier sense. The third item names the hard case: the worthless friend who is affectionate.

reading: For kings with victorious spears the verse names as sweet learning the facts by spying through a spy, doing justice after examining everything fully, and knowing how to share out, with attachment, to all living beings.
nuance: This is the one verse of the chapter that names its audience (வேந்தர்க்கு). Line 3 is obscure: பற்றினலாய் and பாத்தூற்று are not clear, and 'sharing out to all beings' rests on பாத்து ('dividing'); line 4 (வெற்வேறில்) is corrupt.

reading: The verse names as foremost sweet not speaking out of twisted envy, as sweet living upright after crushing and driving out anger, and as sweet letting go, without snatching, of whatever one sees and desires.
nuance: The first item faults envy voiced (உரையாமை), not envy felt; the list runs from tongue to temper to hand.

reading: The verse names as sweet knowing youth to be old age, hearing that one's kin are free of fear, and knowing as poison women with broad, soft, bamboo-like shoulders and the grace of tender shoots.
nuance: The first and third items are renunciant insights that see through youth and through desire; the second, about kin, belongs to the householder and sits oddly between them. The third speaks of women only as objects of a man's desire.
domain_note: a man who would master desire

norm.note: a renunciant view of the period that names women's bodies as poison to the man who desires them

reading: The verse names as sweet the excellence of weapons for one who has few men and as foremost sweet the warlike daring of one who has friends, and reports that the feast for guests of one whose kin stand by him is held sweet beyond all measure.
nuance: Each item is conditional on what one has: few men, then weapons; friends, then enmity can be taken on; kin, then the feast. The last item is reported with என்ப ('they say') and given the strongest praise, so the household's hospitality is ranked above the fighter's strengths.

reading: The verse names as foremost sweet that one who eats by going for alms does not clamour, as sweet the dignity of not grieving while living in a borrowed lodging, and as sweet having no want that, from great greed, abandons dharma.
nuance: துச்சில் is the Kural's word (340) for the body as the soul's borrowed lodging; the second item can be read literally, of a poor man in borrowed rooms, or with that image. The third item says poverty (ஒற்கம்) is not itself the fault; the fault is the want that greed turns into abandoning dharma.

reading: The verse names as sweet living on in one's own town even at a tenfold cost, as very sweet the excellence of not pounding and eating the seed-grain, and as sweetest of all the firm core of learning, faultlessly and over many days, what has worth.
nuance: பத்துக் கொடுத்தும் is unclear: 'even paying tenfold' or 'even giving up a tenth'. The first two items are about holding on in hard times, to one's place and to next year's seed, and the book's last item adds learning as the third thing one does not consume.

title: இன்னா நாற்பது 0-20
theme: The invocation and the first twenty verses each count four painful things, setting failures of worship, kingship, friendship, learning and the household beside plain images of things without their ground (a scentless flower, an unfenced cane field, a weapon in weak hands), so that a fault of conduct is read as one more thing cut off from what makes it work.
source_issues: Verse 0 line 2: Project Madurai's variants பொற்பன வெள்ளியை and மன்றப்பின்னாது; tamilvu has no invocation with this number.
Verse 1 line 3: the variant ஊணின்னாது would reverse the third item ('eating in a brahmin's house is not painful'); the site lacks this verse.
Verse 2 line 3: புநடைவை is likely a corruption of புடைவை; with the variant உடையின்னாது the item would reverse, and its sense cannot be fixed.
Verse 4 line 2: கருவிகண் may be கருவிகள் misprinted.
Verse 5 line 2: உறைசேர் against tamilvu உறை சோர் (leaking); the variant புரைசேர் also noted.
Verse 10 line 1: பொருளணர்வார் is likely a misprint for பொருளுணர்வார்.
Verse 11 line 1: variant மனைவி தொழி லின்னா; line 2 டியர்த்த against tamilvu யாத்த.
Verse 12 line 4: முலையிள்ளாள் is likely a misprint for முலையில்லாள்.
Verse 15 line 3: variant விழைவின்னா; line 4 நாணப் against tamilvu நாணுப்.
Verse 18 line 1: மடிந்திருந்தல் may be a misprint for மடிந்திருத்தல்; line 4 variant அகம்வறியாளர்.
Verse 14 line 1: variant வணரொளி.

reading: The invocation counts four things as painful, all failures of worship: not worshipping the feet of the three-eyed Lord, living without thinking of the white god of the golden palmyra, forgetting the one who bears the discus, and not worshipping the feet of the one who bears the spear.
nuance: The four gods are named by emblems only: three eyes (Siva), the golden palmyra banner and white colour (most likely Balarama), the discus (Vishnu) and the சத்தி spear (most likely Murugan). The dative தார்க்கு puts the pain on the one who neglects worship, so the book opens by counting a lack in the person, as its verses go on to do.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: the beauty of a house that has no tie of kin, the good looks of a son who has no father, eating while staying in the house of brahmins, and a mantra that does not take effect.
nuance: The first two items are beauty without the bond that should frame it (a house without kin, a son without a father). The third is unclear: the verse does not say whose pain it is, the outsider eating in a brahmin house or the brahmins whose house is used, and Project Madurai's variant ஊணின்னாது would make it 'not painful'. மந்திரம் may be a ritual formula or a counsel; வாயா விடின் says only that it does not come off.

norm.note: a rule of the period about eating in a brahmin's house and about the efficacy of mantra, stated without saying who is barred

reading: The verse counts four painful things: a fowl and a dog entering a brahmin's house, the unruliness of a wedded wife, wearing a garment that lacks its proper பாத்து, and the land of a king who does not protect it.
nuance: The first item is a pollution and birth rule: பார்ப்பார் names brahmins as a birth group, and the fowl and the dog are counted as defiling their house. The second makes a wife's lack of restraint (அடங்காமை) a pain for the house, a gender norm of the period. The third line is corrupt (புநடைவை, likely for புடைவை), and பாத்து may mean a border or one's own share, so the item cannot be fixed.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period (animals defiling a brahmin household) beside a norm of the wife's restraint

reading: The verse counts four painful things: living under fierce kings of bent sceptre, swimming long water without a float, association with men of harsh speech, and living in wavering confusion.
nuance: The second item is the image for the rest: under a cruel king, among harsh speakers or in an unsettled mind, one is in deep water with nothing to hold. The last item names its sufferer, உயிர்க்கு, so wavering is a pain to life itself.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: for ploughmen without oxen, the wet of the soil passing unused; turning one's back in battle with weapons lost; provoking those who have fortune; and doing harm to the very strong.
nuance: The first item is a matter of timing: the soil's moisture (ஈரம்) goes by while the ox-less farmer cannot plough. The last two are prudential: the pain is the one the provoker brings on himself. கருவிகண் in line 2 may be கருவிகள் misprinted, or 'where weapons are exchanged'.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: guarding sugarcane that has no fence, living under an old roof that lets the rain drip through, a kingship that rules without justice, and a deed done without secrecy.
nuance: The two images of unprotected keeping (cane without a fence, a house without a sound roof) come before the two cases they illuminate: rule without முறை and action without மறை. The pairing of முறை and மறை in lines 3 and 4 is the verse's own chime.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: harsh words even from those of virtuous mind, men of martial mind slackening in battle, the giving of those who are themselves in distress, and the words of the crooked.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are set against each other, அறமனத்தார் and மறமனத்தார்: each failure is the opposite of the person's own nature. The third item counts a gift as a pain when the giver is in trouble, which the verse leaves without reason: the pain may be the giver's, or the gift's poor fruit.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: a weapon held by one without strength, the beauty of a flower without scent, the boldness of one without clear judgement, and the speech of one who does not know how to reply.
nuance: Each item is a thing cut off from what makes it work: the weapon from strength, the flower from scent, daring from conviction (தேற்றம்), speech from the power to answer (மாற்றம்).

reading: The verse counts four painful things: the lack of good nature in those whose hearts seem as clear as day, the lack of real affection in friends made in laughter, the flight of those who rose up in hostility, and the friendship of the ungracious-minded.
nuance: Three of the four items are about friendship and its counterfeits. பகல் போலும் நெஞ்சத்தார் can mean hearts open as daylight or hearts even as the balance (பகல், the middle); either way the pain is a fair appearance with no character behind it. நார் is the fibre of affection that binds.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: an old town without toddy to the drinkers, the absence of generous patrons to those who seek gifts (named first among pains), the beauty of the ungenerous, and the gait of a horse without harness.
nuance: The first two items name their sufferers in the dative (களிகட்கு, பரிசிலர்க்கு), and set the drinker's want of toddy beside the bard's want of a patron, perhaps with irony. முன் gives the bard's lack the first rank; the third item then turns to the ungenerous rich, whose looks are no comfort.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: reciting a song where there is no one who grasps its meaning, going alone down a narrow path dense with darkness, going to those who have no grace, and attempting liberality when one has no wealth.
nuance: பொருள் closes the first and last lines: a song without hearers who understand its meaning, generosity without the means. The verse thus sets the wasted gift of words beside the impossible gift of goods.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: the shoulders of a wife who is not of one mind with her husband, friendship bound with petty men who have no room in them, association with the intemperate, and coming where one's creditors can see one.
nuance: The first item places the pain in the embrace itself (தோள்): physical closeness without agreement (உடம்பாடு). The last is shame rather than danger: the debtor's pain is being seen.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: crossing the wasteland at the risk of one's head, the pride of one who lives by carrying a net, living with one's mind set on புலை, which is painful to life, and the desire for womanhood of one who has no breasts.
nuance: The second item denies pride to a man who eats by carrying the net, an occupation tied to birth groups in this period, so it ranks people by work. புலை in line 3 may be flesh (as in புலால்) or baseness, or the outcaste; the verse does not fix it. The fourth item is a gender norm whose subject is unclear: a breastless woman longing to be counted a woman, or a man's desire for her; இள்ளாள் is likely a misprint for இல்லாள்.

norm.note: a period ranking that denies pride to a netting occupation, and a norm that ties womanhood to the body

reading: The verse counts four painful things: a king riding an elephant without a bell, boldness spoken by those without courage, submission to kings who will not bend, and a house where people like a disease live.
nuance: The bell on the war elephant announces the king; without it his progress is unheralded or unsafe. The third item is the courtier's pain: bowing to kings who give no regard in return.
domain_note: the king and those who serve him

reading: The verse counts four painful things: being deceived by women with curling five-plaited hair, the fallen fruit of a mango hung with clusters, parting from one who is like a joined doll, and the moment when those who should understand do not understand.
nuance: Three of the items come from love: the deceit of women (a gendered claim of the period), the parting from a beloved, and the failure of understanding between those who should know each other's minds. The fallen fruit sits among them as an image of sweetness spoiled by its fall.

norm.note: a period claim that women deceive, stated as one of the pains of love

reading: The verse counts four painful things: riding a poor horse without a bell, the purpose of an undertaking explained by the unlearned, the fine wishes of those who have nothing, and being shamed among many people.
nuance: The second item is counsel on an undertaking (கருமப் பொருள்) when the counsellor is unlearned; Iniyavai Narpathu 32 uses the same phrase for counsel given by those who know. புல்லார் புரவி may be a horse of the base or a grass-fed nag.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: storing great wealth without enjoying it, union with enemies who should not be approached, the good looks of a man without eyes, and accounts kept by one who does not know numbers.
nuance: The last two items are paired: a handsome man without eyes and an innumerate man doing accounts are both the same lack of sight, one bodily and one learned.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: a fool entering among the worthy who are full and self-subdued, going about when it has grown dark and dim (very painful), the penance of those who do not live subdued by endurance, and abandoning the mother who bore one without caring for her.
nuance: ஆன்றவித்த and நோன்றவிந்து echo each other: the worthy are those who have subdued themselves, and a penance without that subduing is a pain. The last item is the one duty in the verse; the rest are misplacements.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: the mind of a strong man lying idle, facing the chest of one who has valiant warriors, going through the hard forest of the wasteland, and association with the poor in mind.
nuance: The first item imagines strength (உரன்) present and the mind (உள்ளம்) asleep, a strong man whose power goes unused. மனவறியாளர் are those empty of mind; the variant அகம்வறியாளர் says the same.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: lack of learning in one born to a good family, good seed sown in the ground failing to sprout, women of good quality lacking modesty, and union where there is no family standing.
nuance: குலம் frames the verse: the first and last items are about it. The good seed that does not sprout is the image of the first item, birth without learning. கலத்தல் குலமில் வழி makes union (perhaps marriage, perhaps any mixing) outside family rank a pain, a birth norm. நலத்தகையார் are most likely women, and their lack of நாண் is a gender norm.

norm.note: a period norm against union outside family rank, beside a norm of women's modesty

reading: The verse counts four painful things: the koel's voice calling in the rainy season, harsh words spoken by those without valour, the failure of the rain's plenty to a town, and ploughing with a sluggish ox.
nuance: மாரி opens lines 1 and 3: the koel's song out of season and the rain that fails in season. The verse moves from the unseasonable to the town's want and ends in the field, with the ox.

title: இன்னா நாற்பது 21-40
theme: The last twenty verses of Innaa Narpathu each count four painful things, mixing bodily dangers, failures of skill and learning, faults of speech and friendship, and the pains of poverty and patronage, so that a moral fault is weighed on the same scale as a snake in the house or a stone in the areca nut.
source_issues: 21 line 4: ஒத்திலா is read as ஓத்து இலா (without Vedic recitation); the short vowel is likely a misprint.
24 line 4: tamilvu has யாம் என்பவரோடு for யாமென் பவரொடு; the sense is the same.
27 line 2: the printed dative கிழமை யுடையார்க் sits awkwardly with களைந்திடுதல்; the variant கிழமை யுடையாரை is followed.
34 line 1: ஒழுக்க மிலாளார்க் has an unexpected long vowel (variant ஒழுக்கமிலாளர் குறைவுரைத்தல்); line 4 கழிப்புவாய் மண்டிலங் கொட்பு is obscure and its sense cannot be fixed.
35 line 2: the division மரத் தோசை (மரத்து ஓசை) and the variant குழலினிய leave the line's sense unclear.
37 line 3: அறியாண் is likely a misprint for அறியான்.
39 line 3: printed கொடுத்த விடாமை against tamilvu கொடுத்து விடாமை; the reading of the third item turns on it.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: giving to people who are not content with the way they were given to, going to eat with those who do not share their food, sickness that comes in old age, and the word of a brahmin who lacks Vedic recitation.
nuance: The first two items look at the shared meal from both ends, the gift wasted on the ungrateful and the guest at a house that does not share. The fourth is a birth-rank norm: the brahmin is measured by his ஓத்து (printed ஒத்து), and his speech without it is counted a pain, not an authority.

norm.note: a birth-rank norm of the period: a brahmin's word is valued by his Vedic recitation and without it is counted a pain

reading: The verse counts four painful things: seeing kings who have no elephants, eating flesh to swell one's own flesh (ranked painful before all), the taste of honey turned sour, and a town cut off by a forest stream.
nuance: Each line carries its own intensifier, and முன் 'first, before all' puts the flesh-eater at the head. The other three are things that have lost what makes them work: a king without his elephant force, sweetness gone sour, a town without a road; flesh-eating is filed among them as a corruption of the body's food.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: keeping the gate of an old town that has no wall, washing clothes while sitting at the bathing ford, the talk of people who are like a beaten drum, and penance taken up by one without self-restraint.
nuance: All four fail for want of the thing that should hold them in: a wall behind the gate, clean water at the ford, a closed mouth, restraint under the penance. அறைபறை அன்னவர் is the Kural's own image for the base who broadcast what they hear (1076).

reading: The verse counts four painful things: living in an old town without protection, sitting beside people of evil ways, desire grown ripe, which is painful to life itself, and friendship with those who say 'we'.
nuance: யாம் என்பவர் 'those who say we' is read here as the self-asserting, who make every bond about themselves; the line could also mean those who merely claim to be one's own. The third item is not desire as such but desire that has ripened (முதிரின்), with harm to உயிர் named.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: seeing the troubles of friends, seeing the pride of enemies, dwelling in an old town without order, and gambling with dice one has made one's own.
nuance: The first two lines are a pair, the friend brought low and the enemy raised high, both pains of watching. நட்ட கவறு is unclear: from நள் it is dice one has grown attached to, matching நட்டார் 'friends' in line 1; from நடு it would be set or planted dice. The reading of the fourth item depends on which.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: letting go of a bond tied with the great, saying 'we will do even hard things', telling one's own suffering to those who do not care, and doing evil to the great.
nuance: The great open and close the list: first the bond with them let go, last harm done to them, with two faults of speech (the boast, the complaint to the uncaring) between.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: destroying the standing of the eminent, casting off those with a close claim on one, beauty in those without means, and falling into old age within youth.
nuance: The second line is read with the variant கிழமை யுடையாரை, 'casting off those who have a claim'; as printed (யுடையார்க்கு) the verb is harder to place. இளமையுள் மூப்புப் புகல் may be ageing early or living as the old do while still young.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: an unlearned man riding a prancing horse, the worth of words spoken by an incapable man, the grace of speech in the mouths of the poor, and an unlearned man holding an assembly.
nuance: The unlearned man frames the verse, on a horse at the start and before an assembly at the end, two kinds of display he cannot carry. Between them speech loses its weight twice, once for want of skill and once for want of wealth.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: making a great cobra dance without knowing its signs, jumping into water to play without knowing where the stakes stand, begetting children without sense, and a secret heard by one who cannot keep it.
nuance: Every item is handling something dangerous without the knowledge it needs; the line on children puts them in that series, so a child without sense is counted with a mishandled snake and a leaked secret.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: leaping high from the long branch of a tall tree, going against an elephant in fierce rage, a house where a snake lives hidden, and a path where a fierce tiger lives.
nuance: This is the one verse of the chapter with no moral item: four plain bodily dangers. It shows the scale the other verses measure faults against.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: singing to a lute not set to its mode, men who cannot reckon telling the days for conduct, the sound of a drum without its clay, and the enmity of those without coolness of temper.
nuance: Three items are instruments out of true (an untuned lute, a reckoning without number, a drum without its paste) and the fourth is a person out of true; Kural 573 makes the same move from an unfitted melody to an eye without kindness. The second line is read as an unlettered man fixing auspicious days; the sense is not sure.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: going about without guarding oneself, the backbiting of those who will not speak to one's face, association with those who lack goodness, and the fall of those of ancient standing.
nuance: முன்னை உரையார் names the backbiter by what he fails to do, speak in front, so the fault is set against open speech rather than against silence.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: the matter of business a drunkard speaks of, walking in a thorny forest, killing a beast caught in a flood, and association with those of deceitful mind.
nuance: The third item faults killing an animal at the moment it is helpless in the flood; the pain lies in the unequal kill, not in hunting as such.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: speaking of kinship to those without good conduct, even an excellent book to those who do not want it, friendship with people of despised occupation, and a whirling circuit whose sense is obscure.
nuance: இழித்த தொழிலவர் ranks people by occupation, and in this period occupation and birth-group largely coincide; the verse does not name the trade, so the line may rank by birth or by base work. The first line has a variant (குறைவுரைத்தல், telling one's wants), and the fourth line (கழிப்புவாய் மண்டிலங் கொட்பு) cannot be fixed: it may be circling at a place of exorcism or at the mouth of a pit.

norm.note: a rank norm of the period: friendship with people of a despised occupation is counted a pain

reading: The verse counts four painful things: the cloud ceasing its rain for those who live here, a wooden sound sweeter than the flute, illness that befalls small children, and a handsome man who is a fool.
nuance: The second line is obscure: as printed it is the sound of wood that should be sweeter than the flute, perhaps a wooden instrument gone harsh; the variant குழலினிய does not settle it. The fourth line counts beauty as a pain when sense is missing, as 27 does when wealth is missing.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: a man without wealth longing to be liberal, want of money in a city of tall mansions, eating by watching for the houses one may go to, and the friendship of those who desert one at the time of ruin.
nuance: The four make a sequence of a falling householder: the wish to give without means, poverty set against a rich city, living off others' doors, and last the friends who leave.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: a fragrant flower that gives little scent, a man who does not know the ford going down into the water, an ignorant man being questioned, and holding rancour against the small.
nuance: Three items expose a lack (scent, knowledge of the ford, an answer); the fourth turns from lack to cruelty, rancour aimed at those weaker than oneself.

reading: The verse counts four painful things: the folly of going after another man's wife, kings without valour entering battle, riding a fierce horse bareback, and work done by one without skill.
nuance: The list makes desire for another's wife one of four ventures undertaken without the strength or skill they need, and it uses the Kural's own word for it, பேதைமை (141).

reading: The verse counts four painful things: liberality in one who has nothing to give, a stone in the areca nut one has bitten, a poet not being sent off by the one who gave to him, and a poet not singing where he has been received.
nuance: The last two lines look at patronage from both sides: the patron who holds the poet back (கொடுத்த விடாமை, tamilvu கொடுத்து விடாமை) and the poet who does not sing when he is taken in. The reading of the third item turns on that printed form.
domain_note: the last two items concern patron and poet

reading: The verse counts four painful things: fierce daring in a man of restraint, self-conceit in one without standing, seizing what was left in trust, and the speech of those who will not be checked when checked.
nuance: அடக்கம் opens and closes the list: in item 1 the restrained man's martial boldness (மீளிமை) is a pain, perhaps because it is out of his nature or because it is terrible when roused; in item 4 the unrestrainable talker. துடக்கம் in item 2 is read as standing or footing; it may also mean a tie.

title: சிறந்த பத்து 1-10
theme: The first ten ranks one good above another in each line, and repeatedly puts what is kept or practised (conduct, retention, truthfulness, health, shame, chastity, reverence, not dwindling) above what is possessed or displayed (study, brilliance, liberality, youth, beauty, lineage, a large beginning).
source_issues: show flags every saying of this ten (1-10) as site_diff: the online text's verses at these numbers are different sayings, so the edition's numbering or order of the tens differs from the site's.
Line 1 of saying 1 is the frame line repeated at the head of every ten (1, 11, 21 ... 91); it belongs to the ten, not to saying 1 alone.
Saying 10 is spaced முற்பெரு கலின்பின், which divides முற்பெருகலின் பின் at the wrong place.
Saying 9's கற்செய்கை is doubtful as written; the sense of the ranked thing cannot be fixed from the line.

reading: The opening saying ranks the possession of right conduct above recitation of learning.
nuance: Line 1 (ஆர்கலி யுலகத்து மக்கட் கெல்லாம், 'for all people of the sea-roaring world') is the frame repeated at the head of every ten, so the book's first ranking is addressed to everyone, not to one birth or order. ஓதல் is recitation, learning by repeating a text, which is what conduct is set against.

reading: Being held in awe by others' eyes is ranked above being loved.
nuance: கண்ணஞ்சப் படுதல் is literally 'being feared by the eye': most plainly, being looked on with respectful fear. It could also mean being shrunk from in sight, which would make the saying harsher. The saying names no ruler; the frame addresses everyone, so the awe here is a standing a person holds, not only a king's.

reading: Not forgetting what one has learnt is ranked above native brilliance.
nuance: மேதை is quickness of mind one has without effort; the saying puts a discipline (keeping what was learnt) above a gift.

reading: Truthfulness is ranked above liberality in giving.
nuance: வண்மை, open-handedness, is the virtue the bardic poems praise most in a patron; the saying sets a virtue of speech above it.

reading: Freedom from bodily disease is ranked above youth.
nuance: The saying separates two goods usually counted together: youth without health is not the better thing.

reading: A sense of shame is ranked above the possession of beauty or good qualities.
nuance: நலனுடைமை can be bodily beauty or excellence in general; either way an outward or possessed good is set below an inner restraint. The saying names no gender.

reading: The saying ranks chastity above the possession of a good lineage.
nuance: The saying does not name a woman, but கற்பு in this literature is chiefly the wife's virtue, so the ranking reports a norm for women. It also demotes birth: lineage is outranked by conduct, as conduct outranks study in saying 1.
domain_note: a wife, since கற்பு is the period's word for a woman's marital fidelity

norm.note: a norm of the period ranking a woman's chastity above her family's standing

reading: Serving and honouring the learned is ranked above learning itself.
nuance: வழிபடுதல் is the word for worship and service; the learned are given the reverence due to a deity or teacher.

reading: The saying ranks கற்செய்கை above subduing those who hate one; the ranked thing is most plausibly the practice of learning, against revenge on enemies.
nuance: கற்செய்கை is unclear as written: கல் may be learning (கல்-, to learn) or stone, giving 'deeds of firmness'. Either way something built in oneself is set above striking down a foe; the second reading of the word cannot be fixed from the line.

reading: Not dwindling afterwards is ranked above swelling greatly at the start.
nuance: The saying names no subject (wealth, friendship, fortune); it is a rule about any course, valuing what holds over what begins large.

title: அறிவுப் பத்து 11-20
theme: The ten of knowing (அறிவுப் பத்து) names, line by line, the outward sign by which a hidden quality is recognised: great or small birth by kindness or pride, kindness by giving, friendship by help, learning by discernment, theft by trickery, all lapses by a lapse of speech or understanding, and ability by deeds.
source_issues: 11 line 2: the comparison site's text lacks this line; the shared frame line 1 is printed with verse 11 here and the saying is line 2.
13 line 1: our text reads சேரா; tamilvu reads சோரா (e/o vowel sign), which gives the plainer sense 'unfailing'. The (பு) in நல்நட்(பு) is an editorial restoration.
15 line 1: tamilvu reads ஏற்றம் உடைமை எதிர்கோளின் for ஏற்ற முடைமை எதிர்கொளின் (word division and e/o vowel sign).

reading: Birth into a great house is said to be recognised by the kindness, the moistness of heart, a person shows.
nuance: Line 1 is the frame that heads every ten; the saying is line 2. ஈரம், literally moisture, is the softness of heart that the next line ties to giving, so the two lines make a chain. பேரில் (பேர் இல், a great house) ranks families, but the test it names is conduct, not descent.

norm.note: a claim of the period that a great house of birth shows itself in the conduct of those born to it

reading: Possessing kindness is said to be recognised by one's giving.
nuance: The inner quality is read only through the outward act: a feeling that does not give is not counted as kindness.

reading: A good friendship that does not fail is said to be recognised by the help given in it.
nuance: Our text reads சேரா, 'not joined'; tamilvu reads சோரா, 'not slackening', which gives the plain sense followed here. With சேரா the line would speak of the good friendship of those not joined by kin, which is possible but strained.

reading: Having learned is said to be recognised by one's power of seeing, the discernment learning gives.
nuance: காட்சி can be insight or judgment, and less likely outward bearing; on either reading learning is proved by what the learner perceives, not by what he recites.

reading: Eminence is said to be recognised by the way one goes forward to meet and receive others, or by how one meets an encounter.
nuance: எதிர்கொளின் (tamilvu எதிர்கோளின்) is either the courteous going out to receive a guest or superior, or the facing of an opponent or trial. The first fits the ten's run of social virtues; the line does not decide.

reading: Birth in a small house is said to be recognised by swagger and pride.
nuance: This is the mirror of line 11: the great house shows in kindness, the small house in பெருமிதம். சிற்றில் may mean a mean or poor family rather than a birth-group; either way the line reads a family's rank from a fault of conduct.

norm.note: a claim of the period that low birth shows in arrogant conduct

reading: Being a thief is said to be recognised from the doing of trickery.
nuance: குத்திரம் is fraud or a crooked trick, not theft itself: the line calls a man a thief from the deceit in his acts before any goods are taken.

reading: From a lapse in speech, every other lapse a person has is said to be recognised.
nuance: Here the order of the ten turns: what is known (எச்சோர்வும், every lapse) comes after its sign. The item is the thing known, read with the sign சொற்சோர்வு.

reading: From a lapse in understanding, the other lapses too are said to be recognised.
nuance: Built on the same frame as line 18, it moves the telling lapse from the tongue to the mind; the two lines together make speech and understanding the two places where all failing shows.

reading: Excellent manly ability is said to be recognised by what one actually does.
nuance: The ten closes on deeds: after birth, kindness, friendship and learning, the last test is performance.

title: பழியாப் பத்து 21-30
theme: The ten that people do not blame: inborn temper in the untrained, the lowly's lack of eminence, the difficulty of great things and the esteem of rare ones, an uncompletable shortfall, an unjust king (by one living in his land), good kin's omissions, a strange land's customs, the poor man's lack of generosity, and the conduct of the small.
source_issues: 21: the frame line that opens every ten (ஆர்கலி யுலகத்து மக்கட் கெல்லாம்) is printed as line 1 of verse 21; the saying itself is line 2.
21 line 2: the other witness (the site text) lacks this line, so the saying of 21 rests on one witness.

reading: People of sense do not fault those who have no binding discipline for the nature they were born with.
nuance: யாப்பு is literally a binding or tie; here most likely the binding of training or restraint, so the native temper of the untrained is excused as nature, not chosen fault. It could also mean those with no tie of kin or allegiance. Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten and is printed with this verse.

reading: People of sense do not fault those of no eminence for lacking the qualities of the eminent.
nuance: The line mirrors 21: a lack (மீப்பு இல்லோர்) and a quality (மீக்குணம்). மீக்குணம் can be the higher virtues one should not demand of the lowly, or an overbearing, upward-reaching temper one should not grudge them; a third reading takes மீப்பு இல்லோர் as those with no one above them, whose haughtiness is not blamed. The sense cannot be fixed from the line alone.

reading: People of sense do not complain that a great thing is hard to come by.
nuance: 23 and 24 are a chiasm: பெருமை and அருமை change places, so greatness and rarity are made to entail each other.

reading: People of sense do not grudge the high esteem in which a rare thing is held.
nuance: Read with 23: the price of a rare thing and the difficulty of a great one are both accepted as following from what the thing is.

reading: People of sense do not blame a deed that falls short because it could not be carried through in full.
nuance: குறைவினை can be a work left short or a small task; நிறையச் செய்யா says only that it was not done fully, not why. The line excuses the shortfall, not idleness, on the most natural reading.

reading: Those who live in the country of a king who keeps no justice do not openly censure him.
nuance: இருந்து is a participle attached to the predicate, so the most natural reading is prudence: one who lives there does not speak against the king. Another reading is that people are not blamed for staying on in such a land. Either way the line counsels the subject, not the king.
domain_note: a subject living under an unjust king

reading: People of sense do not blame good kinsfolk for failing to do what they ought to have done.
nuance: The excuse is for good kin (நற்கேளிர்) and for omission (செய்யாமை), not for harm done; the adjective limits the forbearance.

reading: People of sense do not find fault with the customary conduct of a country they do not know.
nuance: ஆசாரம் is the same word the Acharakkovai uses for its whole code of conduct; here it is tied to a தேசம் and so allowed to differ from place to place. அறியா may mean a land one does not know or whose ways one does not understand.

reading: People of sense do not blame a poor man for not being open-handed.
nuance: The line sets the limit of others' judgment, not the poor man's own duty; it says nothing on whether he should still try to give.

reading: Even the most excellent do not blame the conduct of small people.
nuance: The உம் in சிறந்தோரும் marks the eminent as the ones most entitled to blame, and so the ones whose restraint matters. சிறியோர் may be the young or the mean in mind.

title: துவ்வாப் பத்து 31-40
theme: The ten of துவ்வாப் பத்து set ten things that look like goods (wealth, daring, a life, a gift, an undertaking, help, a bond, a companion, old age, pleasure) each against a plain lack or a vice and find them no better, so that each good is emptied by the fault that comes with it: blame, excess, shamelessness, disregard, failure to act, falsity, ingratitude, folly, disgrace and not sharing.
source_issues: 31: the comparison site's text lacks line 2 (பழியோர் செல்வம் வறுமையில் துவ்வாது), the saying itself; our text has it after the frame line.
31: வறுமையில் has the -இல் ending where the other nine lines of the ten have -இன் before துவ்வாது; possibly a variant or misprint for வறுமையின்.
32, 36: the printed spacing splits words across sandhi (கழிதறு கண்மை for கழி தறுகண்மை, பொய்வே ளாண்மை for பொய் வேளாண்மை).
39: கதத்தின் is the comparison word; its sense in this line is doubtful.

reading: The wealth of those who carry blame is reckoned no better than poverty.
nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 31 is line 2 alone. துவ்வாது is read through the ten as 'does not rise above'; the verb's plain sense is to eat or enjoy, so the wealth that is 'no better than poverty' is also wealth that cannot really be enjoyed. Here the comparison word is வறுமையில், with -இல், where the other nine have -இன்.

reading: Reckless daring that goes beyond measure is reckoned no better than the state of a பேடி.
nuance: The printed கழிதறு கண்மை is கழி + தறுகண்மை split by the line's spacing: not daring itself but daring in excess. பேடி is a gender word for one neither man nor woman, used in the period as the type of the man without courage; the saying turns that type against the over-bold, so the two extremes meet.

reading: A life without shame is reckoned no better than going hungry.
nuance: The measure is bodily want: whatever such a life has to eat, it is counted as a hungry one, which is the force of துவ்வாது (it does not eat or enjoy).

reading: Giving done without care for the receiver is reckoned no better than refusing.
nuance: பேணில் is read as பேணு + இல், giving without cherishing or honouring the one who receives; the manner of the gift cancels the gift.

reading: Taking a task upon oneself and not doing it is reckoned no better than being a dullard.
nuance: செய்யாமை மேற்கோள் is read as an undertaking (மேற்கோள்) marked by not-doing; it could also be read as taking up the vow of not acting, which would make it idleness rather than a broken undertaking. சிதடி means a fool and also one who is blind.

reading: False benevolence, help that is only a show, is reckoned no better than baseness.
nuance: பொய்வே ளாண்மை is பொய் + வேளாண்மை split by the spacing. The measure புலைமை is formed from புலை, a birth-group term of the period that ranks people as low; here it names baseness as a quality, and the saying states no rule about persons, but the word's caste sense lies under the comparison.

reading: Turning one's regard away from those one has taken from is reckoned no better than cruelty.
nuance: கொண்டு may mean having received a benefit or having taken someone as one's own (a friend, a dependant); either way கண்மாறல், turning the eye away, names the breach of a bond already accepted, which is ingratitude rather than mere unkindness.

reading: The company and support of a fool is reckoned no better than being alone.
