Old age that has fallen into disgrace is reckoned no better than anger, on the most direct reading of கதம்.
nuance: கதம் most often means anger or heat of temper, and the comparison of a disgraced old age to anger is hard to see; the word may carry another sense here (a sting, a hurt), so the measure of this saying cannot be fixed.

reading: Enjoying pleasure by oneself alone is reckoned no better than solitude.
nuance: The same measure, தனிமை, closes 38: unshared joy is counted as the very loneliness the solitary man suffers, so pleasure kept to oneself is no pleasure.

title: அல்ல பத்து 41-50
theme: The அல்ல ten denies a thing its name when one inner condition is missing: a spouse who does not know the other's nature, a house without an excellent wife, kin without tenderness, a friend without consent, learning without submission, giving off aram's road, penance not rightly undertaken, and age that does not know rebirth.
source_issues: show flags saying 41 as site_diff: the online text lacks line 2 (நீரறிந்து ஒழுகாதான் தாரம் அல்லன்); line 1 is the frame line repeated at the head of each ten.
Saying 41 pairs தாரம், ordinarily 'wife', with masculine ஒழுகாதான் and அல்லன்; this may be a scribal or editorial masculinisation of a line about a wife.
Saying 42 (தார(ம்)மா ணாதது) and 48 (ஈயாத(து)) carry bracketed editorial supplies.
Saying 43 has ஈரலில், taken as ஈரம் இல் (ஈரல் alone is 'liver').
Sayings 49 and 50 are spaced across word boundaries (நேர்லா ததுநோன் பன்று; மறுபிறப் பறியா ததுமூப் பன்று); நேர்லாதது is an unusual form of நேர்தல்.

reading: One who does not conduct himself with knowledge of the other's nature is said not to be a spouse.
nuance: தாரம் ordinarily names a wife, yet the participle and predicate are masculine (ஒழுகாதான், அல்லன்). Either the line, as written, applies the word for a spouse to the husband who does not know his wife's nature, or the masculine endings stand for an older feminine reading (the woman who does not act knowing her husband's nature is no wife). The masculine reading is followed here because it is what the text has. நீர், 'nature', names whose nature only by context. Line 1 is the frame line of the ten.

norm.note: a rule of the period on what makes a spouse: conduct fitted to the partner's nature; if the line is read as feminine it is a rule for a wife's conduct

reading: A household life whose wife is not excellent is said not to be a household life at all.
nuance: The saying puts the whole worth of வாழ்க்கை, the life of the house, on the wife's மாண்பு; it says nothing of the husband here, though the line before it, read as written, set a condition on him.

norm.note: a norm of the period that measures the household by the wife's excellence

reading: Kin-friendship that has no moistness of heart is said not to be kin-friendship.
nuance: கிளைநட்பு joins the kin-group (கிளை) and friendship (நட்பு): the saying holds that relation by blood does not by itself make the bond; ஈரம், wetness, the tenderness of heart, does. ஈரலில் is taken as ஈரம் இல் with an unusual spelling; ஈரல் by itself would be the liver.

reading: A man whose hand never loosens to give is said not to be one whose name stands high like a mountain.
nuance: சோராக் கை is a hand that does not slacken or let go, taken here as the closed hand of the miser, since the ten names defective things. சொன்மலை is read as சொல் + மலை, 'a mountain of word', i.e. great renown; it could also mean one whose word stands firm like a mountain, which would make the saying about the miser's promises. Either way the closed hand forfeits a standing of the word.

reading: One whose heart does not agree with one is said not to be a friend.
nuance: நேர்தல் is to agree, consent, come straight; நேரா நெஞ்சம் is a heart that has not come into accord, whatever the outward dealings. The verb returns in 46 and, as நேர்லா, in 49, so three sayings in the ten turn on consent or undertaking.

reading: What is learnt without submitting or consenting to the learning is said not to be learning.
nuance: நேராமல் may mean without the heart's assent, without submitting to the teacher, or without the formal undertaking (or fee) by which a pupil is accepted. All three make learning depend on a relation entered into, not on the content gained; the line does not fix which.

reading: Strain endured without coming to live well by it is said not to count as strain.
nuance: வருத்தம் here is taken as the labour of effort, measured by whether one comes to live (வாழ்தல்) by it. A second reading is open: grief suffered by one who has not lived rightly is not true suffering, i.e. it is deserved. The line does not decide between them.

reading: What is not given along the way of aram is said not to be giving.
nuance: ஈனை is read as giving (ஈதல், ஈகை). The test is not the size of the gift but the road it travels, அறத்தாறு; the saying does not say what that road requires. The bracketed (து) is an editorial supply.

reading: What is not undertaken in the proper manner is said not to be a vow of penance.
nuance: நோன்பு is a vow or observance of restraint. The line is built as a twin of 48: அறத்தாற்றின் / திறத்தாற்றின், giving judged by aram's road, penance by its own proper road (திறம்). நேர்லா is read as a form of நேர்தல், to undertake, so the penance is defined by the manner in which it is entered on.

reading: Age that does not know of the birth to come is said not to be true old age.
nuance: மூப்பு is ordinarily just age; the saying makes it a state reached by knowing, not by years. மறுபிறப்பு assumes rebirth as a thing to be known. The ten ends where 39 in the previous ten also judged old age, there by its disgrace, here by its ignorance.

title: இல்லைப் பத்து 51-60
theme: The ten of இல்லைப் பத்து names, line by line, the thing beyond which there is no greater of its kind: children as gain, knowing ஒப்புரவு as a fitting acquisition, attainable and unattainable desire as the best and worst desire, withholding as cruelty, lack of understanding as death, desire as poverty, renown as legacy, begging as disgrace and giving to askers as distinction.
structure_note: Line 51 carries the frame (ஆர்கலி யுலகத்து மக்கட்கெல்லாம்) shared by the ten. The lines fall in pairs: 53 and 54 are the same desire with and without fulfilment, and 59 and 60 are asking and giving to the asker; 57 (desire as poverty) leads into 59 (begging as disgrace).
source_issues: 51: the comparison site's text lacks line 2 (மக்கட் பேற்றின் பெறும்பே(று) இல்லை), the saying itself; our text has it after the frame line. பெறும்பே(று) carries an editorial bracket for the elided final vowel.
58, 60: word division is irregular in print (எச்ச மில்லை for எச்சம் இல்லை; சிறப்பில்லை run together).
59: ஊஉங்கு is written with the lengthening vowel (அளபெடை) for ஊங்கு.

reading: Of all gains a person can have, none is said to exceed the gain of children.
nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 51 is line 2 alone. The line is unconditional: it says children, not good or wise children, which is where it parts from Kural 61 and Innaa Narpathu 29.

reading: No acquisition is said to be more fitting than knowing one's duty of ஒப்புரவு to the world.
nuance: The saying ranks the knowing (அறிதல்), not only the doing, and calls it a தகுவரவு, a fitting thing to come by: the duty is counted as a gain to the one who knows it, not a cost. வரவு as 'gain, what comes in' is our reading; it can also mean simply an arrival or attainment.

reading: No desire is said to be better than a desire that can fittingly be fulfilled.
nuance: வாய்ப்புடை can mean 'having the chance of coming to pass' or 'fitting, proper'; on the first the line praises realistic desire, on the second lawful desire. 53 and 54 are a matched pair, the same word with and without its negative.

reading: No desire is said to be worse than a desire that cannot come to pass.
nuance: The fault named is not the object of the desire but its futility: வாயா, 'that does not come about', makes wanting the unattainable the worst kind of wanting. If வாயா is read as 'unfitting', the line instead condemns improper desire.

reading: No cruelty is said to exceed hiding from others what one is able to give.
nuance: Refusal is classed as கொடுமை, cruelty, an active harm, not merely as a want of generosity; and the measure is இயைவது, what one can manage, so the poor man who cannot give is not touched by it.

reading: No death is said to be worse than being a person without understanding.
nuance: Bodily death is outranked by a living state: the senseless man is already dead in the sense that matters. உணர்வு may be taken narrowly as moral awareness or broadly as understanding.

reading: No poverty is said to be greater than desire.
nuance: Poverty is moved from what one has to what one wants: a man of means who still craves is, on this saying, the poorest of all.

reading: No legacy is said to be greater than renown.
nuance: எச்சம் is what a person leaves behind, and the word also means offspring; read against 51, the ten gives children the first place among gains in life and fame the first place among what outlasts it.

reading: No disgrace is said to go beyond that of begging.
No distinction a person can reach is said to exceed that of giving to those who ask.
nuance: The ten closes on the counterpart of 59: the same act of asking is the asker's worst disgrace and the giver's highest distinction.

title: பொய்ப் பத்து 61-70
theme: The ten of பொய்ப் பத்து calls ten things false, each a state or wish of a person who lacks what it needs: good life for the wise man aside, the eminent without anger, the drinker without lapse, gain without timing, safety without foresight, rising without bearing one's lot, greatness without bearing lowliness and its mirror, justice from the greedy, and penance from the impure.
structure_note: Line 1 of 61 frames the whole ten. 61 alone turns the pattern round (a gift that rules out a bad life); 67 and 68 are a mirrored pair; the ten moves from the private faults of anger and drink to the king's justice and the ascetic's penance at its close.
source_issues: 61 line 2: the core text has a repaired misprint (பேரறவி read பேரறிவி, as tamilvu), and the site's text lacks this line; the reading follows the repaired line.
62: பெருஞ்சீர் ஒன்றன் is doubtful as printed; the pattern of the ten wants a person-noun such as பெருஞ்சீரோன், and the reading assumes it.

reading: That a person of great understanding should fail to live well is called false.
nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 61 is line 2 alone. Every saying of this ten has the shape 'for such a person, such a thing is a lie': a state or wish is denied to a type of person, and the ten works by naming what the person lacks or has. Here the denial runs the other way from the rest: great understanding rules out a bad life, where the other nine name a lack that rules out a good.

reading: On the most direct reading of a doubtful line, that one of great eminence should be without anger is called false.
nuance: ஒன்றன் makes no clear sense as printed; the ten's pattern wants a person-noun (one of great eminence, perhaps பெருஞ்சீரோன் with தன்), and the reading assumes that. Read so, the line does not praise anger: it says the eminent are never in fact free of it, which may be a warning about the powerful rather than a licence. If ஒன்றன் is kept as 'of one thing', the sense cannot be fixed.

reading: That a drinker of toddy should be free of lapses is called false.
nuance: சோர்வு is a slip or a letting go, of attention, of speech or of a secret; the line does not say drink makes a man wicked, only that it makes him unreliable.

reading: That one who does not know the right time should get what he aims at into his hand is called false.
nuance: கையுறல் is 'coming into the hand'; the failure the line names is not of effort or strength but of timing alone.

reading: That one who does not know what is coming should be able to guard himself is called false.
nuance: மேல்வரவு is literally 'what comes upon one' or 'what comes later'; the line makes knowing it the condition of any self-protection, so guarding is first a matter of foresight, not of defences.

reading: That one who chafes against the work or trouble that falls to him should seek to rise is called false.
nuance: உறுவினை can be the task in hand or what one's past deeds bring upon one; காய்வோன் is one who resents or burns against it. On either reading the line ties rising to accepting what falls to one, but whether that is the labour of the work or the burden of fate the words do not settle.

reading: That one who will not bear lowliness should seek greatness is called false.
nuance: நோனாதோன் is one who does not endure: the line makes the patient bearing of small estate the way to great estate, not its opposite.

reading: That one who will not bear greatness should seek lowliness is called false, the exact mirror of 67.
nuance: The line swaps the two words of 67, and its sense is less plain. It may mean that one who cannot carry high station has no real choice of humility, since only the great can stoop by choice; or that one who cannot bear another's greatness wishes him low, and that wish is vain. The first keeps the ten's pattern of a wish denied by a lack; the second reads சிறுமை as the other's fall.

reading: That one with a craving for wealth should do justice is called false.
nuance: முறைசெயல் is the doing of justice, the king's or the judge's work; பொருள்நசை வேட்கை doubles the word for desire (நசை, வேட்கை), so the fault named is not having wealth but hunger for it.
domain_note: the king or anyone who sits in judgement

reading: That one who is not pure should perform penance is called false.
nuance: வாலியன் is the clean or pure one; the line does not say whether the purity is of mind or of body, but nothing in it points to a ritual rule, and in a ten about inner lacks it reads most naturally as purity of mind. The penance of the impure is not called useless but false, a show.

title: எளிய பத்து 71-80
theme: The ten of எளிய பத்து pairs a desire with what comes easily to it: the love of fame, kindness, hardship and bearing a load brings heaven, giving, pleasure and shared food, while the love of strife, tale-bearing, pleasure, food and women brings battle, betrayed secrets, pain, disease and blame. The last line breaks the pattern with a lack, not a desire: those without support easily meet killing.
source_issues: 71: புத்தேள்நா(டு) prints the final syllable in brackets, an editorial restoration of the sandhi form before எளிது.
72: உறழ்வெய் யோருக்கு has the dative -உக்கு where the other lines of the ten have -க்கு (வெய்யோர்க்கு); possibly a variant or a metrical filler.
77: உண்டிவெய் யோர்க்குப் உறுபிணி has ப் doubled before a vowel, irregular sandhi; probably a misprint for யோர்க்கு, carried over from lines 78-79.
80: சார்பு இலோர்க்கு breaks the ten's வெய்யோர்க்கு pattern and is printed with a space before இலோர்க்கு; the line may be a variant.
71-80: the printed spacing splits வெய்யோர் as வெய் யோர் throughout the ten.

reading: For those who long for fame, the world of the gods is easily reached.
nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 71 is line 2 alone. The ten's pattern is a dative of the one who desires (வெய்யோர்க்கு) and a thing that comes easily (எளிது) to that desire; here the desire is a good one and its yield is heaven, so the ten opens on a reward before it turns to the harms a desire brings on itself.

reading: For those who love to contend, a fierce battle comes easily.
nuance: உறழ் is to vie or oppose. எளிது can be read two ways here: the contentious man finds battle easy to face, or battle easily falls to his lot. On either reading the battle is the yield of the appetite for rivalry, not a choice made on its merits. The line is not addressed to the king or soldier as such: it names a temper anyone may have.

reading: For those who love kindness, giving what is asked for comes easily.
nuance: ஈரம் is moistness of heart, the same word the second ten uses for the kindness that giving reveals (12). நசைகொடை is read as a gift answering desire (நசை), the asker's wish; the line places the ease of giving in the giver's disposition, not in the size of his means.

reading: For those who love tale-bearing, spreading abroad what was secret comes easily.
nuance: குறளை is malicious talk carried behind a person's back. மறைவிரி is a compound, the opening out of what was hidden; the line makes the betrayal of confidences the easy consequence of a taste for gossip, so the one who enjoys slander is no safe keeper of secrets.

reading: For those who willingly take on hardship, pleasure comes easily.
nuance: Read with 76, which reverses its two words: the pair is a chiasmus in which each object of desire turns into its opposite. வெய்யோர் with துன்பம் is odd if taken as 'love suffering'; the sense is those who choose or embrace hardship, toil or austerity.

reading: For those who crave pleasure, pain comes easily.
nuance: The mirror of 75. The line blames the wanting (வெய்யோர்), not pleasure itself: pain is what the craving draws on, not something hidden in every pleasure.

reading: For those who love food, serious disease comes easily.
nuance: உண்டிவெய்யோர் is the lover of food, the glutton; the line does not say how much is too much, only that the appetite itself brings disease near. The printed யோர்க்குப் before a vowel is irregular (see source_issues).

reading: For men who lust after women, grievous blame comes easily.
nuance: பெண்டிர் is plural and unqualified: the line does not say 'another's wife', so the blame is laid on a roving appetite for women in general rather than on one forbidden act. The audience is male; the line makes no rule for women's conduct, so it carries no norm.
domain_note: men; women are named only as the object of the desire

reading: For those who are willing to bear a burden, eating after sharing one's food comes easily.
nuance: பாத்தூண் is food eaten after it has been divided and shared, the Kural's word for the householder's habit of feeding others. பாரம் is most plainly a load or charge; the reading taken is that one who willingly shoulders responsibility (for kin, guests, dependants) finds sharing food no hardship. The sense of பாரம் here is not certain, and the line could also be read as a load taken on in giving, so the verse is marked uncertain.

reading: For those who have no one to lean on, violent killing comes easily.
nuance: The closing line breaks the ten's pattern: not a desirer (வெய்யோர்) but one who lacks (இலோர்). சார்பு is support, refuge or protection. Two readings are open: those without protectors are easily killed, or those with no ties to restrain them kill easily. The first fits the dative 'to whom it is easy' as an outcome that befalls, like 76-78, and is taken here; the second cannot be ruled out.

title: நல்கூர்ந்த பத்து 81-90
theme: The ninth ten calls things poor (நல்கூர்ந்தன்று): goods and acts that lose their worth because the condition that would give them force is missing, such as a land without a just king, desire and adornment in the very old, sulking where one is not cherished, words where words do not carry, anger that inspires no awe, and visits where there is no friendship.
source_issues: 81: the comparison site's text lacks line 2, the saying itself; our text has it after the frame line.
81, 89, 90: parenthesised letters (அரச(ன்), உட்(கு), நட்(பு)) are editorial restorations in our text.
83: our text has உறவோனை; tamilvu has உறைவோனை ('one who dwells with you'). The sense is close either way.
87: our text has சொற்சொல்லாவழி; tamilvu has சொல் செல்லாவழி, which gives the better sense and is read here.
83-90: the printed spacing splits words across sandhi (நல் கூர்ந்தன்று, போற் றாவழி, முதிர்வுடை யோன்).

reading: The land of a king who rules without justice is said to be impoverished.
nuance: Line 1 is the frame shared by every ten. Here நல்கூர்தல் is literal as well as figurative: an unjust reign makes the country itself poor, not only the king's name.

reading: The desire of a woman who is very old is reckoned a poor, wretched thing.
nuance: மிகமூத்தோள் is feminine: the saying names a woman, where the next old-age line (86) uses the masculine முதிர்வுடையோன். The judgement is of fitness to age, a norm of the period about women's bodies, and the line gives no reason beyond the frame.

norm.note: a period judgement that an old woman's desire is unbecoming

reading: Joining with one who is close to you yet bears you enmity is reckoned a poor thing to do.
nuance: Our text has உறவோனை, one related to you; tamilvu has உறைவோனை, one who lives with you. Either way the person is near and hostile, so the sense holds: alliance with an enemy within gains nothing.

reading: The pleasure that comes to a man lying sick is reckoned poor.
nuance: கிடந்தோன், the one laid down by disease: the pleasure is real but cannot be enjoyed, so it counts for little.

reading: Sulking where one is not cherished is reckoned poor.
nuance: Read as தன் போற்றாவழி, where the other does not cherish one; the printed spacing (தன்போற் றாவழி) splits போற்றா. Sulking is a lover's play that works only when the other cares enough to appease it.

reading: Ornament on the body of one who is very old is reckoned poor.
nuance: முதிர்வுடையோன் is masculine, so this old-age line, unlike 82, is about a man; adornment cannot restore what age has taken.

reading: Speaking where one's word does not carry is reckoned poor.
nuance: Our text reads சொற்சொல்லாவழி, 'where a word is not spoken', which gives little sense beside சொலவு; tamilvu's சொல் செல்லாவழி, 'where a word does not go', is read here. On our text the line might instead say that talk is poor where nothing worth saying is said.

reading: Drawing near to one who is empty within is reckoned poor.
nuance: அகம் வறியோன் may be one empty of heart (without love or understanding) or one whose house is bare; the first fits a ten on worthless acts better, but the second, approaching a poor man to ask, cannot be excluded.

reading: Anger where it inspires no awe is reckoned poor.
nuance: உட்கு is the dread a person commands; anger in one who has none is empty show, measured by its effect rather than judged as a vice.

reading: Going to a place where there is no friendship is reckoned poor.
nuance: சேறல், going or visiting: the visitor where no friendship waits gets nothing and loses standing, so the ten closes on a social act as it opened on a political one.

title: தண்டாப் பத்து 91-100
theme: The last ten pairs each wish with the practice its seeker never leaves off: rising with lofty speech, growth with renown, learning with reverence, steadfastness with penance, a good life with deliberation, plenty with toil, safety with just rule and love with hinted speech, and in its centre it sets pleasure and pain each as the price of the other.
source_issues: 91: the comparison site's text lacks line 2 (ஓங்கல் வேண்டுவோன் உயர்மொழி தண்டான்), the saying itself; our text has it after the frame line.

reading: Someone who wants to rise high is said not to give up lofty speech.
nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 91 is line 2 alone. உயர்மொழி may be one's own elevated, worthy speech or the high words of the great that one heeds; the line does not say whose words they are. தண்டான் is read through the ten as 'does not leave off, does not slacken in'; each line pairs a goal with the practice its seeker never drops.

reading: Someone who wants to grow great is said not to leave off winning wide renown.
nuance: வீங்கல் is swelling or growing large, a bodily verb used of fortune; பல்புகழ், 'many-fold fame', suggests renown gathered from many deeds rather than one, so the line asks for a steady run of creditable acts.

reading: Someone who wants to learn is said not to slacken in reverent service.
nuance: வழிபாடு is worship and devoted service; the line does not name the teacher, but in a saying about learning the one served is most naturally the teacher or the learned. It makes reverence a means of learning, not a reward for it.

reading: Someone who wants to stand firm is said not to leave off doing penance.
nuance: நிற்றல், 'standing', is left without an object: it may be steadfastness in one's path, lasting in the world, or remaining in a higher state. தவம் is the renouncer's discipline, so the line is read as addressed to him, though the frame addresses everyone.

reading: Someone who wants a good life is said not to leave off careful deliberation.
nuance: வாழ்க்கை can be living in general or the life of the household; சூழ்ச்சி is the weighing of means that the Kural assigns to ministers, here required of anyone who wants to make a life.

reading: Someone who wants abundance is said not to shrink from toil.
nuance: மிகுதி is surplus, more than enough; வருத்தம் is pain of effort, the same word the Kural uses for the body's strain in labour.

reading: Someone who wants pleasure is said not to shun the pain that comes with it.
nuance: Read with the ten's predicate, the line makes pain the price a seeker of pleasure keeps paying; 98 reverses the pair, so the two lines together say each brings the other.

reading: Someone who wants pain, the line says in reverse of 97, does not hold back from pleasure.
nuance: Taken literally the saying is a paradox; on the reading taken here it names the unchecked pleasure-seeker by where he ends, since pleasure pursued without stop brings pain. A reading in which the one who seeks hardship (as in penance) still does not refuse all pleasure is possible, but the mirror of 97 favours the first.

reading: Someone who wants security is said not to leave off acting by just order.
nuance: ஏமம் is safety or protection; முறை is the word for justice done by a ruler, so the seeker of security is most plausibly the king, though the line does not name him and a householder's fair dealing is a possible wider reading.
domain_note: the ruler, whose safety the line ties to just rule

reading: Someone who wants love is said not to give up speaking by hints.
nuance: குறிப்புச்சொல் is words that suggest rather than state; the line makes indirection the lover's constant practice, the last of the ten and the only one in the akam field.

title: நான்மணிக்கடிகை 0-20
theme: Two invocations to Vishnu, by likeness and by deed, open twenty verses that each set four 'gems' under one predicate: where things are born, how their worth is tested, what adorns, binds, harms or lays waste, and what each thing ends in. Natural images (gems, beasts, crops, fire) sit in the same row as conduct, so that a virtue is shown to have a source, a test and an end like a thing.
source_issues: 0 and 0b: the book opens with two invocations, keyed 0 and 0b.
6 line 2: repaired from a misprint (பிறானக் read பிறனைக்), as tamilvu; the reading differs from the site.
6 line 4: the text has மன்னர்ச் செலவு; tamilvu has முன்னர்ச் செலவு. The reading takes the general sense and notes both.
7 line 3: பார்ககும் is a misprint for பார்க்கும், as on lines 1 and 2.
10 line 3 and 20 line 2: stray spaces split words (சான் றோரை, நட்டோ ரை).
14 line 1: repaired from a misprint (கிளைக்குழம் read கிளைக்குழாம்), as tamilvu; the reading differs from the site.
18 line 4: the line கேளிர் ஒரீஇ விடல் recurs as line 4 of verse 85.

reading: The invocation sets four likenesses between the world and Mayavan: the moon is like his bright face, the rayed sun like his discus, the lotus flower opening on its stalk in the old-watered field like his eye, and his colour like the fresh bloom of the kaya flower.
nuance: The first three likenesses run from the world to the god (the moon resembles his face), the fourth runs back (his colour resembles the flower), so the sky, the field and the bloom are all read as copies of him. The items here count the god's four features, since the comparison is made for them; மதிமன்னு may also be taken as 'in whom wisdom abides', which would leave the moon unnamed and the face without its likeness.

reading: The second invocation names four deeds of the son: he put the earth inside his belly, crossed the whole earth with his foot in three steps, lifted the hill that sheltered the cows from the cold rain, and destroyed the impregnability of Sho.
nuance: It calls the god only மகன், 'the son', and lets the deeds name him: swallowing the earth, the three strides, the lifted hill (Govardhana by tradition) and the fall of சோ (by tradition Bana's fortress). The verse has no count word; the four deeds are four relative clauses closing on the one noun.

reading: The verse gives four prohibitions: never despise people as lowly; whatever one would gain, never take anything such that the hand of those one should not take from is above one's own; however it burns within, never rage at those born in small houses; and never hastily say what should not be said.
nuance: The four gems here are four negative commands, each verb fronted (எள்ளற்க, கொள்ளற்க, சீறற்க, கூறற்க), so the form turns from naming things to naming restraints. The second and third turn on the giver's or the other's standing: the giver's hand placed above the receiver's, and the small house one is born in. சிற்றில் may mean a poor house as much as a low one; the verse restrains contempt for such people rather than ranking them.

reading: The asunam beast does not live once the drum is beaten, the strong do not live once their spirit is lessened, the bamboo in the dense forest dies once it puts out grain, and nobility does not live once a word unworthy of it is spoken.
nuance: Two of the deaths come from outside (the drum, a word) and one from the thing's own fruit (the bamboo dies of seeding), so the verse does not say whether nobility is killed by another's slander or by its own unworthy speech: சொற்பட allows both. The fourth item makes nobility a living thing that can die while its bearer lives.

reading: One knows a gem's worth by washing it, a horse's worth after harnessing and mounting it, gold's worth by burning it free of dross, and the use of one's kin by being ruined.
nuance: Each worth is known only by an ordeal applied to it, and the last ordeal falls on the tester, not the tested: one learns what kin are worth by suffering ruin oneself. The verb அறிப repeats four times, so the verse is a list of tests rather than of goods.

reading: Fragrant agil is born in the belly of the kalli, bright orpiment in the belly of the deer, costly pearls in the great sea, and no one knows in what family a good woman is born.
nuance: The first three are precious things born of mean or unlikely sources (a thorny spurge, an animal's belly, salt water), so the closing question is not idle: a good woman's worth cannot be read off her family. The verse does not rank families; it denies that family predicts the person.

reading: The bright gem is born of stone, high delight is born of the beloved's word, the way of virtue is born of gentle compassion, and everything is born of wealth.
nuance: The last line widens suddenly: after three particular births it makes wealth the source of all things, which sits beside, and does not cancel, the line that gives virtue its own source in அருள். உயர்மதம் is elation, not pride.

reading: Faultless conduct is like fortune, living by the right path is like great virtue, taking someone up and then turning one's face from him is like killing him, and going before those who do not esteem one is like degradation.
nuance: Two goods are made equal to greater goods, two wrongs to greater wrongs. புலை in the last item is the word for the degraded or outcaste condition, used here as a measure of shame, not as a rule about persons. The text reads மன்னர் ('kings'), so the last item may be going to kings who do not esteem one; tamilvu has முன்னர், 'before', which gives the general sense.

reading: There is no sleep for those who plan to steal, none for those who set their heart on a beloved woman, none for those who plan to make bright wealth, and none either for those who guard that wealth.
nuance: The thief and the lover lead to the two kinds of rich man, so earning and guarding wealth are ranked with stealing and longing as kinds of sleeplessness. The last item is set apart with உம் ('the guardians too'): having wealth gives no more rest than wanting it.

reading: Regret over what is past does not show before the learned, failure does not show before those who have set their love on a thing and pursued it, virtue does not show clearly to those who do what is wrong, and before those who rage everything fails to show and is ruined.
nuance: Each item is something that does not appear before a kind of person, but the sense turns: the first two are evils kept away by a virtue, the last two are goods hidden by a vice. உறாமுதல் is rare and may mean 'not attaining' or 'the source of loss'; the reading of the second item rests on that guess.

reading: They say paddy and sugarcane are the ornament of the land, the lotus the ornament of a pond, modesty the ornament of a woman's beauty, and one's own ornament is virtue for the world one goes to.
nuance: The last item turns the ornament inward and forward: the first three adorn something seen, the fourth adorns the self and is worn into the next world. The third item states a gendered norm: modesty is named the ornament of women's beauty, not of the worthy in general.

norm.note: a gender norm of the period: modesty is assigned to women as the ornament of their beauty

reading: They bind a bull elephant to a post to stop its rage, bind the great serpent with a mantra, bind the base with iron after goading them, and the worthy are bound by courtesy.
nuance: All four are 'binding' (பிணி), so courtesy is placed among restraints: the worthy are not free of control but are controlled by the gentlest means. The base sit between the beasts and the worthy and need iron.

reading: One must not be embittered by the harsh things others do, must hold as good the good others did, must always let go of one's own anger, and must destroy the deed that wrecks one's prosperity.
nuance: The first two items are a pair about others' acts (their harm not resented, their help remembered), the last two about one's own (one's anger, one's ruinous deed). The fourth item uses அடல், 'killing', for a deed, so the restraint asked is violent toward oneself.

reading: All snakes harm with their teeth, the killing elephant with its tusk, women harm with their face when sulking at those they love, and sages give harm by their penance.
nuance: Each harms with its own proper organ or power, and the sage's power is the penance itself: the verse sets the ascetic's curse beside the snake's bite as a natural weapon. Women's harm is the sulk at a lover, a small pain placed between two deadly ones.

reading: A drum is better than a lute out of tune, a woman firm in self-containment is better than men without worth, going hungry is better than eating with one's dignity undone, and entering fire is better than parting from those one is bound to.
nuance: Each item prefers a plain or painful thing to a fine thing gone wrong: the crude drum to the spoiled lute, hunger to dishonoured food, fire to separation. The second item sets a woman's நிறை above worthless men, so worth outranks sex here. The last makes parting worse than burning.

reading: Liberality grows in the bed of plenty, the throng of kin rises sweetly in the pit of sweet speech, concealment rises in the graceless pit of harsh speech, and begging rises quickly in the pit of poverty.
nuance: Every item is a plant in its bed or pit, so dispositions are crops of conditions: plenty grows giving, poverty grows begging. Two are good crops and two bad, and the begging grows 'quickly'. The division of lines 2 and 3 (where வன்சொல் belongs) is not certain.

reading: If one wants pain, rise to beg; if one wants to last in this world, plant fame; if one wants what goes along with oneself, do virtue; if one wants to win, give up anger.
nuance: The first item is irony in the form of the other three: begging is offered as the sure means to the wish for pain. The pattern 'if you want X, do Y' makes each virtue an instrument, and the last one inverts expectation: one wins by giving up anger, not by using it.

reading: Sailors split the deep of the sea, the man with a leaping horse can break the deep of an army, the man who holds himself swims the faultless deep of penance, and the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly.
nuance: குட்டம் ('depth') is repeated for sea, army, penance and assembly, so the assembly is made as dangerous as the sea or a battle line, and each is crossed only with its own means. தன்னுடையான் is the self-possessed: the means for penance is mastery of oneself.

reading: Friendships end in falsehood, youth's beauty truly ends in old age, wealth, weighed up, ends in excess, and life ends at its own allotted measure.
nuance: Each thing carries its own end (இறுவாய்): friendship is undone by its own falsehood, wealth by its own excess, so the first three ends are made from within. Only life's end is a fixed measure, தகுதி, not a fault.

reading: Excellent women are the prosperity of a house, being upright is the prosperity of a man's work, people saying 'this king of the angry red spear is good' is the prosperity of the land, and casting off kin is the prosperity of ruin.
nuance: The last item is an ironic turn on the predicate: after three things that build, casting off kin 'builds' ruin. The third makes the land's prosperity a matter of the king's name in people's mouths, not of his wealth. The same last line recurs at verse 85.

reading: If the husband shakes, the doe-like wife trembles; if the learned man shakes, the meaning shakes; if the land he holds is shaken, the king's sceptre shakes; and if the tune shakes, the song shakes too.
nuance: Each pair is a dependence: the wife on the husband, the sense on the learned man, the sceptre on the land, the song on the tune. The third reverses the usual order: the king's rule depends on the land, not the land on the king. அதிர் may be 'tremble' or 'roar'; on the second the first item would say that a husband's anger makes his wife tremble.

reading: Lack of a bright-browed wife is waste to a house, lack of friends is waste to the region one travels to, lack of elders is waste to the assembly one sits in, and a body without learned understanding is waste to oneself.
nuance: Three items are absences in a place (house, foreign region, assembly); the fourth puts the absence inside the person, so the unlearned body is itself a ruined house. பாழ் is waste ground, not merely loss.

title: நான்மணிக்கடிகை 21-40
theme: Twenty four-gem verses on what ruins and what sustains (disunity, bad company, enmity, the giving hand), the stages of learning, kinds of joy and refuge, and a birth-ranking set against verses that deny birth any hold on fortune.
source_issues: 28: five lines where the other verses have four.

reading: Disunity ruins strength, falsehood ruins a man's gold-like body, the vessel it is poured into spoils the taste of milk, and joining with those one should not join ruins a lineage.
nuance: Each gem has the same verb, சிதைக்கும், so the verse is a list of what ruins what; the milk spoiled by its vessel is the image that explains the last gem, bad company spoiling a family. ஒருவனை on line 1 can go with the disunity (it ruins a man's strength) or with the falsehood of line 2; the reading takes the second.

reading: Unfailing clarity is what brings renown, folly is what makes one overstep and act without regard for others, bewilderment is what makes one a blind man who sees nothing, and learning is what gives eyes cleared of darkness.
nuance: கற்பு here is learning, not chastity: it is set against மம்மர், the blindness of bewilderment, and gives eyes free of darkness. The four make two pairs, a gain against a fault and a blindness against a sight.

reading: The elephant bears its load even when it struggles, the child that is beaten still runs to its mother crying 'mother', friends even when angry do nothing that makes one tremble, and there is no time when the hostile live together with one.
nuance: Three bonds hold under strain (each with பினும், 'even if') and the fourth, the enemy, never binds at all. மலைப்பினும் வாரணம் தாங்கும் is taken as the elephant bearing its rider though it rages; it may mean a protector who stands firm though attacked.

reading: The good of laughter grows among friends, the good of a fine assembly shines through good will, the good of a swift chariot is won through its driver, and the good of a town is weighed by the one who dwells in it.
nuance: Each நலம் depends on someone other than the thing itself: friends, kindness, a driver, an inhabitant. உள்ளான் may be the town's leading man rather than any resident.

reading: The verse, in the second person, names four things: if one fears anything, to fear fearlessness; not to fall short of what befits one, to the full of one's means; not to swerve from what the heart knows even for a crore of wealth; and not to pry into a task left with friends.
nuance: Each of the first three plays a negative noun against its own verb (அஞ்சாமை அஞ்சுதி, எஞ்சாமை எஞ்சல், கோடாமை கோடி); the second is the hardest to construe and may mean not leaving undone what one can do.

reading: Rearing other living beings to torment them is a fault, buying flesh at a price and eating it is a fault, saying what should not be said is a fault, and killing is a fault too.
nuance: The buyer's eating and the killer's act are counted as two separate faults, and a fault of speech sits between them; அலைப்பான் may mean rearing beings for slaughter rather than for torment.

reading: All the people live looking to the sceptre, infants live looking to their mother's breast milk, the world lives looking to the rain from the sky, and Death rejoices looking to the world's dying.
nuance: Three dependencies on a giver are closed by a fourth that inverts them: Death too 'lives looking', but to the world's end, and is glad of it.

reading: As one learns, deep ignorance lessens; as it lessens, freed of meanness, one grasps the nature of this world; grasping it, one walks the path of truth; and that path sets fame in this world and enters the high world beyond.
nuance: The four gems are links of one chain, each clause's result the next clause's condition, so learning leads by stages to the other world. The verse runs to five lines where the rest have four.

reading: Water stays where there is a hollow, sin stays where many cast blame, desire stays where it crowds in destroying, and understanding stays where something befalls oneself.
nuance: Each thing is placed by where it 'stands' (நிற்பது, -உழி), so the last makes understanding something that shows itself in one's own trouble. அழித்துச் செறிவுழி is hard; it may mean where desire, having broken restraint, presses close.

reading: Nothing is mightier than fortune, nothing suits a man better than learning, of all things nothing is more painful than poverty, and nothing is firmer than the strong hand that never says 'there is none'.
nuance: Four superlatives: the pain of want (line 3) is answered by the giving hand (line 4). வன்பாட்டது, read as 'firmer', may instead mean harder in labour.

reading: Blazing fire appears with smoke as its seed, joy appears with laughter as its seed, enmity sprouts with a man's own former intent as its seed, and once sprouted it becomes the seed of suffering.
nuance: The seed image runs through all four, and the last turns the third forward: enmity is both a sprout of one's own intent and the seed of further pain. முன்னம் may also mean a prior deed.

reading: Women who do not look ahead are like a disease, loving people are like an ornament to the world, men of mean understanding are like weeds in a crop, and the hard-hearted are like stone.
nuance: The only item that names a sex judges women, and பின்நோக்கா ('not looking behind') is unclear: heedless of consequence, or not looking after the household. The other three are men or people at large.

norm.note: a judgment of the period on women's conduct, likening heedless women to disease

reading: There is no birth better than the brahmin's, whatever one does; no kin more excellent than the mother; no beauty equal to prosperity; and nothing to compare with youth.
nuance: அந்தணர் here ranks a birth-group above all others, a caste ranking stated as fact. என்செயினும் ('whatever one does') can close line 1, making the brahmin's birth best whatever he does, or open line 2, making the mother the best kin whatever she does; the caste claim is much stronger on the first reading.

norm.note: a birth-rank of the period: the brahmin's birth ranked above all others

reading: Iron is split by iron, those who have drunk water rinse the mouth with water, rare things are won, on examination, by rare means, and great things are reached through great men.
nuance: Two physical cases of like working on like (iron on iron, water on water) prove the two moral ones; the mouth-rinsing is cited as a familiar act, not laid down as a rule.

reading: The frenzy of valour shows before kings, the joy of virtue shows when one gives to those who have nothing, the joy of conceit falls upon the poor, and the joy of the base blares through the town.
nuance: Four kinds of களி (elation) are told apart by where they show. வியக்களி நல்கூர்ந்தார் மேற்றாம் may mean a poor man's empty pride or the boast of the rich made over the poor.

reading: Flower-like eyes brighten with collyrium, an upright flame in the dark night grows with ghee, the kuruku leaf sprouts when rain pours and thunder roars, and friends flourish the more when one gives.
nuance: The verb தளிர்க்கும் ('puts out shoots') makes all four things grow from what they are fed. Whether the friends flourish when one gives to them, or one flourishes when friends give, the line allows both; குருகிலை is an uncertain plant name.

reading: Laughter is sweet among friends, a store of wealth is sweet if one gives it out with one's own hand, a woman of good kind is sweet if she tends and serves, and music is sweet in the hearts of those who understand song.
nuance: Each sweet thing is sweet only under a condition (among friends, if given, if she serves, to the knowing), so the verse ranks the condition above the thing. The woman's sweetness is made to depend on her service.

norm.note: a period norm making a woman's worth depend on her tending and service

reading: For those who hide what they have, the end they come to is always downfall; for those who beg, the refuge is those who give; for a wide army, the support is valour; and for living beings, the refuge is others' not eating flesh.
nuance: செல்சார் ('the place one goes to') is a refuge in three items and an ironic destination in the first: the hoarder's only refuge is ruin. The last item gives the creatures' side of abstaining from flesh.

reading: Craftsmen make what they have seen, the learned do what they have heard to be so, those close to one do the sweet things one desires, and fortune does what the unresentful intend.
nuance: The first three are sources of action (sight, hearing, another's wish); the fourth gives fortune itself to the patient. புலனாள்வார் is read as the learned, and அமைந்தார் as intimates; both words allow other senses.

reading: Fortune does not abide by rank of birth, mighty Death does not take its food by doing what it is told, desire does not stay hidden however hard one hides it, and justice stands as the king is.
nuance: Three things no human order controls are set beside a fourth that depends wholly on one man, the king. திணைவகையான் may mean by class of birth or by kind of person.

title: நான்மணிக்கடிகை 41-60
theme: Twenty verses of four gems each, many defining a common word anew (stranger, mother, the sweet eater) or naming what thrives, withers, burns or dies before an unfit receiver, ranging from the king's army to household giving, karma and the constant order of the world.
source_issues: 43 line 1: the site's text lacks line 1 (flag site_diff); the line is kept here as the corpus gives it.
48 line 2: நந்துஞ் before கரும்பெல்லாந் has the wrong sandhi nasal; நந்துங் is expected.
53 lines 1-2: the semicolons are the editor's; the verse names five things where the work's form leads one to expect four.
57 line 3: the doubled பிறப்பார் and the division அறனின் புறுவர் leave the line hard to construe.
59: the verse has five lines where the other verses of the chapter have four.

reading: All lives, at birth, do not leave though told to go and, at death, do not stay though told to stay; wealth swells of itself when the good lady consents, and when ruin comes even what was in plain sight vanishes.
nuance: The first two gems are one sentence about உயிரெனைத்தும், split by birth and death; the third gives no subject for what grows, and நல்லாள் is most likely Fortune (Tiru), so the swelling is of wealth. The four together set coming and going, gain and loss, beyond anyone's command.

reading: The glory of fighters withers without war, every tree withers without roots that go down, the tall neytal withers without a sluice to bring water, and the glory of kings withers away without an army.
nuance: Two natural images sit between two martial ones, so the army is set down as the root and the water-channel of a king's glory rather than its ornament.

reading: Those called strangers are those without good nature, those called dear to everyone are the worthy, the excellent one called father is one's teacher, and the one called mother is the deed one did before.
nuance: Each gem redefines a kinship word: stranger and beloved by character, father as the teacher, and mother as one's own former deed, the source from which one's present life is born. The last turns the household's closest word into a word for karma.

reading: Fortune perishes the moment shame is lost, action is ruined of itself by the five once they have taken their course, the green crop's unfailing goodness perishes without water, and the friendship of friends perishes when the good they gain changes.
nuance: ஐவர் 'the five' is read here as the five senses running their own way; the line gives no noun, and பொறி on line 1 can mean the senses as well as fortune. The fourth gem treats friendship's end on lost advantage as a natural fact, like a crop without water, rather than as a vice.

reading: A kindness dies before those who do not know kindness, a guest who has come dies before those without welcome, a song of rare composition dies before those who do not know melody, and a lover's sulk dies in the heart of one who does not understand sulking.
nuance: All four are offerings that live only in a receiver able to take them: gratitude, hospitality, art and love fail not through the giver but through the one before whom they are set.

reading: Scent tells that a flower is there, spoken words tell, when weighed, the quality of a person's doing, the mind tells the evil packed within, and nothing tells the intention beforehand as the face does.
nuance: The four are signs and what they disclose; the last is a ranking, since nothing discloses earlier (முன்) than the face, and the face outruns even the mind of line 3.

reading: The people of the great earth have nothing without rain, there is no rain where there are no ascetics, no penance where there is no king, and no king where there are no householders.
nuance: The gems form a chain, each resting on the next, so the whole order of world, rain, penance and kingship rests at last on the householder.

reading: A cool woven garland flourishes by its flowers, the bees all flourish by pollen, people flourish by faultless deeds, and honey flourishes by its own buds.
nuance: கரும்பு is read as the bee, which suits தாது (pollen), not as sugarcane; நறா may be honey or toddy. Three things of the flower frame one human one, so a person's deeds are to him what blossom is to garland and honey.

reading: Anger is at all times hard for the eminent, living apart from one's companions is hard for those born into a family, sharing out food is hard for those who hold back, and saying 'there is nothing' to those who beg is hard for anyone.
nuance: Three gems tie a difficulty to a kind of person; the fourth widens it to everyone, so refusing a beggar is set as harder than the others. வரைந்தார் is read as those who set limits on giving.

reading: Food burns when it enters a body that takes no pleasure in it, speech burns those without brightness of mind, a man's former deed, which knows no bound, burns him, and even a king is burned by the army that has joined him.
nuance: Each thing meant to sustain or serve turns on its holder: food, words, one's own past acts and one's own army. The last carries the theme to the king.

reading: Scorning a person is itself a thing to be scorned, words of counsel are things to be pondered, the path of dharma is a thing to join after knowing it within, and the meanings of the many books are things to be examined.
nuance: Each gem gives the right act toward a thing (to deride, to ponder, to join, to sift), and the first turns back on the scorner: contempt is matter for contempt.

reading: There are tanks that hold rivers within them, there are subjects whom glorious kings desire, there are songs that reach the ancient Veda, and there are acts of beneficence equal to sacrifice.
nuance: Each gem says a lesser thing can equal a greater: a tank a river, a subject the king's desire, a song the Veda, giving a sacrifice. வேளாண்மை is read as beneficence, as in the Kural, though it can also mean husbandry.

reading: The verse says the vellalan is the one who owns oxen, the brahmin the one who does not accept, the cock the one that wins with a single strike, the woman of household life one who has wisdom with her beauty, and the commander the one who holds his army close.
nuance: The verse counts five, not four. வேளாளன் and பார்ப்பான் are birth-group names, and the verse defines each by a mark (oxen; not accepting), which can be read as naming what each group should have or as limiting the name to those who have it. ஏலாதான் is read as one who does not accept gifts; it may mean one who does not take up some work.
domain_note: defines the marks of birth-groups and roles

norm.note: defines birth-group names (vellalan, brahmin) and the wife by the marks the period expected of them

reading: Kings who own elephants delight in their fury and love to ride swift horses, good men delight in the modesty of good women with curved earrings, and the bad delighting in the bad is ruin.
nuance: Three delights are named as fitting to their owners, and the fourth turns the pattern: when like delights in like among the bad, the delight is ruin.

reading: No organ excels the eye, no kin is closer than the husband, no wealth is brighter or fuller than children, and no god is to be counted with the mother who bore one.
nuance: Four superlatives each name the first of its kind; the second speaks from a wife's place (கொண்டான், the man who took her) and the fourth sets the mother above any god.

norm.note: ranks the husband as a wife's closest kin, a household norm of the period

reading: Those who love the learned are like the learned, those without kindly regard and those who join enemies are like enemies, and the small-minded who do not plainly say what has befallen them are like an anthill where a snake lives hidden.
nuance: The grouping of lines 1 and 2 is unclear: கண்ணோடார் may stand alone or with செற்றாரைச் சேர்ந்தவர். The verse judges people by what they cling to and by what they conceal.

reading: The excellent gain excellent deeds, those who are not wanted gain unwanted deeds too, those who delight in dharma are born again everywhere, and those who renounce belong to heaven.
nuance: Line 3 is hard to divide: பிறப்பார் is doubled, and அறனின் புறுவர் can be read as those who rejoice in dharma. On the reading taken here it sets household dharma, which leads to rebirth, against renunciation, which leads to heaven.

reading: The days and the two lights exist always, disease and labour are always alike, givers and takers are always the same, and those born and those who die always exist.
nuance: Where most verses on this theme stress that the person passes, this one stresses that the pattern stays: sun and moon, sickness and work, giving and taking, birth and death are permanent features of the world.

reading: The one who eats sweetly is the one who eats without killing life, the one fit to be shunned is the one who lives with a turned-away face, the one called lonely is he who has done no good, and the one called pleasant is he whose conduct no one resents.
nuance: Each gem redefines a common word by conduct: sweet eating by not killing, loneliness by having done no good. The verse runs to five lines where the others have four.

norm.note: names eating without killing as the sweet way of eating, a diet rule of non-killing

reading: The one who eats after giving is the one who plants fame, the one who eats from another's hand is called a kaangi, going before those who are not one's own becomes plainly laughable, and begging from one who does not know one's plight becomes enmity.
nuance: காங்கி is a rare word; it plainly names the dependant who lives from another's hand. The first two gems set giver against taker, the last two count the costs of asking.

title: நான்மணிக்கடிகை 61-80
theme: Verses 61 to 80 each set four things in one frame (what thrives by being drawn on, what is known by what, what is better than what, what lies within a kind), so that household, learning, wealth and speech are judged by the same patterns of sign, measure and increase.
source_issues: 71 line 2: the text has ஆற்றல் வகைய வறஞ்செய்கை and தொட்ட (line 2); the tamilvu text reads அறம் செயல் and தோட்ட. The reading does not turn on the difference.
66 lines 2-3: இன்புறூங்உங் is an odd spelling, probably for இன்புறூஉம்; it appears twice.

reading: The verse names four things that thrive by being given to: fire when ghee is sprinkled on it, the gods who grant boons when approached and praised, the milch-cow when the stall is opened for her calf to suckle, and hospitality when vessels are laid out and guests are fed well.
nuance: The verb நந்தும் (thrives) is repeated for fire, cow and guest-feeding, so the verse makes a single law of increase by outflow: the cow thrives by letting the calf drink, the household's hospitality by feeding. நாகர் is read here as the celestials; the verse does not say more about them.

reading: A man's freedom from blame is to be seen in his children, his want of true friends is learned in his ruin, his prosperity is known by how his wealth moves, and by praise even those who did not esteem him are brought to esteem him.
nuance: கேட்டால் can be 'by ruin' (கேடு) or 'by hearing'; the reading takes ruin, which makes adversity the test of friendship. The last item breaks the 'know X by Y' pattern: புகழ்ச்சி may be one's fame or flattery offered to others, and the line does not settle which.

reading: Within each kind some excel: among eyes some are dear to the one who looks, among women some are excellent without beauty of form, within a country there are good towns, and among songs there are songs that win distinction.
nuance: The four gems share one form (within X there are Y that excel), so worth is placed inside a class rather than given to the class. The first line is compressed; காதற்றாம் is taken as 'dear', but the clause could be read otherwise. The second item separates a woman's worth from her looks.

reading: People worship fire seen as the flame of a wick and scorn it seen as the blaze of firewood; likewise, in one family, the world passes over the elder who grew old without learning and praises the youth of the one who learned.
nuance: The first two gems are one fire valued by its setting; the last two turn that image on a household, so age, like the substance of fire, does not decide worth. The ranking is inside ஒருகுடி, one family, where seniority would normally rule.

reading: What the man with wealth desires comes to be, a cluster of sprouts comes from seed if there is water, a host of fortune comes if the bright red lady looks on a man, and if she is grieved it perishes.
nuance: ஒண்செய்யாள் is the goddess of fortune. The verse runs from wealth's power to its dependence: the rich get what they want, but the wealth itself waits on her glance, as sprouts wait on water. The fourth gem is the third reversed; one could count three things and a consequence.

reading: The tiger gains its sheen by eating flesh, cattle delight in the grass of wet land, all the low delight in rice from paddy, and the high delight in their own proper standing.
nuance: கீழ் and மேல் rank people, but the verse ranks them by what satisfies them, not by a birth rule; it states no rule of who may eat or be fed, so it carries no norm. It sets the low with the tiger and the cow as creatures pleased by food, and the high apart, pleased by வரிசை (their rank and its due).

reading: Deeds that will recoil show it only afterward, whatever they bring, but to those who knew in advance they show it beforehand; for those who have gained things the heart is ever craving; and the deeds of those without craving do not fail.
nuance: The syntax of lines 1 and 2 is dense, with பின்னவாம் and முன்னவாம் played against each other; the reading is one defensible parse. The verse pairs foresight with freedom from craving as the two things that make a deed safe.

reading: Those without wealth are better than those who have it and only guard it, the poor are better than those who have stored it up, those who bear are better than those who swell up and revile, and those who do not break are better than those who did.
nuance: Each gem is a ranking (X is better than Y), so the verse praises poverty only against hoarding, not in itself. பைத்தெழுந்து pictures the reviler rising like a cobra's spread hood. The last line is obscure: சிதையாதவர் may be those who do not ruin others or those who do not falter, and செய்தார் those who did harm or did a deed and spoiled it.

reading: A son tells of his father's goodness, a man's face tells the desire that stands within him, one who has entered a wide well-watered field tells its nature, and the sky tells the nature of the land.
nuance: Every gem is a sign that discloses something hidden, so the verse is about inference: the son is evidence of the father as rain is of the land. The third item may contrast with the fourth: one learns a field by going into it, a land by its rain.

reading: A town is good if many live in it, a man's mind is good if he learns without fault, the sharp-horned bull gains glory by the herd of its own kind, and a family gains glory by the food it gives.
nuance: Two gems say what makes a thing good (நன்று) and two what gives it glory (வீறு); in each the worth comes from what surrounds or flows from it, except the mind, which is made good from within by learning.

reading: A bridled horse is as its rider makes it, a man's doing of virtue is according to his strength, the width of the sluices is according to the tank that was dug, and the ways of those who live are according to their means.
nuance: Every gem says 'according to' (வகைய, அனைய), so virtue is measured like a horse, a sluice and a household budget. The verse does not excuse doing little; it sizes the duty to the capacity.

reading: Aeons pass reckoned by years and the night watches by naazhigai; clear understanding is found in those who are clear without delay; and the harsh delight in harsh words.
nuance: The first two gems say great spans are made of small units. தாழியா and தெற்றென்றார் are hard; the reading takes them as 'without delaying' and 'the clear-minded', which makes the third gem a claim that clarity shows itself at once. The last gem explains harsh speech by the speaker's nature.

reading: If the learned man stumbles he rises again, if the unlearned fool falls his leg breaks, and, considered well, any means made with single-minded care becomes a seed that does not fail.
nuance: The verse counts three things, not the book's usual four: the learned man's fall, the fool's fall, and the single-minded means. The third gem gives the reason for the first two: learning is a means made with care, and so it holds when one slips.

reading: Poets are like gods, those who live in one town are like kin, among kin those who cherish and serve one are like parents, and those who love the learned are like the learned.
nuance: Each gem lifts one group to the rank of another (gods, kin, parents, the learned), so nearness and devotion confer standing. The last gem lets the unlearned share the rank of learning through love of the learned.

reading: Something is choked off the moment a lie is born, a physician names the disease the moment he is asked to speak, good people should be let go the moment they ask to leave, and the rightful heir, when he asks, should be given his share by division.
nuance: Every gem turns on போழ்தே (at that very moment): each act is due at once. The first line does not name what is filled in and lost when a lie is born (trust, merit or friendship); the reading leaves it open.

reading: By the tongue one knows the sweet, by smelling with the nose one knows all flowers, with the eyes one sees ornaments, and what is to be reasoned is reasoned by thought, sitting together.
nuance: Three senses are each matched to their own objects, and then thought (எண்ணம்) is given as a fourth faculty with its own object. தொக்கிருந்து (gathering together) makes reasoning a shared act, as in counsel, where the senses work alone.

reading: There is no bound within which born lives do not die, no strengths that do not decline, no one who has gained unaging youth, and no one who has passed through prosperity without ruin.
nuance: All four gems are negations (இல்லை, இல்), so the verse is a list of things that do not exist. It draws no counsel from impermanence; it only states it.

reading: A man is known by his speech, a pool by its soft water, nobility by helpfulness toward anyone, and toddy by the joy it brings to the body.
nuance: Each thing is known by a sign that comes out of it. Toddy closes the list without blame: the verse uses it as a plain case of a thing known by its effect, set level with nobility. யார்கண்ணும் (toward anyone at all) is what makes oppuravu a test of worth rather than favour to kin.

reading: Is it not the tongue that cuts friendship, does not the undiscerning fool let go even when tightly bound, is not craving caught in the net of many books, and does not a resolve set amid enmity come to ruin?
nuance: All four gems are rhetorical questions with அன்றோ. The second and fourth lines are hard: வீங்கிப் பிணிப்பின் is read as 'though bound tight', and மாறுள் நிறுக்கும் துணிபு as a resolve weighed or set among foes. The third gem makes learning a net that catches craving.

reading: If one gives, one should give food; if one lets go, one should let go of the hoard while life remains; if one lifts, one should lift the kin who have fallen; and if one destroys, one should destroy anger.
nuance: The verse is built on four conditionals (கொடுப்பின், விடுப்பின், எடுப்பின், கெடுப்பின்), each naming the best object of a verb. உயிரிடை ஈட்டை is unclear: it may be the hoard one holds while alive, or gain got from living beings; the reading takes the first.

title: நான்மணிக்கடிகை 81-104
theme: The last twenty-four verses keep the four-gem form: each names four things under one verb or likeness (dies beneath, is death to, stays, grows, is a fault, is evil, is the light of). They range over learning and its absence, speech, the base and the worthy, women's conduct, kin and friendship, and close with chains from speech or the wife to understanding and release.
source_issues: 96 line 2: சாயிறுந் is probably a corruption of சாயினும் ('even if they die').
99 line 1: எண்ணொக்கும் is doubtful; the sense 'like the eye' would need கண்ணொக்கும்.
104 is nearly the same verse as sirupanchamoolam:89 (variants கிழமை/கிளமை, வசைமனம்/பகைமை, அருள்மனம்/ஆரருள்); one book has likely taken it from the other or both from a common stock.
89 line 4 (அணங்கல் வணங்கின்று பெண்) is obscure as written.

reading: Beauty and youth are said to die beneath poverty, lineage and family standing beneath want of learning, paddy beneath a tank that has no water, and a draught ox beneath a load beyond its strength.
nuance: Every item repeats கீழ்ச்சாம், 'dies beneath': each good thing is killed by what should be under it and is missing or too heavy. Lineage, in the Kural's terms a matter of birth, is set among things that need a support from below to live.

reading: The good, those who walk the good path, and the base outcasts all have no town they call their own, while for those with something in hand every town is their town.
nuance: The refrain 'no town is their own' must mean opposite things: the good and the renouncer belong everywhere, the base are kept nowhere. The last line turns it again: for the man with means every town is his, so the belonging the first two earn by virtue the rich buy. கடைகள் (the lowest) is a word of contempt; whether it ranks people by birth or by conduct the verse does not say.

reading: For the unlearned man his own speech is death, for the soft-leaved plantain the fruit it bears is death, for those who do wrong dharma is death, and death too is the woman who lives wickedly in the house.
nuance: Each death comes from inside the one it kills: one's own words, one's own fruit, the dharma one breaks, one's own wife. The plantain, which dies after fruiting, is the image that holds the four together.

reading: Cultivated land gains its glory by water, a port town its greatness by the goods it trades, kings their glory by the land they rule, and a dancer his name by his dancing.
nuance: The king stands in a row with a field, a port and a dancer: each is great by the one thing it works on, so the king's glory is borrowed from the land he holds, not his own.

reading: The verse names striving after one alone as the excellence of women's work, striving always after the good as the mind of the அந்தணர், striving for the land another rules as the excellence of kings' work, and leaving one's kin as striving after one's own ruin.
nuance: All four turn on ஊக்கல், striving, so the verse assigns each station its proper object of effort; the fourth breaks the pattern by naming a striving that ruins. ஒன்றூக்கல் for women is most likely single devotion to the husband. The அந்தணர் are given a mind rather than a rite, which leaves open whether the word names a birth-group or the virtuous.

norm.note: a period norm assigning women the single-minded devotion that is their proper work, beside the work proper to andhanar and kings

reading: The verse says one must not steal, since harsh things follow; must not cast off what is worthy; must not befriend the small; and must not take up enmity with anyone.
nuance: Four negatives in -ஆமை, each with வேண்டும். Only the first gives a reason (கடிய வருதலால்). யார்மாட்டும் can close the third line (befriend the small with no one) or open the fourth (take enmity with no one); the sense survives either way.

reading: The verse bids one increase friends by leading them to the good, stand proud against enemies when the time is known, eat sparingly wherever one is, and curb anger where it cannot take effect.
nuance: The four imperatives rhyme (பெருக்குக, தருக்குக, அருக்குக, சுருக்குக): two increase, two decrease. Friends grow by what one does for them, not by numbers. The anger rule is limited to where anger 'does not go', leaving open anger where it can prevail.

reading: Sloth stays with those bound for ruin, cruelty stays with those who neglect care, good women stay within the bound of the shame they cherish, and the elephant stays at the post planted for it.
nuance: The verb நிற்கும், 'stays', joins a vice that settles in a person with a restraint that holds one. Good women's shame is set beside the elephant's post: the bound is chosen and cherished (பேணிய), yet it is a tether.

norm.note: a period norm that good women keep within the limit set by நாண், compared to a tethered elephant

reading: The verse says learned அந்தணர் know the Veda, kings know victory joined with just rule, bowing is always the ornament of the worthy, and the last line sets a woman's humility apart, on one reading as her not being a torment.
nuance: Each station has its proper excellence and the worthy have humility for theirs. The last line (அஃதன்றி அணங்கல் வணங்கின்று பெண்) is obscure: it may say a woman's bowing is not being an அணங்கு to her husband, or that a bowing woman is no அணங்கு. அந்தண் புலவர் may also be 'gracious learned men'.

norm.note: a period norm setting a separate humility for women beside the Veda of the andhanar and the victory of kings

reading: A woman of good character keeps to the way she was set in, one without a bond goes as she pleases though guarded, desire goes where it went though checked, and a killing, though hidden, rests on the killer.
nuance: The common claim is that inner nature outruns outward control: guarding, blocking and hiding all fail. Desire and murder are the general cases that make the point about women more than a point about women.

norm.note: a period view of women's conduct as fixed by character, against which guarding them is useless

reading: Where hardness of eye grows strength grows, where the sweet looks of soft-spoken women grow kin grow, where the gentle eye of the worthy grows dharma grows, and where the hard eye of the base grows sin is great.
nuance: The same வன்கண் opens and closes the verse: in the first line it is daring that brings strength, in the last the hard eye of the base that brings sin. The eye is the measure throughout: hard, sweet, gentle, hard again.

reading: Not learning in youth, being liberal when one has no means, anger when one has no kin, and eating from the hand of those not one's own are each named a fault.
nuance: Every fault is a virtue or need out of its time or place: learning missed in its season, giving without the means for it, anger without kin to stand behind it, food taken from strangers. The last is about dependence, not purity.

reading: Killing is evil in every place, letting one's children grow up unlearned is evil, the beauty of good women is evil if they stand without shame, and lineage is evil when its principle is gone.
nuance: Only killing is evil without condition (எல்லா விடத்தும்); the other three are goods that turn evil when something is lost. A family's standing is made to depend on its கொள்கை, its held principle, not on birth.

norm.note: a period norm making women's beauty a fault when it is not held in by நாண்

reading: The verse defines ஆசாரம் as learning, the rule of wealth as having enjoyment joined with dharma, justice as showing favour to no one, and says the king who rules with discernment does not lack inner searching.
nuance: A run of definitions (X என்பது Y). Calling ஆசாரம் simply learning is a strong claim beside the ritual sense of the word in the Acharakkovai. The division of the last two lines is not certain: உண்ணாட்டம் இன்மையும் இல் may mean the discerning ruler never fails to look inward, or that he lacks no inner inquiry.

reading: The drunkard knows the misery of toddy, the highest of birds knows the misery of thirst, the man of many wives knows the misery of want, and the thief knows the misery of concealment.
nuance: Each misery is known only from inside: the one who suffers it is the only witness. புள்ளினுள் ஓங்கல் is most likely the bird said to drink only rain; the verse does not name it.

reading: Wounding words appear in the mouths of the graceless, deceitful words do not appear in the mouths of the learned even when they die, evil talebearing does not appear in the mouths of the worthy, and deceitful words appear in the mouths of the base.
nuance: Two pairs of mouths: graceless and base speak, learned and worthy do not. கரப்புச்சொல் is repeated, once withheld and once spoken, which makes the verse a mirror. சாயிறுந் is probably a corruption of சாயினும், 'even if they die'.

reading: Those without beauty have no standing before bejewelled women, the unlearned man has none if he enters a fit assembly, and even a learned man has none if he falls among the unlearned and foolish.
nuance: Three items, not four: the verse names three who lose standing (பாடிலர், பாடிலன், பாடிலனே), and splitting கல்லாதார் பேதையார் into two audiences would not be defensible. The turn is the third: learning, which saves the second case, does not save one in the wrong audience.

reading: A gem does not lose its worth though it is soiled, dirt sticks to iron though it is smeared and polished, and the base, though bound and scoured, show their own dirt.
nuance: Three items: gem, iron and the base. The washing is the point: the gem needs none, the iron does not hold it, and the base, even scrubbed while held fast (பாசத்துள் இட்டு), show their nature again.

reading: Not parting from the worthy one keeps company with is like the eye, living with those who do not care for one is like a wound, the rebuke of friends is like the lute, and a house without a woman of good character is like a ruin.
nuance: Four likenesses in ஒக்கும். The first word எண்ணொக்கும் is doubtful: as written it could mean 'like sesame' or 'like reckoning', and a reading 'like the eye' assumes கண். A friend's rebuke heard as lute music is the turn of the verse.

reading: If the tank is small the water overflows, if the household's income is small the wife takes over, if earlier penance was small deeds overrun one, and if strength is small the enemy overruns.
nuance: ஊரும் carries the verse: water spills over, and the others ride over the one who is too small to hold them. பெண்ணூரும் most likely means the wife overrides the husband when he brings in too little; it is a claim about the household, not a rule. மேலைத் தவம் is penance done before, perhaps in earlier lives.

reading: Reviling yields reproach, doing obeisance yields thriving kin, wealth one has made yields enjoyment, and grace that has softened yields dharma.
nuance: A four-step table of causes, each with ஆகும். Enjoyment is tied to wealth and dharma to grace, not to wealth: the verse keeps the two apart.

reading: There is no one who knows everything, no one who knows nothing at all, no one whose faults hide every virtue, and no one who has learned all the arts.
nuance: The single closing இல் negates all four, so the verse is four 'there is none'. It denies both extremes of knowledge and both extremes of character at once. கணன் (the full count of the arts or treatises) is a rare word.

reading: The light of a house is its wife, the light of wives is worthy sons, the light of beloved sons is learning, and the light of learning is understanding that brings fame.
nuance: A chain: each light is lit by the next, so the house finally shines by understanding. The wife is the first link but not the last.

reading: Sweet speech makes close kinship, harsh speech without sweetness makes a reviling mind, a tongue of gentle speech makes a mind of grace, and with that mind one reaches the release that does not perish.
nuance: A chain from the tongue to release: speech shapes the mind, and the mind gains வீடு. Harsh speech yields a fault in the speaker's own mind (வசைமனம்), not only others' anger. The verse is nearly the same as Sirupanchamoolam 89.

title: கல்வி payiram-10
