theme: Under the heading கல்வி, with the payiram and the invocation, ten verses on learning: it must be had in youth, the learner feels his ignorance grow, learning that does not clear confusion is worthless, the learned are at home everywhere, hearing excels solitary study, a young Chola judges by inherited craft, only the learned or the better can judge learning and goodness, the learned are restrained, and their faults are seen by all.
source_issues: 4 line 1: ஆற்றவும் கற்றவும் is awkward and may be a corruption of ஆற்றவும் கற்றார்.
0: the invocation lacks a main verb and its first line (அரிதவித்து ஆசின்று) is obscure.
10 lines 1-2: வேற்றுமை இல்லார் and கதிப்பவர் are of uncertain sense.

reading: The prefatory verse says that the king of Munrurai, bowing at the feet of the Lord who sits in the shade of the pindi tree, made all four hundred old proverbs into four-line venpas and set them out sweetly.
nuance: The pindi (asoka) tree is the tree under which the Jain Arhat is shown seated, so the bow places the work in a Jain frame without naming the faith. The proverbs are called பண்டை, already old: the poet claims to have set them in verse, not to have made them, and names himself only by his seat, முன்றுறை மன்னவன்.

reading: The invocation sets the feet of the one who quelled the enemy within and knew without flaw beside the rising of those in the wide sea-girt world who have seen and known them as their due, and clinches it with the proverb that the steam of a great thing is great.
nuance: The sentence has no main verb: the feet stand at the head and the worshippers' rise is compared to something left unsaid, so the sense is carried by the proverb, that what issues from a great thing is itself great, here the standing that comes to those who know the great one's feet. அரி may be the senses' enemies or delusion; ஆசின்று உணர்ந்தவன் reads as one who knows without fault, an epithet of the omniscient one.

pazhamozhi.literal: the steam (or breath) of a great thing is great

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the greatness that passes from the worshipped one to those who know his feet

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those who know the great one's feet rise high in turn

reading: The verse asks whether one who would not learn in the youth that is fit for it can expect to gain learning in old age, and answers with the proverb that no one ever took toll after the wilderness road was passed, nor wages after the tree was cleared.
nuance: Both halves of the proverb are about payment that can only be taken while the work is still to be done: once the road is crossed or the tree is moved, the claim is gone. Youth is cast as that moment for learning. மரம்போக்கி may be the felling of a tree or the plying of a boat (மரம், a raft) across water; either way the wage falls due before the task ends.

pazhamozhi.proverb: சுரம்போக்கி உல்குகொண்டார் இல்லையே யில்லை மரம்போக்கிக் கூலிகொண் டார்
pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who took toll after the desert road was crossed, none who took wages after the tree was cleared

story.act: no story; the proverb is the instance, a payment that lapses once the work is past

pazhamozhi.applied_to: learning not gained in youth cannot be claimed in old age

reading: Because a man lapses at every word he speaks, the one who, without flagging, laments at each stage of study that he has not yet learnt, ponders one thing and labours until he knows it, knows the truth of the saying that the more one learns the more one finds oneself unlearned.
nuance: The verse makes the sense of one's own ignorance a working method, not a mood: the lament drives the next round of pondering and labour (உற்றொன்று சிந்தித்து உழன்றொன்று அறியுமேல்). The first line gives the reason as the lapses that each spoken word exposes. The grammar of lines 1 to 3 is loose and the subject is supplied.

pazhamozhi.literal: how, with each learning, one is the more unlearned

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the earnest learner who measures himself after each lesson

pazhamozhi.applied_to: true study shows the learner how much remains unlearnt

reading: A lamp is bought for a price only after everything is weighed to be sure it will not flicker, and if the lamp itself should spread confusion, lord of the hill country, what use is it, for no one pays money to buy darkness.
nuance: The verse never names learning: the lamp stands for it only through the heading, and the point is that knowledge bought at a cost is worth having only if it clears confusion (மருள்). One may also read it as advice to test a teacher or a text before taking it, as one tests a lamp before paying.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one gives wealth to buy darkness

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the purchase of a lamp that gives no light

pazhamozhi.applied_to: learning that leaves one confused is worth nothing for its cost

reading: Those who have learnt deeply are the wise, and there is no land in the four directions they do not go to; those lands are not foreign to them but their own, so, as the proverb says, they need no food for the road.
nuance: The proverb turns belonging into provision: the learned carry nothing because every land feeds them as its own. Line 1 as printed (ஆற்றவும் கற்றவும்) is awkward; the reading takes it as 'those who have learnt much'.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no need of food for the journey

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the learned traveller

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned are at home everywhere and need nothing carried

reading: The wise do not become like the frog in the well that thinks there is no sweet water to drink anywhere else, and even beside reciting a treatise sweetly all day without tiring, the proverb holds that hearing is better than learning.
nuance: The frog image gives the reason for the ranking: one's own text, however diligently recited, is one well, and hearing from others is what shows there is water elsewhere. So the verse ranks listening above solitary study, not above learning as such. கணக்கு is the treatise or text conned by rote.

pazhamozhi.literal: hearing is better than learning

story.act: the frog in the well takes its well for the only sweet water there is

pazhamozhi.applied_to: listening to others frees the learner from the narrowness of his own text

reading: When grey-haired elders said a young man could not see a case through to its end, the Chola tied on grey hair, judged the case by his words to their satisfaction, and so proved the saying that a family's craft is half known without being learnt.
nuance: The proverb credits the king's skill to birth, not study: his line's craft of judging comes to him half-made. That sits oddly under a heading on learning, and against the counted works that rank learning above lineage. The disguise answers the elders on their own terms, appearance, while the judgement answers them on substance.

pazhamozhi.literal: a family's craft is half-known without being learnt

story.act: a young Chola king, doubted by grey elders, put on grey hair and judged their case to their satisfaction
story.tradition: identified by tradition as Karikalan; the verse does not name him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: inherited capacity: the king judges well though young

reading: Only the deeply learned can discern the scholarship of the deeply learned, lord of the town of flowering waters; it is not open to common people, for a snake knows the feet of a snake.
nuance: The proverb rests on the belief that a snake's legs are hidden from all but other snakes: learning is not merely hard for outsiders to judge, it is invisible to them.

pazhamozhi.literal: a snake knows a snake's feet

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the learned judging the learned

pazhamozhi.applied_to: only peers in learning can judge learning

reading: If the goodness of the good is to be known, those better than they will know it and others will not, lord of the great hill where peacocks dance, for spear is split only by spear.
nuance: The verse is about goodness of character, not learning, though it stands under the learning heading; it pairs with 7 but asks more, since the knower must be better (அவரினும் நல்லார), not merely equal. அயில் is a spear point or iron: a hard thing is cut only by what is as hard or harder.

pazhamozhi.literal: they split iron with iron

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the judging of goodness

pazhamozhi.applied_to: only those better than the good can know their goodness

reading: Those who do not know the restraint that the widely learned have found praise themselves in their heedlessness, lord of the fair hill country where the falls strike the rock, for a full pot does not slop its water.
nuance: Self-praise is traced to two lacks at once: not knowing the learned man's restraint, and பொச்சாப்பு, forgetful heedlessness. The proverb implies the half-filled pot without saying it.

pazhamozhi.literal: a full pot does not slop its water

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the quiet of the truly learned against the boasting of the shallow

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned are restrained, the half-learned boast

reading: When those who have learnt the prescribed texts and live conspicuously in their town go beyond the texts of those who teach and do blameworthy things, it is a spot fallen on the face of the moon.
nuance: The fault is no larger in the learned, but more visible, because they are seen across the town as the moon is seen across the sky. Lines 1 and 2 are hard: வேற்றுமை இல்லார் may mean those of steady conduct or those without distinction of rank, and கதிப்பவர் may be those who expound or the revered; the reading takes the general sense.

pazhamozhi.literal: a blemish fallen on the surface of the moon

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the misdeed of a learned and well-known man

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the faults of the learned are seen by all

title: கல்லாதார் 11-16
theme: Under the heading கல்லாதார், six verses on the unlearned and the learned in company: the unlearned man's right judgements are luck, his insights falter when spoken before the learned and count for nothing unspoken, and the learned man who speaks among the unlearned turns his good words bad and lapses in conduct; the unlearned who challenge the learned want what they cannot do.
source_issues: 11 line 1: சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய் is probably a misprint for கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய் (learning and hearing from the learned); the reading assumes the correction.
12 and 13 share an almost identical first line (கல்லாதான் கண்ட கழிநுட்பம்), while 14 has சுழிநுட்பம்; either may be a copying variant.
13 line 3: வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும் carries an editorial bracket and its sense is obscure.
16 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at முடவன், leaving தானும் நடவான் outside, though the clause belongs to the proverb's image; the quotation marks may be misplaced. பிடிப்பூணி is obscure.

reading: Those who have neither learnt for themselves nor heard from the mouths of the learned do not understand things clearly, and if such a man ever lights on the truth it is no more his doing than a fruit picked up under the naaval tree.
nuance: The verse names two routes to knowledge, one's own study and listening to the learned, and denies the man who has taken neither; the proverb then grants that he may be right on occasion and takes the credit from him, since the fruit fell and was not earned. As printed, line 1 reads சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய், which makes poor sense under the heading; the reading assumes கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய்.

pazhamozhi.literal: a fruit got under the naaval (jamun) tree

story.act: no story; the proverb stands for any windfall that drops to whoever happens to stand below

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an unlearned man's occasional true judgement is luck, not knowledge

reading: When an unlearned man voices before the learned some very fine point he has hit upon, it falters, because, as the saying goes, no answer comes without a question going before it, and no deed without a dream going before it.
nuance: Only the first half of the paired proverb does the work: among the learned every statement is met by questions, and the unlearned man's insight, never tested by questioning, gives way under them. The second half (the dream before the deed) rides along as the proverb's usual partner. The verse is addressed to a woman (நல்லாய்!); the address is a frame, not the counsel's audience. Its first line is shared, nearly word for word, with verse 13.

pazhamozhi.proverb: வினாமுந் துறாத உரையில்லை; இல்லை கனாமுந் துறாத வினை
pazhamozhi.literal: there is no answer that a question does not precede, and no deed that a dream does not precede

story.act: no story; the proverb states a general order of things, question before answer and omen before act

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the unlearned man's insight collapses when the learned question it

reading: Since the very fine point an unlearned man has found is hard for him to show, there is no sense in his rating himself highly as one of the good, for even those able to bend others by speech have said nothing if they do not speak.
nuance: Read with 12, the verse closes the unlearned man's last exit: spoken before the learned his insight falters (12), and kept unspoken it does not exist for anyone (13). Line 3 is obscure: the printed வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும் carries an editor's bracket and its sense, perhaps those who can overawe or come at others in anger, is not certain; the reading takes the line only as 'even the powerful in speech'.

pazhamozhi.literal: if one does not speak, nothing is said

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the able speaker who stays silent, and through him to the unlearned man whose insight cannot be shown

pazhamozhi.applied_to: insight that cannot be put into words earns no standing

reading: The deep subtleties that learning yields, spoken before the unlearned, turn every good thing said into a bad one, lord of the land of high hills, just as for those who have no kin even a city is like a forest.
nuance: The image makes the audience a kind of kin: the learned man among the unlearned is as friendless as a stranger in a crowded city, and what is good in his words finds no one to receive it, so it does harm instead. The text has சுழிநுட்பம் here where 12 and 13 have கழிநுட்பம்.

pazhamozhi.literal: to those without their own people even a city is like a forest

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the learned speaker who finds no hearers of his own kind

pazhamozhi.applied_to: learned speech among the unlearned is not merely wasted but turned to harm

reading: For a man nothing is worse than making a fine, well-wrought speech among the unlearned, since there is no lowness greater than a lapse of conduct and no height greater than conduct.
nuance: The verse classes the choice of audience as conduct: holding forth among the unlearned is an இழுக்கம், a lapse that lowers the speaker, not merely a waste of eloquence. The proverb's ozhukkam and izhukkam pair is the pair of the Kural's chapter on conduct, here used as a known saying.

pazhamozhi.proverb: இழுக்கத்தின் மிக்க இழிவில்லை இல்லை ஒழுக்கத்தின் மிக்க உயர்வு
pazhamozhi.literal: no disgrace exceeds a lapse, no elevation exceeds right conduct

story.act: no story; the proverb is a general maxim on conduct

pazhamozhi.applied_to: speaking learnedly among the unlearned is a lapse that lowers the speaker

reading: For the unlearned to provoke those who live by learning, take up a contest of words and rise itching for a fight is like a lame man who cannot even walk wanting to sport with an elephant.
nuance: The proverb's point is the gap between the wish and the means: the lame man cannot walk, yet wants a game with the strongest of beasts. பிடிப்பூணி is obscure; it may tie the elephant to a she-elephant (பிடி) or to a fetter, and the reading leaves it as 'an elephant' only. சொற்றாற்று and சுனைத்து are also uncommon; the reading takes them as a fight in words and an itch to rise.

pazhamozhi.literal: a lame man's wish to play with an elephant

story.act: no story; the lame man of the proverb is a type, applied to the unlearned who pick a quarrel with the learned

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the unlearned man's challenge to the learned is a desire far beyond his strength

title: அவையறிதல் 17-25
theme: Under the heading அவையறிதல், nine verses on knowing the assembly: the skilled speaker reads his hearers' desire, does not answer back or speak out of turn, and wastes no counsel on fools, while the unlearned and shameless who push into the company of the wise talk emptily, mock the restraint of the learned, and are silent among the good but boastful among the mean.
source_issues: 21 line 4: the proverb opens with a quotation mark ('பாண்சேரி) that is never closed.
21 line 4: பாண்சேரி பற்கிளக்கு மாறு is obscure, and the proverb's sense is unclear from the text.
23 line 4: மிளகுளு வுண்பான் (worm-eaten pepper) is obscure, and the proverb's point is uncertain.
25 lines 1-3: நடலை இலராகி and உடலா ஒருவற்கு are of doubtful sense.

reading: The skilled speak only after seeking out their hearers and learning what they want in the matter to be spoken, as bees go where their desire leads, for no one carries into an assembly the things that will lose there.
nuance: The verse makes the hearers' desire (வேட்கை), not the truth of the matter, the speaker's first measure; the bee image in line 3 repeats வேட்கை so that the speaker's skill is to follow desire as the bee follows scent. The address to a woman (வாட்கண்ணாய்!) is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: people do not enter an assembly carrying things that will be defeated

story.act: no story; the proverb states what anyone entering a contest of an assembly avoids

pazhamozhi.applied_to: speech that does not meet the hearers' desire is a losing case brought into the assembly

reading: When one person has spoken his piece, it is not fitting to take it up and answer back so that the two become opponents, for, lord of the great-hilled land, it goes ill even a little when two dogs play together.
nuance: The proverb's point is that dogs' play turns into a fight; a counter-reply in assembly is play of the same kind. Lines 1-2 are compressed and could also be read as forbidding a second man to join in answering one speaker; the reading takes இருவரா as the exchange becoming a two-sided quarrel.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is unpleasant when two dogs play together

story.act: no story; two dogs at play, which soon fall to snarling

pazhamozhi.applied_to: answering back a speaker in assembly turns discussion into a quarrel

reading: In an exchange two men have closely begun, if the one whose turn is to speak afterwards pushes forward and speaks first, his is the talk of one who does not know speech, like wrapping the nose of a man whose knee is torn.
nuance: The proverb mocks a remedy put on the wrong place: speaking out of turn answers what has not yet been raised and misses the wound. பின்னை உரைக்கப் படற்பாலான் may instead mean the one who is to be addressed later; on either reading the fault is pre-empting the order of the exchange.

pazhamozhi.literal: bandaging the nose of a man whose knee is torn

story.act: no story; a misplaced dressing for an injury elsewhere

pazhamozhi.applied_to: speaking before one's turn in a dispute misses the point at issue

reading: Those who, having neither learnt nor listened, bandy words in the midst of an assembly of the learned are themselves to be feared, lord of the hills where bright cascades leap, for even the gods have no power against those who have lost all decency.
nuance: The fear runs the unexpected way: not the unlearned fearing the learned, but the learned well advised to fear the unlearned talker, because shamelessness (பரிசழிந்தார்) cannot be answered by argument. The verse joins the two routes of 11, study and listening, as what these talkers lack.

pazhamozhi.literal: even the gods are powerless against those who have lost their decency

story.act: no story; the proverb sets the shameless beyond even divine power

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned cannot prevail over shameless unlearned talkers and should avoid them

reading: Those who, not knowing how to enter, have entered among men of broad understanding and then out of contentiousness utter empty, mean words are doing just what the saying of the bards' quarter and its talk of teeth describes.
nuance: The proverb's sense is not clear from the words: பாண்சேரி பற்கிளக்குமாறு is 'the way the bards' quarter tells of teeth', perhaps boasting of what the poor have chewed, or teeth to be lost in a quarrel; the reading leaves it open. The verse's own counsel, that entering without knowing how leads to vain contention, is clear.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way the bards' quarter speaks of teeth

story.act: an allusion to a saying about the bards' street and teeth whose point the verse does not spell out

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the empty contentious talk of one who has pushed in among the wise

reading: For those who know neither honour nor shame, their minds confused, to enter among men who know wisdom, sit there and speak questioning that wisdom is laughable, like the venture of one who goes in to see an elephant's tusk.
nuance: The verse puts the fault in character before learning: it is the lack of மானம் and நாண் that lets the man sit among the wise and question them. The proverb may hold a pun, since நகை is both laughter and teeth: one who would see an elephant's tusk must get close to a dangerous thing, and the attempt is absurd.

pazhamozhi.literal: laughable is the going-in of one who wants to see an elephant's tusk

story.act: no story; a man pushing close to an elephant to inspect its tusk

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the shameless man who questions the wise makes himself ridiculous

reading: Those who live chattering in bad assemblies, when they enter a good assembly and speak scorning the knowledge of men whose learning has passed all measure and keeps their tongues in check, are like a man eager to eat weevil-eaten pepper.
nuance: The learned are silent because of their learning (நாவடங்கக் கல்வி அளவிறந்து மிக்கார்), and the chatterer reads that silence as emptiness and mocks it. The proverb (மிளகுளு, worm-eaten pepper) seems to mean relishing what has no savour left, but its point is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: the eagerness of one who eats worm-eaten pepper

story.act: no story; a man relishing spoiled pepper

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the chatterer's mockery of the restrained learned is a taste for what is worthless

reading: To roll up one's tongue on seeing a good assembly and then praise oneself in a mean assembly that does not understand the good is the way of a man who, afraid of the fierce flank of his enemies, strings his bow inside his house and shoots at the pot in the middle of it.
nuance: The verse pairs two faults as one: silence from fear before the good and self-praise before the mean are the same cowardice, brave only where nothing answers back. The proverb's bow drawn at home against a household pot is the clearest image in the chapter.

pazhamozhi.literal: stringing a bow inside the house and shooting at the pot in its middle

story.act: a man who fears to face the enemy's fierce side shows his archery at home on a pot

pazhamozhi.applied_to: silent among the good and boastful among the mean is cowardice that performs where it is safe

reading: To speak sound counsel to someone in a crowded assembly of thoroughly dull men who, untroubled, do not grasp the good, is like sifting flour in the sea.
nuance: நடலை இலராகி (being without trouble or pretence) and உடலா ஒருவற்கு (to one who does not dispute, or does not agree) are both doubtful; the reading takes the first as the fools' complacency and the second as the hearer counselled. The proverb's loss is total: the flour is not spoiled but simply gone.

pazhamozhi.literal: like sifting flour in the sea

story.act: no story; flour strained into the sea is lost

pazhamozhi.applied_to: counsel spoken among dull men is wholly lost

title: அறிவுடைமை 26-33
theme: Under the heading அறிவுடைமை, eight verses on what understanding is worth: it is the garment that all other excellence decorates, one wise man outshines a crowd of fools, the senseless cannot be set right, the wise win the wise through the wise and keep out of company that does not value them, real ability cannot be hidden, and understanding stays where wealth comes and goes with fortune.
source_issues: 27 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at மதியம்போல், taking the moon simile into the proverb; the proverb proper may be only பன்மீனும் காய்கலா வாகும் நிலா.
28 line 2: சொற்குறி கொண்டு துடிபண் உறுத்துவபோல் is obscure and its relation to line 1 uncertain.
31 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at அறியும் in the middle of line 3; the split அறியும் / பெரிதாள் பவனே may be a copying division.

reading: A man who has no excellence through understanding cannot be made excellent by anything else, since jewels of gem and gold, sandal paste, garlands and every such ornament come only after the cloth.
nuance: The proverb does not dismiss ornaments; it orders them. Understanding is the cloth, the thing whose lack is nakedness, and the other goods are adornments that only make sense on a clothed body. பொறியின் in line 2 is read as 'finely wrought', qualifying the gem and gold jewels.

pazhamozhi.literal: all ornaments come after the garment

story.act: no story; the proverb states the order of dressing, cloth first and jewels after

pazhamozhi.applied_to: other excellences adorn only a man who first has understanding

reading: Even if a thousand men without understanding gather, they do not equal one excellent man in the wide world, just as the many stars cannot give the moonlight that the moon gives as it clears the spreading dark.
nuance: The argument is against number: excellence is a difference of kind, so adding fools does not approach one wise man. The quotation marks open at மதியம்போல், so the simile is printed as part of the proverb.

pazhamozhi.literal: the many stars cannot shed moonlight as the moon does

story.act: no story; the proverb sets the single moon against the crowd of stars

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one man of understanding outweighs any number of the senseless

reading: Those who lack good sense cannot be set firm in anything, unlike a drum that is brought to its beat by a spoken cue, lord of the good land where shining falls drop over the rock slopes, as the saying is, 'where learned knowledge has not gone in'.
nuance: The sense is hard to fix. Line 2 is taken as the drummer who strikes the துடி to word-signals, the responsive instrument against which the senseless are measured; the proverb's கடை is taken as the conditional 'when ... has not', so that instruction fails where learning has not first entered. Other divisions of line 2 are possible.

pazhamozhi.literal: when learned knowledge has not gone in

story.act: no story; the proverb names the condition under which a person cannot be steadied

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the senseless cannot be set right where no learning has entered

reading: For men of firm understanding, winning over those whose understanding matches their own worth is, lady with a deer's eyes, like the valiant great kings' binding an elephant by means of an elephant.
nuance: The proverb pictures the capture of a wild elephant with a trained one: the wise are drawn in only by someone of their own kind. ஆணம் in line 1 is taken as firmness or support; it can also mean affection, which would make the bond warmer. The address to a woman is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like binding an elephant with an elephant

story.act: kings capture a wild elephant by using a tame one

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wise are won over only through those of equal understanding

reading: Those who have taken stock and understood alongside the discerning do not push in among people who have no regard for them, for they surely know others' natures, lord of the shore of loud waves, just as the jackal does not show itself to the reapers.
nuance: The understanding in question is social: knowing who will not value one and keeping away. The jackal is not cowardly in the image but shrewd; it knows the reapers with their sickles will strike. பரியார் is read as 'those without regard'.

pazhamozhi.literal: jackals do not show themselves to the reapers

story.act: no story; the jackal in the harvest field keeps out of the reapers' sight

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the discerning keep out of company that does not value them

reading: Need anyone put into words, for those who have themselves arranged both the fitting and the unfitting, what these are, lady of wide red-streaked eyes beneath bow brows, since he who manages much is the one who knows much?
nuance: Read here as a rhetorical question: one who has handled both good and bad affairs already knows them and needs no instruction. புனைந்திருந்தார் could also mean 'those adorned with' fair and foul qualities, which would turn the verse toward a person whose character speaks for itself; the proverb fits the first reading better.

pazhamozhi.literal: the one who handles much knows much

story.act: no story; the proverb credits knowledge to the one with wide charge of affairs

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the experienced need no telling what is fit and unfit

reading: Can men of widespread strength be hidden by covering them with moss, lady with bamboo-smooth shoulders and spear-like eyes, when no one can hide with his hand the sun that moves in the sky?
nuance: The verse is about திறல், ability or power, rather than understanding as such; it fits its heading only if the editor took ability as the outward show of understanding. The moss is a thin cover, as the hand is against the sun: the attempt to suppress is mocked as much as the greatness is praised.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who can hide with the hand the sun moving through the sky

story.act: no story; the proverb mocks a hand raised to cover the sun

pazhamozhi.applied_to: real ability cannot be concealed by those who would suppress it

reading: Fine jewels beyond price and plentiful wealth come back even after they have strayed, if their owners have fortune, lord of the great hills, but since understanding never parts from one at all, firmness, as the saying goes, gains more than fortune.
nuance: The verse concedes more than most praise of learning does: lost riches really can return. Its point is that their return depends on fortune, while understanding needs no return because it never leaves. The subject of பிரிவின்று is unstated and is supplied from the heading as understanding; திட்பம் is taken as the steadiness of that possession.

pazhamozhi.literal: firmness gains more than fortune

story.act: no story; the proverb ranks steadiness above luck

pazhamozhi.applied_to: understanding, which never leaves, is worth more than wealth that returns only by fortune

title: ஒழுக்கம் 34-42
theme: Under the heading ஒழுக்கம், nine verses on keeping one's own conduct: conduct as richness added to good birth, taking a good word from any mouth, walking by one's own way, the limits of advice to the fixed, mending one's own faults before others', choosing ruin before a lasting scar, curing undeserved reproach, the shameless untouched by blame, and the evil tongue that spares no one.

reading: For those of excellent descent who come shining from an old line to live as men of conduct is, the verse asks the lord of the watered town where ripe coconuts drop into the fields, like rich milk with ghee on it poured out.
nuance: The verse treats old lineage as a good in its own right and good conduct as what is added on top of it, abundance upon abundance, as the ripe coconut falling into the paddy field doubles a fertile land. The proverb is hard: நெய்த்தலைப்பால் உக்கு விடல் could also be read as a waste (spilling the cream-topped milk), but that sits ill with the praise in lines 1-2; the reading takes it as richness overflowing.

pazhamozhi.literal: milk with ghee on its top, poured out

story.act: no story; the proverb stands for richness added to richness

pazhamozhi.applied_to: good conduct in the well-born adds excellence to an excellence already given by birth

reading: As fragrant agil comes from the kalli and an omen from the black crow's call, one should not scorn a good word from whatever mouth it comes, says the verse to the lord of the hill country of loud clear falls, for if a dog has caught a monitor lizard even brahmins eat it.
nuance: The two opening images are low sources of something prized: a scented wood from a thorny spurge and a meaningful sign from a despised bird. The proverb takes the extreme case: பார்ப்பார், the brahmins, a birth-group named here for its strict abstention from flesh, will eat what a dog (itself an impure catcher) has brought in, if it is good. The caste term is not used to rank people but to set the hardest test of a rule against a low source.

pazhamozhi.literal: if a dog catches a monitor lizard, even brahmins eat it

story.act: no story; a type case in which the lowness of the bringer does not stop even the strictest eater

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a good word is to be taken whatever the lowness of the mouth that speaks it

norm.note: the proverb presumes the period's norm that brahmins abstain from flesh and shun what a dog has touched, and makes its breaking the measure of a good thing's pull

reading: The verse tells its hearer, addressed as அத்தா, not to become like the small men who do not watch their own conduct, do not know the way their kin came and never join the straight path, but to walk by his own conduct, since no one knows that conduct apart from him.
nuance: The proverb can be taken two ways: that only the man himself knows his own conduct, so he must be its keeper, or that others know a man's conduct only from the man himself, so he is its evidence. Both make conduct a thing the self answers for, against the small men who look neither at themselves nor at their forebears.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who can know your walk apart from you

story.act: no story; the proverb is said to the hearer himself

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a man must keep his own conduct because it is known only through him

reading: When someone takes up a course that is not fit and off the path, turning him back and setting him right is beyond even the great, even those of keen and subtle learning and wisdom, for a drum sounds what has been set in it.
nuance: The verse puts the limit not in the adviser but in the advised: learning and hearing (கூர்த்தநுண் கேள்வி) do not reach one who has chosen. The proverb's ஓர்த்தது is what has been resolved or intended; the drum gives back only that, as a fixed man gives back only his resolve.

pazhamozhi.literal: a drum sounds what it has been set to

story.act: no story; the drum stands for the man fixed on his own purpose

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a man set on a wrong course cannot be turned back even by the wisest

reading: To push in anywhere to remove others' faults without removing one's own is, in all the wide world, the goat that clears another's wind and not its own.
nuance: The verse's words தங்குற்றம் நீக்கல and பிறர்குற்றம் are the Kural's own pair (436), turned from a condition of the king's justice into a mockery of any meddler. The proverb's goat is a curer that cannot cure itself; வளி is the wind-disorder of the body.

pazhamozhi.proverb: வெள்ளாடு தன்வளி தீராது அயல்வளி தீர்த்து விடல்
pazhamozhi.literal: the goat does not clear its own wind but clears its neighbour's

story.act: no story; the goat is any healer of others who leaves his own sickness

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who corrects others' faults while keeping his own is absurd

reading: Even when one is told 'I will be ruined', one must do only what brings no scar on oneself, for in the land ringed by the full sea and its long hills, a stone wears away but a word does not.
nuance: கெடுவல் is the man's own ruin, which the verse accepts as the lesser loss; the scar (வடு) is the reproach a deed leaves, and the proverb's word is what is said of the doer, which outlives the hills.

pazhamozhi.literal: stone wears away, a word does not

story.act: no story; the proverb sets the lasting word against the wearing stone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one should choose ruin over a shameful deed, since the report of it lasts

reading: For the evil disease called unfitting reproach, the medicine is excellence of character, and if it is not cured by medicine, says the verse to the lord of the cool sea shore, the disease destroys one's strength.
nuance: பொருந்தாப் பழி is most likely blame that does not fit the man, an undeserved reproach, though it may be reproach that should never attach to him; either way the verse does not tell him to ignore it but to answer it with மாட்சி, as a disease must be treated or it wastes the body.

pazhamozhi.literal: a disease destroys one's strength

story.act: no story; untreated illness stands for untreated reproach

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a reproach must be answered by worth of conduct or it ruins the man

reading: Even the nerunji thorn can do nothing to hurt the inner soles of those who walk with scraping feet, says the verse to the lord of the cool shore of beating waves where the serunthi bends over the wide backwater, and even great reproach is nothing to those who do not care for it.
nuance: The verse is not praise of indifference: the hardened sole stands for the shameless, whom blame cannot reach as it reaches the man who cares. Under the heading ஒழுக்கம் it describes a failure, not a strength.

pazhamozhi.literal: even great reproach does not exist for those who do not mind it

story.act: no story; the proverb names a type, the man who does not heed blame

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the shameless are untouched by reproach as calloused feet by thorns

reading: The world calls even Mal, the lord who bore the hard cold rain for the cows, a mere cowherd, and there is no need to ask whether it is gods or men: the tongue that speaks evil never runs short.
nuance: The parse takes மாலையும் as மால் with உம் (even Mal) rather than மாலை, evening, and கோவிற்கு as 'to the lord'. On that reading the example is a god whose saving act is turned into a slight on his rank; the point is that slander spares no one.

pazhamozhi.literal: the tongue that speaks evil knows no poverty

story.act: Mal, having sheltered the cows from hard cold rain, is still called by the world a cowherd
story.tradition: by tradition the Govardhana episode, in which Krishna holds up the hill against the rain for the cattle; the verse names only the sheltering of the cows

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the evil-speaking tongue finds something to belittle even in a god's saving deed

title: இன்னா செய்யாமை 43-50
theme: Under the heading இன்னா செய்யாமை, eight verses on not hurting others: harm returns on the one who causes it whatever the victim does (43, 46), the self-measure of pain answers the sense of the other as different (44), the scorned dependant and the defenceless strike back by bite or by tears (45, 47), the great cannot be pinched like stone (48), and the worthy do not retaliate against the base, as beneath them and as a waste of their strength (49, 50).
source_issues: 45 lines 3-4: the proverb's quotation opens at கடையடைத்து but has no closing mark, and போற்றான் (the uncaring owner) at the end of line 2 stands outside it though it belongs to the image.
46 line 1: நீயொளியை is obscure as printed and may be a misdivision.
50 line 4: நல்லாநா ராயம் is obscure; the division of the words, and whether நாராயம் is a weapon, cannot be fixed from the text.

reading: One should not hurt anyone at all on the thought that they will bear it, since even for the gods and for those of steadfast love there is no escaping pain for one who makes others suffer.
nuance: The verse closes the excuse that the victim's forbearance licenses the harm: the other's patience does not cancel the rebound on the one who hurts. Line 3 is hard to construe: தேவர்க்கும் and திண்ணன்பினார்க்கேயும் may name those to whom the proverb applies (no one, not even gods, is exempt) or those one must not hurt even when they would forgive; the reading takes the first, and கைகூட is left loosely rendered. The address பூவுட்கும் கண்ணாய் (you whose eyes flowers fear) is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: for one who makes others ache there is no freedom from ache

story.act: no story; the proverb states the rebound of pain as a rule that binds even gods and the steadfast

pazhamozhi.applied_to: hurting someone because they will forgive still brings pain back on the one who hurts

reading: With no gain to be had from the act and only a sense of the other as different from oneself, one must not deliberately do what makes others tremble, for what is painful to oneself is painful to others.
nuance: வேற்றுமை கொண்டு names the cause the proverb answers: treating the other as unlike oneself is what lets one hurt them, and the proverb denies the difference by making one's own pain the measure of theirs. வினைப்பயன் ஒன்றின்றி marks the case as gratuitous harm, with nothing even gained by it. The address to a woman likened to a flowering branch is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is painful to oneself is painful to others

story.act: no story; the proverb is the self-measure applied to anyone who would harm another for no purpose

pazhamozhi.applied_to: gratuitous harm rests on a false sense that others feel differently from oneself

reading: One should not, judging by appearances that they are powerless, scorn and torment even one's own people who have come to depend on one, for a dog shut in and beaten by a master who does not care for it will bite him.
nuance: The verse names the dependants (அடைந்த தமர்) as the victims and the master's belief in their weakness as the error; the proverb shows the weakness is only apparent, and the detail of the shut door (கடையடைத்து) makes cornering the cause of the bite. The proverb's opening quotation mark falls at line 3 and there is no closing mark; போற்றான் at the end of line 2 belongs to the image (the uncaring owner) though it stands outside the marks.
domain_note: the head of a house toward kin and dependants

pazhamozhi.proverb: கடையடைத்து வைத்துப் புடைத்தக்கால் நாயும் உடையானைக் கவ்வி விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: if one shuts a door on it and beats it, even a dog will bite its owner

story.act: a master who does not care for his dog shuts it in, beats it, and is bitten

pazhamozhi.applied_to: dependants scorned as powerless will turn on the one who torments them

reading: The poet tells his heart that it cannot see what lies far ahead and has surely spoken a cruel thing, for he who looks on another's ruin in the forenoon sees his own ruin in the afternoon.
nuance: The verse is addressed to one's own heart, so the cruelty rebuked is an intention or a wish voiced inwardly, not yet a deed; the proverb's கண்டான் (saw) also stops short of doing, and fits one who looks on or wishes for another's ruin. நீயொளியை in line 1 and அடியுளே in line 2 are obscure; the reading takes அடியுளே loosely as 'at the root' (in the end) and leaves நீயொளியை unrendered.

pazhamozhi.proverb: முற்பகல் கண்டான் பிறன்கேடு தன்கேடு பிற்பகல் கண்டு விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: one who saw another's ruin in the forenoon will see his own ruin in the afternoon

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the speaker's own heart, which has voiced a cruel wish

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even a cruel thought toward another returns as one's own ruin, and soon

reading: When the strong torment those who are ill-favoured in looks, those without support, the poor, and those they count enemies over a word, the tears the victims weep, unable to bear it, fall on the strong as Death.
nuance: The verse names four kinds of the defenceless, one of them (மாற்றத்தால் செற்றார், those taken as foes for a retort) defenceless only because the strong have chosen to treat a word as enmity. The tears are made the agent of the strong man's death, with no king or god named as the one who punishes.

pazhamozhi.proverb: ஆற்றாது அவரழுத கண்ணீர் அவையவர்க்குக் கூற்றமாய் வீழ்ந்து விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: the tears they wept, unable to bear it, fall upon them as Death

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the strong who torment four kinds of the weak

pazhamozhi.applied_to: oppressing the defenceless brings death on the oppressor through his victims' tears

reading: To say one will try to bring down those who have much and are held in high esteem is a fault, even if it looks easy, for no one ever pinched a stone off a cold mountain and came away with his hand unhurt.
nuance: நற்கெளி தாகி விடினும் concedes that the attack may look easy, and the proverb explains why the look deceives: the mountain does nothing, the hand is hurt by its own act against something harder than itself. The target is the great in means and repute, not necessarily the virtuous.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one has pinched at stone and kept the hand whole

story.act: no story; the proverb's image of pinching rock on a cold hill is applied to anyone who sets out to bring the great low

pazhamozhi.applied_to: attacking the established great harms the attacker, however easy it seems

reading: If people lacking worth, out of their own incompleteness, torment the worthy, it is not the way of the worthy to torment them back in anger, for when a dog runs up angered and bites, no one has ever bitten the dog back.
nuance: The ground of forbearance is rank, not compassion: the offender is likened to a dog, and retaliating would mean doing what a dog does. கோள் names non-retaliation as the settled stand of the worthy. Line 2's கூர்த்தவரை may mean the worthy are 'keen' or that they 'grow sharp' (angered); the reading takes the second, with the worthy as subject of நலிதல்.

pazhamozhi.literal: if a dog bites, no one bites the dog back

story.act: no story; the dog that runs up and bites stands for the unworthy who torment the worthy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy do not answer the harm of the base in kind

reading: The poet tells a man with a garlanded chest that for the superior to take to heart the wrongs done by the low, who do not keep their hands free of stain, and to rise against them in return is like taking up a fine great weapon against a little jackal.
nuance: Where 49 says retaliation is beneath the worthy, this verse says it is waste: the great means of the superior are spent on a target too small to deserve them. The proverb's நல்லா நாராயம் is obscure; it may name a fine iron arrow (நாராசம்) or a mighty weapon, and the reading keeps only the sense of a great weapon used on a small creature. The address காழார மார்ப suggests a man of rank, perhaps a king, though the counsel is general.
domain_note: addressed to a man of rank, the counsel for any superior

pazhamozhi.literal: taking up a fine great weapon for a little jackal

story.act: no story; the image of a great weapon spent on a small jackal is applied to the superior who avenges the faults of the low

pazhamozhi.applied_to: answering the faults of the low wastes the strength of the great on what is unworthy of it

title: வெகுளாமை 51-59
theme: Under the heading வெகுளாமை, nine verses on not answering provocation with anger: the great are not heated by the small, the man of unquenched anger is to be avoided, a feud dies as one tends one's own good, a mocking jest rebounds on the jester, the talk of strangers and the lies of the hired cannot be stopped and need not be grieved, the learned do not gore back the fool any more than one gores a cow, abuse returned sets one's own house on fire, and nobility comes from enduring rather than punishing.
source_issues: 56: the quotation marks enclose only செய்யாத செய்தா வெனில், the end of a question begun by என்பரிவ; the proverb may properly include the question word.
58 line 2: வயவுரை is obscure and may be a copying error (perhaps for வசையுரை); line 4 is best divided தீ இல்லை ஊட்டும் திறம்.
59 line 1: சுறுத்தாற்றி is a rare form whose sense (provoking) is inferred from context.

reading: Even when the very small do them harm, those made excellent by birth weigh the matter and do not grow angry, for water heated however hot with good firewood never sets the house on fire.
nuance: The proverb grants that the great are heated, as water is by good fuel, and denies only that the heat does harm: water hot enough to scald still cannot burn the house that holds it. The verse grounds this restraint in birth (பிறப்பினால் மாண்டார்), not in learning or effort, and the counsel turns on திறத்துள்ளி, weighing the nature of the offender.

pazhamozhi.proverb: நல்ல விறகின் அடினும் நனிவெந்நீர் இல்லம் சுடுகலா வாறு
pazhamozhi.literal: though heated with good firewood, very hot water cannot burn down the house

story.act: no story; the proverb is the household image of boiling water that scalds but cannot set its house alight

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the well-born may be heated by the harm of small men but their heat does no damage

norm.note: a lineage claim of the period: freedom from anger is credited to those excellent by birth, set against the very small (இறப்பச் சிறியவர்)

reading: A man whose anger never cools has no sense, and the wise say the best course is to keep out of his way, for it is hard to trust one who never becomes clear.
nuance: The counsel is not to bear the angry man but to step aside from him (மாறி ஒழுகல்), and the proverb gives the reason: one who never settles into clearness (தெளியான்) cannot be relied on. The address to the lord of the wave-beaten shore (சேர்ப்ப) is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is hard to trust one who is not clear-minded

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the type of the man whose anger never subsides

pazhamozhi.applied_to: avoid the man of unquenchable anger, since he cannot be trusted

reading: The verse asks whether one must show force at everything that befalls one, and says that for the learned it is enough to guard themselves from anger, since as grass wears away when paddy is grown, a long enmity perishes of itself when one does one's own work.
nuance: The image makes the feud a weed that dies not by being pulled but by being crowded out by the crop: tending one's own field is the whole remedy. தற்செய்ய could also mean 'when one does good to oneself'; either way the action is on one's own side, not against the enemy.

pazhamozhi.literal: a long enmity perishes of itself when one does one's own part

story.act: no story; the proverb is set beside the farmer's sight of grass dying out as the paddy grows

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned need not retaliate, since a feud starves when one simply tends one's own good

reading: Those at whom an unfit jest is aimed take it as abuse, so the jester is like the rat that carries off the lamp and brings harm on itself.
nuance: The verse comes at anger from the other side: the counsel is not to restrain one's own anger but not to rouse another's with a mocking word, which the hearer takes as reviling (வைதாரா). The rat that drags the lamp's wick sets fire to itself or its nest; the harm returns to the one who started it. Its place under வெகுளாமை rests on that reversal.

pazhamozhi.literal: a rat taking the lamp and causing harm to itself

story.act: a rat that seizes a burning lamp and is hurt by it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the one who makes an unfit jest draws the hearer's anger on himself

reading: When one hears the senseless words of those who do not understand, one should sit as if untouched, for those who try to stop the mouths of heartless strangers are like men who would lock up the public hall.
nuance: The reason given for silence is futility, not virtue: the hall (அம்பலம்) belongs to everyone and has no door to bolt, and the talk of strangers (வம்பலர்) is as open. பரியாதார் போல, 'as if not grieved', admits that the words do hurt and asks only that the hurt not be shown.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who would bar the public hall with a bolt

story.act: no story; the proverb names the absurd effort of locking a hall that stands open to all

pazhamozhi.applied_to: trying to silence the idle talk of strangers is futile, so one should sit unmoved

reading: If worthless men, having eaten their fill at the hands of one's enemies, speak lies about one for their sake, there is no cause for grief, the verse tells a woman, since what is charged is a thing one never did.
nuance: The slanderers are hirelings: கையார உண்டமையால் makes their lies a return for food given by those who bear a grudge (காய்வார்). The comfort rests on innocence alone; a true charge is left outside the counsel. The quoted words read as the end of a question (what grief is there, if it is said you did what you did not?), so the proverb is only a clause, and its sense depends on the words before it.

pazhamozhi.literal: if it is said one did what one did not do

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone falsely accused by men paid in food

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a false charge spread by hired slanderers is no cause for grief or anger

reading: The learned do not answer in heat the petty talk of those without examined knowledge, for no one gores back a cow that gores him.
nuance: The proverb ranks the unlearned speaker with a beast: the cow's butting is in its nature and returning it would make a man its equal. The image is a cow, not a hostile animal, so the fool's offence is treated as artless rather than wicked. The hill-country frame (honey licked by the monkey) is an address to the lord of the hills.

pazhamozhi.literal: if a cow gores, there are none who gore it back

story.act: no story; the proverb rests on the plain fact that no one butts back a cow

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned do not retort to the empty words of the unlearned

reading: When those who cannot bear hurtful words revile in return with their tongue, the verse tells a woman, that abuse is the way of setting fire to one's own house.
nuance: The proverb is best read as தீ இல்லை ஊட்டும் திறம், 'the way of feeding fire to the house', so the retort burns the one who makes it. Line 2's வயவுரை is unclear; the reading takes it as the reviling word returned.

pazhamozhi.literal: the manner of setting fire to a house

story.act: no story; the proverb names arson against one's own dwelling

pazhamozhi.applied_to: answering abuse with abuse destroys the one who answers

reading: To bear with and go on past those who provoked one and did one harsh things is the way to renown, while punishing them brings no gain, since nobility comes only when one endures.
nuance: The verse sets two fruits apart: renown (புகழ்) from enduring, and nothing (பயனின்றே) from punishing, though it assumes the power to punish is there (ஒறுத்தாற்றின்). The proverb then names the deeper fruit, சால்பு, as something that arrives (வரும்) of itself to one who endures. சுறுத்தாற்றி in line 1 is a rare form; the reading takes it as 'provoking'.

pazhamozhi.literal: nobility comes when one oneself endures

story.act: no story; the proverb is a maxim about how worth is gained

pazhamozhi.applied_to: forbearing toward those who harmed one, not punishing them, yields renown and nobility

title: பெரியாரைப் பிழையாமை 60-64
theme: Under the heading பெரியாரைப் பிழையாமை, five verses on offending the great: belittling them is no wisdom and leaves their standing whole, the insolence of the small is a blind walk to death, the unlearned who needle them hide behind a shrub, a repeated offence is not forgiven, and long association does not save one who strays.
source_issues: 60: Line 4 என்றூடு is obscure; the proverb's sense cannot be fixed.
61: Only a closing quotation mark is printed after வாறு; the opening mark is missing, so the proverb's start is not marked.
62: சொல்வின் in line 2 is probably சொல்லின்.

reading: To treat the great as small is neither wisdom nor grace nor even sound knowing, and it brings harm on the one who does it; a hall where the assembly once sat stays a hall even if it is cut into.
nuance: The verse denies the slight three goods in a row (அறிவு, அழகு, அறிவது) before naming its cost (பாடு). The proverb is hard: on the reading taken here, மன்று is the assembly's hall, and its standing survives damage, so the great keep their greatness even when diminished or slighted. Line 4's என்றூடு is obscure, and the proverb could also mean that a quarrel (ஊடு) broken off still leaves the assembly a place of judgement.

pazhamozhi.literal: the place where the assembly sat is still the assembly hall even if it is cut through

story.act: no story; the proverb's hall stands for anyone whose standing does not end when it is damaged or slighted

pazhamozhi.applied_to: belittling the great does not make them small and only harms the one who belittles

reading: For small men to stand before the great, say a scoffing 'is that so?' and keep behaving with insolent boldness of their own accord is like a man with his senses confused, not knowing his way, who walks into a town and does not see the place where he will die.
nuance: ஆமாலோ is the small man's mock assent, the tone of the insolence rather than an argument. The verse makes the offender blind rather than wicked: his fault is that he cannot see where he is going. Only the closing quotation mark is printed, so the proverb's start is not fixed; it is taken here as lines 3 and 4.

pazhamozhi.proverb: போமாறு அறியாப் புலன்மயங்கி ஊர்புக்குச் சாமாகண் காணாத வாறு
pazhamozhi.literal: like one who, not knowing the road and with senses dazed, enters a town and does not see where he will die

story.act: no story; a dazed traveller who walks into the place of his death without seeing it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the insolence of the small toward the great is a blind walk to their own death

reading: For people of no learning to provoke the great, who excel in every respect, is, the verse tells a woman with full bangles, like hiding behind an erukku bush and driving an elephant to charge.
nuance: கைப்பித்தல், to make bitter, names the offence as needling rather than open attack, and the proverb answers it: the provoker thinks himself covered, but the erukku is a thin shrub no elephant notices. The verse sets the unlearned against the great, so the greatness here is chiefly of learning (எல்லாத் திறத்தும்). சொல்வின் in line 2 is read as சொல்லின்.

pazhamozhi.literal: hiding behind an erukku shrub and setting an elephant charging

story.act: no story; one who goads an elephant from behind a flimsy shrub that will not hide him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the unlearned who needle the great trust a cover that cannot save them

reading: The verse asks, of the lord of a watered town where bees hum like a sweet-toned yaazh, whether anyone will bear with a man who has erred once before and errs again, greatly; does a plantain bear a bunch twice?
nuance: The question form expects 'no': forbearance is spent on the first offence. The proverb is apt because the plantain bears its one bunch and is cut down, so the second offence finds nothing left to give. The subject of பொறுப்பவோ is unstated; under the heading it is the great.

pazhamozhi.literal: does the plantain put out a bunch twice?

story.act: no story; the plantain that fruits once and is spent

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the great forgive a fault once, not a repeated one

reading: When the great see that those who have long been with them have left the right way, they tremble and are greatly pained, says the verse to the lord of a shore grove decked with adumbu creepers; the house of one who acts crookedly will perish.
nuance: நெடுங்காலம் வந்தார் makes the offenders long-standing dependents or associates, not strangers, and the great respond with dread and grief rather than anger; the ruin in the proverb follows the crooked man's own conduct. நலிவார் can also be transitive, 'they will greatly afflict them', which would make the great the agents of the ruin; the reading cannot be fixed.

pazhamozhi.literal: the house of one given to crooked conduct will surely perish

story.act: no story; the proverb names a type, the man of crooked ways and his family line

pazhamozhi.applied_to: long association with the great does not save one who strays from their way

title: புகழ்தலின் கூறுபாடு 65-68
theme: Under the heading புகழ்தலின் கூறுபாடு, four verses on praise given out of place: praising oneself before the work is done, accepting praise even from one's own people, praising boasters who have nothing to boast of, and withholding the good word from a poor kinsman set apart among many kin.

source_issues.issue: Line 2 (மெய்யா உணரவும் தாம்படார்) construes poorly; the reading is tentative.
பார்த்துறான் in line 1 is obscure and may be corrupt; lines 1-3 have loose syntax.
Parenthesised letters in அமரா(து) (66) and நோயின்(று) (67) are editorial restorations of elided sounds.

reading: When the work they undertook has not come off even a little and they cannot yet know its outcome truly, people who praise themselves as having reached full success are like those who say they will sell at a fraction the birds still in the field.
nuance: The fault is timing as much as vanity: the praise runs ahead of a deed not yet accomplished, so it is a claim on a result that may never come, as birds in the field are not yet anyone's to sell. Line 2 (மெய்யா உணரவும் தாம்படார்) is hard to construe; it is read here as 'they have not come to know it truly', i.e. the outcome is still unknown.

pazhamozhi.literal: saying 'we will sell, at an eighth of the price, the birds that are still out in the field'

story.act: no story; the proverb is the boast of a seller who prices birds he has not caught

pazhamozhi.applied_to: self-praise before the work is done is a sale of what one does not yet have

reading: Even when it is one's own people who praise one, one should not settle into it but push it away, the verse tells the man of the bamboo hills, for those who wear ornaments do not put on jewels that do not fit them even if the jewels are their own.
nuance: The proverb turns on தமவேனும்: the jewels are one's own as the praisers are one's own kin (தமர்), and ownership does not make either fit. Praise is treated as something worn, to be refused when it does not sit on the wearer's measure. The address வெற்ப is the akam vocative for a hill chief, used here without any love situation.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who adorn themselves do not wear ornaments that will not fit them, even when the ornaments are their own

story.act: no story; the proverb is the ordinary practice of anyone dressing in jewels

pazhamozhi.applied_to: praise from one's own kin is to be refused when it does not fit

reading: To extol those who have no eminence from mother or father yet speak themselves up with the mouth, though it does no harm, is like calling the dog that curls up at the edge of the hearth a tiger.
nuance: The verse blames the praiser, not only the boaster: the one who echoes a hollow self-report names a hearth dog a tiger. It concedes that the flattery is harmless (நோயின்று), so the fault is falsity and absurdity, not injury. மிகவின்றி with தாயானும் தந்தையாலானும் is read as 'without distinction through either parent'; it could also mean 'not much esteemed even by their own mother and father', which makes the boasters people even their parents do not rate.

pazhamozhi.literal: saying of the dog that lies curled at the hearth's edge that it is a tiger

story.act: no story; the proverb names a timid house dog given a tiger's name

pazhamozhi.applied_to: praising self-proclaimed men of no standing gives a great name to a small thing

reading: A man among his many kin who does not attend to one of them, does not know him well, and keeps him apart because he is poor, like one who in speaking holds back the generous word from him, commits the painful wrong of drawing a line within a single row.
nuance: The proverb pictures a row (நிரை), most naturally a line of kin seated to eat or gathered together, within which one is marked off; the wrong is the partiality inside a body that should be one. The verse fits its heading on praise through line 3: the poor kinsman is denied the good word (வளவியசொல்) the others get. பார்த்துறான் in line 1 is obscure; it is read as 'does not look to him', and the syntax of lines 1-3 is loose.

pazhamozhi.literal: a distinction drawn within the row is painful

story.act: no story; the proverb names any line of people in which one is set apart

pazhamozhi.applied_to: singling out a poor kinsman for lesser regard among kin is a wrong

title: சான்றோர் இயல்பு 69-80
theme: Under the heading சான்றோர் இயல்பு, twelve verses on the nature of the worthy: their worth shines through ruin, poverty and mud and is seen by the discerning; they keep their station in hunger, do not covet, give with knowing folly, speak no wounding word in company, judge their own hidden faults, shun slanderers, and pay for their height, since their faults are seen far and remembered long.
source_issues: 77 line 1: the site's text lacks this line (தீப்பால் வினையினைத் தீரவும் அஞ்சாராய்க்); the reading follows the line as printed in our text.
69 line 3: தாறாப் is obscure, and the quotation marks open at தாறாப் படினும், taking in the counsel with the proverb.
73 line 2: மற்றொன றறிவாரின் lacks a pulli (probably மற்றொன்று அறிவாரின்).
76 line 2: தனக்குத் கரியாவான் has a doubled consonant that should probably be தனக்குக் கரியாவான்.
71 line 2: கூடம் மரத்திற்குத் துப்பாகும் is compressed and its construction uncertain.

reading: Like a peerless gem that will not let the ash heaped over it cling and shows apart in its own brightness, the leading man, even when he is brought low, has a light of his own that matches a hundred thousand men.
nuance: The gem image says two things at once: the covering does not stick, and the shine is the gem's own, not lent by its setting. தாறாப் படினும் is obscure; it is read here as 'even if he falls into a reduced state', which the ash image supports, but the word cannot be fixed. The quotation marks take in the whole of lines 3-4, so the counsel and the proverb are one sentence.

pazhamozhi.proverb: தாறாப் படினும் தலைமகன் தன்னொளி நூறா யிரவர்க்கு நேர்
pazhamozhi.literal: even when he is brought down, a leader's own light is equal to a hundred thousand

story.act: no story; the proverb itself names the type, the foremost man whose worth outweighs a crowd

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worth of the noble shows through any covering of low fortune

reading: Even when they have fallen into want, the exalted keep to the station they stood in, as a tiger, though famine-hunger torments it greatly, will not graze on grass.
nuance: The tiger does not refuse food; it refuses food beneath its kind. So the verse's point is not abstinence but keeping one's station: poverty may take the meal, it does not make the high stoop to what is low.

pazhamozhi.literal: however great its hunger, the tiger does not graze on grass

story.act: no story; the proverb is the tiger's nature taken as an instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the exalted hold to their standing in poverty

reading: As, when a mansion falls, its hall timber serves to raise another, so the great remain of great worth even when they have lost their standing, for what has no substance has no worth.
nuance: The image is of salvage: the house is gone but its timber is still good building stuff, so ruin strips the great of position, not of use. The proverb is read as ஈடு 'substance, strength' and பாடு 'worth, standing'; பாடு can also mean suffering or loss, which would give 'what has no substance has nothing to lose', and the verse's sense depends on the choice. கூடம் மரத்திற்குத் துப்பாகும் is compressed and the line's construction is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: to that which has no substance there is no worth

story.act: no story; the proverb states a rule of worth, read against the timber of a fallen mansion

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the great keep their worth when their status is gone, because it lay in their substance

reading: Whatever befalls those who rose high, the discerning recognise them as what they are, lord of the lovely hills, for to those who know, a gem stays a gem though it has rolled in the mire.
nuance: The weight falls on the knower, not the gem: உணர்பவர், உணர்வார்க்கு. Worth survives the mire only for an eye that can see it, so the verse is as much about discernment as about the noble. இணரோங்கி, read here as 'risen high, flourishing', is uncertain; it may refer to lineage.

pazhamozhi.literal: even when it has wallowed in mud, a gem turns out a gem

story.act: no story; the proverb is the gem in the mud

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the discerning see the noble's worth through any misfortune

reading: Even if they have learnt nothing, the well-born are far better than those who know other things, and there is no need to go and speak finely to them, for nobody sells sewing needles in the smiths' street.
nuance: The verse grants the well-born a knowledge that does not come by learning: to instruct them is to bring needles to the street where needles are made. It ranks lineage above schooling. குடிப்பிறந்தார் is a word of lineage rank, not of a named birth-group. Line 2 is read as மற்றொன்று அறிவாரின் 'than those who know something else'; as printed the line lacks a pulli and the comparison could also be 'they know another thing (of their own)'.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who sells sewing needles in the smiths' street

story.act: no story; the proverb is the trader who would bring wares to the place that makes them

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the well-born need no instruction, having what it would teach

norm.note: a claim of the period that high lineage carries worth and knowledge without learning

reading: We have heard tell of those of old who gave a chariot to a jasmine creeper and a mantle to a peacock, lord of the shore of long waters where the pandanus flowers, and so, by that account, even foolishness done knowingly is an ornament to the worthy.
nuance: The verse does not deny that the gifts were foolish: a creeper cannot ride and a peacock is not cold. It calls the folly an ornament because it was knowing (அறி-மடம்), the act of a giver who saw the absurdity and gave anyway out of pity. The verse names neither giver.

pazhamozhi.literal: even knowing foolishness is an ornament to the worthy

story.act: givers of old who gave a chariot to a jasmine creeper and a mantle to a peacock
story.tradition: by tradition Pari (the chariot to the creeper) and Pekan (the mantle to the peacock); the verse names neither

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the givers' excessive gifts were knowing folly and so adorned them

reading: In the midst of an assembly of many, the worthy who keep to the right part will not say to anyone a word that lodges deep within, for, even if it were the tall one who guarded the herds of cattle, one who speaks will be spoken back to.
nuance: The restraint is argued from consequence, not from kindness: a wounding word in company draws a reply, and no rank, not even a god's, exempts the speaker. நிரைப்புறங் காத்த நெடியோன் points to Mal as the herdsman; the verse does not say which retort he received, and the proverb may simply set the highest case.

pazhamozhi.literal: if one speaks, one gets speech in return

story.act: even the tall one who guarded the herds of cattle would be answered if he spoke so
story.tradition: by tradition Krishna as the herdsman form of Mal; the episode of his being answered is not told

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a wounding word in an assembly brings a retort on any speaker, however great

reading: Looking only to the thought 'this is not fitting for me', being himself his own witness, the southern king thought on his fault and cut off his own hand, while it is those who think 'no one will see' who do unworthy deeds.
nuance: The proverb is a foil: it names the ignoble motive, secrecy, that the king's act refutes. He was unseen, there was no accuser, and he still judged and punished himself, so the standard is internal (எனக்குத் தகவன்று), not the fear of being seen. The counsel is general, the example a king's.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who did unworthy deeds did them thinking 'they will not see'

story.act: the Pandya king, judging his own fault with himself as witness, cut off his own hand
story.tradition: by tradition Porkai Pandiyan, who cut off the hand that had knocked at a house's door at night; the verse names only தென்னவன்

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy judge their own faults though no one has seen them

reading: Before deceivers who have no fear at all of evil deeds and who speak lies and slander as if they were guarding one's interest, the worthy do not join in their words but turn away without fail, like a crow from a bow.
nuance: The slanderer's cover is concern (காப்பாரே போன்று): he backbites as if protecting the listener. The crow does not argue with the bow; it is gone at the sight of it. So the worthy do not refute such talk, they withdraw from it.

pazhamozhi.literal: like the crow with the bow

story.act: no story; the proverb is the crow's flight at the sight of a bow

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy at once withdraw from slanderers who pose as protectors

reading: Even when hunger bends them double, the worthy do not set about desiring what belongs to others, lord of the great sea's shore where birds may nest in the palmyra fronds, for the sea and the forest never meet.
nuance: The proverb makes the separation a fact of nature, not an effort: the worthy and another's goods are as far apart as sea and forest. The shore with birds nesting in the palm fronds may hint that each kind has its own place.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no joining of the sea with the forest

story.act: no story; the proverb is the fixed separation of sea and forest

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy do not covet others' goods even in hunger

reading: Faults in the exalted never pass out of talk, as the talk that clings to long-armed Mal who held women of rowed bangles never ends, lord of the hills where the wild cow suckles its calf, like the brand burnt on the back of a grey bull, which never fades.
nuance: The brand fades from no hide, but it shows most on a pale one: the grey bull, like the exalted, carries the mark visibly and for good. The Mal clause is hard: நிரைதொடி தாங்கிய is read as his holding (embracing) bangled women, the herding-god's dalliance, an old story that is never let drop; the episode cannot be fixed from the words.

pazhamozhi.literal: the brand set on the back of a grey bull, which does not fade

story.act: the talk about long-armed Mal and the bangled women he held is never dropped
story.tradition: by tradition Krishna among the herding women; the verse gives no more than the phrase

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a fault in the exalted is spoken of forever

reading: Though the small commit for many days faults grown hard and ripe, nothing at all ever shows in them, but a fault that befalls the exalted, even a single one, is a lamp set on a hill.
nuance: The verse is a contrast of visibility, not of guilt: the small man's many matured faults pass unseen, the great man's one is seen from everywhere. It does not say the small are better off morally, only that height exposes.

pazhamozhi.literal: a lamp placed on a hill

story.act: no story; the proverb is the lamp on the hilltop, seen from all around

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a single fault of the exalted is seen by all, while the many faults of the small go unseen

title: சான்றோர் செய்கை 81-89
theme: Under the heading சான்றோர் செய்கை, nine verses on how the worthy act: they keep up ஒப்புரவு in want, even by borrowing, speak truth though beholden, do not cast off those they took in or friends who prove faulty, pity an enemy in distress, and, though great by birth, depend on and keep company with the lesser; their poverty outranks the wealth of the small.
source_issues: 87: the proverb தால அடைக்கலமே போன்று is obscure as printed; தால may be corrupt, and the sense of the closing image cannot be fixed from the text.

reading: The worthy man born into a house that practises ஒப்புரவு goes on doing it even when he has no earned wealth, and though no one tends him and he grazes where there is no grass, he grows into what his house is, as a bull's calf becomes a bull.
nuance: The proverb puts the weight on birth over nurture: the calf is neither cared for nor fed and still becomes a bull. The verse does not say the man earns again; it says the habit of the house survives the loss of the means.

pazhamozhi.literal: a bull's calf turns into a bull

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the man of a giving house who is poor and untended

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the habit of helping others, inherited from the house, outlasts poverty and neglect

reading: Even when they are crushed into want and cannot manage, the worthy do not sit back thinking they will see to it when a chance comes; they do what is due even if they must borrow to do it.
nuance: The proverb turns on கடன், which is both debt and duty: the worthy take on a debt (கடங்கொண்டும்) to pay a duty (கடன்). Line 2 names the excuse they refuse, putting off the act until a better time.

pazhamozhi.literal: the worthy will do their duty even by taking a loan

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the worthy man in want

pazhamozhi.applied_to: want is no ground for postponing what one owes others

reading: The verse asks what can be said for those who, in a crowded battle, carry the enemy's lies in their mouths and go over in treachery, and answers that the worthy speak the truth even when they have eaten from another's hand.
nuance: கையுண்டும் most plausibly means having eaten at someone's hand, that is, being beholden to him, so the worthy are not bought by what they have received; it could also be read as having taken something into the hand, a bribe. Lines 1 and 2 are compressed and the sense of அறைபோய் as going over in treachery is a reading.
domain_note: men serving in war, set against traitors

pazhamozhi.literal: the worthy speak the truth even after eating from someone's hand

story.act: no story; the proverb is set against the traitor in battle who repeats the enemy's lie

pazhamozhi.applied_to: being beholden does not bend the worthy man's truth, as it bends the traitor's

reading: The verse says there is no question of 'there' or 'here': those who have taken in people who came to them do not then cast them off as worthless, any more than anyone who has strapped on a drum has gone away without beating it.
nuance: The argument rests on a commitment once taken up: the drum, once worn, is beaten. Lines 1 and 2 are a rhetorical question whose subject is unstated, and ஆண்டீண்டு may mean 'in this place or that' or 'this world or the next'; the reading takes மாண்டிலார் as 'people without worth', the excuse for disowning.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one who put on a drum has gone off without beating it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who has taken in those who sought him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a protection once given is not withdrawn by calling the protected unworthy

reading: The worthy do not turn against those they have cherished even if those people lack good qualities, for feeding the friends one made in the sight of the whole village is a duty.
nuance: The proverb makes the bond public: the friendship was made where the village could see (ஊரறிய), so dropping it would break a pledge others witnessed, not only a private feeling. The verse grants the friends' faults outright.

pazhamozhi.literal: is it not a duty to feed those one befriended before the village
