story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the worthy man whose friends prove of poor character

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friendship made openly binds even when the friend proves unworthy

reading: When the better sort see a plain enemy in distress they still show him kindly regard, even if he is of a kind that does harm, for a snake brought into the assembly of the worthy does not die.
nuance: The case is the hardest one: the enemy is open (தெற்றப் பகைவர்) and still dangerous (நவைக்கப் படுந்தன்மைத்து), and the moment is his weakness, when killing him would be easy. The snake is the image for such a man.

pazhamozhi.literal: a snake that comes before the assembly of the worthy does not die

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the dangerous enemy who falls into the good man's power

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy spare and pity even a harmful enemy in distress

reading: The verse says those far above others by birth, not thinking it too great a lowering, go to those small by birth and live in reliance on them, like a தால shelter.
nuance: பிறப்பிற் சிறியார் and பிறப்பினால் மிக்கவர் rank people by birth; the verse takes the ranking as given and praises the high-born for setting it aside when they need shelter. The proverb is obscure: தாலம் may be the palmyra, a plate, or the earth, and I cannot fix what a தால அடைக்கலம் was. Whether the verse praises humility or reports necessity is read from the heading.

pazhamozhi.literal: like a தால refuge (sense not fixed)

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the high-born who take refuge with the low-born

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the high-born are not shamed by depending on those below them by birth

norm.note: a birth-rank of the period: people ranked as great or small by birth, taken as given

reading: The verse says that when those born in great families conduct themselves as kin with those lesser than they, it is the way the string is joined to the flower.
nuance: The image leaves the gain mostly with the lesser party, the string that is carried with the flower, though the garland needs both. The phrase சிறியார் இனமாய் ஒழுகுதல் could also be read the other way, the lesser keeping company as kin of the great; the reading follows the heading. குடி here ranks families by birth.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way string is joined with flowers

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to great families who take lesser people into their company

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the great raise the lesser by joining them, as a flower lends itself to its string

norm.note: family rank of the period: great and small houses ranked by birth, taken as given

reading: The poverty of the great is better than the wealth the small have come by, which is a thing to be ashamed of, for old ghee never becomes worse than buttermilk.
nuance: The proverb concedes that the ghee is old, that is, that the great have declined, and holds that what they are still ranks above the fresh but lesser thing. நாண attaches shame to the small men's wealth, not to the poverty.

pazhamozhi.literal: old ghee is never worse than buttermilk

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the great man fallen poor beside the small man grown rich

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the declined worth of the great still outranks the wealth of the small

title: கீழ்மக்கள் இயல்பு 90-106
theme: Under the heading கீழ்மக்கள் இயல்பு, seventeen verses argue that the base cannot be changed: good company, instruction, a ruler's grant, punishment, favour and wealth all leave them as they were, and the wise neither trust them, counsel them nor honour them in place of the great. Three verses (96, 103, 106) tie baseness to a way of life, a line of descent or family rank.
source_issues: 92 line 4: நந்துழுத may be divided நம் உழுத or நந்து உழுத; the proverb's sense depends on it.
98 lines 3-4: துடும்பல் is obscure and the proverb's image is uncertain.
99 lines 1-2: the syntax is loose and the sense of the counsel is uncertain.
101 lines 1-2: the word division of அலப்பின் அலவாக்கால் and சிதைத்தெழுப is uncertain.
106 line 4: the quotation marks enclose the main clause (கூதறைகள் ஆகார் குடி) and may be editorial.

reading: The roaring sea does not lose its salt though great floods of fresh water pour into it, and in the same way the base never come to goodness of mind, however good the company they keep.
nuance: Lines 3-4 turn the wording of a familiar couplet inside out: இனநலம் நன்குடைய ராயினும் ... மனநலம் ஆகா, good company in full, and still no good mind. The image is chosen against the idea that water takes on the nature of what it meets: the sea takes in the river and stays salt.

pazhamozhi.literal: the base never become good of mind

story.act: no story; the proverb states the nature of the base as a type, matched by the salt sea

pazhamozhi.applied_to: good company cannot reform the base

reading: Those who have joined the worthy and live as their own people do not go over to the small, even when the small are said to be superior, for, as the verse asks the lord of the fertile town of cranes, can anyone eat sand that has jaggery mixed into it?
nuance: The proverb grants the small some sweetness (அக்காரம்) and still calls them sand: a little attraction does not make the mixture fit to take in. மிக்காரால் என்று is compressed; it may mean 'thinking them great' or 'because others say they are great'.

pazhamozhi.literal: can sand mixed with jaggery be eaten?

story.act: no story; the proverb is an image of something sweetened but still inedible

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those settled among the worthy do not take up with the small, whatever is said for them

reading: The verse asks whether the angry men of cruel work can do what those whose character is to do their own proper work do, and answers with the proverb that not everything ploughed counts as a harvest.
nuance: நந்துழுத can be divided நம் உழுத, 'what we ploughed', or நந்து உழுத, 'what the snail ploughed'; on the second, the snail's trail looks like a furrow and is not one, which suits the contrast between the base and the worthy better. Either way the claim is that the look of work is not its yield.

pazhamozhi.literal: can all that is (snail-)ploughed be counted as ploughing?

story.act: no story; the proverb is a ploughing image whose sense depends on how நந்துழுத is divided

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the cruel and angry cannot do what those of proper character do

reading: There are trees that flower and bear no fruit, people who grow old and still do not understand well, and seeds that do not sprout though sown in a prepared bed, and so for a fool understanding does not appear however much he is told.
nuance: The verse stacks three failures of growth, flower without fruit, age without understanding, seed without sprout, so that telling the fool is the fourth sowing that comes to nothing. The human case sits in the middle of the plant images: old age is treated as a season that may pass without yield.

pazhamozhi.literal: though told, understanding does not appear

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the fool as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: instruction cannot produce understanding in a fool

reading: The verse says not to speak anything to the stubborn who grasp neither reasoned thought nor the ways of the world, since such a man keeps hold of what he has taken up and will not let it go, as cloth that has drunk indigo will not take another colour.
nuance: The image puts the fault in a first impression that has set: the மூர்க்கன் is not empty but already dyed, so new words have nothing to take on.

pazhamozhi.literal: what has drunk indigo does not become anything else

story.act: no story; the proverb is a dyeing image applied to the obstinate as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: it is useless to counsel the obstinate, who hold to what they first took up

reading: Once you have plainly seen a man speak evil, the verse says, do not trust him from then on, for such people behave badly whoever they are, as neem is bitter even if the gods eat it.
nuance: The proverb places the bitterness in the neem, not the eater: even the highest company does not sweeten it. So the one evil word seen is taken as evidence of a nature, not of a lapse.

pazhamozhi.literal: neem is bitter even if the gods themselves eat it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the evil-speaker as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one seen speaking evil should not be trusted again, whatever his standing

reading: Men of the forest life, of cruel deeds, do not behave well even if they are granted a place to live in the settled country, as a quail kept in the hand every day still has its mind on the field.
nuance: செய் in the proverb is the field the quail came from: captivity and daily handling do not move its mind. The verse ranks a people by its way of life (காடுறை வாழ்க்கை) and its work (கருவினை), and denies that settlement changes them; whether it means forest peoples as a group or only those of cruel deeds among them, the Tamil does not settle.
domain_note: the lord who grants them a place to live in his country

pazhamozhi.literal: the quail's mind stays on the field

story.act: no story; the proverb is a captive-bird image applied to the forest men as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: granting settled land does not change those of forest life and cruel deeds

norm.note: a ranking of the period: forest dwellers of cruel work are held unable to be reformed by settlement

reading: The lowest, of black deeds, do not care about the great blame that falls on them, lord of the shore where the great punnai drives off the stink of fish, just as some will eat without fear in a house of weeping.
nuance: The proverb's eater at a house of mourning is shameless rather than cruel: he does what the occasion forbids because the opinion of others has no hold on him. The shore frame sets the punnai's scent against the fish smell, a cleansing the base never receive.

pazhamozhi.literal: eating without fear where there is weeping

story.act: no story; the proverb names the shameless act of eating at a house of mourning

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the base are untouched by the blame they incur

reading: When men have done a very great wrong and do not know the fitting way to make it good, their trying to stand out is, as the verse tells the lord of the shore where the adumbu flowers on the sand, like throwing water from a small dish at a great blaze.
nuance: The sense turns on துடும்பல் and on what தலைசிறத்தல் does here; the reading takes the proverb as a remedy too small for the harm. அகலுள் நீர் may also be the water in a lamp-bowl. Both the image and the counsel are offered tentatively.

pazhamozhi.literal: throwing (at) a துடும்பல் with the water in a small bowl

story.act: no story; the proverb is an image of an inadequate remedy, as far as its rare word allows

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a great wrong is not undone by small or showy amends

reading: Those who could not repay their unworthy enemies take delight, as if a victory had come to them, on hearing the words others speak without regard, and though this gives them nothing to eat or drink, theirs is the drunkenness of one who has not even seen the toddy.
nuance: The syntax of lines 1-2 is loose; the reading takes the base man's joy to come from others' slander of his enemy, an empty gain he could not win himself. The proverb mocks intoxication without the drink.

pazhamozhi.literal: the elation of one drunk without seeing the toddy

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the base man's borrowed triumph

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the base rejoice in what does them no good and is not their own doing

reading: To go on doing evil afterwards as if one wanted to, though one has seen that one was punished with no regard to one's labours, is, lord of the cool sea shore where the broad-faced drum sounds, like a thing that grows a span for every cubit cut from it.
nuance: முழம் குறைப்ப சாண் நீளும்: cut a cubit and it grows back a span. Punishment trims the base man's wrongdoing but does not stop its growth. The verse does not name who is punished; the heading makes it the base.

pazhamozhi.literal: as a span grows back when a cubit is cut

story.act: no story; the proverb is an image of regrowth after cutting

pazhamozhi.applied_to: punishment does not cure the base of wrongdoing

reading: The unlearned base do wrong if they are harassed, and if they are not, not knowing where to go, they spoil things and rise up, as for the jackal there is no good year or bad year for food.
nuance: The reading takes அலப்பின் as 'if pressed' and அலவாக்கால் as 'if not pressed': the base do harm in either case, as the jackal feeds on carrion in famine and plenty alike. The division of lines 1-2 is uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: for the jackal food is no different in a good year or a bad one

story.act: no story; the proverb is a jackal image applied to the base

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the base do wrong whether they are pressed or left alone

reading: The verse asks whether there are any fools whose names go unknown among those who refuse the good words from the mouths of the keen-minded and, leaning on their dark understanding, do harsh things, and answers that there is no bull the village does not know.
nuance: The proverb's மூரி is the rogue bull that every villager has learnt to step around: the fool's harsh deeds make him notorious, so his folly is public, not private.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no bull the village does not know

story.act: no story; the proverb is a village image of the notorious rogue

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the fool who rejects wise counsel and acts harshly becomes known to all

reading: Among all the low who come down in a continuous line, search as one may, those of good character do not appear, lord of the mountain land of groves thick with trees, for among monkeys there is none with a fine face.
nuance: நிரந்து வழிவந்த நீசர் is a claim about descent: character is said to run in a line, and a whole line is denied any good member. நீசர் here ranks people by birth; the proverb makes the line a species.

pazhamozhi.literal: among monkeys none has a handsome face

story.act: no story; the proverb makes the base line a kind, like monkeys

pazhamozhi.applied_to: good character is not found among those of base descent

norm.note: a birth-rank claim of the period: those descended from a base line are held to have no one of good character

reading: To clear out those who are fit and raise up the base who are of no use is, the verse tells a woman of sweet lisping speech like the yaazh, like cutting down the honeyed jackfruit and planting the bitter kanjirai.
nuance: ஊழாயினார் most likely means those who are fit or of the right order; the act described (களைந்திட்டு ... பெருக்குதல்) is one of patronage, removing some and promoting others. The address to a woman is a frame and not the counsel's audience.
domain_note: a ruler or master choosing whom to raise

pazhamozhi.literal: cutting down the jackfruit and planting the kanjirai

story.act: no story; the proverb is an orchard image of exchanging a sweet tree for a bitter one

pazhamozhi.applied_to: displacing the fit to promote the base destroys what was useful

reading: To take the honour due to the great and give it instead to the small is, lord of the town where spotted bees hum on the flowers, like spreading a seat of honour for a dog.
nuance: The fault judged is the giver's: the verse does not say what the dog does with the seat, only that laying it out is absurd and takes from the great what was theirs.

pazhamozhi.literal: like spreading a seat on a dog

story.act: no story; the proverb is an image of misplaced honour

pazhamozhi.applied_to: honour meant for the great is wasted and misplaced on the small

reading: Even if one shows them great favour so that their distress is ended, and they prosper greatly without fault, the worthless do not become men of good family with minds made spotless.
nuance: The patron's favour is given in full (பெருக்கத் தலையளித்து) and their prosperity is granted as faultless, so the failure lies only in what they are. குடி here is the standing of a good house, which the verse holds cannot be conferred. The closing quotation marks enclose the clause of the main sentence; the proverb may have been marked editorially.

pazhamozhi.literal: the worthless do not become (a good) family

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the base as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: favour and prosperity do not raise the base into good family

norm.note: a rank claim of the period: the base cannot become of good family through favour or wealth

title: கீழ்மக்கள் செய்கை 107-123
theme: Under the heading கீழ்மக்கள் செய்கை, seventeen verses on the conduct of base men: their insolence to the great, their denial of the next world, the danger of helping, reforming, provoking or living with them, their self-betraying speech and backbiting past shame, their deafness to counsel, their hidden ill will and whims, and the inverted world in which they rise.
source_issues: 108 lines 2-4: the quotation opens at கண்சொரீஇ, leaving the thrown-away ghee cake of lines 2-3 outside though it is part of the proverb's image; the quotation marks may be misplaced.
111 line 3-4: வெண்மாத் தலைக்கீழாக் காதி விடல் is obscure (வெண்மா, காதி).
112 line 2: கல்எறிந்தாற் போலத் கலாந்தலை has an unexpected த் after போல; probably a typing slip for போலக்.
118 line 3: மரிசாதி is obscure, and the quotation opens mid-line at மன்றஞ்சு.

reading: Petty men who neither perceive by the right way nor have any good nature, thinking the great easy to approach, set them level with themselves and speak unfitting words, and the verse calls this a dog barking at the moon.
nuance: The proverb works in two directions: the barking is the base man's insolence, and the moon, untouched and out of reach, is the great man's standing, so the insult is shown to be both noisy and harmless. எளியர் is what the petty think of the great, not what the great are.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like a dog barking at the moon

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the petty man who speaks slightingly of the great as his equals

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the petty man's slighting of the great is empty noise that does not reach them

reading: Those who say 'is there any next world? get for yourselves all that the mind desires' are, the verse says, like people who have the cake of jaggery soaked in fragrant ghee thrown away and then, eyes streaming, feed on brick.
nuance: The image turns the materialist's offer upside down: he promises the fill of every desire, and the proverb says that what he really hands over is brick in place of a sweet, eaten in tears. The quotation marks open at கண்சொரீஇ, though the thrown-away ghee cake (lines 2-3) belongs to the same image. Whose eyes stream, the speaker's followers' or the speakers' own, the words leave open.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who, eyes streaming, feed (someone) brick

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who deny the next world and urge the fill of present desire

pazhamozhi.applied_to: denying the next world for present desire gives up a real good for a hard and painful one

reading: Those who, having read the mind of graceless base men, go close to them and do them good things without reckoning that trouble will come of it are, the verse says, plucking a tick from a tiger's face.
nuance: The good deed is real and the tick a real relief to the tiger, which is the point: the danger lies in the nature of the one helped, not in the help. கண்ணில names the lack of kindly regard (கண்ணோட்டம்) that makes them repay with harm.

pazhamozhi.literal: plucking off the tick on a tiger's face

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone who does favours for the graceless base

pazhamozhi.applied_to: kindness done to the graceless base puts the doer within reach of their harm

reading: The verse tells the listener to correct his eagerness, asking whether the wicked ever come under control just because they have suffered, for even when chopped straw is worked into it unfit clay will not become a wall.
nuance: The straw stands for the hardship or correction mixed into the base man's life; the clay, not the binder, decides whether a wall stands. ஆர்வம் is the hope of reforming them, and the opening imperative turns the verse on the would-be reformer rather than the wicked.

pazhamozhi.literal: clay that does not bind will not make a wall

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the hope that suffering will reform the wicked

pazhamozhi.applied_to: hardship does not make the wicked tractable, because the fault is in their nature

reading: Men small by lineage, going in to settle a quarrel, rise up even against those who would part the fighters, and the verse likens this to white flour that, beaten to settle it firm on the ground, turns over and spills.
nuance: குலத்துச் சிறியார் is a birth term: it ranks people by the family they come from and lays the quarrelsome temper on that birth, though it could also mean those who are the mean ones of a family. The proverb is obscure; வெண்மா may be white flour or a pale animal, and காதி விடல் is taken here as spilling. The sense that the attempt to calm only overturns things is fairly secure; the image's detail is not.

pazhamozhi.literal: the white flour turning upside down and spilling

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the low-born peacemaker who turns on the peacemakers

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the base sent to calm a quarrel only overturn it further

norm.note: a birth-rank view of the period: quarrelsomeness is attributed to those of small lineage

reading: To keep in one's house, and to anger greatly, those who contradict what they are told, will not live in obedience, and take up a quarrel like a thrown stone is, the verse says, to pull out the axle-pin oneself while sitting inside the cart.
nuance: இல்இருந்து and உள்ளிருந்து answer each other: the defiant are inside the house as the rider is inside the cart, so the ruin is self-made and falls on the one who provokes them. The verse does not forbid keeping such men; it is the provoking (முனிவித்தல்) of them at close quarters that the proverb condemns.
domain_note: the head of a house and its unruly dependants

pazhamozhi.literal: like pulling out the axle-pin oneself from inside

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who provokes the defiant within his own house

pazhamozhi.applied_to: provoking the quarrelsome among one's own household undoes oneself

reading: To look after senseless people who know no shame, feel for no one, do worthless things and cherish nothing, to guide them and live together with them is, the verse says, like putting worms into a wound and binding it up.
nuance: The image makes the harm one's own care: the bandage that should heal the wound seals in what eats it. பேணி and ஒழுக்கி say the companion is not only tolerated but fostered.

pazhamozhi.literal: like putting in worms and binding up a wound

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who shelters and lives with the shameless

pazhamozhi.applied_to: fostering and living with the shameless lets the harm grow under one's own care

reading: The fool who speaks evil words and goes about hiding brings sorrow on himself by his own speech, the verse tells a good lady, as even the frog sunk and hidden in the sand perishes by its own mouth.
nuance: The frog's croak betrays its hiding place, so the proverb joins the two things the verse says of the fool: he hides, and he speaks, and the second undoes the first. The address நல்லாய்! is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: even a frog perishes by its own mouth

story.act: no story; the frog in the sand, betrayed by its croak, stands for the hidden man betrayed by his words

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the fool's own speech undoes the concealment he relies on

reading: Why blame those who speak well like kin when they meet a man and slander him behind his back when he has gone, having no eye for anything higher, since in any case for one whose nose is already cut off there is no further disgrace.
nuance: The verse does not excuse the backbiter; it says blame cannot touch him, because a man already disfigured has nothing left to lose by reproach. புறனழீஇ is the Kural's own word for backbiting (182).

pazhamozhi.literal: for one who has lost his nose there is no disgrace

story.act: no story; the noseless man, past disfigurement, is applied to the backbiter past shame

pazhamozhi.applied_to: reproach is wasted on the backbiter, who is already beyond shame

reading: It is hard to restrain with the tongue the qualityless brutes who speak unstrung words, lord of the shore where ships sway like drunkards, for no one catches the wind and puts it into a leather bag.
nuance: மாக்கள், not மக்கள், puts such men among beasts. The proverb gives the reason talk cannot curb them: their words are wind, which has no body to be held. The swaying ships of the address echo the unsteady talkers.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one catches the wind and puts it in a skin bag

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the attempt to silence loose talkers with words

pazhamozhi.applied_to: speech cannot restrain those whose speech has no substance

reading: Those who do not mind that the ignorant speak and that incapacity is bad, who do useless things, will not take the words of the great and do not guard themselves, are, the verse says, the ones who make others into thieves.
nuance: The proverb shifts the blame for a theft onto the careless owner: the man who leaves himself unguarded has made the thief. Line 1 is loosely joined; தெரியாதார் சொல்லும் திறனின்மை may be the ignorant man's talk and his want of skill taken together.

pazhamozhi.literal: they make others into thieves

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who will not heed the great or guard himself

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the man who will not take counsel and guard himself invites the harm others do him

reading: One who has done a cruelty and will not speak so that its consequence may come to him sits wasting in distress, and the verse closes that for those who fear the public hall there is no remedy at all.
nuance: The proverb seems to say that the wrongdoer who will not face the assembly (மன்று) where wrongs are judged cuts himself off from the only remedy; dread of being judged keeps the cruelty unhealed. மரிசாதி is obscure, and the reading of lines 1-3 is tentative.

pazhamozhi.literal: for those who fear the assembly there is no remedy whatever

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the wrongdoer who will not bring his deed before the hall

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wrongdoer who shuns judgement has no way to make amends

reading: The wicked conduct of the common run of people, who unlike the elders deserve scorn, is, lord of the good land where streams fall from the hill, like madness settled in the village hall.
nuance: The village hall (மன்றம்) is the most public place there is, so the proverb seems to say the base man's misconduct is open, settled and seen by all, not hidden. மன்னும் may mean 'lasting' or be an expletive; the contrast with முதுமக்கள் is not developed.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like madness settled in the common hall

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the misconduct of common, scornworthy people

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the misconduct of the base is a standing public disorder

reading: Those who behave arrogantly and do unfitting things, who do uncaring things after being highly esteemed, and who vex others with a concealing heart are, the verse says, the gravel caught in a sandal.
nuance: The gravel is small, inside what one wears and walks on, and hurts at every step; the image fits men who are close, honoured and hidden in their hearts, not open enemies. பெருக்க மதித்தபின் makes the injury follow on the honour done them.

pazhamozhi.literal: gravel caught within a sandal

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to arrogant, ungrateful and concealing men kept close

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the hidden ill will of those one has honoured galls at every step

reading: To set someone up as one's close man and then remove him without any gain to him is a deed fitted to smallness, and the verse likens it to little children planting a grove.
nuance: Children plant twigs in play and pull them up the same day, so the proverb names the fault as whim: installing and removing without reason. பெறுமாற்றம் இன்றி can mean without his gaining anything or without any cause found in him.

pazhamozhi.literal: little children planting a grove

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who raises a man to intimacy and drops him without cause

pazhamozhi.applied_to: casting off without cause one raised to intimacy is childish smallness

reading: When the worthy, full in speech, live withdrawn and those without self-restraint stand tall and flourish, lord of the hill where bright falls come down, that is the gourd sinking and the grinding stone floating.
nuance: The proverb is an impossibility, so the verse calls the state of things against nature, not merely unjust. The measure of rank is conduct and speech (உரைசான்ற, நிறையுளர் அல்லார்), not birth or wealth.

pazhamozhi.literal: the gourd sinking and the grinding stone floating

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a time when the worthy sink and the unrestrained rise

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the rise of the unworthy over the worthy is an inversion of nature

reading: Those who, without discernment or kindly regard and without fear of evil deeds, speak slightingly to all who come to them and do what all the skilled and accomplished hate are answered by the question whether there is no poison for the people of hell.
nuance: The proverb makes such men hell's own people; whether it means that poison is their due or that they are the poison hell holds, the words do not settle. தீர்ந்த விரகர் are those finished in skill.

pazhamozhi.literal: is there no poison for the dwellers in hell?

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to graceless men who fear no evil and slight everyone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: men without grace or fear of evil are already of hell and merit its poison

title: நட்பின் இயல்பு 124-134
theme: Under the heading நட்பின் இயல்பு, eleven verses on what friendship is: a union closer than the god's half-body, kept by taking a friend's words at their meaning, by not parting, by help in deed, by silence about and patience with faults, by telling one's want to the friend who will cure it; one verse takes friendship from anyone for its yield, and the last says the prosperous man's thousand guests vanish in ruin.

source_issues.issue: The quotation marks set the proverb in lines 1-2, at the head of the verse rather than its close; ஒட்டிய காதல் stands outside the quote, and the extent of the quoted proverb is doubtful.
The proverb ஒன்றேற்று வெண்படைக்கோள் ஒன்று is obscure and may be corrupt.
மணலைநாட in line 3 is odd for the usual address and may be a corruption of மலைநாட.
துனியால் opening the address in line 3 is unusual and may be corrupt; முனியார் in line 2 is ambiguous.
Lines 1-3 are syntactically loose; ஊர்ந்த பரிவும் is hard to construe.
நாட்டப்பட்ட டார்களைக் in line 1 has a doubled syllable, probably for நாட்டப்பட்டார்களை.
அறையார் in the address of line 3 is unclear.

reading: Those who join with friends take them, once united, as a whole body that never parts from them, for even he who bears the khatvanga and the conquering banner took Uma, joined to him in clinging love, on one side of himself.
nuance: The argument is a fortiori: the god took his consort as one half of his body, and friends take each other whole (முழுமெய்யும்), so friendship is pictured as a closer union than the divine pair. Unusually the quoted proverb opens the verse instead of closing it, and lines 3-4 draw the counsel from it.

pazhamozhi.proverb: உமையாள் ஒரு பாலக் கட்டங்கம் வெல்கொடி கொண்டானும் கொண்டானே
pazhamozhi.literal: even he of the khatvanga and the victorious banner took Uma to one side of himself

story.act: the god who bears the khatvanga and the victorious banner took Uma as one side of his body
story.tradition: identified by tradition as Siva in his half-woman form; the verse names him only by his staff and banner

pazhamozhi.applied_to: friends united take each other wholly, more than the god's half

reading: Between those who have befriended without flaw, the words one friend speaks to the other and the meaning those words reach are one, the verse tells the lord of the cool shore of winding backwaters, and to take the words up in another sense and repeat them is, as the proverb has it, to accept one thing and take up the white blade as another.
nuance: The fault is put on the hearer, not the speaker: a friend's words are to be taken at the meaning he intends, and re-telling them in a twisted sense is a betrayal. The proverb's sense is not secure; ஒன்றேற்று வெண்படைக்கோள் ஒன்று is read here as 'accepting is one act, seizing the bright weapon another', a picture of seeming agreement turned into attack.

pazhamozhi.literal: taking up one thing and the seizing of the white weapon is another

story.act: no story; the proverb sets an act of acceptance against the drawing of a weapon

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to twist a true friend's words when repeating them is to turn agreement into attack

reading: Even beasts desire to dwell with those who live with them, and abandoning those one has mingled with is not fitting, the verse tells the lord of the land where bright cascades spread down over the sand, for parting is painful even from a demon.
nuance: The proverb makes the pain of parting independent of the friend's worth: if separation from a பேய் hurts, the hurt is in the bond itself, not in the goodness of the one left. Lines 1-2 are close in wording to Naladiyar 76 (கலந்தாரைக் கைவிடுதல், விலங்கு).

pazhamozhi.literal: parting is painful even from a demon

story.act: no story; the proverb names the least lovable companion

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a bond once formed should not be broken, since parting hurts whatever the companion

reading: The means of removing the distress that has come upon dear ones is not accomplished by words, even when it is offered without grudging, the verse tells the lord of the deep-watered shore where waves roll restlessly, for a tank is never filled by dew.
nuance: Kind words are not denied value, only sufficiency: dew is real water and still fills no tank. முனியார் செயினும் is read as 'even if done without vexation'; it may instead refer to the dear ones themselves, and துனியால் in line 3 is an odd opening for the address.

pazhamozhi.literal: a tank does not fill with dew

story.act: no story; the proverb is the farmer's knowledge that dew cannot fill a reservoir

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friend's distress is removed by deeds, not by speech

reading: There is no need to insist that only the worthy are fit to keep friendship with, the verse tells a woman whose hair smells of the forest, for one should take friendship whoever's it is: will not a dog, once befriended, feed one a good hare?
nuance: The counsel is pragmatic and runs against the usual demand to test friends first: even a low creature, made a friend, brings in game. The heading (the nature of friendship) fits, but the verse values friendship by its yield rather than by the friend's character.

pazhamozhi.literal: if one makes friends with a dog, will it not feed one a good hare?

story.act: no story; the proverb is the hunting dog that brings its master game

pazhamozhi.applied_to: friendship with anyone, even the lowly, can bring profit

reading: Some, thinking 'we have reached the end of it', go on without giving assurance and lose even the care they once showed, and friends who lean on old acquaintance as on a post pay no heed to this new coldness; so a span of respect is better than a cubit of friendship.
nuance: The proverb measures regard (உட்கு, awe or respect) against intimacy and ranks a little of the first above much of the second, a warning that old familiarity without care decays. The syntax of lines 1-3 is loose and who 'leans on old acquaintance' (the neglectful or the neglected) is not fixed; the reading here is tentative.

pazhamozhi.literal: a span of respect is better than a cubit of friendship

story.act: no story; the proverb weighs two measures of length against each other

pazhamozhi.applied_to: friendship that trades on old acquaintance and drops its care is worth less than a little respect

reading: Those whose friendship they took after sifting them like grain, they do not blame by speaking of them among many, and why so, the verse asks the lord of the ford where the neythal opens like waking eyes: people do not tell their dream when they have seen something shameful in it.
nuance: The proverb makes a chosen friend's fault like a shameful dream: it is one's own, seen privately, and telling it exposes the teller. The sifting (கொழித்து) comes first; the silence is owed because the choice was one's own.

pazhamozhi.literal: if they see something base in a dream, they do not tell it

story.act: no story; the proverb is the ordinary reticence about a shameful dream

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friend chosen with care is not blamed in public

reading: Those whom they themselves have set firmly in friendship they do not burn against, even when faults are seen with their own eyes, the verse tells a woman with bamboo-like shoulders and speech sweet as melody, for who is there who would watch their own calf die?
nuance: Two things press the duty: the friend was established by oneself (தம்மாலே நாட்டப்பட்டார்), and the faults are seen, not reported (கண்கண்ட). The calf makes the friend one's own young, whose loss one bears oneself.

pazhamozhi.literal: who is there who would look on while their own calf dies?

story.act: no story; the proverb is the herder's care for his own calf

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one does not turn in anger on a friend one has made, even for faults one has seen

reading: Those who have no fault of their own take even the faults of the friends they have made as 'our fault', the verse tells the lord of the shore where battering waves roll over swelling water, for the forbearance of one is the friendship of two.
nuance: It is the faultless friend who owns the fault (எம்தீமை), so the forbearance is not a trade between two sinners but a taking-on by the one who need not. The same proverb closes Naladiyar 223.

pazhamozhi.literal: the bearing of one is the friendship of two

story.act: no story; the proverb is a maxim about how a bond of two is kept

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friendship survives when one partner takes the other's fault as his own

reading: It is fitting to tell the want that has come upon one to someone who, moved by clear care, will remove it, the verse tells a woman of fine bangles, for those who wish to be cured do not hide their disease from the physician.
nuance: The counsel is to the sufferer, and it carries a condition: disclosure is owed to the one who will remedy (தீர்ப்பனப் பட்டார்), as a sick man tells the healer, not to everyone. அறையார் is unclear; the address is read as praise of the woman's bangles.

pazhamozhi.literal: they do not hide their illness from the physician

story.act: no story; the proverb is the patient who tells the healer everything

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one's trouble should be told openly to a friend able and willing to remove it

reading: While a man has no want, those who eat what is cooked in his house become a thousand, the verse tells a man whose breast bears a garland of opened blossoms, but in the age of Kali the ruined have no friends.
nuance: The verse sets the loss of friends in an age (கலியூழிக் காலத்து), not only in a man's fortune, so the desertion is a mark of the times. It describes false friends under a heading on the nature of friendship, the negative case that proves the rule.

pazhamozhi.literal: for those who are ruined there are no friends

story.act: no story; the proverb is the common experience of the ruined man left alone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the many who feed at a prosperous house are not friends, as ruin shows

title: நட்பில் விலக்கு 135-141
theme: Under the heading நட்பில் விலக்கு, seven verses on the friends to be shunned: those once dear as the eye's pupil who turn to plotting one's life, those kept as a reserve who fail at need, the friend who withdraws to piety when the battle comes, the fools who heed slander, the shameless on whom love is wasted, the friend who breaks and must be broken with, and the double-dealer who will hold to neither side.
source_issues: 137 line 1: the site's text lacks line 1 (பாப்புக் கொடியாற்குப் பால்மேனி யான்போலத்); the corpus keeps it and the reading depends on it.
136 line 1: எயப்புழி appears to stand for எய்ப்புழி.
136 line 3: அச்சிடை இட்டு is of doubtful sense (fear, or an axle or frame).
136, 138: the closing quotation includes a full stop inside the marks.

reading: Even those who befriended one with love as dear as the pupil of the eye may, when it comes to the reckoning, stand as strangers and go about scheming to take one's life, yet Death itself keeps a man until his allotted eating is done.
nuance: The proverb consoles rather than warns: the false friend's plot cannot cut a life short, because the term is Death's and not the plotter's. Death is pictured as an eater who also guards its food until the time of eating (உண்ணும் துணை), so the very power one fears is what protects one from the friend. எண்ணும் துணையில் in line 2 may also mean 'in the time it takes to think', making the friend's turn sudden.

pazhamozhi.literal: Death guards a man for as long as he is to eat

story.act: no story; Death keeps every life until its appointed portion is consumed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a treacherous friend's plotting cannot take a life before its fated term

reading: Those one cherished as a store laid by for the day of weakness do not help with a single thing when trouble comes, the verse tells a woman with fresh bangles, and if they go about after setting one in the midst of danger, that is taking away the ladder after making one climb to the loft.
nuance: The fault grows across the verse: first the reserve friend merely fails to help, then he is the one who has put the man in peril and leaves him there, as the ladder is taken from one already raised. எயப்புழி stands for எய்ப்புழி, the time of exhaustion or want. அச்சிடை இட்டு is compressed; the reading takes அச்சு as அச்சம், danger, though it could be the axle or a frame, which would leave the image of being stranded unchanged.

pazhamozhi.literal: removing the ladder after making someone climb into the loft

story.act: no story; a man is helped up to a loft and the ladder is taken away

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the reserve friend who leads one into danger and then withdraws his help

reading: Those who, like the milk-white one with the man of the snake banner, do not join the battle and strike, but go off on the road and perform great penance for their friends, are those who lift a child onto their shoulders when the festival is over.
nuance: The verse scorns piety put in the place of a friend's duty: the penance may be done in the friend's name, but help that arrives after the need is past is the shoulder offered when the procession has gone. It names its figures only by epithet, the white-bodied one and the bearer of the snake flag.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who lift someone on their shoulders after the festival is over

story.act: the milk-white one did not fight in the battle for his friend of the snake banner but went away on the road doing penance
story.tradition: identified by tradition as Balarama, who left on pilgrimage rather than fight for Duryodhana in the Bharata war; the verse uses only the epithets

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friend who withdraws to pious works when his friend needs him in battle gives help too late to be any

reading: The highest kind of men, even when they look into it, do not find that this friend has a rift with that one, but the lowest, because they take in the tale-bearing spoken to their face, show that the friendship of fools is painful afterwards.
nuance: The verse ranks friends by how they receive slander: the best do not credit a quarrel even when they search for one, the lowest believe what is told them in person. The pain of the fool's friendship comes later, when the slander has done its work. தெரிதலால் is read as 'heeding'; it could mean that the low are known by the slander they speak openly, which would make them the tale-bearers rather than the hearers.

pazhamozhi.literal: the friendship of fools turns painful afterwards

story.act: no story; the fool's friendship, sweet at first, pains in the end

pazhamozhi.applied_to: friends who believe slander against one break the bond and bring later pain

reading: When one has befriended people from the heart and treated them as one's own, what of it if they, having no shame within, do not behave well, the verse asks a deer-eyed woman: they will not care for one even by mistake, and the love is moonlight shed in the forest.
nuance: The proverb makes the loss one of waste rather than injury: moonlight falling in an empty forest harms no one and delights no one. The subject of மறந்தும் பரியலரா is not stated; it may be the shameless friends, who never care, or the wise, who do not grieve over such friends even in passing. On either reading the heart's friendship given to the shameless is spent for nothing.

pazhamozhi.literal: moonlight that falls in the forest

story.act: no story; moonlight spilt where no one sees it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: love given to shameless friends who do not return it is wasted

reading: Toward those who act without fellowship, unlike people who have seen and known one, the right course is to behave not as one who knew them of old but as they do, breaking off, drawing away and casting them out, for the remedy for one who breaks is to break.
nuance: The verse answers the claim of old acquaintance directly: பண்டறிவார் போலாது, 'not like one who knew them before', sets aside the indulgence long friendship usually earns. The proverb's மருந்து treats the break as a cure, not a revenge. கண்டறிவார் போலார் is compressed and may describe them as acting like strangers.

pazhamozhi.literal: for one who has broken away, breaking away is the medicine

story.act: no story; a cure matched to the ailment

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friend who turns unfriendly is to be answered by ending the friendship, not by old indulgence

reading: Those who go both to their great friends and to the enemies, speak to each as if settled without wavering, and yet join firmly with neither are the ones people call a brand burning at both ends.
nuance: The fault is not open betrayal but refusal to belong: the double speaker seems resolved to each side, and the brand that burns at both ends cannot be held by either party. திரிவின்றித் தீர்ந்தார்போல், 'as if settled without change', marks the show of firmness.

pazhamozhi.literal: they are called a firebrand alight at both ends

story.act: no story; a stick burning at both ends that no one can grasp

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who courts both friends and their enemies without committing to either

title: பிறர் இயல்பைக் குறிப்பால் உணர்தல் 142-148
theme: Under the heading பிறர் இயல்பைக் குறிப்பால் உணர்தல், seven verses on knowing others by signs: a small part seen stands for the whole, hidden wrong is seen by others' eyes and leaks through the face, the face mirrors intent, and a person's nature is read from their kin, their birth-group and the company they keep.
source_issues: 143 line 4: கணையினுந் கூரியவாம் has ந் before க, where கணையினும் would be expected; taken as கணையினும் in the reading.
147 lines 1-2: the episode of காப்பான் மடமகள் and மேய்ப்பாட்டது is obscure in the text as given; the reading is tentative.

reading: As one ladleful taken from a great pot shows that all the rice in it is cooked, so in anyone what has been seen should be enough to see the rest, for what is seen becomes the ground of knowing.
nuance: The verse argues from a sample: one part of a person, like one ladle of rice, stands for the whole. யார்கண்ணும் is said twice, so the rule is pressed on every person without exception.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way what is seen becomes the reason

story.act: no story; the cook's test of one ladle is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a little seen of a person is sufficient ground for judging the whole of them

reading: The wicked, thinking the evil they did is hidden as behind a mountain, do not grasp that their evil is plain, for, the poet tells the lord of the shore, eyes are sharper than arrows.
nuance: The mountain image (மலைமறைந்தது) is the wrongdoer's own belief; the proverb answers it with others' eyes, which pierce what he thinks is screened. The address to the lord of the shore (சேர்ப்ப!) is a frame and carries no akam situation.

pazhamozhi.literal: eyes are sharper than arrows

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the type of the wrongdoer who thinks himself unseen

pazhamozhi.applied_to: evil deeds believed hidden are seen by others' eyes

reading: As dampness spreads before a flood arrives, those who carry deceit can be known on sight, the poet tells a bright-eyed woman, for even when they hide it the face tells what the heart has gone towards.
nuance: The flood image makes the face's sign a forerunner: the wetness comes before the water, as the face shows the intent before the act. The claim is specific to கள்ளம், deceit that is being hidden (ஒளிப்பினும்), not to feeling in general.

pazhamozhi.literal: the face tells just what the heart has spread towards

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the deceitful who try to conceal their purpose

pazhamozhi.applied_to: deceit can be read in the face even when it is concealed

reading: As one sees in a mirror the parts of one's own body that one cannot see by looking, so for those who can read faces the face itself is enough to know another's intention, as the son's understanding shows the father's.
nuance: முன்னம், the inward intention, is the old term for what a sign reveals. The proverb's fit is not plain: it may mean that the outward (the son, the face) shows the inward (the father, the mind), as the reading takes it, or that understanding is inherited, which would bear on the observer's skill rather than on the face.

pazhamozhi.literal: the son's understanding is the father's understanding

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the reader of faces

pazhamozhi.applied_to: what cannot be seen directly is known through the thing that reflects it, as the mind through the face

reading: It is hard for one person to discern another's mind, the poet tells a sweet-spoken woman, but everyone takes the colours of their own kin, as birds take many colours according to their lands.
nuance: The first two lines grant that minds are hard to read; the proverb offers lineage (குலம்) as the way round the difficulty, so character is made to follow birth-group as plumage follows habitat. குலம் here is kin or lineage, a birth-group, and the verse uses it to rank natures.

pazhamozhi.literal: birds are of many colours according to their lands

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to people of every kin

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a person's hidden nature can be judged by the colour of their kin

norm.note: a claim of the period that a person's nature follows the kin-group of birth

reading: A keeper's young daughter, though she had come into the hands of a keeper, refused to eat, saying the food was of the pasture, and the poet tells the lord of the misty hill that one's own birth-group comes out strongly however it is hidden.
nuance: The episode is obscure: காப்பான் occurs twice and may name a herdsman and a protector or king, and மேய்ப்பாட்டது is a rare form; the words allow that a girl of herding birth, placed in a higher house, betrayed her birth by a habit about food. சாதி in the proverb is a birth-group term, and the verse uses it to say birth cannot be concealed.

pazhamozhi.literal: even if hidden it will not do: one's own birth-group shows out strongly

story.act: a keeper's young daughter, though in a keeper's hands, would not eat food she called of the pasture

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the marks of birth show through any concealment

norm.note: a claim of the period that the nature of one's birth-group (சாதி) cannot be hidden

reading: No effort of probing is needed: whether even sages are of good nature is to be known by the company they keep, the poet tells a carp-eyed woman, and no witnesses are needed, for there is no cooked meal the neighbours do not know of.
nuance: The test is extended even to முனிவர், the renouncers whose inner state might seem beyond judging. கரியர் are witnesses: the verse sets aside the formal proof of testimony for the evidence of company and common knowledge.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no cooked food that the neighbourhood does not know

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone, sages included, whose nature is in question

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a person's nature is known from their company without inquiry or witnesses

title: முயற்சி 149-161
theme: Under the heading முயற்சி, thirteen verses on effort: one is one's own physician and no helper does one's work, the doer outranks the learned and the old, neither the smallness of a task nor the lack of kin excuses sloth, action must be weighed and done by means that succeed, delegation from sloth and dependence on kings fail, and folded hands before fate end no trouble.
source_issues: 152 line 4: the quotation marks enclose only சென்றது பேரா தவர், which is not a complete saying; the proverb probably begins earlier in line 3.
159 line 3: the proverb opens with a quotation mark ('பாய்பவோ) that is never closed.
160 line 3-4: இழுகினான் ஆகாப்ப தில்லையே is obscure, and the proverb's sense reverses with the reading of இழுகினான்.
161 line 2: வடிந்தற வல்லதற்கு is of doubtful sense.

reading: The verse says one need not go looking for helpers in the thought that one needs them, since no one does for another what that other must do, and closes that each is his own physician.
nuance: Line 3 is a rhetorical question answered at once (உண்டோ மற்றில்லை), so the denial is absolute: the verse does not say helpers are bad, only that the striver's own task cannot be carried by them.

pazhamozhi.literal: each person is his own physician

story.act: no story; the physician image is applied to anyone who waits on helpers

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one's own effort, not a sought-out helper, cures one's own need

reading: The verse calls wise the man who carries a task through to its end even if he has learned nothing, and closes that the man who acts, though young, is the elder.
nuance: The verse detaches அறிவு from கல்வி: wisdom is shown in finishing the work (அற்ற முடிப்போன்), and the proverb moves seniority likewise from years to deeds. The address to the lord of the shore (நீத்தநீர்ச் சேர்ப்ப) is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: the man who does the work is the elder even if he is young

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a type of person

pazhamozhi.applied_to: rank in wisdom goes to the one who completes the task, not to learning or age

reading: The verse names the strivers as those who do வேளாண்மை, tend guests, are strong with the sword in fierce battle and have none of the sloth that drags down effort, and closes that the life of those who do not toil never comes right.
nuance: வேளாண்மை beside விருந்தோம்பி is most likely beneficence to guests rather than farming, as in the old pairing of the two words; the verse then joins household giving and battle valour under one demand for toil (தாளாண்மை).

pazhamozhi.literal: the life of those who do not labour does not become well ordered

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a type of person

pazhamozhi.applied_to: household giving and valour alike need unremitting effort

reading: The verse says that one who sits idle reasoning that a single small effort helps nothing incurs a great fault, and that those who do not stir cannot get through even that very day.
nuance: The quotation marks enclose only சென்றது பேரா தவர், which is not a whole saying; the proverb probably includes அன்றைப் பகலேயும் வாழ்கலார் and perhaps நின்றது. நின்றது சென்றது may mean 'what remains and what has gone' or 'whether it stays or goes'; the reading takes பேராதவர் as those who do not move.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who do not stir (from what has gone)

story.act: no story; applied to the idler who scorns small effort

pazhamozhi.applied_to: neglecting small efforts as useless leaves one unable to live even a day

reading: The verse says no one should sink into sloth saying 'I have no one dear, who else is mine, I am alone', but should strive without weariness, and closes that those without weariness never fail to reach what they set out for.
nuance: முனிவு here is weariness or vexation with the task; the verse turns the lack of kin, usually a reason for pity, into a mere excuse for sloth.

pazhamozhi.literal: for those without weariness there is no failing to reach what they intended

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a type of person

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the friendless man's own unwearied effort is enough to reach his aim

reading: The verse says the clever take up a matter after weighing themselves, weighing their helpers and weighing the gain, and that otherwise, if one does anything with anything, it turns into anything at all.
nuance: The repeated யாதானும் makes the proverb enact its point: random means and random action give a random result.

pazhamozhi.proverb: யாதானும் ஒன்றுகொண்டு யாதானும் செய்தக்கால் யாதானும் ஆகி விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: if you take up anything and do anything, it becomes anything

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a type of person

pazhamozhi.applied_to: action without weighing self, helpers and gain has no determinate outcome

reading: Since the wrath of the broad-shouldered Chola destroyed even the fort that hung in the sky, the verse bids one strive by means that will succeed, and closes that when a sharp arrow is drawn to its base no fortress holds.
nuance: The heroic memory is used for method, not for praise: what brought the sky-fort down was force applied by the right means (முடியும் திறத்தால்), and the arrow drawn full to the head is that means in small.
domain_note: a king or warrior attacking a stronghold

pazhamozhi.literal: if the sharp arrow is drawn back to its base there is no defence against it

story.act: the Chola whose wrath destroyed the fort hanging in the sky
story.tradition: by tradition the Chola known as destroyer of the hanging fort (தூங்கெயில்); the verse names him only as செம்பியன்

pazhamozhi.applied_to: effort applied by an effective method overcomes any obstacle

reading: The verse says no one should bring about his own ruin by saying 'there is nothing in me, I have no kin', and closes that for those whose forearms are long the shoulders are everywhere well rounded and very great.
nuance: The proverb puts strength in one's own body: long arms go with great shoulders, so reach and power belong to the person, not to his kin. எங்காணும் நன்கு திரண்டு is taken with the shoulders; the link of the proverb to effort is implied, not stated.

pazhamozhi.literal: those with long forearms have very great shoulders

story.act: no story; the bodily sign of the strong man is applied to anyone who pleads lack of kin

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one's own capacity, not wealth or kin, is the ground of strength

reading: The verse says that those who, seeking great wealth beyond their land, attach themselves to the good among worthy kings but find no firm footing on the ground, are called by those who see them 'a crow on a pestle'.
nuance: A crow perched on a pestle in use must fly up at every stroke; the verse's நிலத்து நிலைகொள்ளாக் காலர் may mean the courtiers' own unsteadiness or the instability of any footing gained through a king's favour. Its place under முயற்சி suggests the contrast with wealth won by one's own effort.
domain_note: those who seek wealth in a king's service

pazhamozhi.literal: a crow on a pestle

story.act: no story; applied to the hanger-on at court

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth sought through attachment to kings gives no stable place

reading: The verse says that if men take up their own task as foremost, then out of sloth put it in the hands of those with no firm grip, and themselves drop their grip and wander off, the task will show itself greatly spilled and run to waste.
nuance: கடைப்பிடி is said twice, of the deputies who lack it and of the master who lets it go; the failure is double, in the choice of hands and in one's own slackening.

pazhamozhi.literal: it will show itself greatly spilled and running away

story.act: no story; applied to the master who delegates and wanders

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a task handed to the irresolute through sloth comes to ruin

reading: The verse says it is no use for those who will not do with their own effort what they can do to wait, thinking they will have it done later by another, for, lord of the hill land of red-water falls, would those who will not even heat water leap into fire?
nuance: The proverb reads most naturally of the hoped-for helper: one who will not do even a small easy service for you will not do a hard one. It could also be read of the idler himself, who will not do the great thing if he will not do the small.

pazhamozhi.literal: would those who will not even heat water leap into fire?

story.act: no story; applied to the man who waits for another to do his work

pazhamozhi.applied_to: others will not do the hard part of one's task when they will not do the easy part

reading: The verse asks whether suffering ends by sitting with folded hands, saying 'He apportioned everything beforehand', and closes that when the leaf written earlier is faulty there is nothing the one who smears it over cannot make.
nuance: The writer of the leaf is the one who fixed fate (முழுதுடன் முன்னே வகுத்தவன்). இழுகினான் is taken as one who smears out and rewrites the palm leaf, so effort can correct a bad fate; if it is read as 'the slack man', the proverb instead says the leaf does not fail the idler, with a reversed sense.

pazhamozhi.proverb: இழுகினான் ஆகாப்ப தில்லையே முன்னம் எழுதினான் ஓலை பழுது
pazhamozhi.literal: if the leaf written before is faulty, nothing is beyond the one who smears it over

story.act: no story; the scribe's correction of a palm leaf is applied to fate

pazhamozhi.applied_to: effort can rewrite what fate wrote, so passive worship of the fixer of fate ends no trouble

reading: The verse says there is no effort for what is done, no increase for what broke off unfinished, no hardship for one who is thoroughly capable, and closes that in the world there is no name for what does not exist.
nuance: The four clauses share the frame X-க்கு இல்லை Y, so the proverb reads as the last of a series: what was never done earns no name. வடிந்தற வல்லதற்கு is of doubtful sense; taken here as one refined to full capacity.

pazhamozhi.literal: in the world there is no name for what does not exist

story.act: no story; the general truth closes a series of four

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an undone or half-done work gets no renown

title: கருமம் முடித்தல் 162-176
theme: Under the heading கருமம் முடித்தல், fifteen verses on getting a task done through others: fitting one's manner to each person, winning help by affection rather than force, choosing the capable over kin, the senior or the base, allowing the agent his share, and keeping watch after the work is handed over.
source_issues: 174 line 4: the core text repaired ௌ written as ெ + ள in வௌவுண்டார், and the reading differs from the site; the proverb's sense remains uncertain.
176 lines 3-4: the quotation marks open at அரங்கினுள், leaving நிரையிருந்து மாண்ட outside the proverb though it qualifies the board; the proverb's start is doubtful.
171 line 4: the proverb மற்றதென் பாற்றேம்பல் நன்று is run together and can be divided more than one way.

reading: The verse says that toward those who look upright but mean to wreck the matter, and toward those who look false yet bring the matter to completion, the capable act in whatever way suits each, as one sprinkles cold water into hot.
nuance: Lines 1-2 can be construed two ways: either the two kinds of person are judged by deeds rather than looks, or the doer himself puts on an upright face and a false one by turns to suit each. The proverb fits both: hot water is tempered, not thrown out. The point either way is that the manner is fitted to the person, not fixed in advance.

pazhamozhi.literal: sprinkling cold water into hot water

story.act: no story; the proverb is the everyday act of tempering hot water with cold

pazhamozhi.applied_to: conduct toward others in a task is measured to each person's real nature, as heat is tempered

reading: Those who cannot carry the matter through themselves, after stirring the people they had attached themselves to into enmity by evil talk, run off first for their own safety, fearing the clash: they are breakers of the shard-bowl they ate from.
nuance: The fault is double: they start the quarrel with words and leave the fighting to others. The proverb's bowl is a humble broken shard, which sharpens the ingratitude: they wreck even the poorest thing that fed them.

pazhamozhi.literal: they smash the potsherd dish they ate from

story.act: no story; the proverb is the ingrate who breaks the very vessel that fed him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: embroiling one's own patrons in a quarrel and deserting them is ruin of one's own support

reading: Even with those one is closely joined to, the verse tells the lord of the hill country, a task should be taken up so that they are pleased and without slipping from what was said, for a task pressed in haste breaks down and turns into trouble.
nuance: Closeness is the case where one might think haste and bluntness safe; the verse says intimates too must be brought along gently and held to the agreed word.

pazhamozhi.literal: work done in haste falls apart and becomes a misfortune

story.act: no story; the proverb states the general rule that haste ruins work

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even among intimates a task must be carried through patiently and by agreement

reading: The verse tells a woman with tinkling bangles and braided hair that one should not say to the point of hurting 'they have no steady character, they are not straight', but take only the benefit, for those who take the appam and eat it do not count its holes.
nuance: It does not deny the flaw; it says the flaw is not the eater's business once the cake is in hand. The counsel is about getting the work out of imperfect people, not about trusting them.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who eat the appam do not count its holes

story.act: no story; the proverb is the eater who enjoys a holed cake without tallying the holes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one takes the use of a flawed helper without voicing his flaws

reading: To have a thing finished on the spot instead of winning it by serving the other with love until he softens is like one who will not milk when the calf has been let to the cow, and is the way of milking a cow by loosing an arrow at it.
nuance: Milk comes when the calf is let in; the verse makes affection the let-down that force cannot produce. The arrow image also implies that force kills the source it wants to use.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way of milking a cow by shooting an arrow

story.act: no story; the proverb is the absurd milker who wounds the cow instead of letting the calf in

pazhamozhi.applied_to: getting a task done by compulsion instead of patient affection destroys what it seeks

reading: The verse tells a creeper-like woman that if one employs a slothful man he strives only in such a way that the task is never finished, and that forcing work out of one who has gone slack is ploughing with a lazy old bullock.
nuance: பாரித்தவன் is read here as the man gone slack and heavy; it may instead mean one who made large promises, in which case the verse joins sloth to boasting. மூரி is the old or idle bullock that lies down in the furrow.

pazhamozhi.literal: ploughing with a lazy old bullock and leaving off

story.act: no story; the proverb is the farmer whose idle bullock leaves the field unploughed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a slothful agent cannot be driven to finish a task

reading: If one sets a man to do, dragging it out over ten years, a task one holds as central, who will do it without drawing some small share for himself, since not even one's own cart goes without grease?
nuance: காணி is a tiny fraction; the verse expects the agent's cut as the cost of the work, not as theft. ஆணி (linchpin) and the greased cart make one image: the central task and the vehicle both need lubricating. பாணித்தல் may also mean the employer's own delay.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no going, even for one's own cart, without greasing it

story.act: no story; the proverb is the cart axle that must be greased to move

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an agent kept long at a task must be allowed his small share

reading: Even after a task has been handed over to be done, one must keep directing those who would otherwise stall, for a chisel does not go in without being struck, even when it stands on a tender shoot that wilts at a touch.
nuance: விட்டு, 'having let go', concedes the handing over and still demands direction after it. The tender shoot makes the point that even the easiest task does not move itself.

pazhamozhi.literal: the chisel does not go in unless it is struck

story.act: no story; the proverb is the carver's chisel that needs the mallet even on soft wood

pazhamozhi.applied_to: entrusted work still needs the employer's continued prompting

reading: For those who have shown the task to the base, laid it on them and then sat at ease thinking 'they will do it well for us', the verse tells a peacock-like woman with a doe's glance, it is setting a cat to guard the heads of small fish.
nuance: Two faults are joined: the wrong agent, and the employer's idleness after appointing him. The cat is not lazy; it is the wrong nature for the trust.

pazhamozhi.literal: setting the cat to guard the fish heads

story.act: no story; the proverb is the guard whose appetite is the very danger

pazhamozhi.applied_to: trusting the base with a task and not watching it hands the goods to the one who will take them

reading: The discerning do not seek out an incapable man to entrust a task to, but only those of clear knowledge; even when such a man has learnt, come to know something and been rid of faults, it is better to go without than to give it to him.
nuance: முற்றல் is hard: it may be the old, the 'ripe' in years, so that seniority is the false ground being refused; or simply a stiff, unfit man. The proverb's words are also hard to divide (மற்று அதன்பால் தேம்பல், 'to pine for want of it'); the reading takes it as 'better to go without'.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is better to waste away for lack of it

story.act: no story; the proverb prefers want to an unfit remedy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a task should wait rather than go to one without practical capacity, whatever his learning

reading: There is no need to ask whether a man is kin or not: valuable matter should be let go into the hands of the learned man alone, for the learned man heeds his master's word, and even if he does not, salt eaten by the ox is no loss.
nuance: The concession is the striking part: even if the learned agent disobeys, what he consumes is like the salt fed to the working ox, an outlay that returns as work. Kinship is set aside as a test altogether.

pazhamozhi.literal: salt eaten by the bullock is no loss

story.act: no story; the proverb is the farmer's salt that keeps his working bullock strong

pazhamozhi.applied_to: what is spent on a learned agent is not wasted even if he does not always obey

reading: When a task is set to be done under safeguards, one should not put on it careless men who make off once they have had their fill, since there is no wealth that does not cling to those who touch it, as there is no pot that does not cling to those who cook in it.
nuance: The verse treats the handler's taking as a law of nature, like the cook's tasting; the choice it leaves is only of handlers who care for the work. கட்டுடைத்தாக can also mean 'with binding authority', so the safeguard may be the master's own control.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no cooking pot that does not stick to those who cook in it

story.act: no story; the proverb is the cook to whose hands the pot's contents always cling

pazhamozhi.applied_to: whoever handles wealth keeps some of it, so careless handlers must not be chosen

reading: If those who were set up in office prove to have no goodness, the verse tells a wide-eyed woman, there is no need to say 'we will expose them and remove them': drive them off, for no one was ever robbed by agreeing to part with a black goat that was going to die.
nuance: The proverb is hard: இறக்கும் மையாட்டை 'the dark goat that is about to die' and உடம்படுத்து 'having consented' are read here as letting go what is lost anyway at no cost. ஓட்டி may belong to the counsel ('drive them off') or to the address. The counsel is quiet dismissal over public exposure.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one was ever robbed in giving up a goat that was going to die anyway

story.act: no story; the proverb is the owner who loses nothing by parting with a dying goat

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a worthless appointee is best let go quietly, since keeping or shaming him gains nothing

reading: If one greatly raises up men with no inner purity and leaves them in some far place out of reach, that, done without thinking and discerning, is letting a tortoise go into a long pond with the words 'get wet and come back'.
nuance: அகந்தூய்மை here is honesty of mind in an agent, not ritual purity. The tortoise is at home in the pond; sending it there and asking it to return is asking it to act against its nature with no one watching.

pazhamozhi.literal: letting a tortoise into a long pond and saying 'get wet and come back'

story.act: no story; the proverb is the owner who frees a tortoise in its own element and expects it back

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an untrustworthy agent raised high and sent beyond oversight will not return what was entrusted

reading: When one stands nearby saying subtle things about a task, the man who has gone into it without knowing its hidden state perishes, for on the well-made board laid out in rows the war of the dice is easy for those who sit at its edge.
nuance: The verse holds two people: the bystander whose advice is cheap because he risks nothing, and the doer who enters without knowing the inside of the work. புரை may be the hidden flaw or the inner chamber; either way it is what the onlooker does not see.

pazhamozhi.literal: the battle of dice on the board is easy for those sitting at the edge

story.act: no story; the proverb is the onlooker at a dice game who finds every move easy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: advice from outside a task is easy, and the one who acts on it without inner knowledge pays

title: மறை பிறர் அறியாமை 177-182
theme: Under the heading மறை பிறர் அறியாமை, six verses on keeping secrets: kinship and friendship are no ground for disclosure, a mean confidant chosen over worthy kin is a drum struck, love must be known before one confides, everyone passes on what he hears, only the noble keep a secret, and even the affectionate must be examined first.
source_issues: 177 line 4: சீர்ந்தது is a rare form; its sense (what suits or profits one) is inferred from context.
179 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at உயக்கொண்டு, leaving the hunter clause (தின்குறுவான் கொல்வாங்குக் கொன்றபின் அல்லது) outside though it belongs to the image; the syntax is compressed.
180 line 4: the quotation opens after சான்றோர், which is the subject of the proverb's verb உரையார்.

reading: The wise do not, going on the ground that someone is kin or friend, trust him with their weak point, for even the lord who rides the victorious bird and strode across the world did what served his ends.
nuance: அற்றம் is the exposed or unguarded point, the thing one must hide; the verse refuses kinship and friendship as grounds for disclosing it. The proof is drawn from a god: if even he acted for his own advantage, no lesser bond is a guarantee. The sense of சீர்ந்தது is not certain; 'what suited him' is a reading from context.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who does not do what suits him

story.act: the lord who rides the victorious bird and strode over the world, who even so did what served his purpose
story.tradition: by tradition Vishnu, the Garuda-rider, whose striding of the worlds is the Vamana episode in which he won the earth from Mahabali by a request; the verse names neither

pazhamozhi.applied_to: since everyone, even a god, acts for advantage, kinship or friendship is no ground for revealing one's weak point

reading: When one's own people, rich in every excellence, are at hand, to pick out a man with no excellence of mind, take him aside into one's secret counsel and not put him away is like setting the drumstick to the drum's face.
nuance: The fault lies with the one who chose the confidant: passing over worthy kin for a small-minded outsider is itself the beating of the drum, so the leak is the chooser's own act. The syntax of மாற்றா தொழிதல் (not removing him) is loose.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is the way of putting the stick to the drum's face

story.act: no story; the proverb is the act of readying a drum to be sounded

pazhamozhi.applied_to: confiding a secret to a man of mean mind is preparing its public announcement

reading: One should not run ahead to tell one's secret to anyone at all before knowing their love, for no one follows the track of an antelope to carry it off safe, only to kill it as the man who means to eat it kills.
nuance: The image makes the over-eager listener a hunter on the trail: the one who pursues another's secret pursues it to use it. The construction of lines 2-4 (தின்குறுவான் கொல்வாங்குக் கொன்றபின் அல்லது) is compressed and the reading of the image is tentative.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one follows an antelope's path to take it away alive

story.act: no story; the hunter tracks the antelope only to kill and eat it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who has not shown love and seeks a secret seeks it to do harm, so it is not to be told before love is known

reading: Addressing a woman with cloud-like hair and golden bangles, the verse says that even among those who keep friendship pleasantly there is no one who does not pass on what he has heard, and so the worthy do not tell their secret to the base.
nuance: The first half claims more than the proverb: it is not only the base but anyone, even a pleasant friend, who carries on what he hears. The proverb then narrows the rule to the base, so the verse moves from a general distrust to a practical line drawn at the mean. உயவாது shares the root of the Kural's உய்த்து (carrying a secret on).

pazhamozhi.literal: they do not tell a secret to the base

story.act: no story; the proverb states the practice of the worthy (சான்றோர்)

pazhamozhi.applied_to: since what is heard is always passed on, the worthy keep their secrets from the base
