reading: Addressing the lord of the great mountain land, the verse says that only the noble keep the precious secret that others must not know, and that telling it to the small of heart is like setting cotton on top of a palmyra and carding it loose.
nuance: Cotton fluffed on a palm-top is scattered by the wind beyond any gathering back; the image stresses that the loss cannot be undone and spreads in every direction. Keeping a secret is named as a mark of the ஆன்றோர், not merely a prudence.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like placing cotton on a palmyra and carding it

story.act: no story; cotton carded at a height is blown abroad

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a secret told to the small-hearted is scattered past recovery

reading: There is no need to speak one's confidences to the hostile who stand apart as strangers, like the dead, and even with the affectionate, one who trusts without examining perishes.
nuance: The verse moves from the obvious case, the estranged, to the hard one, the loving, and makes examination necessary even there. தஞ்சம் here is what one leans on, the matter one confides; முளிந்தார் (the withered, dried up) is a rare figure for those whose regard has died.

pazhamozhi.literal: one who trusts without having examined will perish

story.act: no story; the proverb states the fate of trust without testing

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even those who show affection must be examined before one confides in them

title: தெரிந்து தெளிதல் 183-195
theme: Under the heading தெரிந்து தெளிதல், thirteen verses on examining before trusting or acting: the giver who does not weigh the asker, the witness who weighs even what he saw, the go-between caught in a quarrel, the near small gain over the far large one, water taken for shallow, the loser who suspects even gods, fair-seeming dependants who rob, and private scrutiny joined to going with the town.
source_issues: 186 line 4: குறுக்கண்ணி is rare and the proverb's image cannot be fixed.
189 line 2: நடைத்தாரா is obscure; the episode behind the nickname is not told.
192 line 1: விரியப் புகுவார் is unclear, and the verse's stance on truth and falsehood is uncertain.

reading: The one who ruled the world, thinking the gift easy for him, poured the gift-water lavishly without knowing the measure of the one who had come to him, and lost it all, for those who begin a thing with a flaw in it there is no affliction that they have not brought on themselves.
nuance: The heavy lengthenings (ஆஅம், மேஎம், தோஒம், தாஅம்) give the verse its sound. The ruler pours water (நீர் பெய்து) as a giver seals a gift; his fault is not giving but giving without weighing the recipient, so the verse fits its heading as trust given without examination.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no affliction that does not come of one's own giving

story.act: a ruler of the world, sure the gift was easy for him, poured the gift-water without knowing who had come and lost his world
story.tradition: by tradition the king Mahabali, who granted three steps to Vishnu in dwarf form; the verse names only one who ruled the world

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the gift-giver who does not weigh the asker brings his ruin on himself

reading: Even kin of good quality speak without weighing their words, so there is no point in grieving at the want of good nature in those not of good family, lord of the land where cascades stir on the rock, for there is no one at all who never slips in speech.
nuance: The argument runs from the greater to the less: if the well-born slip, the lapse of the low-born is no wonder. The verse assumes that good family (இற்பாலர்) yields good nature, and then uses that assumption to excuse rather than to condemn.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one whoever who does not falter in speech

story.act: no story; a general claim about every speaker

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one should not grieve over another's careless words, since even the good let words slip

reading: When the king asked men to show the boundary marks of the land of Pukar of cool flowering waters, the worthy man, ashamed of what he had come to hold, kept it hidden, and so even what one has seen with one's own eyes is to be weighed before it is spoken.
nuance: The episode is compressed and its point is unclear: கொண்டதனை may be what the worthy man had taken or accepted, or what he had grasped of the matter. On either reading the proverb's lesson is that eyewitness alone does not license speech.
domain_note: a witness questioned by the king

pazhamozhi.literal: even what is seen with the eyes should be spoken after thought

story.act: a king of Pukar asked men to show a land's boundary marks and a worthy man, from shame, concealed what he knew

pazhamozhi.applied_to: testimony, even of what one saw, needs weighing before it is given

reading: If, in a quarrel that has flared between two who rose in anger without understanding, someone enters between them out of friendship, the two in their great hatred turn on him and he is caught in the knot at the head of the fight.
nuance: The mediator is not blamed for malice but for misjudging the moment: the two have not understood (உணராது), and a friend's entry turns both angers on him. குறுக்கண்ணி is a rare word; it is taken as a cross-knot or tie in which the go-between is caught.

pazhamozhi.literal: he becomes the cross-knot at the head

story.act: no story; the go-between in a quarrel

pazhamozhi.applied_to: stepping between two who quarrel without understanding draws the anger of both

reading: Better to take what is close at hand though it be only a millet-grain's worth than to get however much from far away, lord of the cloud-ringed hills where herds of stags tear the honeycombs, for no one eats the palmyra's fruit by planting the palm.
nuance: The palmyra takes many years to bear, so the planter does not live to eat the fruit; the proverb weighs gain by its distance in time as well as space.

pazhamozhi.literal: people do not eat the palmyra's fruit by planting it

story.act: no story; the slow-bearing palmyra

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small gain near at hand is to be preferred to a large one far off

reading: The verse says that even when they have set their heart on it people do not do what is unfitting, that what has been spoken with weight must be kept, and that one should do even what one would not do if it pleases one's people, for no one ever impaled his own kin.
nuance: The proverb names the king's harshest punishment, impalement (கழுவேற்றல்), and says it is never turned on one's own people; the counsel to please the people even at some cost to oneself follows from that bond. Lines 1-3 are three loosely joined counsels, and how they lead to the proverb is not certain.
domain_note: one who holds power over his people

pazhamozhi.literal: no one has ever impaled his own kin

story.act: no story; the punishment of impalement, never inflicted on one's own

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one bears with and pleases one's own people rather than treat them as enemies

reading: A man whose head was painfully split, who lost the use of his legs as well, who was dubbed 'the walking duck' and with his lameness got another name, shows why people do not go into water taking it for shallow.
nuance: The cost the verse dwells on is not the injury alone but the new name it brings, a lasting mockery. நடைத்தாரா is taken as 'walking duck', a nickname for a waddling lame man; the episode behind it is not told.

pazhamozhi.literal: people do not go in, taking the water to be shallow

story.act: a man who plunged into water thinking it shallow split his head, was lamed and was nicknamed the walking duck

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one should not enter on anything before testing its depth

reading: Those who have attached themselves to the wealthy, getting at first a little gruel, will get a large portion too, for if a man gets a place to sit in a crowded space, he will get a place to lie down as well.
nuance: The verse is a counsel of patient entry, not of greed: the small first share is the foothold. அரிதாம் இடத்துள் makes the space hard to get, so the first seat is what counts.
domain_note: one who attaches himself to a wealthy patron

pazhamozhi.proverb: இடத்துள் ஒருவன் இருப்புழிப் பெற்றால் கிடப்புழியும் பெற்று விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: one who gets room to sit will get room to lie down too

story.act: no story; a seat in a crowded place grows into a bed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small first share from the wealthy grows into a large one

reading: Can those who truly discern mean speech from good speech live by the way of harsh speech, the verse asks, since mean speech brings a man into trouble, while sweet speech never puts anyone in danger.
nuance: The argument is from the speaker's safety, not the hearer's pleasure: knowing the two kinds of speech is enough to choose the sweet, because only the mean one rebounds on the speaker.

pazhamozhi.literal: sweet speech never brings one into trouble

story.act: no story; a claim about speech

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who can tell good speech from mean will not choose harsh words

reading: Whether men enter openly being of true nature or bring their ends about being of false nature, let them be whatever they are; for each, to be true to his own nature is foremost.
nuance: The verse seems to set truth and falsehood side by side without choosing between them and to prize only constancy of nature; this may be a counsel to the observer to judge each man by his settled nature rather than his professions. The sense of விரியப் புகுவார் is not clear.

pazhamozhi.literal: being of one's own nature is foremost

story.act: no story; a maxim on keeping one's own nature

pazhamozhi.applied_to: whatever a man is, true or false, his constancy to his own nature is what counts

reading: Whoever they may be, those who have lost their property will suspect harm even of the gods, lady who appears like a painted doll, for one who has lost a long spear will search for it even inside a pot.
nuance: The proverb is comic: a long spear cannot be in a pot, yet loss drives the search everywhere. Under its heading the verse reads as a warning that a loser's suspicions are no proof against those he suspects.

pazhamozhi.literal: one who has lost a long spear searches even in a pot

story.act: no story; the absurd search for a lost spear

pazhamozhi.applied_to: loss makes a man suspect everyone, even the gods

reading: Taking clothes and food in the hours of sleep, coming into view when the sunlight spreads, and showing themselves as though they were attached to one, lady of spear-like eyes, there are thieves like peacocks.
nuance: The peacock is a figure of a fair outside; the thieves are fair-seeming dependants who rob by night and appear devoted by day, so the danger is inside the household's own circle. The image is not explained beyond the comparison.

pazhamozhi.literal: the world has thieves who are like peacocks

story.act: no story; dependants who steal by night and appear loyal by day

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those who seem close may be the ones who rob

reading: The verse says not to go away so that those attached to one are left desolate, not to stay on departing from the path of those who renounced, and to examine again and again the fine point one has seen for oneself, without hearing others, and to run along with the town's way.
nuance: The verse joins private, repeated scrutiny with outward conformity: examine for oneself, but act with the town. நீத்தார் may be those who have renounced or those who have left one, and line 2 is uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: run in step with the town's way

story.act: no story; a maxim of going with the community

pazhamozhi.applied_to: having examined for oneself, one acts in step with the community

title: பொருள் 196-204
theme: Under the heading பொருள், nine verses on what wealth does: it overcomes the unreasonable better than force, makes every affair go well, draws the needy and the praise of all, guards the one who guards it, grows from small daily gains, is untouched by petty theft, and leaves the fallen great their standing; one verse warns against scorning a man for his small beginnings.
source_issues: Pazhamozhi 203: the proverb's நரிநக்கிற்(று) has a bracketed ending in our text, an editorial restoration of the syllable; it does not change the sense.

reading: Those who act without understanding and have no merit are best cut off with wealth, for who will hold out once wealth is given; a gift's thrust is stronger than a spear's.
nuance: The counsel sets giving against force as ways of dealing with the unreasonable, and ranks giving higher: the proverb's spear and காணி stand for the two. காணி can name a holding of land or a small fraction of money; either way the gift is the sharper weapon. The verse plays on பொருள் as both wealth and the fitting course (பொருளால் அறுத்தல் பொருளே).

pazhamozhi.literal: the thrust of a காணி is stronger than the thrust of a spear

story.act: no story; the proverb opposes the weapon and the gift as two ways to overcome

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the senseless and unworthy are more surely ended by a payment than by force

reading: For those who have wealth nothing is out of reach and their affairs go well as they intend, while for those who have none the same affairs turn to trouble; the rich see clearly even in the sea.
nuance: The address to the lord of the shining shore (இலங்குநீர்ச் சேர்ப்ப!) is a frame borrowed from the neytal poems. The proverb's sense is not fixed: it may mean that the rich find their way even in a place as trackless as the sea, or that what is in the deep is plain to them.

pazhamozhi.literal: even within the sea they see well

story.act: no story; the proverb states the reach of those who have means

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth makes every undertaking go well, where want turns it to hardship

reading: Those who hold wealth that is hard to come by do not go looking for those who have business with them, since no one who dug a tank went off in search of frogs.
nuance: The tank draws frogs of itself, so the seekers come to wealth and not wealth to them; the verse states this as a law of nature, without praise or blame. The stork asleep on the buffalo's back in the address (எருமைமேல் நாரை துயில்வதியும் ஊர!) is a marutam frame of ease.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one who dug a tank ever went in pursuit of the frogs

story.act: no story; the tank and its frogs are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wealthy need not seek those who need them; the needy come of themselves

reading: No one, the compassionate or anyone else, fails to praise those who have wealth, and this is the saying that the goods of the fortunate are taken by two.
nuance: The point is that even those with அருள், who should be moved by need and not by wealth, join the praise. The proverb's 'two' most likely answers the verse's two kinds of people (the compassionate and the rest), both of whom take from the rich and so praise them; that reading is ours. The address பொருபடைக் கண்ணாய்! is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: the goods of the fortunate are taken by two

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the rich and those who live by them

pazhamozhi.applied_to: praise of the rich is universal because all, good and not, share in their goods

reading: The owner guards what he owns, and what he owns in turn guards him, as the thicket is strength to the tiger and the tiger strength to the thicket.
nuance: The proverb makes wealth and owner each the other's defence: the tiger keeps men from cutting the thicket and the thicket hides the tiger. அடையின் ('if they join') makes the protection depend on the two staying together. The verse thus treats guarding wealth as a gain, not a burden.

pazhamozhi.proverb: புதற்குப் புலியும் வலியே புலிக்குப் புதலும் வலியாய் விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: the tiger is a strength to the thicket, and the thicket becomes a strength to the tiger

story.act: no story; the tiger and the thicket are the instance of mutual defence

pazhamozhi.applied_to: guarded wealth protects the one who guards it

reading: Though one's income be small, if it is gathered every day it grows very great, as gathered light lights the world and gathered drops make a flood.
nuance: Two images carry the claim before the proverb: light gathered (ஒளியீண்டி) and drops gathered (துளியீண்டில்), both repeating the verb ஈண்டு of line 1, so accumulation, not the size of the income, is the whole argument.

pazhamozhi.literal: drops, if they gather, give a flood

story.act: no story; the gathered drops are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small income gathered daily becomes great wealth

reading: Even if the people of one's own town have let us know someone's small beginnings, he should not be despised, for in the old bustling town the calf grazing in the market may also grow into a bull.
nuance: முதல் can be the man's origin or his starting capital; under the heading பொருள் the second is likely, but the verse's argument holds for either. The reason given is time: what is small now grows, so contempt based on knowing someone's past misjudges his future. The address இலங்கிழாய்! is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: the old calf that grazes in the market may also become a bull

story.act: no story; the market calf is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a man of known small beginnings may rise, so he is not to be scorned

reading: Even if many field labourers steal, the wealth of the very rich does not suffer, for the sea does not run dry because a jackal licked it.
nuance: The verse reports the indifference of great wealth to petty loss without judging the thieving labourers (களமர்). The address pictures a town where the dam is opened to drain the water for reaping the ripe paddy, a frame of abundance.

pazhamozhi.literal: will the sea run dry because a jackal licked it

story.act: no story; the jackal at the sea is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: small thefts do not diminish great wealth

reading: Will the great rich whom the land knows cower even when they have become poor and withered; though they lie shrunk and shrivelled, no dog sniffs at a tiger's head.
nuance: The verse says the standing of those once known as great outlasts their wealth: the mean (the dog) do not dare to approach even the fallen great (the tiger). வட்குபவோ asks whether they will be abashed and expects no. The counsel sits under பொருள் but is about honour in loss of wealth.

pazhamozhi.literal: a dog does not sniff at a tiger's head

story.act: no story; the tiger and the dog are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the fallen great are not insulted by the mean, nor do they cower

title: பொருளைப் பெறுதல் 205-212
theme: Under the heading பொருளைப் பெறுதல், eight verses on keeping wealth rather than winning it: look ahead to one's own wealth and kin's, guard it oneself and not through untested kin, the base or the man of no family, keep it in a fit place, do not neglect it and hope to recover it later, and know that wealth let go or lent out does not come back without anger.
source_issues: 208: நொள்வியார் is a rare or possibly corrupt form; the sense, unfit keepers, rests on the proverb.
211: the proverb கடம்பெற்றான் பெற்றான் குடம் is obscure; கடம் may be a debt or a pot.
212: the opening quotation mark falls mid-line 3, so the proverb as printed includes கொண்டார் வெகுடல், which also completes the counsel's clause.

reading: The verse urges looking ahead to one's own wealth and to the prosperity of one's kin and taking care to sustain them, and proves it with the proverb of the snail that took in water having looked to the distance.
nuance: The care is double: one's own goods and the வளமை of one's kin are both to be looked to முந்துற, beforehand. The proverb is read here as the snail that keeps water in its shell against the dry time; சேணோக்கி may also mean looking far off in space, and நந்து can mean 'increase', so the image is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: like the snail that took in water

story.act: no story; the proverb's snail, having looked ahead, holds water for the time to come

pazhamozhi.applied_to: providing in advance for one's own wealth and one's kin's

reading: Unless one guards one's own goods without ever forgetting them, the wise do not put them in the hands of those they have not tested, on the ground that they are eminent or are kin, for no one knows how to bring back what is gone.
nuance: சிறந்தார் தமர் என்று names the two pretexts for trust, standing and kinship, and the verse sets both aside in favour of testing (தேற்றார், those not made sure of). The proverb makes the loss final rather than merely likely.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who knows how to bring back what has passed away

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to wealth handed to untested kin and lost

pazhamozhi.applied_to: kinship and standing are no ground for entrusting wealth without testing

reading: Precious wealth kept in an unfit place is not saved even by guarding it without blinking, since even the unblinking gods, guarding their nectar at that time, had it carried off; so a hard enclosure is better than good watching.
nuance: The verse puns on இமையாது, 'without blinking', and இமையோர், the gods who never blink: the most vigilant guards there are still lost the nectar. The proverb ranks the place over the watcher. The verse names neither the thief nor the episode.

pazhamozhi.literal: a harsh enclosure is better than a good guard

story.act: the gods guarded the nectar and still had it taken from them
story.tradition: by tradition Garuda's carrying off of the nectar; the verse does not name him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a secure place keeps wealth where vigilance alone does not

reading: Handing over the bright wealth one earned by striving and toil to worthless men with a careless 'look after it' is like rice put in a crow's keeping.
nuance: இகழ்ந்து marks the fault as the owner's contempt for his own labour, not only the keeper's baseness; ஊக்கி உழந்து sets the effort of earning against the ease of the handing over. நொள்வியார் is a rare form; the proverb makes the sense, unfit keepers, clear.

pazhamozhi.literal: rice put in the crow's keeping

story.act: no story; the keeper set over the rice is the one who eats it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth entrusted to the base is consumed by the very keeper

reading: Placing gathered wealth in the hands of a man who is not of a good family is, the verse tells a woman, grass fed to a sluggish ox.
nuance: குடிமகன் அல்லான் makes birth the test of a keeper, where 208 made worth the test. மூரி is read as an ox that will not work: the grass is spent and nothing comes of it, so the loss is waste, not theft. The address to a woman is the verse's frame, not its audience.

pazhamozhi.literal: grass fed to a sluggish ox

story.act: no story; the feed is spent on a beast that gives no work

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth entrusted to a man of no family is spent without return

reading: Neglecting what one had at first and then later trying to search it out and get it back is, the verse says, the way of catching a peacock by putting butter on its head.
nuance: The proverb is of a roundabout trick that cannot work: the bird is gone before the butter melts. The verse does not say recovery is impossible, as 206 does, but that the late effort is absurd beside the early guarding it replaces.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way of catching a peacock by setting butter on it

story.act: no story; the proverb is a fool's method of catching a bird

pazhamozhi.applied_to: recovering neglected wealth afterwards is a futile roundabout effort

reading: Those who say that bright wealth once let out of hand does not come back are those who have learned it as it truly happened, for, as the proverb says, he who got the loan got the pot.
nuance: மெய்ப்பட்ட வாறே உணர்ந்தார் grounds the saying in experience, not precept. The proverb is obscure: கடம் may be a debt or a large pot, and the line seems to say that whoever has received the thing holds it. The reading here takes கடம் as the loan.

pazhamozhi.literal: he who got the loan (or the jar) got the pot

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to wealth that has passed into another's hand

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth let go belongs in effect to whoever now holds it

reading: When those who have lent out bright wealth and let it lie then take their moment and say 'give it to us', the borrowers turn on them as if they had taken up a feud, and the anger of those who took turns even past good cheer into bitterness.
nuance: The fault lies on both sides: the lender let the loan lie (கைவிட்டிருப்பார), and the borrower answers a just claim with enmity. நகைமேலும் suggests the friendly ease that made the loan possible is what turns bitter.

pazhamozhi.literal: the anger of those who took turns bitter even over laughter

story.act: no story; the borrower asked to repay grows angry

pazhamozhi.applied_to: asking back a loan left long unclaimed turns the borrower into an enemy

title: நன்றியில் செல்வம் 213-226
theme: Under the heading நன்றியில் செல்வம், fourteen verses on wealth that does no good: ill-gotten gain that perishes as it seems to grow, wealth in weak hands that draws attack, the hoard neither given nor enjoyed, the miser's piety and his lost next birth, giving that passes over kin, the feigned kindness and the false plea of poverty, the honest refusal set against killing hope, and the gift wasted on the ungrateful.
source_issues: 222 line 3-4: the proverb has a closing quotation mark but no opening one; the proverb is taken to begin at அவ்வாயுறைப்.
220 lines 3-4: the opening quotation mark stands before ஆற்றக், so the adverb is inside the proverb as printed.
226 line 3: the opening quotation mark falls after செய்தது, so செய்தது is outside the proverb though it belongs to its clause.

215 line 4, 219 lines 3-4, 221 line 3, 223 line 4: the proverbs and phrases மரங்குறைப்ப மண்ணா மயிர், குடரொழிய மீவேலி, இழந்ததில் செல்வம் பெறுதலும் இன்னார், இடையன் எறிந்த மரம் are obscure and their application is uncertain.
225 lines 1-2 are nearly identical to Naladiyar 111 lines 1-2.

reading: The verse asks whether those who walk the good way would covet the rare wealth gained by those who walk the wrong way, and answers with the proverb that evil things perish even as they seem to prosper.
nuance: The address to the lord of the shore, where the loud water seems to rush in, mirrors the proverb: the wave's advance looks like gain and is followed by its ebb. The ill-gotten fortune is not denied; it is said to be the look of growth that precedes ruin.

pazhamozhi.literal: evil things perish in the very act of seeming to thrive

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the type of man who grows rich by wrong ways

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the good do not desire wealth won by wrong means, since its rise is the shape of its fall

reading: The verse says that when men who lack any resolve proven over time come into wealth of real worth, it is like the mango tree that bears fruit and so draws the throwing-stick upon itself.
nuance: The wealth itself is not blamed: it is called fine (நன்மையின் மாண்ட). The fault is in the holder, who has no tested firmness to guard it, so his gain becomes the reason he is struck. தொன்மையின் மாண்ட துணிவு may mean resolve made excellent by long use or by ancestry; the line does not settle which.

pazhamozhi.literal: the mango that fruits takes the cudgel upon itself

story.act: no story; a fruiting mango is pelted by those who want its fruit

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth in weak hands draws attack on its owner

reading: The verse says those who, even having wealth, neither give to others nor enjoy it themselves, and whose kin also cling and grow tight, are named by the proverb of unwashed hair beside the lopping of trees.
nuance: Line 2 may say that the miser's kin, holding on to him, become tight-fisted in turn, or that they cling to the hoard. The proverb மரங்குறைப்ப மண்ணா மயிர் is obscure: one reading is that they labour at felling trees while their own hair stays unwashed, toil without any enjoyment, which fits தாந்துவ்வார் (they do not enjoy). The image is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: they lop trees, and their hair stays unwashed

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the hoarder who neither gives nor enjoys

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth neither given nor enjoyed is labour without fruit, and the habit spreads to the kin

reading: The verse says that the drum-proclaimed wealth gained by a man who knows neither how to give nor how to enjoy is a dog's coconut.
nuance: A dog may own a coconut but cannot break it open or eat it: the proverb is about possession without access. The booming drum (முழங்கு முரசு) marks royal or lordly wealth, so the verse aims at a ruler or great man, not a small householder.
domain_note: a lord whose wealth is proclaimed by the drum

pazhamozhi.literal: a coconut that a dog has got

story.act: no story; a dog guarding a coconut it cannot open

pazhamozhi.applied_to: great wealth held by one who cannot give or enjoy it is possessed and useless

reading: The verse says that the wealth of one who, though he has seen rulers of the whole sea-girt earth fall and vanish like a dance in a festival town, still gives nothing because giving feels like loss, is the loss of the eye together with its beauty.
nuance: The miser calls giving இழவு, loss; the proverb turns his word back on him, since his hoard is the real இழவு, and a double one, as losing an eye destroys sight and looks at once. The kings who vanished like a festival dance make the argument from impermanence: wealth will go in any case.

pazhamozhi.literal: losing the eye together with its beauty

story.act: no story; the loss of an eye, which costs both use and looks

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the hoard of one who will not give is a double loss, of use and of honour

reading: The verse asks what it matters whether those who, knowing the want of those who beg aloud, wrap up their own goods tightly, fear evil deeds or not, and answers with the proverb: what matter whether a blind eye sleeps or wakes?
nuance: The target is the miser who claims piety: his fear of தீவினை is like the blindness of an eye, the same whether shut or open, because it changes nothing he does. மாவினை may be his goods or provisions (மா, grain or flour) and பொதிகிற்பார் those who bundle them away; the exact object is uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: what if a blind eye sleeps, what if it does not

story.act: no story; a blind eye open or closed sees alike

pazhamozhi.applied_to: fear of sin that does not move a man to give is no different from having none

reading: The verse says that those who give nothing toward the birth that follows and, by the attachment that pursues them, keep their wealth and die, are those who in the pressing hour leave the guts behind and send off the outer fence.
nuance: The proverb குடரொழிய மீவேலி போக்குபவர் is obscure. On one reading it sets the inner thing (the gut, what life depends on) against the outer fence, so the hoarder guards the outside and loses the inside: his wealth stays, his next birth goes unprovided. படரும் பிறப்பு, the birth that spreads onward, makes giving a provision for the coming life.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who, the gut being lost, send off the upper fence

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the hoarder who dies with his wealth

pazhamozhi.applied_to: keeping wealth till death and giving nothing for the next birth protects the outer while the inner is lost

reading: The verse says that failing to relieve the gnawing hunger of those who come with love and of one's own kin, while helping strangers, is wholly like the black palmyra.
nuance: வம்பர் may be strangers or idle, worthless men; either way they are set against kin and those who came in love. The proverb's image is only கரும்பனை, the dark palmyra, and the verse does not say how it applies; on one reading the tall palm gives nothing to what stands at its foot. The opening quotation mark falls before ஆற்ற, so the proverb includes that word.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is wholly of the nature of the black palmyra

story.act: no story; the palmyra stands for help that does not reach those nearest

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving that passes over hungry kin to reach strangers is misdirected

reading: The verse describes men who do not give, have no strength, are harsh of speech and do not help one who has toiled when trouble comes, says that gaining wealth from them is no better than losing it, and calls leaving them leaving behind the stack of an old field.
nuance: Line 3 is hard: இழந்ததில் செல்வம் பெறுதலும் இன்னார் may say that what one gets from such men is as good as lost, or that they are men from whom no wealth comes. The proverb then counsels quitting them, as one leaves an old field's threshed stack with nothing lost.

pazhamozhi.literal: leaving behind the straw stack of an old field

story.act: no story; abandoning a stack already threshed, from which nothing more comes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to leave the ungiving is to lose nothing

reading: The verse says that when the destitute, unable to bear it, have spoken so that their need is understood, to make a show of doing good and then dash their hope by a hard act is to tie the mouthful of grass to a beast's neck and let it go.
nuance: The beast with grass tied at its neck has its food beside its mouth and cannot eat it: the image is of a gift shown and withheld, worse than a refusal. நசையழுங்க, hope crushed, is the same phrase Naladiyar 111 uses of one who keeps the asker waiting.

pazhamozhi.literal: tying that mouthful of grass on the neck and letting it go

story.act: no story; a beast turned loose with its grass bound to its neck

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a feigned kindness that kills the asker's hope torments rather than helps

reading: The verse says that if one who could help, asked by those long close to him, pleads that he has nothing, it is the tree a herdsman has cut.
nuance: The refusal is aimed at old intimates (அடையப் பயின்றார்), not strangers. The herdsman's tree is hacked for leaves to feed his flock and left standing but maimed; on that reading the bond is not cut through but spoiled. ஆற்றுவரா may also read as those askers who could not bear it; the proverb's application is uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: a tree hacked by a herdsman

story.act: no story; a tree lopped by a herdsman for his flock

pazhamozhi.applied_to: pleading poverty to old friends maims the bond without ending it

reading: The verse says that those who stand and beg before men whose minds are hard as wood get nothing, as one gets nothing by seeking alms inside a monastery.
nuance: The பள்ளி is a house of renouncers, who themselves live on alms: to beg there is to beg from beggars. The proverb makes the hard-hearted rich man equal in yield to one who owns nothing.

pazhamozhi.literal: entering a monastery to ask for alms

story.act: no story; begging alms where the dwellers themselves beg

pazhamozhi.applied_to: asking of the hard-hearted rich yields as little as asking of those who own nothing

reading: The verse says that giving what one can and saying 'I have none' are both no disgrace but the way of the world; but if, while one who has come in hope stands waiting, a man does not share and eat, there is no world for him who killed that hope.
nuance: Its first two lines are almost word for word the opening of Naladiyar 111; the two verses part only in the proverb. The fault is not refusal but keeping the asker standing (நிற்ப) and then not sharing. செல்லுலகம் இல் denies him a world to go to after death.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no world to go to for one who killed hope

story.act: no story; the proverb names the hope-killer as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an honest refusal is no fault, but to hold the asker in hope and then deny him forfeits the next world

reading: The verse says such men will not, when need comes through their kin or themselves, do anything and stand as equals, and that all that is given to those who do not rejoice in what was done for them is lost.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are elliptic: they seem to describe men who neither help nor return help in trouble, as if to say what kind of recipient wastes a gift. The proverb judges the gift by the receiver's gladness, not by any return.

pazhamozhi.literal: all that is given to those who do not rejoice is loss

story.act: no story; the ungrateful recipient as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a gift to one who takes no joy in kindness is wasted

title: ஊழ் 227-240
theme: Under the heading ஊழ், fourteen verses argue that fate rules effort, understanding, guarding, service to kings and escape: what is due befalls the highest and the unwilling, gain falls to those whose earlier good deeds or penance earned it, the fortunate have no evil day, the foe is only the agent of one's old deed, and survivors of fire come to escape or to rule.
source_issues: Verse 227: the proverb குறும்பியங்கும் கோப்புக் குழிச்செய்வ(து) இல் is obscure in its key words and may be corrupt.
Verse 230: the proverb line nearly repeats the last line of Naladiyar 109 (உற்றபால there, உறற்பால here).

reading: The verse asks what diligent effort, which reaches its goal with hardship as its companion, can do once the deity has settled the outcome, addressing the lord of a town where bees swarm and hum at the blossoms, and closes with a proverb that digging a set pit is of no use where the kurumbu moves.
nuance: The question is rhetorical and grants effort its full credit first (எவ்வம் துணையாய்ப் பொருள்முடிக்கும்) before denying it any force against தெய்வம். The proverb's terms are hard: குறும்பு may be a marauding band or a wild creature and கோப்புக் குழி a pit laid out as a trap, so the sense would be that a prepared trap is idle where the quarry goes its own way; this is a guess.

pazhamozhi.literal: where the kurumbu moves about, there is no making of a laid-out pit

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone whose effort meets an outcome the deity has fixed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: effort, however hard, cannot prevail where the deity has already settled the end

reading: Even in men of great understanding, pointed out by name, when many contrary turns befall them, their undertakings go after the kind of the fortune that has fallen to them, and so, the proverb says, fate defeats understanding.
nuance: The claim is about outcomes (கருமம்), not about the wise man's judgment going bad: his knowledge is intact and still loses. பொறி here is the mark of fortune, the word the Kural uses in 618.

pazhamozhi.literal: fate overcomes understanding

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to renowned wise men whose works miscarry

pazhamozhi.applied_to: understanding, however great, does not secure the outcome of a man's works

reading: Even the moon, which spreads its broad light across the beautiful sky, is seen to come to harm, the verse tells the lord of the beautiful hill country where falls leap onto the rocks, and so what is bound to befall befalls everyone.
nuance: The moon is the instance, not an ornament: if the brightest and highest thing suffers its waning or its seizure, no rank exempts a person. தீங்குறுதல் does not say which harm, waning or eclipse.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is due to befall befalls anyone

story.act: no story; the moon's harm is the instance, and the proverb is applied to everyone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: no height or brightness exempts anyone from what is bound to befall

reading: Because the elephant tied up at Kazhumalam went to the excellent man of Karuvur, the verse says, whether one wants excellent things or does not want them, it is hard for what is bound to befall to pass without touching one.
nuance: The proverb line is almost word for word the last line of Naladiyar 109 (உற்றபால there, உறற்பால here), so the verse proves its point with a known saying; but where the Naladiyar speaks of unwanted evil, the elephant story turns it to unsought good. The episode is only alluded to: the verse names two places and an elephant that went to a man, and does not say that he was made king.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is bound to befall can hardly be kept from touching one

story.act: an elephant tied at Kazhumalam went to an excellent man of Karuvur
story.tradition: good fortune comes to the one it is due to, whether he seeks it or not

pazhamozhi.applied_to: by tradition the elephant sent out to choose a king, which chose a man of Karuvur; the verse names only the elephant, the two places and the man

reading: Though one guard all night, shouting, the tall fine palmyra that has grown up, its fruit falls only to those it is to fall to, and fortune too, the proverb says, touches only those it is to touch.
nuance: The image sets the watchman who stays up crying out against the one the fruit happens to drop to, so guarding is shown not to confer the gain. The lengthened forms (ஆஅய், ஏஎய், வாஅய்) are metrical.

pazhamozhi.literal: fortune too touches those it is due to touch

story.act: a man guards a tall palmyra all night and its fruit still falls to another

pazhamozhi.applied_to: gain goes to the one fated for it, not to the one who guards it

reading: Can those who did not do great good deeds earlier, without fail, get great wealth later, and what comes of setting out to make wealth by vying with those who have stores, the verse asks, since for those with no capital there is no profit.
nuance: The proverb is a merchant's rule, and the verse makes earlier good deeds the capital, so present striving is trade without principal. வைப்போடு இகலி is unclear: it may be rivalry with those who hold stored wealth, or striving against what is laid up by fate.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no profit for those without capital

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who seek great wealth without earlier good deeds

pazhamozhi.applied_to: without the capital of earlier good deeds, effort for wealth yields nothing

reading: Because the kani-vengai, though it has stood in its place for many days, blossoms only on the good day it seeks out, so wealth, even for those who serve kings so as to please them, gathers only at the time it is due to gather.
nuance: கணிவேங்கை is the vengai whose flowering marks the auspicious time, so the tree is itself a reckoner of days; the courtier's service is likened to its long standing, which does not make it bloom early.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is due to gather gathers at its time

story.act: no story; the vengai's timed flowering is the instance, applied to those who serve kings

pazhamozhi.applied_to: service to kings does not hasten wealth before its due time

reading: Those seized amid clamour, who have suffered the fault of capture, may yet break out and get away, the verse says, for the five who were free of falsehood escaped from the lac house, and there is no place without escape for those who are to escape.
nuance: The first line is obscure: குரைத்துக் கொளப்பட்டார் may be men denounced and taken, and கோளிழுக்கு the disgrace of capture. பொய்யற்ற gives the five a moral quality, but the proverb rests the escape on what is due, not on their truth.

pazhamozhi.literal: for one who is to escape there is no place he cannot escape from

story.act: the five free of falsehood got out of the lac house
story.tradition: those due to survive escape even from the surest trap

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the five of the lac house are, by tradition, the Pandavas of the Bharata story; the verse does not name them

reading: For those who are to prosper, even what was agreed to be surely bad turns out surely good, the verse tells the lord of the cool shore where flowers rich with honey give scent by the spreading waves, since for those who have fortune there is no evil day.
nuance: The proverb answers the reckoning of days: the bad day itself loses its force for one with திரு. ஆவார்க்கு, 'for those who will be', makes the good turn depend on the person's lot, not on the thing.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no evil day for those who have fortune

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those whose lot is to prosper

pazhamozhi.applied_to: for the fortunate even what all judged bad turns out good

reading: Even for those who have come to a king able to give, things do not come to hand, though wanted, except by the way of their lot, so one need not call them dull or small, since for those who did penance curry falls even into their rice.
nuance: The verse defends the unrewarded petitioner against contempt: his failure is his lot, not his want of sense. வீற்று வழி is not clear; it may be 'a separate way', the path one's own fortune opens. The proverb pictures gain falling of itself into the plate of one whose penance earned it.
domain_note: petitioners and dependants at a king's court

pazhamozhi.literal: for those who did penance the curry falls even into the rice

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who gain at court by the merit of earlier penance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: what a king gives reaches those whose earlier penance earned it, and the rest are not to be scorned

reading: For those whose time is to prosper even effort is not needed, and for those whose fortune is to leave, striving is fruitless, the verse tells the lord of the rocky hill country, so whatever one does and whatever one gets, for those not due to prosper nothing prospers.
nuance: The verse names ஆள்வினை and denies it on both sides: needless for the fortunate, useless for the unfortunate. ஆகும் சமயத்தார் makes the favourable lot a matter of timing.

pazhamozhi.literal: for those not due to prosper nothing comes to good

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those whose lot is against them

pazhamozhi.applied_to: effort neither helps the fortunate nor saves the unfortunate

reading: Not knowing that the old deed done in anger long ago has come and is punishing them now, why do people rage at the foes who make them suffer, the verse asks a woman with a lightning waist, since the servant who is sent also burns a town.
nuance: The proverb makes the enemy a mere agent: a town burned on a king's order is burned by his servant, and anger at the servant mistakes the hand for the cause. பண்டுருத்துச் செய்த puts anger at the origin of the deed, so the verse answers anger with anger's own past fruit.

pazhamozhi.literal: a man under orders burns even a town

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the foe who brings suffering as the agent of one's past deed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: anger at those who harm one is misplaced, since they carry out one's own old deed

reading: The Chola's son, who came through alive after being burned, got the great elephant's nape and at last made his flawless sceptre run, and so, the proverb says, there is no deed that those who keep their life cannot attain.
nuance: The proverb fits the heading obliquely: it is less about fate's fixity than about survival keeping every outcome open, though the verse's sequence (burned, saved, mounted, enthroned) implies a lot working itself out. பிடர்த்தலைப் பேரானைப் பெற்று may mean he was carried on the state elephant's neck as the chosen king.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no deed beyond those who keep their life

story.act: a Chola prince survived burning, mounted the great elephant and in the end ruled with a just sceptre
story.tradition: so long as one lives, even kingship from ruin is within reach

pazhamozhi.applied_to: identified by tradition as Karikalan and the burning of his prison; the verse names only the Chola's son

reading: When things greatly to be feared come, those who know what is to be done do not fear their own distress, the verse tells the lord of the bamboo-ringed hill where the bull elephant, fearing the cold, embraces its mate, and the proverb sets this on ground where fate's arrow does not fall.
nuance: The closing proverb is elliptical: it may say the knowing stand as if on ground where fate's arrow cannot fall, or, read as an implied question, that there is no such ground and so fear is idle. The elephant sheltering its mate from the cold may hint that the wise meet danger by acting, not by fearing.

pazhamozhi.literal: on ground where fate's arrow does not fall

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who know what to do when danger comes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those who know their course are not shaken by the fear of what fate brings

title: அரசியல்பு 241-257
theme: Under the heading அரசியல்பு, seventeen verses on the nature of kingship: punishing one's own and sparing no age, even justice to rich and poor, gentle taxation and the futility of favours paid for by extortion, the helplessness of subjects under an unjust king, the need for a measure of severity and a firm mind, keeping no rival power or equal close, not handing office to the unrestrained, forbearance as a ground of rule, and the gain of joining the great.
source_issues: 243: the comparison site lacks this verse (show flag site_diff).
245 line 4: பாலதலை is obscure, and line 3 கோல்தலையே யாயினும் கொண்டீக is unclear.
247 lines 3-4: the quotation opens inside மற்றில்லையே (மற் 'றில்லையே), splitting a word; the proverb's own words are probably யானை தொடுவுண்ணின் மூடுங் கலம் with இல்லை.
252 lines 3-4: the quotation opens after மெல்ல at கவுட்கொண்ட நீர், and பாத்தறிவென் is obscure; the bounds of the proverb are doubtful.
255 line 3: ஒளளியன் is probably a typing slip for ஒள்ளியன்.

reading: The verse says that to think 'these are my own people' is a danger: even if they are one's own, a king who sees unfitting deeds must turn hard-eyed and punish, for a soft-eyed king who cannot punish will not rule.
nuance: தங்கண்ணர் puts kin and favourites inside the reach of punishment, and the proverb's மென்கண்ணன் turns the Kural's praised kindly eye (கண்ணோட்டம்) into a fault once it stops the rod.

pazhamozhi.literal: the soft-eyed man who cannot punish does not rule a kingdom

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who spares his own people

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king must punish wrong even in his own people

reading: The verse recalls that though the worthy hid and shielded the deed for long, even after the time had passed the father drove his chariot over the son who had driven over the calf of a milch cow, and proves by it that justice knows neither old nor young.
nuance: Lines 1-2 (கைகரப்ப, காலை கழிந்ததன் பின்றையும்) seem to say the elders concealed the son's deed and time went by, so the point is that neither concealment nor delay saved him; the exact sense of கைகரப்ப is not certain. The verse names neither the king nor the son.

pazhamozhi.literal: in justice there is no old age or youth

story.act: a father, the king, drove his chariot over his own son, who had run over a cow's calf, though the worthy had hidden the deed
story.tradition: identified by tradition as the Chola called Manu Needhi; the verse does not name him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king's justice does not spare the young, even his own son

reading: The verse says a king who knows justice must, without wavering, deal evenly with the rich and the poor, and that if he swerves and does not deal evenly it is like water flowing on one side and milk on the other.

pazhamozhi.literal: like water running on one side and milk running on the other

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who judges rich and poor unequally

pazhamozhi.applied_to: unequal justice gives the rich milk and the poor water from one source

reading: The verse says that for kings of unfading fitness and cool flower garlands, taking the wealth of those who live in the shade of their feet without hurting them, as if not taking at all, is the right taking, like the bee that eats the pollen and leaves.
nuance: The word division of the proverb (வண்டூதா துண்டு) is unsure; the image is in any case of the bee that feeds on a flower without harming it. அருத்தம் is the Sanskrit artha, wealth.

pazhamozhi.literal: as a bee eats from a flower and leaves it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's taking of his subjects' wealth

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king should take revenue so lightly that the subjects feel no loss

reading: The verse appears to say that even when the subjects live in prosperity, the king should not keep his levy over them excessively high, but take within the measure of his rule, since, as the proverb has it, milk does not keep welling beyond its measure.
nuance: Lines 3-4 are obscure: கோல்தலையே யாயினும் கொண்டீக may mean 'take and give, even at the sceptre's point' and பாலதலை is unclear, so both the instruction of line 3 and the proverb's image are my best guess.

pazhamozhi.literal: roughly, milk does not go on welling beyond (its) head; the image is unclear

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who presses levy on prosperous subjects

pazhamozhi.applied_to: prosperity does not license excess taxation

reading: The verse says that when a giving king harms those who came to him for refuge, turns crooked of sceptre, takes levy from his subjects beyond measure and then shows them favour, it is like cutting off a creature's crest and putting it in its own mouth.
nuance: The irony is in கொடைவேந்தன்: the king's generosity is paid for by the people he gives to, so his gift feeds them their own flesh. சூட்டு is most likely the cock's comb.

pazhamozhi.literal: cutting off the crest and putting it in the mouth

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king whose largesse comes from over-taxing his people

pazhamozhi.applied_to: favour funded by extortion only returns the subjects' own loss to them

reading: The verse asks, addressing the lord of the shore of swelling waves, what the subjects under the white umbrella can do if the king himself is not just, and answers that there is nothing: if the elephant itself takes the food and eats, there is no vessel that can cover it.
nuance: The white umbrella is the sign of protection, so the verse's point is that the protector turned taker leaves no higher recourse.

pazhamozhi.literal: if the elephant takes and eats, no vessel can cover the food

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to subjects under an unjust king

pazhamozhi.applied_to: against an unjust king the subjects have no protection

reading: The verse appears to say that for kings with rutting elephants, letting matters slip out of hand rather than keeping the upper hand over others is a danger, since even those who do penance rightly, like the bird that lives on raindrops, scorn the weak.
nuance: ஒளியாரை and கைகடத்தல் can be read more than one way (those who lack lustre or those who hide; to lose control or to overstep), so the counsel may be either 'keep the upper hand' or 'do not overstep except over the weak'. The rain-drinking bird is the cataka, an image of strict austerity.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who does not scorn the weak

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who lets his power slip

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king who appears weak will be scorned by all, even ascetics

reading: The verse says that if a king of great goodness, not divided in mind, acts with a firm mind, then what can hostile men do even if they gather an army with loud proclamations, for one stone is enough for a thousand crows.

pazhamozhi.literal: one stone for a thousand crows

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a resolute king facing a gathered enemy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a single resolute king scatters a numerous but weak enemy

reading: The verse tells a woman of bright bangles that even a king who bears the wheel of rule is scorned by his own allies if he is not just, and yet that kings need some harshness, however little, since even a cool stick, they say, makes the body rise.
nuance: The verse holds two things together: injustice earns contempt, and a measure of வெங்கோன்மை is still needed. The proverb's sense (that a light rod still raises welts, or still makes one stand up) is not certain. ஆழியான may be the wheel-bearing emperor or Vishnu.

pazhamozhi.literal: even a cool stick, it is said, raises the body

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the measure of severity a king must keep

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king needs a little severity even within just rule

reading: The verse asks the lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea, where the water leaps over the punnai, how others could gain the upper word under a king's command, since a tree does not grow under a tree.

pazhamozhi.literal: a tree does not grow under a tree

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to rivals for power under a king

pazhamozhi.applied_to: no second authority can rise under a king's rule

reading: The verse appears to say, to a woman of bamboo shoulders, that those who made strong the men who served them can destroy or raise them as they will, like water held in the cheek, which one may slowly swallow or spit out.
nuance: The proverb is only கவுட்கொண்ட நீர், and பாத்தறிவென் மெல்ல is unclear; my reading takes the water in the mouth as wholly at the holder's disposal.

pazhamozhi.literal: water taken into the cheek

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to followers a ruler has raised

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those a ruler has raised remain his to make or unmake

reading: The verse tells a woman of soft shoulders that for a king to keep men who aspire to leadership on an equal footing with himself is like living with a snake in one room.
nuance: நிலைமையால் நேர்செய்து may mean raising them to equal rank or keeping them level with one another; either way the danger is ambitious men kept close and strong.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way of living with a snake in a single room

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who raises would-be leaders to his own level

pazhamozhi.applied_to: rivals given equal standing are a constant danger at close quarters

reading: The verse appears to say, to a woman whose smile is like jasmine, that as Death when it takes a life does not stop to examine those who have pleas, so there is nothing one can do when the king suddenly seizes one.
nuance: It is unclear whether the verse warns the subject that royal power is as deaf as Death or reproaches a king who seizes without inquiry; வல்லை (quickly) and அரசாட் கொளின் allow both.

pazhamozhi.literal: what can one do if the king swiftly seizes (one)

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a man caught by royal power

pazhamozhi.applied_to: against the king's sudden seizure there is no plea, as against Death

reading: The verse says that to place the high dignity of great wealth on a man of unrestrained mind who is not upright in conduct is to put a firebrand in a monkey's hand.
nuance: ஒளளியன் is probably a slip for ஒள்ளியன், so 'not upright (or not wise) in conduct'. The proverb's monkey will not keep the fire still, so the damage spreads beyond the man himself.

pazhamozhi.literal: giving a firebrand into a monkey's hand

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to giving high office to the unrestrained

pazhamozhi.applied_to: power given to the unrestrained spreads ruin

reading: The verse says that those who do not quickly grow angry even at those who did them boundless harm are the ones said to rule the world, and people, drawn in by their words, take shelter at their feet like a food-bearing tree in a field.
nuance: ஒல்லை வெகுளார் is 'not angry quickly', not 'never angry'; the forbearance is of speed. The shelter image, கூழ்மரம், is my reading of a tree whose yield feeds those near it.
domain_note: the forbearing as those who rule the world

pazhamozhi.literal: like a food-bearing tree in a field

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the forbearing ruler around whom people gather

pazhamozhi.applied_to: slowness to anger draws people to a ruler's shelter

reading: The verse recalls that the younger brother of Lanka's lord came over himself as ally to Rama of the garland and gained even the kingship of Lanka, and proves by it that none who joined the great and held close to them failed.
nuance: The epic case cuts against kin loyalty: the reward comes from leaving his brother for the great one, and the verse passes no judgment on that.

pazhamozhi.literal: there are none who joined the great and held close to them who did not thrive

story.act: the younger brother of Lanka's lord went over to Rama as his ally and was made king of Lanka
story.tradition: the younger brother is Vibhishana in the Ramayana tradition; the verse names only Rama

pazhamozhi.applied_to: joining and keeping close to the great brings gain, even a kingdom

title: அமைச்சர் 258-265
theme: Under the heading அமைச்சர், eight verses on the king's counsellors: the royal assembly shows their learning, the king's faults are laid on those who shaped him, a king without many counsellors for eyes is helpless in trouble, the king should test and hold the wise, restrained guardians keep his life, good ministers press unwelcome good on him, the wise may even beguile him at the right moment, and the experienced take care never to provoke his anger.
source_issues: 265 line 4: the closing quotation mark is missing; the proverb is taken to run from புலிமுன்னர் to the end of the verse, and the quotation may have been meant to cover only the second image.
264 line 4: the quotation opens at ஒள்ளிய, after அம்புலிமேல், and the quoted words are hard to construe alone; the placement of the mark is doubtful.
259 line 2: பயிரறு is obscure and may be corrupt.

reading: The council of the king of killing anger shows a man's breadth of learning and the skill of his set speech, just as the cool flood that pours down in full at the river's head shows how much rain fell on the mountain.
nuance: The argument runs from effect to hidden cause: the rain on the mountain is not seen, only the flood below, and the learning stored in a man is not seen until the king's assembly draws it out. துணை here is a measure, how much, not a companion. The king is கொல்சின, of killing anger, so the assembly that tests is also a dangerous one.
domain_note: the king's counsellor before the royal assembly

pazhamozhi.literal: the flood shows the measure of the rain on the mountain

story.act: no story; the river in spate is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a counsellor's learning and eloquence are known by what he brings out in the king's council

reading: Addressed to a woman with coral-red lips and few sweet words, the verse says that the faults of an angry king whose sceptre is otherwise blameless are laid on the attendants beside him, since no doll is unlike the one who made it.
nuance: The counsellors are cast as the maker and the king as the doll, so the king's misdeeds are read as the work of those around him; கொள்வர் may mean they take on the blame or that they take on the king's evil ways. பயிரறு, qualifying பக்கத்தார், is obscure: it may be 'whose calling is cut off' or a corrupt word, and the reading does not rest on it.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no doll that does not resemble the one who made it

story.act: no story; the doll and its maker are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king's faults are charged to the counsellors who shaped him

reading: Addressed to the lord of the great hills where the marai deer calls its mate, the verse says that for one who has not made many of those around him his eyes, there is no steadying when distress comes, like a gourd-lute whose strings are cut.
nuance: The lute is still there when the strings are cut, but it can give no sound: the man without counsellors keeps his state but has no response when trouble strikes. The address image, a deer calling its companion, sets beside the counsel a creature that has a mate to call on.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like cutting the strings of a gourd lute

story.act: no story; the stringless lute is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a ruler without many counsellors as his eyes is helpless in a crisis

reading: The verse says that to seek out by close discussion those who weigh good and ill, grasp what others say and know other good things besides, and then hold them firmly, is as a bull rubs against a bull's back.
nuance: The proverb pictures like supporting like: two bulls lean and rub together, each the other's prop. The chooser is not named, but the heading and the testing by கட்டுரை, set speech, point to a king choosing counsellors. வலிப்பது may mean binding them fast or making oneself strong by them; the proverb fits either.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way a bull embraces the back of a bull

story.act: no story; two bulls rubbing together are the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: testing the discerning by discussion and holding them close makes them a mutual support

reading: The verse describes guardians who are full and subdued in mind, speech, body and every deed, who keep watch in thought and never waver, and says that if there are none such to guard him, life goes and perishes.
nuance: The three channels of mind, speech and body, a frame of the Jain and wider ethical codes for restraint, are here demanded of the king's guardians rather than of the ascetic. ஒன்றும் பரியலராய் may mean they are moved by nothing, or that they spare no effort; both make them steadfast. Whose life is at stake is left open; the heading makes it the king's.
domain_note: the king's counsellors as his guardians

pazhamozhi.literal: if there are none to guard it, life goes and dies

story.act: no story; an unguarded life is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king without restrained, watchful counsellors is lost

reading: The verse says that good counsellors make the warring king do the good he does not want to do and stop him when he stands bent on evil, telling him what is for his good even by afflicting him, and so the words of elders are painful at first.
nuance: முன் இன்னா, painful first, implies the sweetness after: the elders' counsel is bitter in the hearing and good in its outcome. The counsel works both ways, pushing to unwanted good as well as holding back from evil, and தன்னை நலிந்து admits that the minister's duty is to hurt the king.

pazhamozhi.literal: the word from the mouth of elders is painful at first

story.act: no story; the elders' bitter counsel is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a good minister's counsel pains the king before it profits him

reading: The verse says that when the wise find the garlanded king in a favourable mood they will even use guile, as mothers soothe their children with idle talk of the moon, and closes with the proverb that it is hard for those who show bright things.
nuance: The counsellor is likened to a mother who points to the moon to quiet a child, steering by a pleasing show rather than by plain speech; அவ்வியம், usually crookedness or envy, is here a tactful deceit. The proverb as quoted is hard to construe: it may mean that what bright show achieves is hard for others to achieve, or that the moon shown is hard to give. செவ்வியல பெற்றால் may instead be 'if they get the right moments'.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is hard for those who show bright things

story.act: mothers beguile their children with empty talk, pointing to the moon

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wise may steer a king by artful indirection when his mood allows

reading: The verse says that those who know the court's ways do not think of anything that would anger the mighty king even when what he does is not evil, for there is no escape for the deer before the leaping tiger, and likewise no load of straw before the wind.
nuance: The proverb is doubled, tiger before deer and wind before straw, both images of a force nothing stands against. தீயன அல்ல செயினும் most likely means even when the king does no wrong, so the caution is not a response to his faults but a standing rule; it could also be read as 'even if he does things other than evil'. சிந்தியார், they do not even think it, puts the restraint in the mind as well as the mouth.

pazhamozhi.proverb: புலிமுன்னர் புல்வாய்க்குப் போக்கில் அதுவே வளிமுன்னர் வைப்பாரம் இல்
pazhamozhi.literal: the deer has no escape before the tiger; just so, a load of straw has none before the wind

story.act: no story; the deer before the tiger and straw before the wind are the instances

pazhamozhi.applied_to: no servant survives the anger of a strong king, so the wise never provoke it

title: மன்னரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகல் 266-284
theme: Under the heading மன்னரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகல், nineteen verses on serving kings: work owed for food already eaten and reward trusted to the commander, no contradiction and no flinching, strength borrowed from the king, not asking and not seeking elsewhere, access and timing above rank, the danger of royal love, a fallen king still a snake, no meddling between kings, no treachery, resentment kept asleep and forbearance not presumed on, and steadiness before slander.
source_issues: 270 lines 3-4: the proverb has a closing quotation mark but no opening one; the span பனைமுதிரின் ... விடும் is inferred.
275 line 2: உரைப்பாரைக்கொன் (று) looks like a misprint for உரைப்பார்க்கொன்று.
280 line 4: a full stop stands inside the closing quotation mark.
269 line 1: விடலமை is doubtful; 276 line 4: the proverb கடிய கனைத்து விடல் is obscure; 278 line 3: தீதரம் is unusual.
273 line 1: மன்னரைத் சார்ந்தார் has தச் where sandhi expects ச் (மன்னரைச் சார்ந்தார்).

reading: Addressing a woman of fine jewels, the verse asks what place there is for shrinking back from a task the bannered-chariot kings have assigned, for those who live by sharing those kings' food, since no one drinks the toddy and then goes limp.
nuance: கூட்டுண்டு, eating together with or from the king, makes the service a debt already taken. குழை (to soften, droop) is read here as losing nerve; the proverb may also mean that one who has drunk cannot then pretend to be sober, and the sense is not fully fixed.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who drinks toddy and then wilts

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who lives on the king's food cannot slacken on the king's work

reading: When the king of the victorious spear gives a command, to say 'we have received nothing' is folly; one should do the work without grievance, for it is the one who says 'do' who says 'eat'.
nuance: The verse answers the servant who bargains before working; reward is placed after the work and in the same mouth as the command.

pazhamozhi.literal: he who said 'do it' is the one who says 'eat'

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the servant should do the king's work first and trust the reward to follow from the one who commanded it

reading: When the king puts his own men at the head, saying 'let our men do this for us', they do not fall back even at the point of the spear; to answer him back is the way of saying 'pool' when he says 'aal'.
nuance: தமர் are the king's own people, and his putting them first is the honour that binds them. பூல் is taken as a plant name chosen for its jingle with ஆல்; the proverb mocks mere contradiction rather than reasoned dissent.

pazhamozhi.literal: when one says 'banyan', the other says 'pool'

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to contradict the king's commission is perverse contrariness in his trusted men

reading: Addressing the lord of the shore where palmyras with fronds stand by the full waves, the verse says that if one does not act to break away or stand off in fear, but conducts oneself so that kings hard to oppose are pleased, everything that the sea does not yield will come.
nuance: The address to a lord of the seashore makes the proverb pointed: even to one whose wealth comes from the sea, the king's favour yields what the sea does not. விடலமை in line 1 is read as 'acting so as to leave'; the word is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: all that is not got from the sea will be got

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: pleasing the king without flinching brings every gain

reading: Tasks fit to win the king's glad consent, each taken up in its proper measure, when they ripen in their fruit come back upon the one who did them, as a palm fruit when ripe falls at the foot of its parent tree.
nuance: The proverb has no opening quotation mark in our text; the span is taken from the closing mark and the sense. Whether செய்தான்மேல் ஏறும் means the reward or the responsibility comes to the doer is not settled by the verse; the palm image favours a return to the source.

pazhamozhi.literal: when the palm fruit ripens it falls at the foot of the tree that bore it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the fruit of work done for the king returns to its doer

reading: Addressing a woman whose bright skin bears the spreading sunangu marks, the verse asks whether those who have joined mighty, proud kings will tremble in fear of any one man, for the fine horn of a strong-necked bull is sharp.
nuance: The horn's sharpness is put down to the neck behind it, so the servant's courage is borrowed from the king's strength rather than his own.

pazhamozhi.literal: the good horn of a bull with a strong neck is sharp

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a servant backed by a strong king need fear no single opponent

reading: Whoever the king esteems and is pleased with, other people too esteem in the same way; addressing a woman of soft, well-tended hair, the verse says that, as is known, the vessel into which ghee was poured is the one that pours ghee.
nuance: கொண்டேனை is read as கொண்டு with ஏனை மாந்தரும், 'other people too'. The verse states a fact of reputation, not a merit: esteem flows where the king has poured it.

pazhamozhi.literal: only the vessel that has been filled with ghee pours ghee

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: honour conferred by the king is passed on by others to the one he favoured

reading: Those who have joined manly kings should not, even when they fall into hardship, say 'we want something here'; addressing a man whose chest bears ornaments, the verse says that for the worthy, not wanting gives all that is wanted.
nuance: வேண்டாமை is the word of the renouncer's ethics, here put to use at court: the paradox is that freedom from wanting is the surest way to be given. அல்லுறினும் is read as 'even if they suffer distress'.

pazhamozhi.literal: not wanting brings all that one wants

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy servant who asks nothing of the king even in want receives everything

reading: For those who have served the guardian king fully and stay doing the work he commands, to seek help from elsewhere is like a calf standing by its cow and sucking her throat while the udder is there.
nuance: உதவு அடுத்தல் is read as approaching others for help; the line could also mean that others' help to such servants is superfluous. Either way the king is the udder.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like sucking the mother's throat while the udder is there

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the king's servant who seeks support elsewhere turns from the true source to a dry one

reading: There is nothing that cannot be achieved by those who watch the right moment with distinguished kings and speak with skill; even those who are like life itself to victorious kings fare worse outside, for a hunchback inside is better than a minister outside.
nuance: The kūn, a hunchbacked palace attendant, has the inner rooms and so the king's moments; the minister, however high, does not. The verse ranks nearness at the right time above office. Line 2 உரைப்பாரைக்கொன் (று) is read as உரைப்பார்க்கு ஒன்று.

pazhamozhi.literal: a hunchback within is better than a minister without

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: access and timing in speaking to the king outweigh rank and even dearness

reading: To think 'the kings of the parasol chariots will suit us', and, when they love one fiercely, to return the love and strive on without perceiving anything that lies hidden, is like clearing one's throat at a dangerous moment.
nuance: The proverb is short and its image cannot be fixed: கடிய may be 'dangerous' or 'quickly', and கனைத்தல் a cough or a neigh. The counsel is clearer than the proof: royal love is not a ground for unguarded action.

pazhamozhi.literal: giving a cough where it is dangerous to make a sound

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the favourite who trusts the king's love and does not read what it hides betrays himself

reading: Even if a worthy king has lost all his greatness, those who weigh his station do not face him and mock him, even when he has gone without his great kin and stands alone, for no one slights a snake because it is small.
nuance: நிலைநோக்கி, 'looking to his standing', makes the restraint a judgement of what he still is and may again be; இளைது can mean small or young, and the snake keeps its venom either way.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one belittles a snake for being young

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a fallen and friendless king keeps his power to strike and must not be scorned

reading: To enter among proud kings and speak words that help neither of them is something one cannot afterwards set right for oneself, and that is the bringing of harm: it is eating straw between bulls.
nuance: ஒருத்தற்கு உதவாத சொல் is read as words of no use to either party; it may instead mean words that fail the one king one serves. தீதரம் is unusual and is read as a form of தீது, harm.

pazhamozhi.literal: eating straw between two bulls

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who meddles between rival kings is crushed between them

reading: For those who served many days and secretly took and ate what was the king's to come before him with gold tied up as an offering, hoping he will do them no harm, is tying a water lily with its own fibre.
nuance: The image works because the lily is bound by what grew from it: the gift that is meant to win the king over was the king's own. The verse does not say whether the trick succeeds, only what it is.

pazhamozhi.literal: tying the blue water lily with its own stalk-fibre

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to placate the king with gold taken from him is to give him back what was his

reading: Those who were highly regarded for standing in truth, if they go on doing dark deeds under the king's very hand and take up falsehood, setting themselves against him, fell the palm so that it falls on themselves.
nuance: The servant's standing was built on truth (மெய்ம்மையே நின்று), so his falsehood fells the very trunk that held him up. Our text has a full stop inside the closing quotation mark.

pazhamozhi.literal: they cut down the palm so that it falls on them

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the trusted servant who turns false brings his own ruin
