reading: Even if the fiercely angry king does what one does not want, one should not act in the least on what one holds in the heart, even when one has been caught for whatever one did, for no one wakes a sleeping tiger from its sleep.
nuance: The resentment is granted as real (வேண்டாதவே செயினும்); the counsel is to keep it inside, since the king's quiet anger is the sleeping tiger. Line 3 என்செய்து அகப்பட்டக் கண்ணும் is read as 'whatever one is caught for'.

pazhamozhi.literal: would anyone rouse a sleeping tiger from its sleep

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a servant wronged by the king should not stir the king's anger by acting on his grievance

reading: Why should those who cannot even protect themselves by themselves be angry with kings of leaping horses? Addressing the lord of a beautiful hill where wild cattle leap, the verse says that those who have climbed the kongu tree have no safety.
nuance: Why the kongu gives no safety (brittle wood or thorny trunk) the verse does not say. வாமான்றோ is read as வாம் மான் தேர், the king of leaping horses and chariots.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who have climbed the kongu tree find no safety

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the weak who turn against the king have no refuge

reading: When the king, though seeming unable to bear it, bears with those who have done what does not suit him, to go on doing more and more of what cannot be borne is a boil risen upon a hump.
nuance: The verse turns on பொறாஅன் போலப் பொறுத்தல்: the king's patience is shown with displeasure, and the servant who reads only the patience compounds the fault.

pazhamozhi.literal: a boil that has risen on a hump

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to presume on the king's forbearance heaps a second affliction on the first

reading: Beyond working out how the king may see clearly through the false slander spoken by worthless men, the wise do not dance along with those who rise up in alarm and dance, like the stilts of a dancer to the drum.
nuance: பொய்க்கால் is read as the stilts of a stilt-dancer, which move only as the dancer moves them; the proverb mocks those who are carried by another's alarm. The pun on பொய் (false) links the stilts to the false slander.

pazhamozhi.literal: like the false legs of a dancer to the drum

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wise courtier does not move with the agitation that slander raises but helps the king discern

title: பகைத்திறம் தெரிதல் 285-297 (1/2)
theme: Under the heading பகைத்திறம் தெரிதல் (first part), thirteen verses on dealing with enemies: fear empties every fort, a young enmity must be cut off from its allies, retaliation must not wait, favours do not win a settled foe, the great and their dependents must not be provoked, the weak should flee and live, an old enemy never becomes a friend, and a false friend close by is worse than a flood afar.
source_issues: 288 lines 1-2: the episode of the boundless great one entering hell is obscure, and மன்றி in the proverb may be corrupt.
289 line 4: the proverb has a closing quotation mark but no opening one.
294 line 1: நிற்பாறை is most likely a corruption of நிற்பாரை.
295 lines 1-3: the taunt and இழைத்த திகவாதவர் are of uncertain sense.
297 line 4: அள்ளில்லத்(து) is obscure.

reading: The verse asks whether anyone, by pouring in strength, can make those who lack a footing of their own stand in glory, even when they have strong backers, and answers that for those who fear there is no fortress, whoever they are.
nuance: The verse sets two supports against each other: வன்சார்பு, the strong backing of allies, and தஞ்சார்பு, a footing of one's own; the first cannot make up for the lack of the second. This reading takes both phrases of the same people; if தஞ்சார்பு இலாதாரை is instead the attacker's victims (those without allies of their own), the verse asks whether the strong may lord it over the friendless, and the proverb fits less well.
domain_note: the ruler or chief who leans on allies and forts

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no fortress for those who fear

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone whose own nerve fails, whatever backing he has

pazhamozhi.applied_to: allies and strength poured in from outside cannot save a man without courage of his own

reading: The verse says that an enemy who has risen against one, if rooted out swiftly while still young, does not grow mature, and that once all the friendships of those who had courted him are cut away he is left alone, for a lone tree never becomes a forest.
nuance: Two moves are joined: striking early (இளைதாய போழ்தே) and stripping the enemy of his allies (நண்பெல்லாந் தீர). The proverb proves the second: an enemy isolated cannot spread. The syntax of lines 2 and 3 is loose; தீர்த்து and தீர are read as the removal of the enemy and of his friends.
domain_note: the ruler facing a rising foe

pazhamozhi.literal: a single tree never becomes a forest

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to an enemy cut off from his allies

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an enemy isolated from his friends while still weak cannot grow into a threat

reading: The verse calls it folly to think of harming later those who have already harmed one greatly and risen in hostility, for, it tells a woman whose shoulders are like bamboo, no one ever takes the fangs of a snake that bites swiftly and runs.
nuance: The counsel is against putting off retaliation, not against retaliation: the snake that has bitten and fled cannot be caught afterwards, so the harm stands unanswered. The address to a woman (காம்பன்ன தோளி) frames a political counsel as talk to a beloved, as the hill and shore addresses do elsewhere.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one takes the tooth of a snake that has bitten and run

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to an enemy who strikes and withdraws

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who has been harmed must answer at once, since the chance passes with the attacker

reading: The verse appears to say that even the boundless great one entered hell after seeing it in full, that the pitiless do not relent, and closes with the proverb that when one comes to ruin the community, he is to be put away root and all.
nuance: The first two lines are hard to construe: who the வரம்பில் பெரியான் is and why he entered hell the verse does not say, and the link from that episode to the proverb is not plain. The proverb's own sense, that a destroyer of the kudi must be removed down to the foot, fits the heading on dealing with enemies; மன்றி may be a corruption.

pazhamozhi.literal: when one comes to ruin the people, cast him off till his foot is gone

story.act: a boundless great one entered hell after seeing it in full

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who would ruin the community is to be removed entirely, without pity

reading: The verse says that even when one shows favour to those who are not one's own, to men whose intent is not to be reconciled it plainly does not take, just as saline ground boils from within even when one mixes into it what makes good ground for a wall.
nuance: The fault is placed in the other's குறிப்பு, his settled intent, not in the favour shown: kindness cannot change a mind made up against one. The soil image makes the hostility a property of the ground itself, which treatment does not reach.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way saline ground boils within

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those whose intent is fixed against reconciliation

pazhamozhi.applied_to: favours to a settled enemy do not win him over

reading: The verse says that the wish of one who begs to be let into the house of those who cannot bear to see his face even outside is like a child crying to be carried on the hip by people who, on a great wilderness road, would not let him walk behind them on the proper path.
nuance: The proverb is a picture of misplaced asking: to want closeness (to be taken in, to be carried) from those who refuse even distance (to be seen, to be followed). The verse is about the asker's want of self-respect as much as the host's enmity; its link to the heading is through the hostile host.

pazhamozhi.literal: crying for the hip, as a child wails to be carried

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who seeks entry where he is hated

pazhamozhi.applied_to: seeking intimacy from those who cannot bear one's face is a child's futile wailing

reading: The verse says one should not seek enmity with the very great, for the demon who took it on without care was caught in battle, and even those who have the greatness of penance have never clapped Death on the back.
nuance: The example is a warning against one's own strength: the அரக்கன் is cast as a figure great in penance who still fell, so even power won by austerity does not make the great safe to offend. The proverb turns the point to death, which no penance mocks.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one ever clapped Death on the back

story.act: a demon who took on enmity with the great without heed was caught in war
story.tradition: identified by tradition as Ravana; the verse says only அரக்கன், fused with கொண்டு in கொண்டரக்கன்

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even those mighty by penance must not provoke the great, since none escapes the death that follows

reading: The verse says that the small, taking folly as their prop, behaving with hostility toward those who have attached themselves to the great, are, lord of the hill where the packs of wild dogs fear the noise, like the bear that by crying out rouses the fierce dog.
nuance: The target here is not the great but their dependents (பெரியாரைச் சார்ந்தார்), and the danger lies in waking the protector. எண்கு is the bear; புலம்புகின் is read as its crying out, though it may mean when it is alone.

pazhamozhi.literal: the bear rouses the fierce dog

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the small who provoke the dependents of the great

pazhamozhi.applied_to: attacking those under a great man's protection wakes the great man against oneself

reading: The verse says it is a danger for the weak to scorn those strong in strife and stand against them, and bids them go far off and survive by whatever means, for the man who does not die will yet touch the bangle on the forearm.
nuance: The counsel puts survival above standing: என்செய்தே யாயினும், by doing anything at all. The proverb's bangle is most plausibly the joys of later life (the embrace of a bangled arm), held out to the one who lives, so retreat is presented as a gain deferred, not a disgrace.

pazhamozhi.literal: the one who does not die will touch the bangle on the forearm

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the weak man who flees a stronger foe

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the weak should escape a strong enemy by any means, since the living may yet prosper

reading: The verse says that the small, standing with a single resource, doing many things to inflame those who stand victorious, is, lord of the hill where the bees war with the mountain, a thing that by no means comes out well.
nuance: The image is of the bees that sting the cliff on which they hang their hives: an attack that cannot hurt its target. ஒன்றொடு நின்று is read as the small man's single strength against the victor's many; line 1 is likely corrupt (நிற்பாறை for நிற்பாரை).

pazhamozhi.literal: it is not a thing that came with good

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the small who provoke the victorious

pazhamozhi.applied_to: provoking the proven strong ends in harm to the provoker

reading: The verse seems to say that those who rise roaring and swagger, asking whether a kite will not peck at the tongue of whoever spoke against them, if they fight and enrage men who do not swerve from what they have resolved, become the food of those who eat behind the offering.
nuance: Those who eat behind the bali offering are most plausibly the crows, so the swaggerers end as carrion. The quoted taunt in line 1 and the phrase இழைத்த திகவாதவர் (those who do not exceed what they set) are both hard; the reading follows the most likely sense.

pazhamozhi.literal: the food of those who eat outside the offering

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to boasters who provoke the steadfast

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those who swagger against firm men end up dead

reading: The verse says that as everything with a tuber sprouts in one way when it gets the cool rain of the thundering sky, one should not keep those one has come to favour coiled about one's roots, for old enmity never becomes friendship.
nuance: The tuber image explains why old enmity does not end: it lies dormant underground and sprouts as soon as its season comes. விழைந்தவரை is read as former enemies one has come to like; வேர்சுற்ற puts them at the root, the place where a sprouting tuber does most harm.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no old enmity that becomes friendship

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to reconciled enemies kept close

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a former enemy kept close will turn when his chance comes

reading: The verse asks what those who live elsewhere can do, even if a flood is the enemy, and says that a false, excessive friendship that has come close with deceit is like a debt eaten in one's own house.
nuance: The contrast is distance: an enemy as great as a flood harms those far off little, while the deceitful friend at hand consumes from within, as a debt run up in the house eats the household. அள்ளில்லம் is obscure; it is read as the near house, one's own.

pazhamozhi.literal: the debt eaten in the near house

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the deceitful friend at one's side

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a false friend close at hand is worse than a great enemy far off

title: பகைத்திறம் தெரிதல் 298-310 (2/2)
theme: The second part of the heading பகைத்திறம் தெரிதல் (verses 298-310) treats the craft of enmity: an open enemy is better than a false intimate, anger should stop when the enemy is dead, the petty are not worth fighting, allies in number outweigh one's own prowess, and above all an enemy is beaten by turning others against him, a rear threat, an outside power, the division within his own camp, and finally by the four means of words, gifts, division and measured force.
source_issues: 301: the proverb உருவு திருவூட்டு மாறு and the episode (a man of sword-might who shows a radiance and is spared) are elliptic; the hero is not named.
304: the opening quotation mark falls mid-line 3, so போகாதே is part of the proverb.
307: the opening quotation mark falls mid-line 3, so ஆற்றுவான் is part of the proverb.
309: மலிந்தடைதல் and காக்கொள்ளு are hard; the reading of the proverb is uncertain.
302: வலியலாந் தாக்கு is obscure; the proverb's sense is uncertain.

reading: The verse asks whether those who take up open enmity and keep apart are worse than those who, caring nothing for a man, attach themselves to him as his own and bring him blame in this life and sin for the next, and answers that blindness is better than dim sight.
nuance: செம்மைப் பகை, 'straight enmity', is set against the false kinsman: the proverb ranks a known lack (blindness) above a sight that seems to see and misleads (மைம்மை, a clouded eye). The harm of the false friend is counted in two worlds, blame here and sin hereafter, which the open enemy cannot cause.

pazhamozhi.literal: blindness is better than clouded sight

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the false intimate set against the open enemy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an open enemy is less harmful than one who poses as one's own

reading: To go on raging beyond measure, unsettled, even after one has fought and killed those who would not agree, is like flooding the stubble with water after the crop has been reaped.
nuance: The proverb's point is waste: water given to a reaped field feeds nothing. The verse does not blame the killing; it blames the anger that outlives its object. The address வெற்ப!, 'man of the hills', is the poet's frame, not the audience.

pazhamozhi.literal: watering the stubble after reaping

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anger that continues after the enemy is destroyed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: rage after the enemy is dead is labour without fruit

reading: Even if the great take on the enmity of men of hard strength, to take on the enmity of men of low standing brings them nothing, for even a light shower can bring a flood.
nuance: The proverb seems to give the reason: a small shower can still swell to a flood, so the petty enemy can do great harm while the great man gains nothing by fighting him. வெண்பாட்டம் is taken here as a light or rainless-looking shower; if it means something else the link between counsel and proverb is less sure.

pazhamozhi.literal: a light shower brings a flood

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the great who quarrel with the petty

pazhamozhi.applied_to: enmity with the low profits the great nothing and may still harm them

reading: When men surrounded a man of sword-might in his day and came to kill him, he showed a shining radiance, and seeing a nature they could not bear they gave up the attempt; so form brings fortune.
nuance: The verse tells an episode without naming its hero: a man hemmed in by would-be killers who is saved by the radiance he shows. Who he is cannot be fixed from the words. உருவு திருவூட்டும், 'form feeds fortune', makes bearing or presence itself a defence against enemies.

pazhamozhi.literal: form feeds fortune

story.act: a man of sword-might surrounded by killers showed a shining radiance and they gave up
story.tradition: the verse names no one; an epic episode of a hero revealing his radiant form to those who would seize him is possible, but no identification is made by the words

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an awe-inspiring presence turns enemies away

reading: To keep one's mouth shut on seeing the strong and to override the weak is the way of superiority, since against the strengthless an attack is strong.
nuance: The proverb is hard: வலியலாந் தாக்கு may be 'the attack on those without strength' or a word-play on வலி. Read with its heading the counsel is strategic, not moral, but மேன்மை யுடைமை may also be ironic, mocking a 'superiority' that is quiet before the strong and loud before the weak. The address to the man of the hills where the elephant fights the tiger can support either reading.

pazhamozhi.literal: the blow against the strengthless is strong

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to choosing whom to oppose

pazhamozhi.applied_to: strength is best spent on the weak and withheld from the strong

reading: When enemies stand ready to kill, a single man should not trust in himself at all, for those who gather to him, even if they have no merit, are many, and nothing has more power than numbers.
nuance: The verse grants the allies may be worthless (நன்மை யிலராய்) and still prefers them: in battle number outweighs quality. வியவற்க is a warning against self-admiration as much as self-reliance.

pazhamozhi.literal: nothing has more might than numbers

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the lone man facing enemies

pazhamozhi.applied_to: in war many allies, even poor ones, outweigh one man's own prowess

reading: If one able to crush you comes against you, you must find someone who will harass him from behind, for however hard a ram presses forward with its head, it will not advance with a dog at its back.
nuance: The counsel is to open a second front: the enemy is stopped not by meeting him but by threatening his rear. The proverb's quotation mark opens mid-line 3, so போகாதே belongs to it.

pazhamozhi.literal: a ram will not go forward with a dog behind it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a stronger enemy's advance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a strong enemy is checked by setting another on his rear

reading: To stir up enmity so that allies take arms against each other, by making one say 'with me and this elder brother of mine here, there is nothing left for valour to do', is to throw a bone between dogs.
nuance: The quoted boast is the tool of division: flattering one partner that he and his brother are enough sets them quarrelling over the glory. Who speaks the line, the plotter or the flattered ally, is not certain from the syntax; the proverb fixes the sense as sowing discord.

pazhamozhi.literal: throwing a bone in among dogs

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to dividing allied enemies

pazhamozhi.applied_to: enemies who stand together are broken by giving them something to fight over

reading: One who would defeat his natural enemy should, for his own safety, first incite an outside enemy against him and, by kindness, kindle that one's anger and make him easy to his hand; that is stirring with a small monkey's hand.
nuance: இயற்பகை is the enemy by nature or position, அயற்பகை the stranger who is his enemy. The proverb is the image of using another creature's hand to stir what one will not touch oneself: the outside power takes the burn.

pazhamozhi.literal: stir with a small monkey's hand

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to using a third power against one's enemy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: fight a natural enemy through another's hand, kept friendly by favour

reading: Since one word breaks another, one should remove enemies through an enmity worked against them, for division is found in everyone, and one man able to act will kill the hundred.
nuance: The verse moves from speech (மாற்றத்தை மாற்றம் உடைத்தல்) to division to the proverb: because every group has its fault lines, one capable man who works them outmatches a host. நூற்றுவர், 'the hundred', may point to the hundred brothers of the epic, but the verse does not say so.

pazhamozhi.literal: the able one will kill the hundred

story.act: a capable man destroyed a hundred
story.tradition: by tradition the hundred may be the hundred brothers of the Bharata war; the verse names neither them nor their slayer

pazhamozhi.applied_to: division within a host lets one able man overcome it

reading: For those able to discern, it is a sure gain to win over the enmity that lives inside their enemy, as we see liquor cured by liquor; is that not removing thorn with thorn?
nuance: The verse gives two proverbs, one in the counsel (கள்ளினால் கள்ளறுத்தல்) and one quoted. Both make the same point: the cure of a thing is its like, so the enemy's own inner enemy is the best weapon against him.

pazhamozhi.literal: removing thorns with a thorn

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to using the enemy's inner foe

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an enemy is undone by the enmity within his own camp

reading: When someone has gone in day after day to crush and kill another, and sees that the weakened one does not fall, to come to him in fullness of friendship is like taking to one's guard when the arrow has missed.
nuance: The line is hard: மலிந்தடைதல் is taken as 'approaching warmly', and காக்கொள்ளும் as 'taking guard' after a missed shot. On this reading the failed oppressor should turn friend before the survivor turns on him. If கா is read otherwise, the proverb's image changes.

pazhamozhi.literal: when the arrow misses, take guard

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to an attacker whose victim survives

pazhamozhi.applied_to: when an attack fails, make peace before the enemy recovers

reading: Except by speaking sweetly and openly, by giving fine wealth, by drawing men over through division, and by striking well and in due order those who have come into the middle, enmity is not ended by snapping a stick and throwing it.
nuance: The verse names four means against an enemy, sweet words, gifts, division and force, in that order, with force last and 'in due order' (முறையால்). The proverb dismisses the rash gesture: an enmity does not end with a show of breaking. அறையான் is taken as 'by splitting'; it might mean 'by speech'.

pazhamozhi.literal: enmity does not end by breaking and throwing

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the rash way of ending enmity

pazhamozhi.applied_to: enmity ends by conciliation, gifts, division and measured force, not by a gesture

title: படைவீரர் 311-326
theme: Under the heading படைவீரர், sixteen verses on the soldier: deeds over words, loyalty that cannot join the enemy, silence about one's own valour, courage that weighs the match and is not the fool's ignorance, scorn for those who bully the weak, hide behind walls, kin or reputation, or eat the king's food without fighting, and the refusal of a daughter to a king that can end only in war.

reading: The verse says the worthy, having weighed the matter, close with the enemy in fierce battle whether the foe wins or they do, while those who sit within the guarded fort and rage with many words are compared to water poured into a யாப்பு.
nuance: தூக்கி, 'having weighed', comes before the indifference to outcome: the weighing does not decide whether to fight but is the mark of the worthy who fight anyway. யாப்பு is taken as a binding or enclosure that does not hold water, so the talk runs off; the exact object is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: water poured into a binding (an enclosure that does not hold it)

story.act: no story; talk of rage from behind the walls runs away like water poured into what cannot hold it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: big talk from safety is wasted where the worthy go out and fight

reading: The verse asks whether one who would give his body for his king when need comes could ever join that king's enemies, and answers with the proverb that two bulls in open enmity do not drink at one ford.

pazhamozhi.literal: two bulls do not drink water at one ford

story.act: no story; two bulls set against each other will not share a watering place

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the loyal soldier and his king's enemy cannot meet on common ground

reading: The verse says that when those who did great deeds stand silent and those who did nothing talk at length and blame the king, it is like the ox that, guarded from slipping, pulls the load out of the mud, while the dead weight rises where it does not.
nuance: The proverb's syntax is hard: வாங்கும் எருது (the ox that pulls) stands against சாக்காடு, read here as the useless, dead-weight beast, with எழாஅமை and எழல் set against each other. The general sense, that the doer is silent and the idle make the noise, is clear from lines 1-2; the image is not.

pazhamozhi.literal: where the pulling ox does not rise up, the dead weight rises

story.act: no story; an ox drawing a cart from the mud and a useless beast set side by side

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the silent doer against the complaining idler who blames the king

reading: The verse asks whether those who say 'we will take the battle' when their garlanded king looks at them need make the charge a common one, and says that whoever it falls to should take it up and give it, as the town is charged with the begging bowl of the Jain monks.
nuance: அமணர் are Jain ascetics, and the proverb assumes that the whole town feeds them, each house in turn. The application is unclear: it may mean that a battle pledged in the king's sight is everyone's charge, as the monks' bowl is the town's, or that no one may push it onto the common stock. The reading follows the second.

pazhamozhi.literal: the Jain monks' bowl is the charge of the town

story.act: no story; the alms-bowl of the Jain monks, which the townspeople fill

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a pledge made before the king is a duty for whoever it falls on

reading: The verse says that those who killed the strutting foe should, while others praise them, never speak of their own valour even in elation, closing with the proverb of theft that is not bundled up.
nuance: The praise is to come from பிறர், others; the warrior's own word about himself is what is to fall. சோரம் பொதியாதவாறு is read as stolen goods that cannot be wrapped and hidden, so the deed shows itself; it could also mean that self-praise exposes a man as a theft does. Either way the claim is that valour needs no telling.

pazhamozhi.literal: as a theft is not wrapped up

story.act: no story; something stolen that cannot be bundled out of sight

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the warrior's deed speaks without his boasting

reading: Addressed to the lord of the surging shore where the long dark punnai drops puffed flowers like crushed lizard eggs, the verse says the taunting talk of those who spoke does not overwhelm the great, as a jackal's howl does not reach the sea.
nuance: Line 1 is compressed: உரைத்தாரை மீதூரா மீக்கூற்றம் is read as the loud claims of talkers that do not rise above their object. The shore address is the akam style used for a counsel of war.
domain_note: the warrior or lord of the shore

pazhamozhi.literal: as a jackal's howl does not reach the sea

story.act: no story; a jackal howling at the sea

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the noise of small men does not touch the great

reading: Addressed to a woman with bow-like brows, the verse says that even when men are able, to rush upon the enemy in battle without being their match is harm, like striking the hand against a stone.

pazhamozhi.literal: like striking the hand on a stone

story.act: no story; a hand struck against a stone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: attacking an unequal foe hurts the attacker

reading: The verse says that one who has entered the assembly of kings should not take fright because the strong enemy has mountain-like elephants, nor talk in turn and leave, but resolve to do one thing, for no one stills the waves before bathing in the sea.
nuance: உரைநடை மன்னருள் is read as the council where kings talk; நிரையுரைத்து is speaking one after another. The proverb removes the excuse of waiting for the danger to pass.
domain_note: a warrior in the royal council

pazhamozhi.literal: no one bathes in the sea after stilling its waves

story.act: no story; bathers do not wait for the sea to fall calm

pazhamozhi.applied_to: act despite the strong enemy instead of waiting for safety

reading: The verse says that petty men's soldiering is to say nothing against those who stand guard and are able, and to ride pitilessly over those who cannot resist, like a barber's razor sharpened only to cut a colocasia leaf.
nuance: சில்லார், 'the few' or 'the small', names a kind of man, not a number. சேப்பிலை is read as the soft leaf of the சேம்பு plant: the edge is real but spent on what offers no resistance.

pazhamozhi.literal: sharpening a barber's razor for a colocasia leaf

story.act: no story; a razor honed and then used on a soft leaf

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the courage of the petty is spent only on the weak

reading: The verse says that the incapable, though they shut themselves behind a fortress wall and feel secure, are caught through their fear, as a frightened bird is startled in its very body though it hides in the dark, being in the open though in darkness.

pazhamozhi.literal: in the open though in darkness

story.act: no story; a timid bird that shows itself by its own start even in the dark

pazhamozhi.applied_to: walls do not hide or save the fearful

reading: The verse says that those who cannot with spirit make the enemy perish in the raging battle, yet with arrogance eat their king's food as if they were doers, are those who take cloth with a கருக்கு.
nuance: The proverb is obscure: கருக்கு may be a jagged edge (the serrated stalk of the palmyra) or the dusk. Read as getting cloth by tearing at it or taking it in the dark, the image is of gain by false or rough means; the counsel, eating the king's food without doing his work, is clear.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who get cloth with a கருக்கு

story.act: no story; a man who gets cloth by an improper means

pazhamozhi.applied_to: drawing the king's pay on a show of deeds not done

reading: The verse says that those who turned aside from battle and were well known to have done so, saying 'our people were such men before; to whom shall we tell it', and live on food under cover of their kin's name, are like a mother who lives hidden behind her son.
nuance: எமர் மேலை இன்னரால் is read as an appeal to the ancestors' deeds; தமர் மறையால் is shelter behind one's kin. The proverb inverts the proper order: the mother should be the son's cover, not the son the mother's.

pazhamozhi.literal: as a mother lives with her son as her cover

story.act: no story; a mother sheltering behind her son

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the coward living on his family's earned name

reading: The verse says that the fool's daring, propped on his failure to perceive the many dangers, is not true daring, and that daring holds only as it is ingrained, closing with the proverb that the fear that comes of knowing is very great.
nuance: பொறிப்பட்டவாறு can be 'as it is stamped in' (by nature or by fate); the verse seems to say courage cannot be put on by ignorance. The proverb then admits that knowledge brings fear, so true courage is the knowing man's, holding against a fear he feels.

pazhamozhi.literal: the fear of knowing is very great

story.act: no story; the proverb states the fear that understanding brings

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the courage of ignorance is not courage

reading: The verse asks what want of young warriors one has who has no one stronger than himself to face, and answers that cats, though mightier than tigers, get no milk where there are no rats.
nuance: தன்னின் வலியானைத் தானுடையன் அல்லாதான் is read as the king with no stronger foe; he feels no need of warriors, so their worth goes unrewarded. புலியிற் பெருந்திறல is the warriors' mightiness, said of the cats with irony.

pazhamozhi.literal: cats get no milk where there are no rats

story.act: no story; household cats are fed while they have rats to catch

pazhamozhi.applied_to: warriors are valued only while there is an enemy

reading: The verse says of those who are reputed to have generosity, conduct and grasping intelligence but lack the strength to march on the enemy's possessions, that the bearing of an army is better than an army.
nuance: The proverb may be praise or irony. Read with lines 1-3, such men serve only as the look of a force, its படைத்தகைமை, not its striking power; it is uncertain whether that is meant as their use or their shame.

pazhamozhi.literal: an army's bearing is better than the army

story.act: no story; the proverb weighs an army's appearance against its strength

pazhamozhi.applied_to: men of good name but no drive to attack serve only as display

reading: The verse says that if the king demands the young girl with eyes like two carp, even her brothers will not consent, and there is nothing but the sweet sight of them swinging their mighty shoulders as they declare battle, for no one salts a raw plantain.
nuance: This is the Sangam theme of a girl refused to a king, and war that follows, told here as a certainty with a kitchen proverb. தன்னையர் are the girl's elder brothers, not her father. The proverb is read as 'there is no other treatment for it'; the exact sense of salting a plantain is not sure.
domain_note: the girl's kin as warriors against a king

pazhamozhi.literal: no one rubs salt into a raw plantain

story.act: no story; a kitchen practice that is not done

pazhamozhi.applied_to: war is the only answer when a king demands a daughter of a proud house

title: இல்வாழ்க்கை 327-337 (1/2)
theme: The first half of the heading இல்வாழ்க்கை, eleven verses on the household: money as the seed of its work, cherishing the wife who shared its toil, keeping up appearances in want, the wife who tends guests unbidden, the father's charge over his children, a mother's favour, the bard who pleads for a straying husband, a glance that hides modesty, not entering a friend's house alone, the futility of confining women, and the great sparing the poor as hosts.
source_issues: 330 line 2: விரும்தோம்பி is a misspelling of விருந்தோம்பி.
334 line 3: தொழுதையுள் மாலையும் மாலை மறுக்குறுத்தாள் is obscure and may be corrupt; the verse's sense is uncertain.
332 lines 1-2: the dice comparison is compressed and its grammar loose.

reading: The verse says, to a woman, that womanhood of great charm is not without modesty, the life of the body is not without food, and the household's undertakings cannot be carried out without money, and clinches it with the proverb that there is no conjuring trick without a seed.
nuance: The first two clauses are given as plain preconditions so that the third, money for the work of the house, takes their certainty. சம்பிரதம் is a juggler's or conjuror's feat, most likely the trick of making a plant spring up, which still needs a real seed: even the marvel has a material cause. The line on modesty is a statement of the period about what makes a woman, not a counsel the reading endorses.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no conjuring feat without a seed

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to any undertaking that seems to come from nothing

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the work of the household needs money as its seed

norm.note: a norm of the period that a woman's womanhood requires modesty

reading: The verse says that wives who have shared the toil of the household with their husbands are, once this is seen, to be cherished without parting, and that men who are not content with what they themselves have obtained and keep reaching for more are like those who dig too deep and come upon a snake.
nuance: உரிமை is the wife's right place in the house, and உழந்தமை is labour shared there, so her claim to be kept is earned by toil. Who 'does not rejoice in what they got' is not stated; read with the proverb it is most likely the husband who looks past the wife he has, and over-digging finds harm, but it could be read of anyone discontented with his lot.

pazhamozhi.literal: if one digs too deep, there are some who see a snake

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the man who seeks beyond what he has

pazhamozhi.applied_to: discontent with one's own lot and partner turns up harm

reading: The verse says that even when the ruin within the house is great one should keep a bright face outside, and even when one has no bed at all, since nobody asks those who are well dressed whether they have eaten.
nuance: The proverb is an observation about how the world reads people, not a moral claim: the clothed are presumed fed. The counsel is the household's dignity before others, and it accepts concealment of want as part of it.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one asks those who are clothed about their food

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the impoverished house that keeps up its outer show

pazhamozhi.applied_to: keeping one's outward state hides an inner want

reading: The verse says that those whose wife, by nature reading the unspoken sign, tends the guests who come and who live secure in their wealth without trouble have, as it were, set up a water-lift in the sea every day.
nuance: The wife acts on what the husband has not said (சொல்லாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறியும்), so the hospitality is hers. துலாம் here is the counterpoised pole that lifts water from a well; set up in the sea it never runs dry. Line 2 reads விரும்தோம்பி, a slip for விருந்தோம்பி.

pazhamozhi.literal: they have set up a water-lift in the sea

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the house whose wife tends guests

pazhamozhi.applied_to: such a house draws from a store that does not fail

reading: The verse says, to a deer-eyed woman, that by whatever means the head of the house must make his children stand on the right path, for the doll one has made oneself becomes a thing that afflicts its maker.
nuance: இறைவன் here is the master of the house, the father, not a god or a king. அணங்கு can be a goddess or an afflicting spirit; with the warning of the first lines it is most likely the latter, so the child one formed carelessly becomes one's own torment, but the proverb could also say that what one shapes well becomes one's object of worship.

pazhamozhi.literal: the doll one made becomes an afflicting spirit to oneself

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the parent and the child he forms

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a father answers for the children he shapes

reading: The verse says that at dice, though the wealth staked on both sides is equal, an onlooker at the side leans to one player, and that so even among children who are all of great worth a mother has one she favours, asking whether mothers' sides among their children are any different.
nuance: The proverb is a question; read with the dice image it grants that partiality is natural even where merit is equal, rather than condemning it. The first line's ஒக்கும் வகையான் உடன்பொருள் is compressed and the grammar of line 2 is loose, so the dice scene is reconstructed.

pazhamozhi.literal: is a mother's leaning among her children anything other?

story.act: the bystander at a game of dice who takes one player's side though the stakes are equal

pazhamozhi.applied_to: favour among equals is natural, even to a mother

reading: The verse has a wife tell the bard that while her husband presses his body to the breasts of bangled young women he should not speak what is not the way, since no one can wake a man who only feigns sleep.
nuance: This is an akam situation set under the household heading: the bard comes to plead for the husband who keeps courtesans. The proverb of feigned sleep is most likely said of the husband, who strays knowingly and cannot be reformed by words, though it may also be her refusal to be taken in by the bard's excuses.
domain_note: a wife answering the bard who pleads for her husband

pazhamozhi.literal: one who feigns sleep is hard for anyone to wake

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the husband who goes to courtesans knowing what he does

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a man who strays by choice will not be turned by pleading

reading: The verse says that the startled-doe gaze of finely jewelled women hides the modesty that lives in it, as a garland spoils another garland, and closes that this is how excellence cuts excellence.
nuance: The sense is that one beauty, the frightened glance, covers another, the modesty, so that a grace is lost to sight by a grace; but line 3 (தொழுதையுள் மாலையும் மாலை மறுக்குறுத்தாள்) is obscure, and both who 'spoiled the garland' and what the garland stands for are guesses. The counsel has little to do with the household heading.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way excellence cuts excellence

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a woman's glance that hides her modesty

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one grace may conceal another

reading: The verse says that even men of pure mind should not enter alone even the house of a friend, because when the town is loud with talk of wrong no witness can stand, as no dam holds when the water rises.
nuance: The innocence of the man is granted: the point is that the town's clamour is a flood, and a pure mind is no defence against it. கரி is a witness; the line says that once rumour rises there is none who can testify to the truth.

pazhamozhi.literal: when the water rises there is no dam

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to rumour overwhelming the innocent

pazhamozhi.applied_to: avoid the occasion, for a rumour once loosed cannot be checked

reading: The verse says that women of fine jewels who excel by their own restraint cannot be held by confinement, and that one without it, though bound by force until she suffers, is like a dog's tail, which never comes straight.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 and the proverb face two ways: the woman with நிறை needs no prison, and the one without is not changed by it. The verse keeps the assumption that women's conduct is a matter for guarding and says only that force cannot do it.
domain_note: the husband who would guard a wife

pazhamozhi.literal: a dog's tail never becomes straight

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the woman without restraint whom force cannot amend

pazhamozhi.applied_to: confinement neither makes nor mends a woman's restraint

norm.note: a norm of the period on guarding women's chastity by confinement

reading: The verse says that those who have grown very great should not go as passing guests to the poor, for the strain of those who give beyond their means is like a sparrow cutting its own thigh, whose entrails faint.
nuance: The duty is laid on the guest, not the host: the poor man will feed a great guest beyond his means, so the great should spare him. குறங்கு is the thigh; the sparrow that cuts its own flesh to feed others (perhaps its young) has so little that it collapses.
domain_note: the great who visit the poor

pazhamozhi.literal: when the sparrow cuts its thigh, its entrails faint

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the poor host who gives more than he has

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a great guest ruins the poor host who must receive him

title: இல்வாழ்க்கை 338-347 (2/2)
theme: The second part of இல்வாழ்க்கை, ten verses: a gift spoiled by withholding a sweet word, penance as an even mind not a sect's mark, prompt return of a deposit, the use of even a small companion, the bar on flesh for renouncers and for the graceless, service to the one who feeds one, bearing the anger of kin one has fed, and ingratitude as cutting one's own branch and burning the house one ate in.
source_issues: 339: செத்துக and சகத்தனாய் (line 2-3) are odd forms; the line is read as 'whether hacked or smeared with sandal'.
341: விண்டோ யும் (line 2) has a stray space, read as விண்தோயும்.
344: ஒன்றிண்டாம் in the proverb is read as ஒன்றிரண்டாம்.
345: தான்காயான மன்னே (line 2) looks corrupt; the opening quotation mark falls inside மற்றியாரே, so the proverb as printed begins with றியாரே.

reading: The verse says that to give clothing, medicine, shelter, food and the like and relieve a man's want, and then to send him off without a sweet word, is like killing a buffalo for a feast and being stingy over the spice.
nuance: The costly things are all given; what is withheld is the one thing that costs nothing, the word at parting (விடுத்து). The proverb's காயம் is the seasoning, cheap beside the slaughtered buffalo, so the meanness is measured by how little was saved.

pazhamozhi.literal: a man who has slaughtered a buffalo grudges the spice

story.act: no story; the proverb's feast-giver kills the buffalo and then stints on the seasoning

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a large gift spoiled by withholding a sweet word when the receiver is sent off

reading: The verse says that the marks each sect takes for itself are not penance, and that penance is the worth of one who keeps an even mind whether he is hacked or smeared with sandal paste and so lives on in the world, like the middle pin of a yoke.
nuance: The middle pin (பகலாணி) holds the yoke balanced between the two oxen, so the image is of a mind that leans to neither the wound nor the perfume. The verse sits under இல்வாழ்க்கை but its counsel is about penance; the heading does not fit it. செத்துக and சகத்தனாய் are odd forms, and the sense of line 2 is read from the pairing of cutting and sandal.

pazhamozhi.literal: like the middle pin of a yoke

story.act: no story; the yoke-pin stays at the centre whichever way the oxen pull

pazhamozhi.applied_to: true penance as an equal mind toward harm and honour, not the sect's outward mark

reading: The verse says that when someone has placed a thing in one's hand, one should hand it back at the moment he comes to take it, and not put him off thinking that he will not claim it and it has become one's settled wealth, for base wealth does not stay hidden.
nuance: The fault named is delay, not denial: the keeper need only stall (நீட்டித்தல்) for the deposit to begin turning into his own. புலை here qualifies wealth, the ill-kept thing, and is not a caste word.

pazhamozhi.literal: base wealth does not stay; it comes out into the open

story.act: no story; wrongly held wealth neither lasts nor stays concealed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: returning a deposit promptly when it is asked for

reading: The verse tells the man of the good land whose hills touch the sky that it is good to have a companion, since even a crab freed a brahmin from the danger of a snake, and that there is nothing which is of no use to something.
nuance: The point turns on நண்டேயும், 'even a crab': the companion need not be great to save one. பார்ப்பான் names the traveller in the tale and carries no rule. The heading இல்வாழ்க்கை fits only loosely.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is nothing that is of no use to something

story.act: a crab kept as a companion saved a brahmin from a snake

pazhamozhi.applied_to: having a companion, however small, against sudden danger

reading: The verse says that for those who have put away strong desire that is hard to let go and stood on the good path that is hard to walk, to eat flesh got through another's suffering is to swim across the sea and then drown in the water of a calf's hoofprint.
nuance: The sea is the craving already crossed; the hoofprint is a small appetite left over, so the ruin is the more absurd for the size of what was overcome. கற்றடி is read as the calf's hoofprint (கன்று அடி). The heading இல்வாழ்க்கை does not fit a verse addressed to renouncers.

pazhamozhi.literal: having swum the sea, to sink in a calf's hoofprint

story.act: no story; a swimmer crosses the ocean and drowns in a puddle

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the renouncer who has overcome great desire and then eats flesh

norm.note: the abstention from flesh of the period, made a condition of the renouncer's path

reading: The verse says that those who kill in rage and long rejoice in it, and do not walk in grace through understanding, do not refrain from killing other lives and living on their flesh, and that this is like spoiling the curd to cook something else.
nuance: The order runs from rage to killing to eating: flesh-eating is the last step of a habit that began without அருள். The proverb is read as giving up the good thing at hand (the curd, grace) to make some other dish; the image is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: to spoil the curd and cook something else

story.act: no story; the cook ruins the curd to make another dish

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those without grace who kill and eat flesh

norm.note: the rule against killing and flesh of the period, grounded in grace

reading: The verse tells the lord of the shore where waves roll that those who know a thing well should always plan the good of the one who gives them a measure of grain, and closes with the proverb that there is no trade in which one becomes two even by going over the sea.
nuance: The giver of a நாழி is the one who feeds the speaker, a patron or master. The proverb can be read two ways: that no trade, however far, doubles the capital as serving one's provider does, or that one gains nothing by seeking a richer master abroad. ஒன்றிண்டாம் is read as ஒன்றிரண்டாம்.
domain_note: a dependent toward the one who feeds him

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no trade in which one becomes two, even by crossing the water

story.act: no story; overseas trade does not double what is sent

pazhamozhi.applied_to: steady care for the welfare of the one who provides

reading: The verse says that one who gave two measures to a man as his own does not flare up even when that man rages at him like Yama, and asks who else but our own, scorning us as 'that one' and 'this one', would lick our ghee.
nuance: The giver bears the kinsman's anger because the gift made him one of his own; only kin take such liberty and still eat from the house. The line division and the subject of காயினும் are uncertain, and line 2 is corrupt.

pazhamozhi.literal: who else would lick our ghee?

story.act: no story; only one's own people take freely of the household's ghee

pazhamozhi.applied_to: bearing the rudeness of kin one has fed

reading: The verse tells the lord of the high hills of bright gems that to plot ruin with others against those who sought one out and cared for one well as their own is thoughtlessly to cut the branch on which one sits.

pazhamozhi.literal: to cut down the branch one was sitting on

story.act: no story; the sitter saws through his own perch

pazhamozhi.applied_to: plotting with others against one's benefactor

reading: The verse says that when someone has looked after a man and his kin as old friends and relieved their want, to join with those who have broken with him and speak against him behind his back is like setting fire to the house where one has eaten.

pazhamozhi.literal: like setting fire to the house where one ate

story.act: no story; the guest burns his host's house

pazhamozhi.applied_to: backbiting a benefactor in league with his enemies

title: உறவினர் 348-356
theme: Under the heading உறவினர், nine verses on kin: one must feel dependants' trouble as one's own and feed them, good kin remove distress, stand by in trouble even after enmity and help at last like late rain, their hurtful counsel is to be borne, and one taken as kin follows his kinsman; but even brothers should not share a roof long, and dice among kin, as the Bharata shows, make them strangers.

reading: If a man does not feel that what befalls those who depend on him has befallen himself, as though it were his own, what is the use of him, for that is like pounding husk and getting only sore hands.
nuance: The verse doubles the identification: the dependants' trouble must be taken as one's own (தமக்குற்றதேயாக) and spoken of as 'ours' (எமக்குற்றது). Kinship without that feeling is not merely cold but wasted effort, which the proverb makes concrete. The hill-country address is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: like pounding chaff and only hurting one's hands

story.act: no story; the proverb names labour that yields nothing

pazhamozhi.applied_to: keeping dependants without sharing their trouble as one's own is fruitless toil

reading: Even if a man on whom others have come to depend trusts them as wholly his own, unless he sees that those he has chosen do not go in want, what way have they to go on, for all else is false and only cooked food is true.
nuance: The syntax of lines 1 to 3 is compressed and the sense of தீர்ந்தாரா and செல்லாமை is not certain; on the reading taken here, the patron's trust in his dependants' loyalty counts for nothing unless he feeds them, which is what the proverb's அட்டூண் (food that has been cooked) clinches.
domain_note: the man on whom kin depend

pazhamozhi.literal: everything is false; only food that has been cooked is true

story.act: no story; the proverb sets the meal actually served against every other profession

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a bond with dependants is proved by providing for them, not by trusting them

reading: When someone falls into distress, those called his good kin are the ones who remove it by the way of good deeds, and that is the medicine that has become a tree in one's own house.
nuance: The verse defines good kin by their act (வினைமரபின் ... நீக்கும்), not by birth; the proverb's tree growing in the house yard is a remedy that needs no search, so kin are help near at hand.

pazhamozhi.literal: the medicine that has grown as a tree of the house

story.act: no story; the proverb names a remedy growing at home

pazhamozhi.applied_to: good kin who remove one's distress are a remedy close at hand

reading: Taken truly, what do outsiders ever do for one another; but one's own people, even if they seem never to do anything, will do it, as rain, they say, will rain even when it has held off.
nuance: The contrast is between பிறர் (others) and தமர் (one's own). The proverb concedes the delay: kin, like rain, may fail for a season, but their help is certain in the end. The address to a woman is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: rain, they say, will rain even if it has not rained

story.act: no story; the proverb rests on the certainty of rain after a dry spell

pazhamozhi.applied_to: kin help in the end even when they seem to fail

reading: Those of one family, even if they were hostile before, stand behind a man and do not leave him when overwhelming trouble comes, while others will not come in even if he treats them as gold, for outsiders are not those who draw close.
nuance: முன்னின்னார் (unpleasant before) and பின்னின்னார் (standing behind afterwards) are a pun on the same syllables; the loyalty is owed to shared family (ஒருகுடியார்), not to past kindness, and the outsider's failure is set against favours given him (பொன்னாச் செயினும்).

pazhamozhi.literal: others are not the ones who draw near

story.act: no story; the proverb states the outsider's distance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: in trouble one's family closes in and strangers stay away

reading: Even if they speak so that it hurts, it is good to hear counsel for one's good from the mouths of kin, for a mother's treading does not make her young lame.
nuance: The address in line 3 (birds treading on flowers in the ripe fields) prepares the proverb's image of a mother bird treading her chicks. The hurt of kin's words is real (உளைய) but cannot cripple, because of who gives it.

pazhamozhi.literal: a mother's treading does not make one lame

story.act: no story; the proverb draws on a mother hen or bird treading on her young

pazhamozhi.applied_to: hurtful counsel from kin is to be heeded because it does no lasting harm

reading: When someone, valuing you, has taken you as his own, then whatever befalls, you do what he does, and what trouble is there in that, for the thread goes where the needle goes.
nuance: Who values whom in line 1 is not fixed; the reading here takes the subject of கொண்டக்கால் as the one who accepts and the addressee as the accepted kinsman who then follows him. The address in line 3 is to a man of the hills (இன்னொலி வெற்ப).

pazhamozhi.literal: the thread goes the way the sewing needle goes

story.act: no story; the proverb is the needle and thread

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one taken as kin follows his kinsman's course whatever it costs

reading: Even for those who mingled together in the womb, living long in one place together is painful, for sharing a dwelling is unpleasant even with Tiru who sits on the lotus.
nuance: The heading praises kin, and this verse turns: brothers born of one womb (கருவினுட் கொண்டு கலந்தாரும்) should not stay long under one roof. துச்சு is taken as a shared or borrowed dwelling; the proverb's goddess of fortune makes the point that even the best companion palls.

pazhamozhi.literal: sharing a dwelling is unpleasant even with the goddess of fortune

story.act: no story; the proverb names Tiru on the lotus as the most welcome of housemates

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even brothers should not live together long

reading: In the Bharata too, the twice fifty, staking their inheritance, faced the five in war, became strangers to them and broke apart; therefore one does not play dice with those one loves.
nuance: The verse reads the epic as a case about kin: the dice turned brothers' sons into ஏதிலர் (strangers). It does not name Dharma's loss but makes the stake their own share (தம் தாயமா).

pazhamozhi.literal: people do not play at dice with those they love

story.act: the hundred staked their inheritance at dice against the five, went to war with them and became strangers

pazhamozhi.applied_to: gaming among kin destroys kinship

title: அறம் செய்தல் 357-371
theme: Under the heading அறம் செய்தல், fifteen verses on doing aram: the rich give easily, aram rather than the hoard is the reserve for need, it serves both worlds, it must be done before illness and death and while the rare human birth lasts, begun aram must not be dropped, a few days of the best will do, guarded wealth is lost anyway, grace is its root, and aram or penance practised falsely binds the deceiver.
source_issues: 360 line 4: the proverb வேள்வாய்க் கவட்டை நெறி is obscure; வேள்வாய் cannot be fixed.
362 lines 1-2: தக்கமில் and தொக்க வகையும் முதலும் are hard to construe; the reading rests on the proverb.
363 line 3: the opening quotation mark falls after மலைத்தழு(து), which has a bracketed ending in our text; the crying belongs to the proverb's image though printed outside it.
364, 366 line 3, 359 line 3: the proverb opens mid-line.
365 line 3: பிணிமூப்(பு) and அருங்கூற்(று) carry bracketed endings, editorial restorations of the syllable.
366 line 4: நட்டறான் can be divided more than one way, giving opposite senses to the proverb.
369 lines 3-4: the proverb ஊர்ந்துருளின் குன்று வழியடுப்ப தில் is unclear.

reading: For those whose wealth lets them live enjoying the best, doing aram and becoming gracious is, the verse tells the lord of the hills where bamboo clashes with bamboo, only like setting something more on top of a load already carried.
nuance: The proverb is read for its ease: the rich already bear wealth, and adding giving to it costs them little. It could also be read as an added weight that the rich should take on gladly; the image does not settle which.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is the way of putting more on top along with the load

story.act: no story; the proverb's porter takes a little more on a load already borne

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram and grace come easily to those who already have wealth

reading: The verse says not to take stored wealth for a reserve, but to enjoy it, give it out on both sides and do aram looking to the fit occasion, and calls that the true reserve for the time of need.
nuance: The proverb's phrase எய்ப்பினில் வைப்பு, the store kept for the time of exhaustion, is taken from the hoard and given to aram. இருபாலும் 'on both sides' may be oneself and others, or this world and the next.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is called the store for the time of exhaustion

story.act: no story; the proverb's saving for hard times is redefined

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram done at the fit place, not the hoard, is the reserve for need

reading: When the worthy come by abundant great wealth, the verse tells a slender-waisted woman, they make it a protection even for where they go after death, like one who chews the green cane and also boils it into jaggery.
nuance: The proverb is read as using the cane both ways, tasting some now and turning the rest into a sweet that keeps, so wealth serves both the present and the hereafter. It might instead set chewing against boiling as waste against keeping.

pazhamozhi.literal: chewing the green sugarcane and making jaggery of it

story.act: no story; the proverb's cane is both eaten and turned into a sweet that lasts

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy use great wealth so that it also protects them in the world to come

reading: Aram wins fame for one still in this world and is sweetness for one who has passed to the other, so for one who does good aram every day, both worlds are like a forked road whose two branches both go well.
nuance: ஈனுலகு and தேனுலகு pair this world and the sweet world above. வேள்வாய்க் கவட்டை is obscure; it is read as the fork where a road parts, both ways being good.

pazhamozhi.literal: the path at the fork

story.act: no story; the proverb's forked road leads well either way

pazhamozhi.applied_to: daily aram serves in both worlds

reading: Those who did not readily do the many kinds of good deeds before death, but think of the way later and turn to aram when they see illness, find nothing in it, as a man who sees a dog finds no stone to hand.
nuance: ஆய்வின்றி is read as 'without hanging back'; it could also mean 'without discernment'. The proverb says the means is missing at the moment of need, not only that time is short.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way one does not see a stone when one sees a dog

story.act: no story; the proverb's man finds no stone when the dog comes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram put off until illness comes fails

reading: When one gets wealth by blameless work and the gathered kinds and the capital are all of that, to be angered when told to do aram generously with it is like spurning milk sweetened with sugar.
nuance: Line 1's தக்கமில் and line 2's தொக்க வகையும் முதலும் are hard; the sense rests on the proverb. செருக்கும் is read as refusing in pride.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way one spurns milk with sugar

story.act: no story; the proverb's man spurns sweetened milk

pazhamozhi.applied_to: resenting the call to give from honestly earned wealth refuses one's own good

reading: Making those who will not take up good aram take it, checking them with an eye to the lasting good in the endless world, is like mothers who shake the struggling, crying baby that will not feed and pour milk into it.
nuance: The verse approves compulsion for the other's good: the unwilling are made to take aram as an infant is fed against its will. குலைத்தடக்கி is read as shaking and holding down. The quotation mark falls after மலைத்தழு(து), so the crying is outside the proverb as printed though it belongs to its image.

pazhamozhi.proverb: உண்ணாக் குழவியைத் தாயார் அலைத்துப்பால் பெய்து விடல்
pazhamozhi.literal: mothers shaking a baby that will not feed and pouring milk into it

story.act: no story; the proverb's mothers force-feed a refusing infant

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the unwilling should be made to take aram for their lasting good

reading: If even those who do aram look to where it is rightly placed and give with discernment of the ways, it is good for them where they go, their wealth grows as they give it out, and when aram is done, what is not aram departs.
nuance: புறஞ்செய்ய is read as giving outward to others. The proverb's அல்லவை, the things that are not good, leave when aram is done.

pazhamozhi.literal: when aram is done, the things that are not good leave

story.act: no story; a general saying

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram given with discernment brings good hereafter and removes evil

reading: Since human birth is hard to come by, the verse urges aram as far as one can, for without fail dreaded disease, old age and hard Death come together, and the stupor comes that puts one to sleep.
nuance: The whole of lines 3 and 4 is set as the proverb. துயக்கு and துஞ்ச make death a sleep of bewilderment rather than an event.

pazhamozhi.proverb: அஞ்சும் பிணிமூப்(பு) அருங்கூற்(று) உடனியைந்து துஞ்ச வருமே துயக்கு
pazhamozhi.literal: dreaded disease, old age and hard Death join, and stupor comes to put one to sleep

story.act: no story; the proverb names the three that come together at life's end

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the rare human birth should be used for aram before death

reading: If a good aram, planned to be firmly bound so that many are not burdened by how it falls out, meets obstacles and breaks off midway, it would have been better to be one who never planted it.
nuance: நட்டறான் is read as 'one who has not planted'; it could also be read as one who plants and does not cut it off, which would make the proverb a call to carry the aram through. Either way the half-done aram is the fault.

pazhamozhi.literal: rather than fall abandoned midway, better to be one who did not plant

story.act: no story; the proverb's planting abandoned midway

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an aram begun must be carried through, or it were better not begun

reading: Even if one cannot do aram on many days, the verse tells a woman whose waist seems to wilt under her girdle to do it on some days with the best things, for good aram does what nothing else does.
nuance: The proverb is read as 'hear: good aram does what (nothing else) does'; it could also mean that aram's doing is never undone. The counsel trades frequency for the quality of what is given.

pazhamozhi.literal: hear: good aram does what (others) do not

story.act: no story; a general saying addressed to the listener

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram done even on a few days, with the best, is worth doing

reading: Birds snatch drying grain in the blink of an eye even while those watching are watching, and for bright wealth won by tending and guarding too, those who eye it are more than those who keep it.
nuance: பார்ப்பார் here means those who look out for it, the covetous, set against காப்பார், keepers; it is not the birth-group word. The verse does not name aram: under this heading the lesson is that wealth will not stay kept, so it is better given.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who watch for it outnumber those who guard

story.act: no story; the proverb's birds that take grain from under the watcher's eye

pazhamozhi.applied_to: guarded wealth is still lost to the many who covet it

reading: Having seen the two aged parents one cannot do without perish, will anyone still hold wealth to be the true thing? The verse urges aram in a fitting way, for once a thing rolls, no hill stands in the path to stop it.
nuance: இருமுது மக்கள் is read as the two aged parents. The proverb is read as life rolling toward death with nothing to check it; ஊர்ந்துருளின் and குன்று வழியடுப்பது leave the image unclear.

pazhamozhi.literal: when it rolls, no hill blocks the way

story.act: no story; the proverb's rolling thing that nothing stops

pazhamozhi.applied_to: death comes unchecked, so wealth should go to aram

reading: Those who know fully that grace is what aram rests on know its root; those who plainly leave that root and abandon it keep a conduct that guards nothing, like letting the hare go to eat a crow.
nuance: முதல், the root or capital, makes அருள் the source of aram; the proverb ranks the forsaken thing above what is taken, the hare above the crow.

pazhamozhi.literal: letting go the hare and eating the crow

story.act: no story; the proverb's hunter drops the better prey for the worse

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram without grace gives up the root for a lesser thing

reading: Those who have both penance and aram in this life, if they practise them falsely, earn blame not only in this life but in the next: it is a rope with which they bind themselves.
nuance: சலமொழுகல், practising with deceit, is the fault; the image turns the means of merit into the means of the deceiver's own bondage.
domain_note: those who profess penance or aram

pazhamozhi.literal: the rope with which one binds oneself

story.act: no story; the proverb's self-binding rope

pazhamozhi.applied_to: false penance and aram bind the false one in both worlds

title: ஈகை 372-386
theme: Under the heading ஈகை, fifteen verses on giving: giving to get more is angling, the hoard ends with the king while a small gift to the starving is rain in the waste, discerning giving neither drains nor dwindles wealth but renews it like tank and well, the best giver reads the need, the habitual giver gives even in want as Pari's daughter did in drought, a gift measures the patron's worth, giving for fame is wage work, crowds of askers and incapable patrons defeat the asker, and wealth not given in time is lost past remedy.
source_issues: 372: the quotation mark opens inside the word வேண்(டு)'அயிரை, so the proverb's first word is split by the mark.
378: துறைக்தோணி is likely a misprint for துறைத்தோணி.
382: மண்ணசுற்றிக் looks corrupt; the sense of encircling or removing the foes' land is guessed.
384: பெறாஅஅன் has a doubled alapedai vowel, likely a misprint for பெறாஅன்.

reading: Those who give a small thing and by that act look to gain a large one are, the verse tells the lord of the river town where spread flowers mingle in the water, like anglers who throw away the small ayirai fish to haul in the varal.
nuance: The verse does not call such giving wrong in so many words; the angler's image makes it plain that the gift is bait and the giving a kind of trade. Its place under the heading ஈகை implies the censure.

pazhamozhi.literal: they are those who let go the ayirai they wanted and pull in the varal

story.act: no story; the angler who sacrifices a small fish as bait to land a bigger one

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving a little in order to get much back is fishing, not giving

reading: What the concealers have laid up helps no one in the end except as a provision for kings who drive them out and seize it, while giving even one thing to help those crushed by want is rain falling in the dry wilderness.
nuance: The verse sets two ends of wealth side by side: the hoard feeds the seizing king, the small gift feeds the destitute. துரப்புடைய may mean kings given to driving people out or to pursuing; either way the hoard passes to royal power.

pazhamozhi.literal: rain poured in the middle of the dry wilderness

story.act: no story; rain in the wasteland stands for a gift where need is greatest

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small gift to those in deep want is worth more than any hoard

reading: Wealth that lay gathered over many years and idle, once a capable man gives it out with discernment, does not quickly run dry, any more than the water a tank has long held runs out.
nuance: The giver must be வல்லான் and must give தெரிந்து, with discernment: the claim that giving does not exhaust wealth is made for discerning giving, not for any scattering. வல்லே (quickly) qualifies the running out.

pazhamozhi.literal: water that a tank has held a long time

story.act: no story; a long-filled tank stands for long-gathered wealth that giving will not soon drain

pazhamozhi.applied_to: discerning giving from long-gathered wealth does not soon exhaust it

reading: The excellent givers are those who see what a suppliant has in mind, judging from his very manner, and give that; the verse tells the lord of cool hills where the owl hoots in the millet field that no one drops a stone into a begging bowl.
nuance: The proverb is read as: what goes into the bowl must be what the bowl is for, so the gift must answer the asker's need, and the best giver reads that need before it is spoken.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who puts a stone into a begging bowl

story.act: no story; the alms bowl takes food, not stones

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a gift should fit what the asker needs, which the best giver reads unasked

reading: Even when they have nothing left to call people in and give, those long used to giving freely are the ones who can wipe away the distress of those who depend on them, as a great horse, even wasted, shows its difference once it is in harness.
nuance: தூஉய்ப் பயின்றார் is read as those practised in scattering (giving lavishly); it could also mean those practised in purity. வாய்ப்புத்தான் before the quotation is hard to construe.

pazhamozhi.proverb: வாடியக் கண்ணும் பெருங்குதிரை யாப்புள்வே றாகி விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: even when it has wasted, a great horse becomes distinct in its harness

story.act: no story; the thoroughbred, though thin, shows its breed once harnessed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the habitual giver keeps relieving his dependents even when his means are gone

reading: Let those who came to one who gave a thing to each who asked go off saying they have made him poor; the verse tells a woman with five-plaited hair that, for anyone at all, there is no one who has become poor by giving.
nuance: கொண்டார் is read as the takers who leave thinking they have stripped the giver; it could also be his own people who complain that he has ruined them. அடுத்தேறல் in the address is obscure.

pazhamozhi.literal: there are none who became poor by giving

story.act: no story; the proverb denies that giving impoverishes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving does not impoverish the giver, whatever onlookers say

reading: Have those who conceal their wealth, thinking it will dwindle if they give to askers, never seen for themselves, the verse asks the lord of the shore where a boat rides at the landing on the swelling sea, that a well springs fresh each time it is drawn?

pazhamozhi.literal: the well springs up each time it is drawn

story.act: no story; a well refills as water is drawn from it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving does not diminish wealth but renews it

reading: Only the foolish say a gift goes by the rank of the suppliants; the deeds of patrons who, concealing nothing, have worn generosity as their ornament are all great in the measure of their own worth, as a water-flower rises to the measure of the water.
nuance: The verse moves the measure of a gift from the receiver to the giver: வரிசை (rank, due measure) belongs to the patron's சீர், not to the suppliant's standing.

pazhamozhi.literal: water flowers are bounded by the water

story.act: no story; a water flower's height follows the depth of water

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a gift's greatness follows the patron's worth, not the suppliant's rank

reading: When a great poet had composed his song, a patron, to make good the want spoken in his words, said 'give to him as he asks; may you live long'; there is no need to spell out such men by name, for givers themselves know the measure of their own worth.
nuance: The first two lines seem to tell a particular episode of a patron answering a poet, but neither is named; அடுத்தர and தொடுத்தின்னார் என்னலோ வேண்டா are hard to construe, so the episode is reported only as far as the words allow.

pazhamozhi.literal: givers themselves know the measure of their own worth

story.act: a patron answers a great poet's composition by bidding that he be given what he lacks and blessing him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a true giver gives by the measure of his own worth without needing to be told

reading: Even in a time of drought without rain, Pari's young daughter gave a bard gold, putting it in the pot of water on the fire to serve as his food; there is no doorstep to which nothing at all comes.
nuance: The proverb can be read two ways: every house, even in drought, has something to give, or every house will in time receive something. The episode of gold put in the cooking pot in place of rice is the verse's own; it does not say the daughter was poor, only that the rain had failed.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no front yard where nothing comes

story.act: in a rainless season Pari's young daughter put gold in the pot of water and gave it to a bard as his food

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving goes on in every house, even when the means of giving fail

reading: For the strong, whose generosity makes even their foes hand over what they own so that fame stays with all who receive, and who can encircle and take their foes' land, what is hard to give? The man who has a daughter does not fear loss.
nuance: The proverb's father has already reckoned with giving his daughter away, so loss holds no fear for him; the verse applies this to the conquering king, for whom wealth given is wealth that can be won again. மண்ணசுற்றிக் looks corrupt, and the first two lines are hard to construe.

pazhamozhi.literal: he who has begotten a girl does not fear loss

story.act: no story; the father of a daughter is resigned to giving her away

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king strong enough to take what he gives does not fear the cost of giving

reading: The giving of those who give lavishly without regard to return and without discernment, looking only to fame, is, the verse tells the lord of the cool shore where the sea leaps roaring like strong horses, the way of working for wages and eating.
nuance: பயன்நோக்காது seems to clear these givers of seeking return, but the proverb turns it back: fame is their wage, so giving aimed at fame is still paid work. பாத்தறிவு, the sense that divides the deserving from the rest, is what they lack.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way of working for hire and eating

story.act: no story; the hired labourer eats by his wage

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving for fame is wages, not giving

reading: Even a man who never refuses, when many ask him for the same one thing, thinks of the distress of those who will go without and, unable to bear it, hides even what he has; so for living by begging, numbers are bad.
