nuance: The giver's concealment here comes from pity, not meanness: he hides the one thing because he cannot bear to disappoint the rest. The proverb's counsel falls on the askers.

pazhamozhi.literal: for eating by begging, many together is bad

story.act: no story; a crowd of askers defeats the one they ask

pazhamozhi.applied_to: suppliants who come in numbers make even a generous giver withhold

reading: People of great show and great desire who attach themselves to those who cannot satisfy that desire are, the verse tells a woman with heavy earrings and kohl-lined eyes like the river's kayal, going the way of axle grease that soaks in and is gone.
nuance: The image of axle grease that sinks into the wheel and is lost is read as the suppliant's hope and effort spent for nothing; தோற்றம் பெரிய may describe either the seekers' show or the patrons'.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way axle grease sinks in

story.act: no story; grease rubbed on an axle soaks away

pazhamozhi.applied_to: seeking from a patron who cannot give wastes the seeker

reading: When vast wealth slips its guard and runs off and a great king seizes it, what can those who never gave it away do? Even for great renouncers, when overwhelming things befall, there is no remedy.
nuance: The proverb is read as saying that excess, whether of wealth or of misfortune, admits no cure, so wealth should be given before the king takes it; நீத்தப் பெரியார் widens the point to renouncers, which fits the heading only loosely.

pazhamozhi.literal: when excessive things arrive there is no remedy

story.act: no story; the hoard swept away to a seizing king

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth not given in time is lost past remedy

title: வீட்டு நெறி 387-399
theme: Under the heading வீட்டு நெறி, thirteen verses on the way to release: self-mastery outranks wealth and birth, the senses must be guarded early, the finished household should give way to renunciation and the undecided lose both lives, no fortune escapes Death, desire and pride in town life are costly, the renouncer must cut even the smallest tie, and birth ends when its supports are gone.
source_issues: All verses of this chapter (387-399) are flagged site_diff: the comparison site lacks them, so the text could not be checked against a second witness.
398 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at பயின்றது but has no closing mark; the proverb is taken to run to the end of the verse.
392 line 3: திச்சென்று is obscure and may be corrupt.
396 line 4: the proverb குழிப்புழி ஆற்றா குழிக்கு is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
397 line 2: சுடரே ரனைத்தாய் is oddly divided (perhaps சுடர் ஏர் அனைத்தாய்).
388 line 4: கொல்லி is obscure; it may stand for கொள்ளி.

reading: Wealth that does not run short however it is counted, good birth and the possessions that kings hold are set aside, and so is being named by kings as men of worth: for this life and the next, the verse says, owning oneself comes first.
nuance: தம்மை உடைமை, 'having oneself', is read here as self-mastery, the possession that the external goods of wealth, lineage and royal favour cannot replace; the verse ranks it above even a king's acknowledgement, the honour a court poet might value most.

pazhamozhi.literal: possessing oneself is the chief thing

story.act: no story; the proverb is set against a list of outer goods: uncounted wealth, birth, royal property and royal recognition

pazhamozhi.applied_to: self-mastery outranks wealth, birth and royal esteem in this world and the next

reading: Those who do not, early in life, guard the five so that they are held in check, grow excellent here by the three they have taken up, and so make a safeguard for the road taken when the body falls away, are said by the proverb to have set the drum upon the kolli.
nuance: The five are most naturally the senses; the three begun may be thought, word and deed, or in a Jain frame right faith, knowledge and conduct; the verse does not say. கொல்லி is obscure: if it stands for கொள்ளி, the funeral firebrand, the proverb mocks those who beat the drum only when the pyre is lit, which fits the verse's stress on சிறுகாலை, but this is a guess.

pazhamozhi.literal: they set the drum on the kolli

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who leave provision for the afterlife until too late

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the safeguard for the next world must be made early, by restraint of the senses

reading: Once a man has made friends, quieted his enmities, gone after and joined the sharp-toothed women with waists like the drum, and set up a household, the proverb asks what use after that is a body that does not renounce.
nuance: The household is not condemned: friendship, peace and marriage are listed as tasks completed, and the question falls only on what comes after them. Renunciation is cast as the use of the body, so the body that stays in the house past its work is called useless.
domain_note: a man whose household tasks are done

pazhamozhi.literal: what is the use of a body that does not renounce?

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the householder who has done everything the house asks

pazhamozhi.applied_to: after the household is complete, renunciation is the body's remaining use

reading: Those who take up neither the householder's life nor the life without a house, and stand in the middle while the good life passes, never resolving to go wholly to one side, are said by the proverb to have lost both ends of the carrying pole.
nuance: The verse does not rank the two lives; it condemns only the failure to choose. இருதலையும் கா கழித்தார் pictures the carrier's pole with a load at each end: the undecided drop both, so the image makes indecision itself a loss, not a neutral pause.

pazhamozhi.literal: they have lost both ends of the carrying pole

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who hover between household and renunciation

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one must commit wholly to one of the two lives, or lose both

reading: Wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth and good birth may all be present, yet because Death is not turned aside by honouring or fearing it, the proverb asks who knows of anyone who leapt over Death and survived.
nuance: The construal of மதித்தஞ்சி மாறும் அஃதின்மையால் is not secure: it may mean that Death cannot be made to turn back by esteem or fear, or that the six goods give no way of escape for all that people value them. Either way the six goods are listed only to be cancelled at one stroke.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one knows of having leapt over Death and lived

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who trust in wealth, youth, beauty, strength and birth

pazhamozhi.applied_to: no gift of fortune or birth exempts one from Death

reading: The hunger that besets the body, of no help to the three aims one keeps, is as old and as fertile as anything that has come down from of old; since what is eaten is known to go into the belly and turn foul, the proverb says one's own desire becomes an arrow, enters within and destroys.
nuance: The three that one keeps (கொண்டொழுகும் மூன்று) are probably aram, porul and inbam, which hunger serves none of. திச்சென்று is obscure and the reading 'turns foul' is a guess from context. அம்பாயுள் is divided here as அம்பு ஆய் உள், desire turning into an arrow against oneself; other divisions are possible.

pazhamozhi.literal: one's own desire becomes an arrow, enters within, and finishes one

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the craving of the belly for food that only turns to waste

pazhamozhi.applied_to: desire for food harms the one who feeds it

reading: Those who do not clearly weigh how far their wealth and their span of life will go with them, who swell with pride at a little and live delighting in the town instead of living in the hermitage, are said by the proverb to be eating the honey of the thorn bush.
nuance: பள்ளி is the dwelling of renouncers, in a Jain text likely the monks' retreat, set against பதி, the town. The proverb's honey is sweet but gathered among thorns, so the pleasure of town life is not denied, only priced.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who eat the honey of the thorny mulli plant

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the proud town-dweller who has not reckoned how long wealth and life will last

pazhamozhi.applied_to: pleasures taken without counting their end are sweetness bought with wounds

reading: The speaker tells his heart that it goes after the hard-hearted, longing for their way, and has today been brought low, and bids it go and not die, as others do, pointing to the house and speaking fondly of it, for wives and children are many bonds.
nuance: The verse is an address to one's own heart, so the counsel is self-persuasion. வன்னெஞ்சினார் may be the hard-hearted world the heart longs after, or it may praise the renouncers as hard against attachment; the sense of the first two lines turns on this. கட்டம் may be a bond or a hardship; both suit the proverb.
domain_note: a man urging his own heart to leave the house

pazhamozhi.literal: wives and children are many bonds

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the heart that clings to home as death nears

pazhamozhi.applied_to: attachment to wife and children holds the heart back from release

reading: The verse asks the lord of the hill country, where the roaring cascade falls on the millet field, what further tie is left for those who have renounced after giving up even their dear children and the wealth they earned, and says that clinging still would be like the elephant passing through while its tail does not.
nuance: The proverb inverts the scale: the elephant (children and wealth) has gone through the gap, and it is the tail, the smallest remnant of attachment, that sticks. The verse thus says the hardest part of renunciation is not the great surrender but the trifle kept after it.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way the elephant goes through but its tail does not

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a renouncer who keeps some small tie after leaving children and wealth

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small attachment kept after a great renunciation defeats it

reading: Though people fear that the fruit of deeds gathered over many births will come home to the body, the verse says we see them unable to do anything at all at the place where it must be discharged, and closes with a proverb about what a pit cannot do for a pit.
nuance: கழிப்புழி, 'where it is to be worked off', seems to be the present life in which the deed's fruit falls due. The proverb குழிப்புழி ஆற்றா குழிக்கு is hard to construe; it may say that what fills one hole cannot fill another, or that a pit cannot be filled from within itself. The application is therefore uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: at the pit's place, they are of no avail for the pit (sense unclear)

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who fear karmic fruit yet do nothing when it must be worked off

pazhamozhi.applied_to: fear of deeds' fruit is useless without acting when the fruit comes due

reading: A flame burns with the wick, the lamp-bowl and the ghee as its supports, and when one looks closely, so the self that runs free of its supports cuts off birth; the proverb says that when the water is gone, what depends on water is gone too.
nuance: The lamp is an image of dependence: the flame is real but lives only on what holds it, so release is put as the end of supports, not the destruction of the self. The verse names no subject for ஓடிப் பிறப்பறுக்கும்; the self or the knower is supplied. சுடரே ரனைத்தாய் is oddly divided in the text.

pazhamozhi.literal: when the water dries up, what relies on water dries up too

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to birth, which ceases when its supports are removed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: cutting the supports of attachment ends rebirth

reading: Knowing that the people of the sea-girdled world are lovers of whatever path they follow, the verse tells the lord of the forest country that people practise nothing else, and closes with the proverb that what is practised becomes heaven.
nuance: The first lines are hard to construe: அந்நெறி காதலர் may mean that people love the path they are used to, so that habit rules them, or that they love 'that path' of release. The proverb then says either that habit makes its own heaven or that steady practice of the good wins heaven.

pazhamozhi.literal: what one has practised becomes heaven

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to people's attachment to the path they follow

pazhamozhi.applied_to: practice persisted in becomes the next world one reaches

reading: The verse says not to run along the many paths of the widespread doctrines but to think on, understand and take up the complete vision, which gives greatness without limit, and closes with a proverb that the paramburi always comes to a pathakku.
nuance: நிரம்பிய காட்சி, 'the full seeing', in a Jain text may name right faith or right vision, the first of the three jewels, against the doctrines of other schools. பரம்பூரி and பதக்கு (a grain measure) make an obscure proverb: it may say that whatever is filled heaped comes in the end to one fixed measure, so that the many ways yield one result, but this is a guess.

pazhamozhi.literal: the paramburi always comes to a pathakku (sense unclear)

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who run after many doctrines instead of one complete vision

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one complete vision is worth more than many scattered creeds

title: சிறுபஞ்சமூலம் 0-20
theme: After an invocation and a verse offering the book as rain against famine, the chapter counts things under one predicate (amrita, beauty, laughable, poison, painful, death, the tongue's death) across the household, the king's service and a Jain code whose crown is not being born again by giving up lying, theft, women and meat.
source_issues: Verse 1 line 1: கொலைபோய் is read as கொலை பொய் (killing, lying); போய் is likely a misprint for பொய்.
Verse 7: show flags that the site's text lacks lines 1 and 2; their construal is uncertain.
Verse 8 line 4: நஞ்றென்றல் is likely a misprint for நன்றென்றல், as in line 3.
Verse 11 line 3: சுவிச்செயலும் is likely a misprint for கவிச்செயலும் (verse-making).
Verse 19 line 1: தேவறே is likely a misprint for தேவரே.
Verse 20 line 1: கள்ளான்கு தென்றும் is doubtfully divided; கள்ளான் சூதென்றும் is the likely reading.
Verse 16 line 3: கோய்வாயிற் கீழுயிர்க்(கு)ஈ துற்று is hard to construe and may be corrupt.

reading: The poet bows without fault to the feet of the one who knew everything, put away the three and does not age, praises him fully, and says he will tell some venbas of firm use to the people of the world.
nuance: The one praised is named only by three attributes (all-knowing, rid of the three, ageless) and by no deity's name; the verse does not say what the three are.

reading: The verse calls on its hearers to tell the Sirupanchamoolam as a rain that ends a great famine, setting out fitting conduct and setting aside the four that are not to be done: killing, lying, meat and theft.
nuance: The verse puns on பஞ்சம் (famine) inside the title's பஞ்ச மூலம். The four are read from கொலைபோய் புலால்களவோ(டு) with போய் taken as பொய் (a lie); ஓர்நால் counts these four, and ஒத்த ஒழுக்கம் is the frame they serve, not a fifth item. Lines 1-2 are hard to construe.

reading: Enjoyment lies with the man who has wealth and dharma with the man who has grace, and the man of grace does no blameworthy deed, does not come near sin and does not carry backbiting to others' ears.
nuance: Divided into five: two possessions, then three refusals of the gracious man. Wealth gets one clause and grace the rest of the verse.

reading: A chaste woman, a man who has learned and is restrained, a land of good surroundings, a king whose banner reaches the clouds and who is good to his land, and a soldier who does his work as it should be done are each named amrita.
nuance: Only the soldier is amrita on a condition (ஆகவே செய்யின், if he does it rightly). Line 3's மேகமே may instead name the rain cloud as a separate amrita for the land, which would make six things; we read it as the height of the king's banner.
domain_note: three of the five belong to the realm: land, king and soldier

reading: The subtlety an unlearned man thinks he has found, a proud carriage of the neck by a woman who lacks both ears, and a man with nothing saying he gives unattainable wealth to the needy and is generous are, the verse says, laughter to the good when they hear of them.
nuance: Three things, not five; all three are claims that outrun what the person has, so the laughter is at pretension, not at lack. காதிரண்டும் இல்லாதாள் may mean a woman without ears or without ear ornaments.

reading: The verse says that one who would be rid of the body should practise high penance, one who would end want here should give, one who would be rid of folly should learn, and one who does not desire another man's wife will gain fortune.
nuance: Read as four counsels with fortune (திரு) as the closing reward, so four items. இடம்பொழிய and மடம்பொழிய are hard to divide, and அறிமடம் may be one word (feigned ignorance) rather than அறி plus மடம்; the third item is our best construal. Ending the body means not being born again.

reading: Elephants are the beauty of an army, slenderness the beauty of a woman's waist, unbending speech the beauty of conduct, the same unbending the beauty of the sceptre, and unwavering courage the beauty of soldiers.
nuance: கோடா (not bending) is used once and carried by அதுவே to the sceptre, so truthful speech and just rule are made one quality.

reading: The verse defines five titles by conduct: the ascetic is one who holds to the book of the one free of attachment, the leader is one who has mastered every matter, the பார்ப்பான் is one who shares his food out of devotion, the worthy man is one who is aware of blame, and one who eats with care sees no disease.
nuance: பார்ப்பான் is a word for the brahmin by birth; here the verse defines him by an act, sharing food, not by birth. Lines 1-2 are missing from the site's text, and பற்றினான் may also be read with the brahmin (holding to the primal one's book).

norm.note: a varna term defined by conduct: the verse names who counts as a பார்ப்பான் by sharing food

reading: Kindly regard is the beauty of the eye, not going where one should not the beauty of the feet, saying exactly how much the beauty of reckoning, the hearers' saying 'good' the beauty of music, and the people's saying it is good that he does not oppress his land the beauty of a great king.
nuance: The last two beauties are both a judgment by others (கேட்டார் நன்று என்றல், நன்று என்றல்): the song and the king are beautiful by what listeners and subjects say.

reading: The tongue dies, the verse says, in one who kills and eats, in one who goes as a false witness, in the unlearned before those who know the good, in a debtor when he sees even once, and in the well-born when he has eaten and comes to know of it.
nuance: The tongue's death is losing the power to speak for shame. கடவான் is read as the debtor (one who owes) facing his creditor, and the last item as the well-born man struck dumb on learning what or from whom he has eaten; both construals are ours.

reading: Its own eggs are death to the spider, its long horns death to the beast, its hair death to the animal that cannot turn, its own young death to the crab, and words of abuse death to the tongue.
nuance: Each creature is killed by something of its own; the list sets abuse beside them, so the tongue's ruin comes from itself, not from the one abused.

reading: The worth of a man without shame, the vow of a man without conduct, the generosity of a man without food, the soldiering of a man without strength and the verse-making of one who does not know good Tamil are laughable, the verse says, when weighed by speech.
nuance: Each item is a virtue claimed by one who lacks its ground. The fifth turns the book's ridicule on poets.

reading: Killing is poison, enjoying meat is a cruel poison, overcoming one who is no match is poison, harming at length one who trusted is poison, and speaking ill of a young girl without inquiry is poison.
nuance: Only eating meat gets the stronger கொடுநஞ்சு, so the verse ranks eating above killing. நஞ்சூனைத் fuses நஞ்சு and ஊனை. மா(று) அல்லானை is read as 'one who is no match'; நீடாங்கு செய்தல் and இளங்கிளியை (a young parrot, or a girl addressed as one) are doubtful.

reading: Distress among friends is painful, not giving is painful, ties with those who are not friends are painful, the suffering of the pure is painful, and, the poet tells a woman, a vow taken and left short is painful.
nuance: கண்டல் அவர் in line 3 is hard to place; read with the fourth item it makes it 'seeing the suffering of the pure'. The address பூங்கதுப்பினாய் (you of the flowered hair) is the frame, not an item. Three things are fused with இன்னா in the text, so their `thing` carries it as written.

reading: The verse names as the virtue of each: for a woman, walking the way of the man who married her; for a son, following his father's way without fail; for kin, the same; for soldiers, not leaving the hot front of spears; and for a king's land, living by his sceptre.
nuance: Every item is a following: wife after husband, son after father, soldier at the front, people under the sceptre, so the verse makes one virtue of keeping to one's place in an order.

norm.note: a rule of women's conduct of the period: the wife is to walk her husband's way

reading: Bearing with a wrong is greatness, sitting brooding on harm done is smallness, and it is good to live so that the enmity one made comes to an end and so that the wealthy and the good have no cause to laugh.
nuance: Four items, not five: two set greatness against smallness, two name a good way of living. பல்பொருளார் நல்லார் may be read as the subjects (the wealthy and good, living so none laugh at them) rather than the ones who laugh.

reading: Before people without worth, anger is good, nobility bad and arrogance good, the verse says, for goodness shown there is like good meat in the mouth of a dog that bit and rose barking.
nuance: Three items, the inversion of the house virtues made explicit (கதம் and மதம் are fused with நன்று in the text); the closing image says kindness spent on the base is wasted like meat in a dog's mouth. Line 3 (கோய்வாயிற் கீழுயிர்க்(கு)ஈ துற்று) is hard to construe.

reading: Making friends, humbling enemies, lying with broad-hipped women of sharp teeth, and keeping love for those within one's house are named the fruit gained by a body that has not renounced.
nuance: Four fruits, all of the unrenounced body (துறவா உடம்பு), so the verse grants the householder's life its gains while marking them as the lesser body's. ஓட்டித் தொடங்கினார் is doubtful.

reading: One who does not lie though he would gain gold, does not steal, does not turn to soft women though long-haired women want him, does no harm, and, knowing the body will leave, does not eat flesh out of craving, will hardly take a body again.
nuance: The reward is not this world's but release from rebirth (பேர்த்துடம்பு கோடல் அரிது). Each abstention is set against its strongest temptation (gold, women who desire him). வையாமை and நையாமை are uncertain: we read 'not setting on' and 'not afflicting'.

reading: Those who have learned are gods and the unlearned, on examination, ghouls; those who did not earn wealth early are wretches; and those who say they had no sorrow before and were the handsome ones are two-legged oxen.
nuance: Four items. The scale runs from god to ghoul to beast, and the last item mocks those who live on their past.

reading: One who does not steal, never gives himself to gambling, does not befriend the black-hearted, does not move his tongue to take life, and refuses meat will never, worn out, take on a body of flesh again.
nuance: The line division கள்ளான்கு தென்றும் is read as கள்ளான் சூது என்றும். The closing pun sets the refused flesh (ஊன்) against the flesh-body (ஊனுடம்பு): refusing the one, he is not given the other.

reading: The payiram says that Makkariyasan, pupil of Makkayan, whose hand is like rain ending the other famine of not learning, made the Sirupanchamoolam to remove the ills of many in the world.
nuance: It joins the title's two senses: the five roots as medicine (நோய்நீக்கும்) and பஞ்சம் as famine, here the famine of the unlearned (கல்லா மறுபஞ்சம்).

title: சிறுபஞ்சமூலம் 21-40
theme: Twenty verses of about five things each, opening with a matched pair on the precocious and the dull, then moving through renunciation in youth, a bad wife, teacher and pupil, penance defined by conduct, a ladder of giving, penance and knowledge, beauty as speech, and the soldier who spares the surrendered.
source_issues: 22 line 2: மூவாது மூவர்நூல் தேற்றதார் does not construe; the parallel with 21 suggests a reading such as 'though aged, do not grasp the books'.
23 line 3: தொக்(கு)ஈர் பசுவால் is obscure.
24 lines 3-4: கிளைமைத் துறமது is doubtfully divided.
25 line 1: பிறன்பொருள்வெள வன்மின் appears to have வௌவன்மின் split, with ௌ written as ெ + ள.
26 line 1: கோல்தகுதல் is obscure.
29 lines 1-3: the first half and துணங்கு are hard to construe.
35 line 3: போதும் is likely a misprint for போகம் (enjoyment), which the triad of fruits requires.
37 line 2: show flags a repaired ௌ and a reading that differs from the site.
39 lines 1-2: பாத்தில்லார் உண்டார் அடிசிலே and தோழரில் are hard to construe.

reading: There are trees that fruit without flowering, and those who know the good and are skilled in books are elders without having aged; there are seeds that sprout without being sown, and to the intelligent understanding reaches without being told.
nuance: Two nature images each answered by a kind of person: the tree that fruits unflowered is the young man who is already an elder in knowledge, the seed that sprouts unsown is the quick mind that needs no telling. Divided into five, taking நன்றறிவார் and நூல்வல்லார் as two descriptions; they could be one. Verse 22 is its exact negative.

reading: There are trees that flower yet do not fruit, and men who, though grown old, do not grasp the books; there are seeds that do not sprout even when buried in a bed, and to the fool understanding does not reach even when told.
nuance: The mirror of verse 21, image for image: flowering without fruit is age without learning, the buried seed is the fool who is told and still does not take it. Line 2 as printed (மூவாது மூவர்நூல் தேற்றதார்) does not construe cleanly; the reading takes it as the aged who have not understood the books, as the parallel with 21 requires. Four things, not five.

reading: Those who rely on five things (bodily form, youth, the beauty that has come to them, a family that bows to no one, and lineage) and do not renounce while young never see the unshaken state that has no end.
nuance: Two of the five are pride of birth (குடி, குலம்), set beside the body's goods as things that hold a man back. The deadline is youth itself (இளங்கால்): renunciation put off past youth is the failure. Line 3's தொக்(கு)ஈர் பசுவால் is obscure; it may speak of being dragged by bound attachment, and the reading leaves it out.

reading: The verse names as the doings of a bad wife drinking toddy, living apart from her husband, going without shame into other people's houses, prying with intent into others' affairs, and keeping close ties with bad women.
nuance: All five faults lie outside the kitchen and the husband's presence: drink, absence, other houses, other people's business, bad company. காணில் in line 1 is hard to place (if one looks, or when he is seen). Line 3-4's கிளைமைத் துறமது is doubtful; it may instead mean cutting off her own kin, and the fifth item is held loosely.

norm.note: a rule of the period for a wife's conduct, listing what marks a bad wife

reading: The verse urges joining those of great character, not seizing another's wealth, giving up the friendship of the dark-natured and guarding against evil speech, for Death's coming is certain and the reckoning is not mere talk.
nuance: Four commands and then their ground: the coming of காலன் is certain, and the last line (வழக்கு is not mere mouth-talk) says the judgment that follows is real. The list's force comes from the fifth item, which is not a command at all but the reason for the other four.

reading: The sky-bird's nest, lac, the white silkworm's work, the fit of a stick and honey are things no one can make at will; the skilled should not say they achieve whatever they set out to, for to each single being some one thing comes without fail.
nuance: The five are works of creatures (the weaver bird's nest, the lac insect, the silkworm, perhaps the termite or bee, the honeybee) that no human craftsman can copy, set against the boast of the skilled. கோல்தகுதல் is obscure and the fourth item is a guess. The point is a limit on human skill: every being has its own one gift.

reading: The man set in dharma stands on the good path, the unrestrained outsider does not leave the low path, and the one who befriends outsiders picks up toddy, theft and gambling and, practised in them, shows them as of old.
nuance: The verse turns on நாட்டான்/நட்டான், the one established and the one who befriends: vices are learned through company. The construal of lines 2-4 is uncertain; the division takes two persons and three vices.

reading: The teacher is one who seeks no gain from men, the pupil who suits him serves him with love, the pupil who learns everything has cast off the three, and for one who has not cast them off all that he holds remains a disease of the heart.
nuance: Divided into four: teacher, loving pupil, the pupil who has cast off the three, and the one who has not. The three are not named; in a Jain work they are most likely desire, anger and delusion, the three the invocation says the Lord destroyed (மூன்றொழித்து). Learning without that riddance is called a sickness, not a lesser good. ஆண்ஆக்கம் may mean worldly gain or a man's advancement; the reading takes gain.

reading: The verse sets out a student's observances: hair kept as a tuft like a closing neytal bud with the rest trimmed, a term of a month, and the student's work of reciting the text and listening, coming to the teacher with a bow and circling him to the right.
nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to construe: உய்தல் ஒருதிங்கள் நாளாகும் may give the interval for trimming the hair or a period of study. துணங்கு in line 3 is obscure. The second half is clearer: recitation, listening, bowing and circumambulation of the teacher.

norm.note: a rule of the period for a student's tonsure and his ritual approach to the teacher

reading: There is no one who knows everything, no one who knows nothing at all, no one wholly without fault with every virtue held in him, and no one who has learned the whole body of the treatises.
nuance: Four negations, each closed by the single இல் at the end. The second is the surprise: as no one is all-knowing, no one is wholly ignorant either, so the verse limits contempt as much as pride.

reading: If a man does no harm to living beings, forgets the pain that befalls him, does no hurtful wrong to another, and gives up desire and anger, the diseases that are faults, then penance is not lowly but sweet.
nuance: Penance is defined wholly by conduct, with no rite or austerity named. மறத்தல் (forgetting) the pain that comes goes further than enduring it. The conclusion answers a doubt the verse assumes: that penance is a lowering of oneself.

reading: The verse says that he who performs sacrifice is the brahmin, chastity is the excellence of a bright-jewelled woman, he who listens is the flawless great scholar, a poet's excellence comes from his mind, and in the world one's good comes through the father.
nuance: Each line names a person by the act that makes him what he is called. பார்ப்பான் is a birth term, but the verse ties it to the act of sacrifice (வேட்பவன்), not to birth; it reports that norm, it does not argue it. The last item gives the father, not one's own deeds, as the source of standing in the world.

norm.note: the period's definition of the brahmin by the sacrifice and of a woman's excellence by chastity

reading: The verse says that only he who lays up is the liberal man and he who hands out is a merchant, that only he who leads to the higher state is a teacher, and that the one so led, keeping the body's hedge and never beginning to eat flesh, is sure to go there.
nuance: The first line is a paradox whose sense is uncertain: the 'laying up' is perhaps the store of merit made by giving, and the 'handing out' giving for return, so that the merchant gives and the liberal man saves. The closing rule makes abstaining from flesh the test of whether one has been led upward.

reading: Blame comes of reviling, homage comes of doing good, a thriving family comes of what was done before, enjoyment comes of wealth, and dharma comes of grace that has melted.
nuance: Five effects, each with its cause. The division of lines 1-3 (வசை / வணக்கம் / செழுங்குலம்) is uncertain; செழுங்குலம் may instead be the fruit of homage. The last two repeat verse 2's pairing of wealth with enjoyment and grace with dharma, and add that the grace must be நெகிழ்ந்த, softened.

reading: Surveying the good dharma of householders and the dharma of renunciation, the verse says that giving brings enjoyment, penance brings heaven, and knowledge brings release.
nuance: Three ranked paths with three ranked fruits, and heaven is only the middle one: release belongs to knowledge, not to penance. Only three things, not five. போதும் in line 3 is read as போகம், enjoyment; as printed it does not construe.
domain_note: surveys both the householder's and the renouncer's dharma

reading: The beauty of the hair, of the eye-catching chest, of the nails, of the ears and of faultless teeth is not beauty; the beauty of speech fitted to learning is beauty.
nuance: Five bodily beauties are denied and a sixth affirmed, so the verse counts six; the last undoes the first five. The true beauty is not learning as such but speech that fits the books (நூற்கியைந்த சொல்).

reading: The verse says, addressing a young woman, that the worthy do not eat food got by bowing, do not sleep in a friend's house, do not seize another's property that has gone astray, do not look down on one after joining with him, and do not take up baseness after a quarrel.
nuance: The subject is unstated, and taken as the worthy. புலை in line 4 is read as baseness of conduct, not as the caste term. தொழீஇ அட may also mean food cooked by one made to bow, that is, by a servant forced to it.

reading: Not lying is good, wealth is good, not killing so that a life suffers is good, not exalting oneself before many is, when weighed, worth esteem, and the minds of the excellent shun unworthiness however small.
nuance: Wealth stands between the two vows as a plain good, with no ranking among the three. Lines 3-4 are hard to divide; the reading takes பேணாமை as not making much of oneself and மாணாமை as unworthiness that the excellent mind will not admit.

reading: To put a treasury, many accounts, oversight, a kitchen of food and a household in the charge of men without understanding to match their size is like setting a crow to guard cooked rice.
nuance: The five are offices of trust in a great house; பாத்தில்லார் உண்டார் and தோழரில் are hard to construe and the last two items are held loosely. The measure of the appointee is understanding fit to his body: a big man with a small mind.
domain_note: the master who appoints officers to his stores and accounts

reading: Those who have dropped their clothing, those who chew grass, those who have entered running water, those who have laid down their weapons and those who have fled with nothing left: these five, the verse says, true soldiers never go near.
nuance: All five are signs of a beaten or helpless enemy: stripped, grass in the mouth in surrender, taking to the river, weapon down, in flight. The restraint is made the mark of the true (செவ்வகை) soldier, not a mercy he may choose.

title: சிறுபஞ்சமூலம் 41-60
theme: The chapter gathers counsel on the household and the realm: which women a man avoids and which men guard a woman, a wife's excellence and her hold on her husband, the farmer's care and ruin, the fortress and the minister, and the rewards of learning; several verses on women and marriage state period norms of gender and astrology.
source_issues: Verse 41 line 1: பூவாதான் with final ன் where the list of women needs பூவாதாள்; line 2 ஓவாதான் likewise.
Verse 54: the count word says five (என்றைந்தும்) but line 1 names four parts; a part may be lost.
Verse 52: the count word says ஐந்து but six phrases are listed.
Verse 59 line 1: நாளும்மா டோ போற்றிப் looks corrupt (perhaps மாடு ஓம்பி or மாடோம்பி); line 3 என்றிலை is obscure.
Verse 46 line 4: மன்றுசார் வாசு மனை is obscure; வாசு may be corrupt.

reading: The verse names five women whom men who know keep away from, recoiling as from an enemy: a girl not yet come of age, a woman past her menses, a woman bearing the sign of renunciation, a woman who at no time guards herself, and any other man's wife.
nuance: The list widens the Kural's single prohibition (another's wife) into a set of women barred by age, bodily state, vow and conduct. இலிங்கி is a woman who bears an ascetic's sign; ஓவாதான் கோலம் on line 2 may describe her garb ('the dress of one who never leaves it'), and the division of line 2 is our construal.

norm.note: a rule of the period on which women a man may approach, set by age, menses, vow and marriage

reading: The verse says a woman's excellence lies in knowing the household's ways in proportion to its income, not angering kin, eagerly tending guests, and always worshipping, with a clear mind, the one who brings her fortune and the gods.
nuance: திருவாக்கும் is read here as the one who makes her fortune, most likely the husband, so worship is owed both to him and to the deity; if it qualifies தெய்வதை instead, the list has four items. Income comes first, as in the Kural's definition of the wife.

norm.note: a period norm defining a wife's excellence by household management, hospitality and worship

reading: The verse says that if one finds a man who knows the five (the agreement of birth-stars, the auspicious hour, the agreement of planets, the yoga and the qualities) and whether the couple are fit to be joined, one should have him fix the wedding day.
nuance: Astrology is given here as a learned craft with five parts, and the counsel is to seek out its expert. தோள்கூட்டல் உற்றானும் அல்லானும் ('one fit and not fit for the joining of shoulders') is read as the reckoning of the couple's match; it could also mean the bridegroom and others.
domain_note: fixing the day of a marriage

norm.note: a ritual rule of the period: the wedding day is fixed by astrological reckoning

reading: The verse names five qualities (guarded restraint, a greatness that does not covet, dignity, modesty and reserve) and says a woman without them, even if she were Lakshmi herself with jewelled breasts like kongu buds on a golden hill, is hard to bring within one's bounds.
nuance: நாண்ஒடுக்கம் is split into two to reach the count; read as one, there are four. The verse ranks the five above beauty at its divine limit, but its measure is whether the husband can hold her, not her own good.
domain_note: a wife, as the husband sees her

norm.note: a period norm on the qualities that keep a wife within her husband's bounds

reading: Addressing a long-haired woman, the verse traces a chain the world repeats without end: as the ridge of the field rises the water rises, as the water rises the paddy rises, as the paddy rises the undiminished people rise, and as the people rise the king rises.
nuance: Each item is the cause of the next, so the list is a ladder, not a set: the king's height is the last effect of a field bank. ஓவா(து) உரைக்கும் உலகு gives it as a common saying.

reading: The verse names the conduct of a good house: wasting nothing, raising up those who depend on it, blaming no one, sharing with everyone without hiding, and not milking so that the calf dies.
nuance: The calf whose milk is taken is set in the same list as dependants and guests, so the house's care reaches its animals. The closing மன்றுசார் வாசு மனை is obscure; we take it as praise of such a house before the common ground, and எத்துவமும் as 'anything at all'.

reading: Addressing a woman, the verse says those who understand well never kill the hope of those who long for them, the meal of their kin, their own generosity or their fame, and will not consent to kill whatever they might gain by it.
nuance: The verse plays on கொல்: hope, a meal, generosity and fame are 'killed' by neglect, and the last 'killing' is the literal one, refused at any gain. The fifth killing has no object of its own in the Tamil, so we give four items and read the close as the frame.

reading: The verse says the wise have examined five things as a fortress (deep water, forest, saline waste, a lofty hill reaching the sky, and the people) and that the rule is to establish as king the one who has them.
The verse names five ruins for the ploughman: negligence, pride in wealth, leaving work unfinished, quarrelling, and falling out with the skilled worker.
nuance: The last two ruins are social: a farmer is ruined by quarrels and by losing the craftsman he depends on, not only by his own sloth.

reading: The verse sets not killing as good and killing, not learning letters, and anger as bad, and calls a place where kin are wholly free of blame, without the good having to speak first, a town where many may live.
nuance: The first four items are verdicts of good and bad in the same breath, so illiteracy and anger are weighed on the scale of killing. The last two lines are hard to divide; we read them as the place where such conduct prevails.

reading: The verse says fasting with desire put away is good, hosting guests without reckoning a return is good, and scorning the weak is bad, and that those who do not go to others' houses are rare and those who do not eat from others' hands are great.
nuance: The list joins the ascetic's fast and the householder's guest, then turns both into a pride of self-reliance: not entering others' houses, not eating from their hands.

reading: The verse names the medicines by which women bring the husband to yield: bearing children, innocence, beauty, living with him in accord, restraint in food, and not being restless in speech.
nuance: The verse says ஐந்து but the Tamil yields six phrases; we give six, though மடனுடைமை மாதுடைமை may have been counted as one. The medicine works on the husband: the wife's virtues are named as her means of holding him.

norm.note: a period norm naming a wife's qualities as means of holding her husband

reading: Addressing a garlanded man, the verse names the five who guard a well-adorned woman, when one considers it: the husband who took her, her brother, her maternal uncle, her son and her father.
nuance: கொண்டான் கொழுநன் is read as one person, the husband who took her, which gives five; read as two it gives six. Every guardian is a man of her family.
domain_note: the men of a woman's family

norm.note: a period norm placing a woman under the guard of the men of her family

reading: The verse says that if a woman lets her lily-red mouth, eyes, mind and long brows run many ways and does not guard her restraint, she is held like the bent-earringed dancer whom scorners make to perform on a tall bamboo pole.
nuance: The count word says five but four parts are named (mouth, eyes, mind, brows); a fifth may be lost or ஆம்பல் may have been counted apart. The guard here is her own நிறை, not a man's watch. The pole dancer of the close is our reading of an obscure image.

norm.note: a period norm on a woman's guarding of her own glance, speech and mind

reading: The verse says the learned man wins gold, the good poet wealth and the debater fame, while the unlearned and those outside the company of the learned win only laughter among the good.
nuance: The rewards are graded by the kind of learning: gold, wealth, fame. என்பெறும் வாதி may be a question ('what does the debater gain? fame').

reading: The verse calls it wisdom to bring the good to light, forget the bad, be quickly a staff of strength to living beings, turn deceit away from others' property, and, for a man of honour, to perish.
nuance: The list ends on a hard turn: after four acts of care and honesty, the fifth wise act is to die, and only for the man of honour (மானத்தான் ஆயின்).

reading: The verse says the king's minister, with his great power to split anything open and know it, acts only after closely measuring his own position, the state of the work that must not fail, the state of the houses of those who oppose him in strength, and the matchless order of things.
nuance: The Tamil names four நிலை; the minister's own power in the last line may be the fifth root. We give four items.

reading: The verse names five qualities (wealth, enjoyment, fearlessness, a grace that does not leave even at the hour of death, and rare dharma) and says the man who has them is the one a king of sharp spear can trust.

The verse says the farmer, in a good field, stores straw, tends the cattle daily, readies the small tools and tends the manure before he sets the fitted plough to the soil, and those who recite the texts hold a finer plough.
nuance: The last line turns the farmer's labour into an image for study: the scholar's plough is the subtle one. Line 1 (மா டோ) and line 3 (என்றிலை) are doubtful, so the division is ours.
domain_note: the farmer, set beside the reciter of texts

reading: The verse names five claims and says it has never yet seen anyone who makes them: that not receiving is good, that giving is bad, that falling short is good for those without character, that falling short is good even when learning fails, and that doing much penance is bad.
nuance: The division turns on sandhi (நன்றீதல் may be நன்று ஈதல்) and on how far என்பாரை reaches. The first claim sits oddly among absurdities, since refusing gifts is praised elsewhere; it may be read as 'refusing to give', or the closing may govern only the last claim.

title: சிறுபஞ்சமூலம் 61-80
theme: Most of these twenty verses count acts of giving and care (water and shade, tanks and wells, alms to fasters, food to the maimed, the dying and the hungry low, care of mothers and newborns) and attach a fruit to each list, from kingship and heaven to long life and health, set among verses that strip the ascetic's outward forms, spread the sin of killing along the chain to the eater, and divide what company governs from what the mind does.
source_issues: 61 line 1: அடங்காய் and பெண்வியக்க are hard to construe; the reading of the first three items is uncertain.
63 line 3: சிதவலிப்(பு) is unclear; read as சிதவல் (a rag).
66 line 2: ஓர்த்(து) பால்மறைத்(து) உண்பான்மேய் is obscure and may be corrupt.
68 line 4: வேகும்பம் is unclear.
70 line 1: செந்தார்க்கு may be a misreading of செத்தார்க்கு.
76: the site lacks this verse (text flag site_diff), so it rests on one source.
77 line 2: கண்கண்பட்(டு) looks like a doubled syllable.
78 line 4: வாண் is probably a misprint for வார்.

reading: The verse names five who live close to a man (kin who wear him down like a file and will not be checked, a wife who makes herself a wonder to others, a servant who stands unmoving like a tree, a son who turns against him, and a neighbour who watches like a hidden disease) and says that if these five are his, a life needs no other disease.
nuance: The predicate makes the household itself the sickness: every one of the five is someone a man cannot easily leave. Line 1 is hard (அடங்காய், பெண்வியக்க), தொண்டு is read as the servant whose simile மரம்போல் runs onto line 2, and கரம் may mean poison rather than hand, so the first three portraits are readings, not fixed.

reading: The verse calls good the gift of water, the gift of shade, and charity within one's own house when the householder eats only after sharing, calls the founding of a temple and a hall great virtue, and says that together these bring great enjoyment.
nuance: The list climbs from a drink of water to a founded building, and நன்று gives way to பேரறம் at the fourth item, so the verse ranks as it counts. Only the third item carries a condition (பாத்து உண்பானேல்): charity at home counts if the giver eats after sharing. பார்அறம் is not certain in sense. The fruit named is பெரும்போகம், enjoyment, not release.

reading: The verse lists small gifts (a handful of alms, a little given afterwards, alms of gruel, salt that the giver had himself begged and brought, and a torn rag) and says that those who give them without calling them of small use gain a very great fruit hereafter.
nuance: The gifts are a poor man's: salt he begged for himself (எடுத்திரந்த உப்பு) and a rag. The condition is the giver's attitude (சிறுபயம் என்னார்), not the size of the gift. பின்னிறை and சிதவலிப்பு are uncertain words, so the boundaries of the second and fifth items are a reading.

reading: The verse names five things that melt (butter that sees the hot fire, wax, earth that meets water, salt, and a father whose son has come to him) and says that one who gives with a heart melted like any one of them gathers fruit like a hill, however small the gift.
nuance: The five counted things are images, not gifts: they measure the giver's heart. Four are matter softened by heat or water; the fifth, the father at his son's approach, is the one human case and is set last, so the list ends where giving's feeling is most familiar.

reading: The verse says that one who carries out five works (digging a tank, setting its bank, clearing a road, breaking ground into a ploughed field, and digging a well whose water is shared) goes sweetly to heaven.
nuance: All five are works on land and water that others use after the doer. The reward is சுவர்க்கம், heaven, not release; the Jain works keep these merits in the round of births. உளந்தொட்டு is read as breaking hard ground for the plough. The count word is fused with என்று as written (என்றிவ்ஐம் பாற்படுப்பான்).
domain_note: the man of means who builds for the village

reading: The verse names outward forms of ascetics (wrapping the body, stripping it bare, smearing it, growing the hair long, and eating hidden and guarded) and says that if these are a virtue truly thought out one should bear what is said, but otherwise, in the Kali age, renunciation is false and household life alone is true.
nuance: The five forms answer to the mendicant orders of the period (clothed, naked, smeared, long-haired), though no sect is named. The close is a strong judgement for a Jain work: in கலி the household is the true path and renunciation a lie, unless the renunciant's virtue is truly considered. Line 2 (ஓர்த்து பால்மறைத்து உண்பான்மேய்) is obscure, so the fifth item is a reading.

reading: The verse says it is good to live remembering the house one was born into, holding firmly to oneself, knowing how others regard one, not living so that others say 'let him die', but so that the worthy say for many years 'may he live'.
nuance: The five run from the inside out: one's birth-house, oneself, others' regard, others' curse, the worthy's blessing. Two opposite speeches by others (சாவ, வாழ்க) close the verse, so a life is judged by what is said of it.

reading: The verse names four practices (drawing out and cutting short, long bathing in the waters of a ghat, and staying in by day) that do not remove the blemish, and says that one who leaves these four and restrains the five senses, wanting nothing, is released.
nuance: The verse has two counts, நான்கு and ஐந்து: four rejected practices and the restraint of the five senses that it approves; they are given as five items, the last of a different kind. What is drawn out and cut short (food, hair, the body) is not said, and வேகும்பம் on line 4 is unclear.

reading: The verse names five who share in a killing (the one who killed, the one who agreed to it, the one who took the killed thing without hesitation when it was fat, the one who cooked it and the one who ate it when served) and says the sin should be reckoned as bound on all five.
nuance: The chain runs from the act to the meal, and the eater, last, is the one least likely to think himself guilty; the verse closes the gap the eater relies on.

norm.note: the Jain rule against flesh-eating of the period, stated as a share in the sin of killing

reading: The verse names five kinds of people (those lying in prison, those who fast for the ... (perhaps the dead), those who have lain many days in ..., those who eat only every other day, and those who eat nothing from the crescent to the full moon) and says that those who gave to them will live as kings in all fullness.
nuance: Four of the five are fasters by vow; the prisoner, first, goes hungry by force, so the list joins chosen and imposed hunger. செந்தார்க்கு and உறைக்கிடந்தார் are uncertain (செந்தார் may stand for செத்தார், the dead).

reading: The verse lists five acts that, it says, the authors of the old books declared great virtue: delivering a child, caring for a pregnant woman, taking up an infant, sheltering in one's house an unmarried girl who has conceived, and sheltering a man who is ruined.
nuance: The verse appeals to authority (முதுநூலார்) rather than to a fruit. The unmarried pregnant girl is counted among those to be taken in, not cast out; the verse names her condition plainly.

norm.note: a period view of the unmarried girl who has conceived, whom the verse counts it great virtue to shelter

reading: The verse says that a single mouthful given, without asking who they are, to those who have lost their strength, the old, those who sit facing north to die, those wasted by disease, and those ruined by losing their land, makes the giver a king.
nuance: இன்னவராம் என்னாராய், 'not asking who they are', makes the gift blind to the recipient's worth, in a book that elsewhere rewards gifts to ascetics. வடக்கிருந்தார், those who sit facing north to die, stand here among the needy rather than the heroic.

reading: The verse lists acts of care around birth (guarding the pregnant woman from distress, not neglecting her when the embryo is harmed, help at the delivery, taking up the infant without shrinking from it, medicine for the child, and not frightening it) and says that, examined, the greatness of virtue lies in these.
nuance: The verse has no count word. It is divided here into six on the six negated or verbal nouns, but விலங்காமைக் கோடல் may join குழவி, and இலங்காமை after கருப்பஞ் சிதைந்தால் is unclear, so five is as defensible.

reading: The verse sets out the pains of bringing a life into being (failing to conceive, the suffering of pregnancy, being unable to nurse after the birth, the hardship of rearing once begun, and the incapacity that follows) and says that those who know these well find, on sifting, that not eating and not killing are good.
nuance: The five pains are given as items; the predicate the verse draws from them is உண்ணாமை and கொல்லாமை. உண்ணாமை is read as not eating flesh, beside not killing, but it may mean fasting. ஏலாமை and சால்பவை வல்லாமை are uncertain.

norm.note: the Jain abstention from eating flesh and killing of the period, argued from the pains of bearing life

reading: The verse says that those who in former days cured the gathered diseases of five kinds of sufferer (சிக்கர், the blind or dull, those whose mouths are eaten as by termites, the afflicted, and those with piles) now live free of any disease.
nuance: முன்னாளில் and இந்நாள் are read as an earlier birth and this one: present health is the fruit of past healing. The disease words (சிக்கர், சிதடர், துக்கர், துருநாமர்) are rare and their senses are uncertain.

reading: The verse names five duties: not taking sides, taking on another's suffering, not being swayed, giving food to the hungry even if they are the low who are not worthy ascetics, and holding back excessive anger.
nuance: The fourth item ranks recipients (தவமல்லாத் தக்கார், இழியினர்) and then sets the ranking aside: the hungry are fed even if low. இழியினர் here ranks people; it may be birth-rank or low conduct. தக்கம் படாமை and பாடேற்றல் are uncertain.

norm.note: a ranking of recipients by worth and lowness (இழியினர்) of the period, which the verse sets aside for the hungry

reading: The verse says that those who gave to the wounded, to those with no one to care for them, to those whose life is ebbing, to those who have lost their eyes and to those without both legs, people sunk and broken, will live gladly to the end.
nuance: Line 3 (ஆழ்ந்து நெகிழ்ந்தவர்க்கு) sums the five as those sunk and broken; it is read as a summary, not a sixth item.

reading: The verse names five who live beyond eighty: one who shares his food in a time of famine, one who does not hoard, one who goes fearlessly into a breaking army and strikes, one who gives before he eats and holds nothing back, and one who makes offerings for children.
nuance: The list joins the householder's sharing with the soldier's courage under one reward, long life. காவாதான் may belong with the next clause (one who, not guarding himself, enters the army), and குழவி பலிகொடுப்பான் may be one who feeds children or one who offers for them.

reading: The verse lists what the wise (implied) shun: they do not keep a woman without bounds, do not climb an anthill, do not befriend the worthless or a warring king, do not go where a fierce elephant like a hill is let loose, and do not travel the road where a cruel tiger prowls.
nuance: The list sets people (a woman without bounds, the worthless, the warring king) among natural dangers (anthill, elephant, tiger), so the human ones are read as hazards of the same kind. வையார் may mean 'do not keep' or 'do not revile', and மன்னைப்புற்று is unclear. The verse has no count word; six are given.

norm.note: a period view that sets the woman 'without bounds' among dangers to be shunned

reading: The verse says the way of the worthy does not perish while the unworthy sink on a fallen way; blame and fame come from one's company, but understanding comes from one's own mind.
nuance: The last two lines divide what company governs (reputation) from what it does not (மதி, understanding). The count of five is a reading of a verse without a count word.

title: சிறுபஞ்சமூலம் 81-96
theme: These sixteen closing verses mostly grade conduct and learning: five marks of the good giver and the lay vows set above scripture, the trick of the calf-skin placed beside killing, two tiers of the learned, five dogs answered by five easy virtues, a ladder from sweet speech to release, virtues fitted to the station where they cost most, and a ranking that puts Ganga worship below restraint, ending with worth proved only at death.
source_issues: 83 and 89: the site's text lacks line 1 (text flag site_diff), so those lines rest on one source.
81 line 1: கைலாரா is hard to construe.
86 line 1: கண்ணும் is unclear as the first of the five arts.
87 line 4: பருத்தி பகர்வழி does not fit the list clearly.
91 line 1: the spacing வா யால்நிர யம் looks broken (வாயால் நிரயம்).
96 line 1: வாயல் is unclear and may be a misprint; line 2 தீக்சொற்க is probably a misprint for தீச்சொற்க.

reading: The verse names five marks of a man (he does not grieve over what has passed, does not crave what is out of his hand, takes no pleasure in base things, speaks softly, and gives what the poor ask with a heart that melts) and says such a man is praised by the gods in sweet words.
nuance: The last two marks belong together: the soft word and the melting heart are the manner of the gift, so the list ends in giving done well, not giving alone. கைலாரா is hard to construe; read here as what has not come into the hand.

reading: The verse names five marks of a man (he sees his house, lovely to the eye, as a wilderness, others' wealth as a potsherd, others' wives as the mother who bore him, he does not go between people stringing harsh words, and he does not kill) and asks what he would lack even without the recitation of the many scriptures.
nuance: The five line up with the Jain lay vows: non-attachment, not stealing, not desiring another's wife, no slander or untruth, not killing. The closing question sets this conduct above scriptural recitation; பல்லவர் ஒத்தினால் is read as ஓத்து, scripture, which the spelling leaves open.

reading: The verse says that those on the side of virtue do not milk a cow by showing it a stuffed calf-skin, do not drink milk so drawn, do not do what brings blame and sin, and do not seize creatures living content in what they have, ruining their homes to Death's delight.
nuance: The first two items are one practice seen from milker and drinker: the deceit worked on the cow whose calf is dead taints the milk too. The list runs from that small cruelty to the killing of creatures, so the trick on the cow is placed on the same line as killing. The construal of கறந்தபால் with பாற்பட்டார் is a reading.

reading: The verse names five things not wanted where elders are seated (laughter, private counsel, partiality to friends, enmity, and song or idle talk) and says the ancient treatises set this down after those who knew had examined it.
nuance: It cites old treatises as its authority, an appeal the verses around it rarely make. நட்டார்க்கு வாரம் is read as favouring one's friends, a fault of judgment in an assembly rather than of manners.

reading: The verse names five branches of knowledge (grammar of sound, true knowledge, logic, the religious systems, and release as the wise have seen it) and says one who knows all five is, on reflection, a learned man of the first rank.
nuance: சத்தமெய்ஞ் ஞானம் is divided as சத்தம் and மெய்ஞ்ஞானம். The verse ranks learning, and ranks it by subject: release closes the list as the highest thing to be known. It is the first of a pair; verse 86 names the middle rank.

reading: The verse names five arts (one read as the art of the eye, arithmetic, the lute, the making of unguents, and cutting and arranging leaves) and says one who knows these five is reckoned a learned man of the middle rank.
nuance: Set against verse 85, the pair grades learning: doctrine and release make the first rank, crafts and accomplishments the middle. The first item, கண்ணும், is unclear; it may name an art of the eye such as painting or the reading of signs, or be only 'also'.

reading: The verse names five men who are dogs: the shameless, the one who does not befriend well, the one who does not honour the great, the one in another's service, and the one with nothing in his hand who goes to the quarter of the jewelled courtesans.
nuance: பருத்தி பகர்வழி, the lane where cotton is sold, is hard to fit; it may mark where the penniless man loiters or compare him to a dog in that lane. பிறர் சேவகன் may mean a servant or a soldier of another man. Verse 88 answers this list item by item.

reading: The verse says, to a woman addressed, that modesty comes easily to womanhood, laughter to a friend, steadfastness to a soldier, and reverence to the great, while arrows seldom fly at a man of compassion.
nuance: It reverses verse 87 point by point: shame, friendship, the சேவகன் and honour of the great return, now as what comes easily. The last item turns from easy to rare, which is the list's twist. ஏண் is read as steadfastness and அளியன் as the compassionate man; both are readings.

norm.note: a period claim about women: modesty treated as natural to womanhood

reading: The verse traces a chain: sweet speech makes kin, harsh speech without good nature makes enemies, gentle speech brings unceasing grace, and that grace, in a good mind, becomes release that does not perish.
nuance: The things are steps, not peers: speech leads to grace, grace to release, so the list is a ladder from manners to salvation; the Tamil gives four steps, not five.

reading: The verse says penance befits a young man, refusing food befits a rich man, and beauty befits a chaste woman, but a man with shoulders strong and fair who lacks understanding becomes like a red ant in the shade.
nuance: Each virtue is fitting where it costs most: penance while youth pulls the other way, fasting when food is at hand. The fourth item turns from fitting to unfitting. தழல் may belong with a third தக்கது, and the image of the ant in the shade is read as a nuisance where one rests; the count of four is the Tamil's, not the title's five.

norm.note: a period norm: a woman's beauty counted fitting only with chastity

reading: The verse sets out claims that heaven comes by falsehood and hell by truth, and that wealth and a dark-eyed maiden make life sweet, and tells the woman addressed that if this were true, it would be no harm to take up any penance at all.
nuance: Read as a reductio: the inverted claims about heaven and hell are absurd, so the conclusion drawn from them is mocked. The spacing of line 1 (வா யால்நிர யம்) and the sense of the close are unsure, and the verse may be read otherwise. It gives four claims, not five, divided at each instrument (falsehood, truth, wealth, the maiden).

reading: The verse says household life is better than a mean dharma and worth guarding, since one can walk with the truly virtuous, and that those who cooked, served and then ate, feeding the virtuous, will live in this life too cooking, serving and eating in plenty.
nuance: It does not set household above renunciation as such, only above புல்லறம், a poor or false dharma. The repeated அட்டிட்டுண்டு makes the reward the same act again: feeding now brings the means to feed later. The verse argues rather than counts; the three items are its three claims.

reading: The verse says giving is good and withholding evil, joining the good is good and joining those who are not is evil, and that one who keeps hearing and stands firm has a penance that carries him, riding, to the flawless high state.
nuance: The first four items are two pairs of good and evil; the fifth is an instruction whose fruit is the high state. Hearing and holding firm are themselves called a penance.

reading: The verse ranks conduct: not going where others are eating, where enemies are brought low, or where counsel is taken, is foremost; ending quarrels of words after reflection is high penance; and, beside these, the worship on the bank of the Ganga is lowest.
nuance: The three ranks (தலை, உயர், கடை) put restraint first and pilgrimage worship last, so a celebrated rite is counted but placed beneath manners of speech and presence. உரைப்பூசல் கோறல் may instead mean wordy quarrels and killing; கோறல் usually means killing.

reading: The verse names five (the chaste wife, the soldier, the flawless ascetic of severe penance, the man upright in dealings with wealth, and the worthy who keep a trust without flaw and judge cases) and says their rightness should be known when they have died.
nuance: The test is deferred to death: none of these virtues can be certified while the life can still fail. The list spans house, war, renunciation, trade and judgment, so the claim covers every station.

reading: The verse names conduct it calls aram (following the right path, not grieving, truthfulness, attending to intent, and turning in disgust from words joined with evil speech) and says the learned who would be saved examine and let the rest go.
nuance: Several words are unclear: வாயல் may be a misprint, and வழிப்படரல் and குறிப்படரல் could mean pursuing a path or a sign in either a good or bad sense. The division into five is a reading.

title: திரிகடுகம் 0-20
theme: The invocation counts three deeds of the god's feet, and the twenty verses that follow each count three things under one predicate (a medicine, the ruin of ignorance, a road to grief, a mute's dream, an undying body), mixing household, social and royal conduct so that unlike acts are judged as one kind.
source_issues: 0 lines 1 and 3: அளந்துதூஉம் and உதைத்தூஉம் stand beside பாய்த்ததூஉம் on line 2 and look like shortened or misprinted forms of அளந்ததூஉம் and உதைத்ததூஉம்.
1 line 2: the text was repaired from a misprint (தெடார்ச்சியும் read தொடர்ச்சியும்); the reading differs from the site.
3 line 3: the count word is fused with the verb (புகலுமிம் மூன்றும்), so the usual இம்மூன்றும் does not appear as a separate word.
10 line 4: the count word is spelt இம்முன்றும் with a short u, probably a misprint for இம்மூன்றும்; the same closing line recurs at verse 63.
14 line 3: the other witness has செறுவோடு for செறுவொடு; line 4 recurs as the closing line of verse 46.

reading: The invocation counts three deeds of the dark one coloured like the kaya flower (measuring the wide earth, felling the fragrant kurundham tree, kicking the magic cart that came at him) and names the three together as his feet.
nuance: All three deeds are deeds of the foot (a stride, a leap at the tree, a kick), so the predicate 'these three are his feet' is exact: the book's counting form is turned on the god before it is turned on conduct, and the feet are worshipped as the acts they did.

reading: The shoulders of a wife chaste as Arundhati, unbroken company with the excellent of an old well-ordered family, and the friendship of men whose learning by listening clears away the tangle of words are three things that act as a medicine like the three pungent drugs.
nuance: The predicate gives the book its name: the three are not called good but curative, which implies a sickness they treat. The second and third items are both kinds of company, so two of the three remedies are chosen associates and only one is the house.

reading: Keeping one's own good nature from declining, doing what is asked by people of sweet nature and flawless worth, and walking the way of the knowers of the four Vedas are named the work of the gentle.
nuance: The Veda-knowers enter as guides to a path, qualified by நன்குணர்வின் (of good understanding); the verse sets them beside one's own character and the bidding of the good, so the gentle person's conduct is drawn from three sources, only one of them Vedic.

reading: Living as one of the kin of the unlearned, beating one's wife with a stick, and entering a house in the company of petty men are named three ruins that come from ignorance.
nuance: காழ்கொண்ட qualifies the wife and is ambiguous: 'firm, of settled worth' would make the item 'beating a steadfast wife', while 'harbouring rancour' would make it 'beating a wife who has turned bitter'; either way the beating is counted as ignorance, but the scope of the condemnation turns on the word. The count word is run into the verb (புகலுமிம் மூன்றும்), so count_word records only மூன்றும் and the third thing is cut before the fused verb.

norm.note: a marital norm of the period: the verse counts a husband's beating of his wife among the ruins of ignorance

reading: Setting up one's life in front of one's enemies, walking without a stick into a gathered herd of cattle, and taking by the hand a man who was earlier enraged against oneself are named the doings of one about to die.
nuance: The third item rests on dividing முற்றன்னை as முன் + தன்னை, 'oneself, earlier'; read as முற்று + அன்னை it would be 'one who rages at his aged mother', which makes a different item (taking up with a matricidal-tempered man). The first reading keeps all three items about exposure to a known danger.

reading: Going down into the water at a ford no one uses, joining the shoulders of women who have no desire for one, and arriving worn out as a guest in a strange town are named roads that lead to hard suffering.
nuance: ஒப்ப joins the first two items: union with an unwilling woman is likened to entering water at an unused ford, a danger whose depth is unknown. The third item looks at hospitality from the guest's side, as a hazard of dependence.

reading: Being abashed when others honour one, bearing it patiently when those who do not honour one speak ill of one's ability, and doing deeds of dharma in the manner of the rain-cloud's giving are named the pride called ஊராண்மை.
nuance: The closing word செருக்கு (pride) is paradoxical after three acts of self-effacement: the verse claims that true pride is modesty under praise, patience under scorn and giving without return. காராண்மை is read as the cloud's liberality, which asks nothing back; it might also mean the farmer's labour.

reading: A vaalai fish caught in the trap, a man of no capacity born into a wealthy family, and hard learning acquired by one who is afraid in assemblies are named a dream seen by a sleeping mute.
nuance: The image is exact: a mute's dream is real to him and can never be told, so each item is a good possessed that cannot be brought out. உள்ளல் is taken as a fish trap; if it is a pool or a place, the first item changes from 'caught' to 'stranded'.

reading: Lineage that shows itself in an old assembly, learning that stands out in a gathered good assembly, and a victory in battle that delights the king are named three things that need not speak of themselves.
nuance: Each item carries its own witness (the old assembly, the good assembly, the pleased king), so the claim is that real worth is proclaimed by a setting, not by its owner. வட்டார்த்த is obscure; it seems to describe the clamour of the battle where the victory was won.

reading: Moving away from the company of the great, living in desire for women one has no right to, and resolving on things that are not excellent are named what utter fools love.
nuance: The predicate is காதல், love: the verse says these are not the fool's mistakes but his preferences, which places folly in what is wanted, not in what is misjudged.

reading: A town with no teachers, an assembly with no elders to settle quarrels, and living beside people who do not share their food are named three things that yield no good.
nuance: All three are about a place lacking a kind of person, so the verse measures a settlement by who lives in it: the teacher, the arbiter, the sharer. The third makes a neighbour's stinginess a loss to those beside him.

reading: Watching the dance of one who has not invited one, the unguarded talk of a man who is not drunk enough to fall, and going again and again into the house of one who does not trust one are named three things the whole town finds offensive.
nuance: The second item excuses nothing by drink: it is the sober man's careless speech that is blamed. Each of the three words விளியாதான், களியாதான், தெளியாதான் is a negative participle and the readings ('one who has not called', 'one not drunk', 'one not assured') are inferred; ஊரெல்லாம் நோவது உடைத்து may also mean that these bring pain on the doer from the whole town.

reading: The verse defines three titles by conduct (the man of effort is one who lives without debt, the vellalan is one who does not eat while a guest is waiting, the man of principle is one who does not forget) and says it is sweet to live with these three as kin.
nuance: The form changes here: instead of three things it gives three definitions, each 'X என்பான்' fixing a name by an act. வேளாளன், a name that can denote an agrarian community, is defined by hospitality alone, not by birth or land.

reading: A young member of a family who knows right conduct, a king able to care well for his people, and an ascetic of excellent character without a blemish are named three people hard to find anywhere.
nuance: Each figure is rare because his virtue runs against his station: conduct is not expected of the young, care for subjects is hard for one who rules them, and a flawless life is what the ascetic's vow claims but seldom keeps.

reading: Youth, whose nature is to slip; folly, which is fixed in speaking words of blame; and meanness, which always stands with hostility, are three things the wise do not go near.
nuance: Each item is a state given its defining trait (slipping, blaming, hostility); youth is named as a thing to keep away from, not a time to be used, which makes it a temperament rather than an age.

reading: The luckless wretch who lives by dealing in lies, the hollow man who claims equality when one's fortune has turned and one is low, and the one who attaches himself as fortune runs and looks only to the profit of the business are named three not to be befriended.
nuance: பொறியறை and தட்டை are terms of contempt whose exact sense is unsure ('one bereft of fortune', 'a husk'); ஊழினால் ஒட்டி is read as attaching oneself according to another's fortune. Read so, all three fail a friend at the turn of fortune.

reading: One who has planted lofty fame on the earth, one who has won a chaste wife from among women of spotless worth, and one who has dug a well of drinking water without stint are named three who have gained a body that does not die.
nuance: The 'undying body' is fame's body, but the three routes are unlike: a public reputation, a private marriage and a public work for water. Winning a chaste wife is counted as an achievement equal to the other two.

reading: One who in old age has turned away from what is good, the husband who does not go to his chaste wife at her season, and the mendicant bearing a sect's sign who wants to win by words in disputes are named three who have let go the raft of learning.
nuance: The three let go of learning at the three stages where it should bind most: the old man at life's end, the householder in his duty to his wife, and the renouncer, whose learning turns into a weapon of debate. இலிங்கி names one who bears a sectarian mark, not necessarily a Saiva ascetic.

norm.note: a marital rule of the period about the wife's season (பூப்பு): the husband is held bound to go to her then

reading: Old age, which comes surely from one side, separation, painful at both ends to those who were united, and great disease that melts the body within and eats it are named three things to be feared more than thieves.
nuance: The comparison with thieves makes all three robbers: of youth, of a companion, of the body. Separation of lovers, an akam theme, is counted among the bodily dreads, and ஒருதலையான் and இருதலை play on 'one side' and 'both sides'.

reading: The witless man who runs at a killing elephant, the man who loiters at another's door by night, and the senseless one who plays with a dancing snake not knowing its fury are named, on examination, three who hang by a thread.
nuance: யானைக்கோடும் is read as யானைக்கு ஓடும், 'runs at the elephant', not as 'the elephant's tusk'. The middle item (by night at another man's door) is placed between two acts of reckless courting of animal danger, so the adulterer's risk is treated as physical. தூங்குபவர் may mean those as good as hanged or those who sleep heedless.

reading: One's hope coming to rest on another, falling into sloth while one's dependants go hungry, and being scorned in anger by someone as unlearned are named three things painful to everyone.
nuance: பாசம் here means those bound to one (kin, dependants), so the second item is not sloth in general but sloth at the moment others need one's work.

title: திரிகடுகம் 21-40
theme: Twenty verses each count three things under one predicate (a rope to merit, a sinking mire, those called the world, the pure, husk-pounders, an army that breaks wealth), ranging from household giving and learning to statecraft and release, with a pointed attack on flesh-eating and sacrificial killing.
source_issues: 22 line 2: the source has a blank line inside the verse; the lines after it were kept with the verse.
22 line 3: the other witness reads புகை இருள் (smoky darkness) for பகையிருள்.
26: the verse is printed without a number in the source and numbered 26 by its place.
